title: DJ Dollar Steady Against Yen as China Data Helps Spur Risk Appetite
text:
--Dollar hovers near Y99

--Strong Asian shares, Chinese data lift risk appetite

--New Zealand dollar takes hit after RBN governor talks of intervention

By Alexander Martin

The dollar hovered around the Y99 level during Asian trading Wednesday, as strong Japanese share prices and better-than-expected Chinese data helped lift risk appetite.

Asian stock markets rallied on the back of a fresh record high Tuesday for the Dow Jones Industrial Average, with the Nikkei Stock Average up 1.4% at midday.

"Strong Asian share prices have helped lift the dollar/yen after it fell toward the mid Y98 level earlier in the session," said Kengo Suzuki, forex strategist at Mizuho Securities in Tokyo. But as the Nikkei began paring some of its earlier gains in afternoon trading, the dollar also seemed to be edging lower aginst the yen, he added.

As of 0450 GMT, the dollar was at Y98.96 from Y99.00 in late New York trading Tuesday. It briefly climbed to Y99.16, having fallen as low as Y98.63 earlier in the morning.

Traders and analysts said a large amount of selling orders around Y99.50 will serve as a heavy cap on the pair, and it may take some time before the dollar can breach the key Y100 level.

"Both the upside and downside of the dollar/yen appear limited. Another dose of strong U.S. data may be necessary to lift the pair higher," said Minori Uchida, chief analyst at the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ. He said next week's U.S. retail sales data would be closely watched for cues.

Junichi Ishikawa, market analyst at IG Securities in Tokyo, said that while better-than-expected U.S. labor market data last week saw the dollar rally, it wasn't enough to clear all uncertainty over a U.S. economic recovery.

"The market is probably assuming it can embark on further dollar buying after the release of major economic indicators from next week onwards," he said.

Stronger-than-expected Chinese trade data also helped lift risk appetite, pushing up the Australian dollar, which fell Tuesday after the Reserve Bank of Australia lowered its benchmark interest rate.

China posted an $18.16 billion trade surplus in April, higher than a median forecast of $15.55 billion in a Dow Jones Newswires survey of economists. The Australian dollar climbed to $1.0194 from $1.0172 after the release of the data. As of 0450 GMT it was at $1.0187 from $1.0185, while the euro was at $1.3094 from $1.3079, and Y129.59 from Y129.48.

The New Zealand dollar fell after Reserve Bank of New Zealand Gov. Graeme Wheeler reportedly said the central bank sold the Kiwi to weaken it and is capable of doing so again to protect economic growth.

The Wall Street Journal Dollar Index, which measures the dollar against a basket of currencies, was at around 73.648 from 73.678.

title: DJ  Central Banks in Asia Boost Efforts to Deal with 'Hot Money' Flows-3-
text:
HONG KONG--Central banks in Asia, Australia and New Zealand are ratcheting up moves to deal with an influx of capital that is keeping currencies strong and complicating efforts to manage growth.

New Zealand's central bank said Wednesday it intervened in foreign-exchange markets to blunt the rise of its currency and would continue to do so, a day after Australia's central bank cut interest rates to their lowest level ever and noted the stubborn strength of the Australian dollar. Elsewhere, China is moving to curb bets on the rising yuan while Thailand is mulling effects to curb the strongest level of the baht since the 1997 Asian financial crisis.

Driving the surging flows of capital to the region are the ultra-loose monetary policies of the developed world that have forced interest rates to near zero, leading investors to look for higher-yielding assets such as those offered in Asia. Last week's interest-rate cut by the European Central Bank added to continuing operations by Japan and the U.S. that are pumping capital into the global financial system. The recent pickup in China's currency gains against the dollar has also attracted speculators inside and outside China to dive into yuan, putting pressure on policy makers there to stem the inflows.

"Asia is still where the growth is, relatively speaking. It's quite clear where their [investors'] money will go. Asia is benefiting from that front," said Craig Chan, foreign-exchange analyst for Nomura in Singapore.

Data from provider EPFR Global show that investors have added nearly $8 billion to Asian emerging-market bond mutual funds so far this year, similar in size to the strong growth of capital inflows that occurred in 2010. A World Bank analysis of flows to emerging markets globally showed an increase through April of 42% over the year earlier, to $64 billion.

Another measure: Asia's central banks are again scooping up capital inflows and putting them into foreign-currency reserves. World Bank data show developing Asian economies have added $120 billion in foreign-exchange reserves so far this year to bring total reserves to nearly $4.3 trillion.

While attracting investment from overseas is often a good thing, left unchecked, inflows strengthen local currencies, which causes countries' goods to become less competitive on the global market. In addition, government policy makers worry, money that arrives quickly can leave just as fast, destabilizing local banking, stock and currency markets.

"The dilemma these central banks face is they could respond to inflows by cutting interest rates...but in some economies you have overheating risks and asset bubbles" that would be made worse with easier monetary policy, said Stephen Schwartz, economist for BBVA in Hong Kong.

Philippines, which recently was upgraded to investment-grade status by two ratings companies, has been fighting hot money inflows with several measures, including making it easier for locals to take money abroad and lowering a deposit rate for banks that do cross-border business.

The effect in Asia isn't uniform, as the U.S. dollar has had broad strength globally. Some countries, such as India and Indonesia, have seen their currencies stay weak in reaction to trade deficits. Compared to 2010, when Asian central banks routinely intervened in currency markets, this year has been less dramatic.

China moved Sunday to stanch upward pressure on its currency by forcing banks and exporters to sell yuan in favor of dollars. Regulators also issued a warning to exporters, which have been suspected of sneaking money into the country through accounting maneuvers related to the invoicing of goods. The moves are meant to dissuade Chinese banks and investors from trying to speculate on the strengthening of the yuan against the dollar.

Thailand's central bank has been under pressure from the government to intervene aggressively to tamp down the strength of the baht. The central bank issued a statement on April 30 noting that the "rapid appreciation" of the baht was "not justified by economic fundamentals." The bank promised to work with the government on measures to respond. No official disclosures have been made, but analysts expect either a rate cut or other moves to stem capital inflows.

Nearby, the Philippines has also cut rates on certain deposits last month to slow so-called hot money flows.

So far, though, the moves haven't made much of a dent in these strong currencies. While Australia's central bank on Tuesday cut interest rates for the seventh time since late 2011, the Australian dollar has fallen only about two cents against its U.S. counterpart over that time period.

Buoying the Australian dollar has been strong demand from overseas investors. More than 70% of Australian government bonds are held offshore--double the level in foreign hands a decade ago.

In nearby New Zealand, the head of the central bank said the bank has intervened in currency markets to slow the appreciation of its currency but admitted there was only so much it could do.

"We would not expect, given the strength of the flows, that intervention would materially change the level of the exchange rate, but we could take potentially the tops off rallies," said Graeme Wheeler, governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.

--Rebecca Howard and Rachel Pannett contributed to this article.

title: DJ New Zealand Dollar Steadies; Euro Climbs On Strong German Data
text:
-- New Zealand dollar steadies after RBNZ intervention admission triggers losses overnight

-- Euro rallies after German industrial production rose in March economists had expected a decline

-- Norwegian, Polish central bank rate decisions due later Wednesday

By Jessica Mead

The New Zealand dollar settled near its weakest levels for the month Wednesday after suffering heavy losses overnight on the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's admission it had intervened to prevent further currency strength, while the euro rallied after better-than-expected German industrial production data.

The New Zealand dollar, or Kiwi, had tumbled almost a cent against the U.S. dollar in Asian trading hours to $0.8361 after RBNZ Governor Graeme Wheeler said the central bank had stepped into the currency market and would do so again to contain the currency, which has risen about 10% over the past year against a basket of major currencies. Given the recent strong performance of the Kiwi, market participants believe the interventions were small in size.

"The takeaway from the RBNZ is that its pain thresholds for New Zealand dollar appreciation have been reached, and the central bank is prepared to step up its resistance by threatening rate cuts and intervention, in our view," said strategists at Credit Suisse in a note to clients.

In European hours, the Kiwi stabilized at around the $0.84 level with currency strategists skeptical that this has marked the start of more frequent interventions, citing Mr. Wheeler's comments that the central bank would expect to take the tops off rallies rather than materially change the exchange rate.

"I don't think we are going to see [the New Zealand dollar] tumble further. People have been buying the currency for diversification purposes, for yield. And as long as they are in that mindset, then they will still be buying it," said Jane Foley senior currency strategist at Rabobank in London, adding that it appears the central bank just wants to take the edge off the currency's gains.

The euro notched up gains after German March industrial production rose 1.2% on the month, confounding expectations for a 0.2% decline. The common currency rallied to as high as $1.3148 against the dollar and nudged briefly back above Y130 against the yen.

The figures are the second successive positive surprise for the economy, following Tuesday's publication of much stronger-than-expected manufacturing orders for March.

In the session ahead, few data releases are scheduled and the focus will be on the Polish and Norwegian central bank rate decisions.

The Polish rate decision is usually announced around 1100 GMT and most economists think the Polish central bank will leave borrowing costs unchanged at 3.25% after the half-point cut in March. Some, however, are calling for a quarter-point cut and others, such as Barclays, are expecting another half-a-point cut.

The Norwegian decision is due at 1200 GMT. It is widely expected that the Norges Bank will keep rates on hold at 1.5% for the seventh consecutive meeting, although some economists anticipate the bank mirroring the recent rate cut by the European Central Bank.

At 1017 GMT, the euro was trading at $1.3139 against the dollar, compared with $1.3079 late Tuesday in New York, according to trading system EBS. The dollar was at Y98.94 against the yen, compared with Y99.00, while the euro was at Y129.96 compared with Y129.47. Meanwhile, the pound was trading at $1.5502 against the dollar, compared with $1.5485 late Tuesday in New York.

title: DJ   New Zealand Central Bank  Admits  Currency Intervention
text:
WELLINGTON--New Zealand's central bank said it had intervened in foreign currency markets and would do so again if needed to contain a soaring local currency that's dragging on tourism and denting the competitiveness of the nation's agricultural exports.

The remarks, by Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Graeme Wheeler, sent the Kiwi tumbling nearly a cent lower to US$0.8361 from US$0.8460 on Wednesday. The governor also said the Kiwi was "overvalued... perhaps significantly," signaling the currency's high level remained a concern.

The New Zealand dollar has risen about 10% in the past year against a basket of major currencies. Official data already shows the central bank has actively intervened by selling New Zealand dollars in recent months, but the Reserve Bank until now hasn't explicitly called it an intervention.

"We've indicated on the record that we are prepared to intervene in the exchange rate," Mr. Wheeler said in a testimony to lawmakers. "We would not expect, given the strength of the flows, that intervention would materially change the level of the exchange rate, but we could take potentially the tops off rallies. And in terms of activity, there has been some."

In December, the central bank sold nearly NZ$200 million in the most significant sale in nearly four years, official data show. The pace of its sales slowed early this year, with the central bank selling only NZ$28 million in the first three months of the year combined. The Reserve Bank is due to release foreign currency transaction data for April later this month and some analysts say the intervention may have gathered pace again.

"Activity may have picked up very recently," Gareth Berry, a currency strategist at UBS said. He added that Mr. Wheeler's remarks Wednesday didn't look like the start of an "aggressive foreign exchange intervention campaign."

Bank of New Zealand economist Stephen Toplis said the market reaction Wednesday was a "storm in a teacup," adding that the central bank was likely to continue selling small amounts of its reserves "as part of their normal operations" whenever the local currency rose sharply.

title: New Zealand  Dollar Down Late as RBNZ Governor Mentions  Intervention
text:
WELLINGTON--The New Zealand dollar was lower late Wednesday following Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Graeme Wheeler's confirmation of some currency "intervention," but moves were pared by traders who decided it was more leaning than intervention.

The New Zealand dollar fell sharply to US$0.8361 around 0050 GMT from about US$0.8460 after Mr. Wheeler told a parliamentary committee that "we've indicated on the record that we are prepared to intervene in the exchange rate. We have also indicated that we would not expect, given the strength of the flows, that intervention would materially change the level of the exchange rate, but we could take potentially the tops of rallies. And in terms of activity, there has been some."

However, the sharp fall was somewhat reversed as market players mulled over the news and decided it wasn't significant intervention in the market but only the central bank's ongoing policy to lean against the currency.

The central bank has been "steadily selling small amounts of the New Zealand dollar against notably the U.S. dollar," said ANZ Senior FX Manager Sam Tuck. "We haven't got the April number but we don't expect it to be much larger than any of the prior months."

In December the central bank sold 199 million New Zealand dollars after selling NZ$64 million in November. The two sales marked the first significant moves by the central bank since mid-2008.

The central bank has also been grappling with an elevated Kiwi--up around 10% in the past year on a trade-weighted index basis--that is making it more difficult for companies in the country, which mostly exports agricultural products, to compete in global markets.

At 0530 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was trading around US$0.8398 compared with US$0.8497 late Tuesday. It was at A$0.8248 late in New Zealand from A$0.8337 late Tuesday.

Earlier Wednesday Mr. Wheeler said at the release of the Financial Stability Report that the New Zealand dollar was "over valued... perhaps significantly" and that it could continue appreciating which is a "significant concern."

The New Zealand April 2015 government bond fell 1 basis points to end at 2.45% and the April 2023 bond was unchanged at 3.20%.

title: UPDATE 2-RBNZ  intervened  to curb NZD as global flood of money raises economic risks
text:
* RBNZ confirms has intervened to lower NZ dollar

* Market participants expect biggest NZD selling since mid-2007

* Analysts: Intervention to have limited impact on NZD strength

(Adds comment, details)

By Gyles Beckford and Naomi Tajitsu

WELLINGTON, May 8 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank confirmed selling its own currency for only the second time since the "kiwi" was floated in 1985, reflecting concerns that a flood of global money could undermine a budding economic recovery.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand usually keeps intervention quiet, and its rare admission came after the currency surged to 20-month highs of $0.8676 last month, undercutting exporters and pressuring an economy finding its feet after devastating earthquakes in Christchurch in the last two years.

The intervention demonstrated the widespread unease among smaller economies over the impact of massive monetary expansionary campaigns in the United States and Japan.

"There has been intervention ... We've indicated on the record that we are prepared to intervene in the exchange rate," Governor Graeme Wheeler told a parliamentary committee on Wednesday.

On Tuesday, the Australian central bank, also grappling with a high-flying currency, cut interest rates to a record-low 2.75 percent.

The Australian dollar is not far from 28 year peaks when measured against a basket of currencies, which is "unusual given the decline in export prices and interest rates," Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glen Stevens said.

The kiwi has surged to similarly uncomfortable levels.

In April, when traders suspect the RBNZ conducted its latest intervention, the kiwi's trade-weighted index, the currency measure closely followed by the central bank, rose to 79.39, a record for the free float era.

During the last quarter of 2012 the New Zealand economy grew at its fastest pace in three years. It is expected to show annual growth of about 3 percent for the next couple of years, led by improving domestic demand and the rebuild of earthquake damaged Christchurch.

The high currency, however, is putting pressure on exporters' earnings.

Wheeler's comments helped drive down the New Zealand dollar

more than half a U.S. cent to a session low, but it is still hovering near a post-float high around $0.8850 hit in August 2011.

And market participants believe the intervention by the RBNZ would do little to weaken the kiwi, which is the 10th most traded currency in global markets.

Wheeler admitted as much: "We've also indicated that we would not expect the strength of the flows from intervention to materially change the exchange rate, although it could potentially take the top off (currency strength)."

The message was not lost on the currency market.

"What he's doing is talking about tools and waving a stick as the currency goes," said Alex Sinton, director, institutional FX, global markets at ANZ.

ATTRACTIVE YIELDS

Currency diversification by sovereign investors and the wall of money unleashed by massive monetary easing campaigns by major central banks have driven the "kiwi" higher.

Investors are drawn to its attractive yields, with the central bank expected to raise interest rates from a record low of 2.5 percent in the next year.

New Zealand's 10-year bond is currently trading around 3.2 percent, compared with a yield of 1.78 percent for its U.S. Treasury counterpart.

Wheeler told the committee the currency may appreciate more if investors expected the country's economy to outperform, raising expectations of higher rates.

The central bank's latest balance sheet, which covers transactions through March, shows scant selling of New Zealand dollars from the bank's reserves during the first three months of the year, after it sold a net NZ$199 million in December.

Market participants said that while the RBNZ's selling in April would be higher than the December amount, it would not be on the scale of the RBNZ's last major confirmed intervention in June-July 2007, when it sold a total of NZ$2.2 billion to stem kiwi strength.

The central bank has appeared to have sold the currency sporadically since then, but Wednesday's confirmation was only the second time the RBNZ has declared its hand since 2007.

"The RBNZ is playing a similar game to many other central banks in attempting to weaken or at least prevent strength in their currencies," analysts at Credit Agricole CIB said in a note. "The bottom line is that more smoothing is likely but a significant push to change NZD direction is highly unlikely."

(Reporting by Gyles Beckford; Editing by Shri Navaratnam)

title: Dollar significantly overvalued, hurting exporters - NZMEA
text:
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) has admitted to intervening in currency markets responding to the appreciation of our currency, say the New Zealand Manufacturers and Exporters Association (NZMEA).

NZMEA Chief Executive John Walley says, "It is good to see the RBNZ make some moves to lower our currency, but they can do much more than "take the top off the rallies". The sharp drop in the currency across the board shows just what action from a central bank can do. If the RBNZ were to commit to a more long term set of actions to bring down the currency, we would see a sustained effect on the dollar. This could be achieved through a co-ordinated mix of currency intervention, monetary policy and other macro-prudential tools."

"We consistently reference the example for the Swiss  Central Bank("http://www.realeconomy.co.nz/206-rbnz_lessons_from_the_swiss.aspx") using the infinite capacity of a central bank to place and enforce a currency ceiling."

"The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has also cut a further 25 basis points off its cash rate to a record low 2.75%. They are taking action against the appreciation of their currency."

"Much of Australia's recent economic success has been built on the back of their strong natural resource based businesses. Now their exporting sector is struggling, largely due to strength of their currency."

"Why is this important for New Zealand? Australia has been a bright spot for exporters in recent times; meaning businesses exporting to Australia for Australian consumption have been doing okay, compared to those selling into the U.S and Europe. The RBA takes action to lower the pressure on the AUS$ and places upwards pressure on the NZ$; this will hurt New Zealand exporters."

"We are pleased to see the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) commit to putting new tools into place for increasing reserves for high Loan to Value Ratio loans as well as some currency intervention."

"Even so, our dollar remains significantly overvalued, hurting exporters."

title: UPDATE: NZ  Central Bank  Threatens  Intervention  to Curb Kiwi
text:
WELLINGTON--New Zealand's central bank threatened to take steps to weaken the local currency, as its strength makes it increasingly difficult for the tiny exporting nation to compete in global markets.

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Gov. Graeme Wheeler said Wednesday the New Zealand dollar is "significantly over-valued," and the central bank will intervene in foreign exchange markets "when the circumstances are right". He also said the central bank could use the country's cash rate as a tool to apply downward pressure on the currency.

Currency levels have become a politically charged issue globally as aggressive monetary policy steps taken by central banks, including the Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan, have contributed to a sharp appreciation in currencies such as the New Zealand and Australian dollars as foreign investors seek out higher-yielding assets.

New Zealand's economy is far from a global powerhouse, but its currency plays an outsize role in the daily foreign-exchange market as one of the 10 most-traded currencies in the world, according to the Bank for International Settlements. In 2010, the kiwi accounted for about 1.6% of global foreign-exchange daily turnover.

So far in 2013, the kiwi, as it is commonly called, has gained around 1.7%. That makes it one of the best performers among Group of 10 nations when compared with the U.S. dollar. Part of its appeal is that the central bank has kept its benchmark interest rate at 2.5%, attracting yield-hungry investors.

Manufacturers and exporters have been lobbying the government to take action as the kiwi's strength undermines the competitiveness of the country's crucial farm exports. Dairy products account for a quarter of the nation's annual exports, valued at around 46 billion New Zealand dollars (US$39 million). Exporters have said that for every 1% increase in the exchange rate, exporters lose around NZ$200 million annually.

The kiwi tumbled following Mr. Wheeler's remarks, made at a gathering of exporters in Auckland, and was trading at US$0.8411 at 0438 GMT versus US$0.8469 before the speech.

Still, some analysts were skeptical about whether Mr Wheeler would follow through on his tough rhetoric.

Annette Beacher, the Singapore-based head of Asia-Pacific research for TD Securities, said Mr. Wheeler is "toothless tiger" and "highly unlikely" to cut the cash rate or directly intervene in the currency. Neither move would have much impact on the kiwi, she added.

Policymakers pledged during a weekend meeting of Group of 20 industrial and developing nations in Moscow to ensure that monetary policy is focused on price stability and growth, rather than on weakening currencies, as countries globally try to devalue their currencies because of falling global trade.

"There are no simple solutions available to the Reserve Bank on the exchange rate challenges we face," Mr. Wheeler said.

title: New Zealand Dollar Weakens; RBNZ Says  Currency  'Over-Valued'
text:
WELLINGTON--The New Zealand dollar ended lower late Wednesday after taking a tumble when the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Graeme Wheeler said the currency is significantly over-valued and the central bank stands ready to intervene.

At 0536 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was trading at US$0.8409, after touching an intraday low of US$0.8394 following the speech. It was buying US$0.8439 late Tuesday. Against the Australian dollar it was at A$0.8113 versus A$0.8170 late Tuesday.

"There are no simple solutions available to the Reserve Bank on the exchange rate challenges we face," Mr. Wheeler told the manufacturers and exporters association in Auckland. "The Bank will intervene when circumstances are right. We will use the Official Cash Rate as circumstances require," he added.

Western Union Business Solutions Corporate Dealing Manager Chris Hunter said, however, he expects the dip to be short-lived as the market will likely shrug off the comments. "There's no real change to the bank's stance here," he said. He said the Kiwi has short term support at US$0.8372 and resistance at US$0.8440.

In the longer term, traders expect the Kiwi to remain supported, in particular given strong dairy prices. BNZ FX Strategist Kymberly Martin noted that the latest GlobalDairyTrade auction, which took place overnight Tuesday, showed average milk prices up 3.1% since the prior auction two weeks ago.

"This was a very strong result, taking prices to +8.9% since the start of the year. This is in line with our broader view that positive New Zealand commodity price trends should help underpin the NZD this year," she said.

Dairy is the backbone of the New Zealand economy, representing around 25% of the island nation's NZ$46 billion of exports in the 12 months to the end of December.

title: UPDATE 1-NZ dollar overvalued, but no quick fixes to lower it - RBNZ
text:
* NZ dollar overvalued, but no quick fixes - RBNZ governor

* RBNZ intervention possible if conditions right

* Intervention likely short term effect, QE won't work

(Adds quotes, comments, market reaction)

By Gyles Beckford

WELLINGTON, Feb 20 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar is significantly overvalued compared with its economic fundamentals, but there are no quick means to bringing it down, including intervention, the central bank governor said on Wednesday, skittling the currency by nearly half a cent.

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Graeme Wheeler said part of the currency's strength reflected global imbalances, a weak U.S. dollar, and New Zealand's improved terms of trade, but he said there were no simple solutions, including intervention.

"Given the strength of recent capital flows, we can only attempt to smooth the peaks of the USD/NZD exchange rate; we cannot determine the level," Wheeler said in a speech to a business group.

He said the RBNZ had four criteria for intervention -- whether the exchange rate was at an exceptional level, whether it was justified, whether intervention would be consistent with monetary policy, and whether it was likely to succeed.

However, he said it was unlikely to have a sustained impact in bringing down the exchange rate but it could ease pressures in the short term.

"When the NZ dollar is coming under upward pressure, we want investors to know that the Kiwi is not a one way bet," Wheeler said.

The New Zealand dollar fell nearly half a cent to a low of $0.8411 after Wheeler's comments.

It also lost ground on cross rates against the Australia dollar, euro, and yen, sending the trade weighted New Zealand dollar index, the RBNZ's preferred currency measure, down around 0.6 percent, after hitting a post-float high last week.

"He said that he was ready to intervene if required, but he added that four criteria have to be met, and they're certainly not met yet," said Tim Kelleher, head of institutional sales at ASB Bank.

The kiwi, along with the neighbouring Aussie and other commodity linked currencies, have risen strongly this year, as central banks have effectively printed money, lowering their exchange rates, in a bid to stimulate their economies.

Last week, the Group of Seven and the Group of 20 called for members to allow market determined exchange rates.

Wheeler reiterated previous comments that quantitative easing measures as practised by some economies would unlikely to be successful in New Zealand.

"Quantitative easing would increase inflation, raise inflation expectations, stimulate asset prices, and lead eventually to higher interest rates," Wheeler said, adding that a Switzerland-style capping of the New Zealand dollar would be highly inflationary.

Wheeler also repeated that New Zealand needed to improve productivity, reduce foreign borrowing, sort out distortions in saving and investment incentives, and cut fiscal imbalances.

title: N.Z.  Central Bank  Kept Up Passive  Currency Intervention
text:
WELLINGTON--New Zealand's central bank continued to apply subtle downward pressure on the nation's currency by reducing its New Zealand dollar holdings for the second straight month in December.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand, or RBNZ, sold 200 million New Zealand dollars (US$168 million) last month after selling NZ$66 million in November in the first significant sales of the currency by the central bank since March 2008.

The New Zealand dollar has remained elevated in recent months, with investors buying the currency on promising growth signs as agricultural commodity prices stay firm, and earthquake reconstruction work looking like giving a boost to the economy this year. But as with Australia, New Zealand's strong currency is hurting many companies reliant on converting foreign income.

The central bank is "not trying to influence the level of the currency," said Bank of New Zealandcurrency strategist Mike Jones. "They're just leaning against the wind."

The RBNZ seldom actively intervenes in the currency market, and Mr. Jones said that while the scale of the buying was limited, the moves were more a "signalling device"--a way for the central bank to indicate that the Kiwi was overvalued and that it would like it to move lower.

title: UPDATE: RBNZ's Wheeler Assures Market It's Business As Usual
text:
--RBNZ Governor Graeme Wheeler says quantitative easing unnecessary, bank has scope to cut cash rate

--Mr. Wheeler says currency market intervention unlikely to have sustained effect

--NZ dollar dips on speech, but pares losses as comments digested

(Recasts the first paragraph, adds details throughout, comments from economists from paragraph nine.)

By Lucy Craymer

WELLINGTON--The maiden speech by Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Graeme Wheeler assured the market that it would be business as usual at the central bank, even as he retained the possibility of currency market intervention or a cut to the official cash rate.

Mr. Wheeler told the Admirals' Breakfast Club in Auckland in a speech Friday that price stability and financial stability remained the Reserve Bank's central objectives for monetary and prudential policy, and this had been reinforced by the newly signed Policy Targets Agreement.

While annual inflation is currently at 0.8%, below the central bank's 1%-3% target band, Mr. Wheeler said the new focus of keeping inflation at 2.0% should "help to anchor inflation expectations around the mid-point" going forward.

The New Zealand dollar knee-jerked lower following the release of the speech, touching US$0.8175, but pared losses as the market digested Mr. Wheeler's comments and is now at US$0.8193.

HiFX Senior Trader Stuart Ive said comments that the RBNZ had scope to cut rates had weighed on the New Zealand dollar, but taken alongside comments about price stability they suggest "he will not cut rates on the basis that the currency is too high" but will only ease if the economy deteriorates.

Mr. Wheeler used much of his speech to address recent calls from opposition parties in New Zealand for the RBNZ to either use quantitative easing to reduce the strength of the New Zealand dollar and improve the economy or to intervene in the currency market. Opposition parties have argued that the high New Zealand dollar has been putting pressure on the export sector.

"New Zealand does not require quantitative easing: the economy is growing at an annual rate of around 2%, and the Reserve Bank has scope to lower interest rates if needed," he said.

He added that while the central bank would like to see a lower exchange rate, foreign currency intervention in unlikely to have a sustainable effect on the New Zealand dollar.

"The bank will remain vigilant on its criteria for intervention and will be prepared to intervene if all its conditions are met," he said.

The RBNZ last intervened in the foreign exchange market in June 2007 and its policy only allows for it to intervene if the New Zealand dollar is deemed to be exceptionally high or low; when it believes the exchange rate is unjustifiable by economic fundamentals; where intervention is consistent with the PTA; and where markets are such that intervention has a reasonable chance of success.

"He is not an uber-dove. He is not going to revamp the monetary policy framework or introduce quantitative easing and declare a futile war on the exchange rate," ANZ economist Mark Smith said in a note after the speech.

The central bank has held the official cash rate at 2.5% since March 2012 and economists expect it will remain at this level until late 2013. Mr. Wheeler's speech hasn't changed this view, with some economists even thinking the newly arrived governor is less dovish than they had expected.

"The over-riding impression we form from this speech is that at this stage it is very much 'business as usual' at the RBNZ under the new governor," Deutsche Bank economist Darren Gibbs said. "The speech reinforces our sense that at this stage the RBNZ has no more than a soft near-term easing bias and that it will still take significant bad news on activity and/or weak inflation indicators to cause the bank to act on that bias."

title: FX  GLOBAL CALL: Our Take on the Day's Big  FX  News
text:
The FX Global Call covers the main talking points from a news meeting involving DJ FX Trader editors in New York, London and Singapore, as well as other FX hot spots when warranted.


 
   By Michael Casey

1. So much for the dollar/yen rally. For all the excitement over what looked like a major shift lower in the yen this week, the Japanese currency has rebounded in the past 24 hours as traders calibrate their expectations for next week's meeting of the Bank of Japan. In London trading the dollar was back below Y80. Meanwhile, options markets are already pricing for the likelihood that dollar/yen won't rise much further, which could be predicated on the belief that the BOJ won't live up to expectations for a heavy bout of quantitative easing. One concern is that although the market had begun to price in the prospect of an asset-buying program as large as Y20 trillion, constant jawboning from government officials on the need to reverse deflation and weaken the yen could give the BOJ cold feet as it seeks to protect its independence. In a BOJ Watch Friday, we reported that people familiar with the BOJ's thinking say an asset-buying program will be discussed at Tuesday's meeting, but they are already concerned about the central bank's substantial, distorting impact on various asset classes.

2. In China, the yuan again hit the upper end of its trading band versus the dollar, as inflows into the country continued amid a general improvement in sentiment about its economic prospects. But a wave of dollar-buying by state banks left the impression that the People's Bank of China was using them to conduct de facto intervention to push the yuan lower toward the end of the day.

3. In Berlin, a senior lawmaker from Germany's ruling coalition hinted that the Bundestag might be amenable to an extension in Greece's bailout program. Hans Michelbach, the senior finance policy spokesman for the Christian Social Union, the Bavarian sister party in German Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservative parliamentary alliance, told us exclusively that the German government was actively seeking to extend the Greece aid program. He said that was a "conceivable path." Support from the German parliament is critical if Greece is to turn an expected agreement with the EU-ECB-IMF "troika" for an extension to 2016 of its fiscal targets into a legally binding agreement and to secure an estimated EUR30 billion in funding needed to pay for the financial shortfall that this would entail.

4. Spain's unemployment numbers were, in Katie Martin's words, "hideous"--rising to 25.02% from 24.62%. But the market has become more or less inured to the depressing drumbeat of bad news out of Spain's economy. Nothing really changes the fact that Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy is going to have to ask for money from the EU sooner rather than later. And that, of course, would be welcomed by the market as it would trigger ECB bond-buying.

5. Portugal is also maneuvering slowly toward the prospect ECB intervention in its bond market. It sold EUR50 million in 2018 notes in a private placement. That could help it attract ECB help because the central bank has said it would only initiate its outright monetary transactions for countries that have proven access to funds from the market.

6. In his inaugural speech as the new governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, Graeme Wheeler initially sparked a bit of excitement by mentioning the prospect of a rate cut and keeping the door open to intervention, which helped push the New Zealand dollar lower early in Wellington trading. But in time, it became clear that there was no real shift in policy and that his positions on these policy options were consistent with those of his predecessors. The "kiwi" recovered and stabilized.

7. Across the Tasman Sea, however, the Reserve Bank of Australia has been surreptitiously engaging in a form of de facto intervention, writes James Glynn in an exclusive piece of analysis. The RBA, it turns out, has been allowing natural inflows of foreign currency into its coffers to drive its foreign currency reserves higher--by $890 million over the past two months. Normally, the central bank would "sterilize" those inflows by purchasing local currency to keep its balance sheet steady, but it hasn't done so of late. It's an important reason that the Aussie dollar is under pressure.

8. In the latest expansion of the Libor scandal, we reported exclusively late in New York Thursday that nine additional banks have received subpoenas from the New York and Connecticut attorneys general as part of the international investigation into interest rate manipulation. The banks are Bank of America Corp., Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi UFJ, Credit Suisse Group, Lloyds, Rabobank, Royal Bank of Canada, Societe Generale, Norinchukin Bank and West LB, according to the person familiar with the matter.

9. And in Singapore's own version of this global investigation--in this case a probe of how the Singapore Interbank Offered Rate (Sibor) is set--the Royal Bank of Scotland has placed a currency trader, Ken Cho on leave, people familiar with the decision tell us. Choy is director of Emerging Markets FX at the bank.

10. The central banks of Colombia and Mexico meet Friday. Both are expected to keep rates on hold.

11. In the U.S., the Commerce Department will release the first estimate of third quarter GDP at 8:30 a.m. EDT. It is expected to show an annualized gain of 1.8%, up from 1.5% in the previous quarter.

title: REFILE-UPDATE 1-New RBNZ head backs inflation goal, douses  intervention  talk
text:
(Corrects spelling of "head" in headline)

 * Inflation, financial system focus of policy

 * Says while NZ$ high, intervention to cap it would not work

 * Approach seen signalling no major changes 

 By Naomi Tajitsu

 WELLINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is focused on keeping inflation in check and the financial system healthy, prerequisites for a stronger economy, the central bank's new governor said on Friday as he doused expectations of measures to lower the currency.

Graeme Wheeler made the comments in his first public speech as governor, a day after the central bank held the official cash rate (OCR) at a record-low 2.5 percent. 

 "Price stability and financial stability remain the Reserve Bank's central objectives for monetary policy and prudential policy," said Wheeler, who took over from Alan Bollard at the end of last month.

 "Our economy is growing at an annual rate of around 2 percent and the Reserve Bank has scope to lower interest rates if needed," he said, but added it was not the role of monetary policy to target growth rates.

 One analyst said the speech showed there would not be any major surprises from a Wheeler-led central bank.

 "He is not going to revamp the monetary policy framework or introduce quantitative easing and declare a futile war on the exchange rate," ANZ senior economist Mark Smith said.

 Wheeler said the economy would benefit from a lower exchange rate if it could be achieved without compromising other policy goals, and so while lower interest rates might initially push down the currency there was unlikely to be a sustained impact.

 "If we reduced the OCR without sound reasons, the exchange rate might drop initially but rise later when the inflationary implications of the rate cut became clear," Wheeler said.

 The New Zealand dollar has gained around 10 percent since hitting its low point for the year in early June. 

 CLEAR CRITERIA

 The RBNZ had clear criteria for currency intervention, including whether it would work, whether the currency was exceptionally high, and whether the market conditions were right -- and Wheeler indicated those conditions had not been met.

 "It makes little sense to risk incurring losses to taxpayers by intervening when currency flows supporting the New Zealand dollar are particularly strong."

 Wheeler also dismissed the practicality of capital controls, saying they would damage the credibility and stability of the financial sector, and increase the real cost of capital.

 The kiwi dollar fell nearly half a cent to a low of $0.8159 after the comments, before settling back around $0.8190.

 Wheeler said his policy agreement with the government had reinforced the importance of controlling inflation, in particular aiming for the mid-point of the 1-3 percent target band.

 "Over time, attaining this outcome should help to anchor inflation expectations around the mid-point."

 He noted the central bank also had macro-prudential tools, such as core funding ratios, capital buffers, sectoral risk weights, and housing loan-to-value ratio limits, to deal with  any inflation bubbles that developed.

 Quantitative easing of the sort undertaken in the United States, Europe, and Japan were not needed in New Zealand, he said.

13 Oct 2012 00:10 EDT DJ  INTERVIEW: NZ Fin Min Says Costs, Risks of Currency Intervention 'Very High'

--New Zealand finance minister says talks with central bankers confirmed view that costs, risks of intervention high

--Says worried about central banks unwinding positions after monetary easing 


 
   By Eleanor Warnock and Ainsley Thomson 
 

TOKYO--New Zealand Finance Minister Bill English said discussions in recent days with countries that have in the past intervened to weaken their currencies reaffirmed his belief that a similar tactic was the wrong strategy for New Zealand.

"It's confirmed for me that the costs and risks of it [currency intervention] are very high, particularly for a small open economy," Mr. English, who is in Tokyo for the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings, said in an interview.

He said during his time in Tokyo, he had spoken with a former governor of Switzerland's central bank and the current governor of Japan's central bank, Masaaki Shirakawa. Both countries have intervened in the past to weaken their currencies.

Since the beginning of 2009, the New Zealand dollar has appreciated about 40% against the U.S. dollar. The New Zealand dollar, which reached a post-float high of US$0.8841 in August 2011, was at US$0.8170 at Friday's market close.

New Zealand's economy is heavily dependent on trade, and a stronger dollar has put a pinch on the nation's exporters by making products more expensive abroad.

Mr. English said his country's strategy to deal with the currency issue would be centered on increasing the competitiveness of its exporters, and expressed hope that the agricultural-product heavy makeup of its exports would make it better positioned to withstand a slowdown in China than its neighbor Australia, which exports large amounts of minerals and energy.

"A slowdown (in China) would affect us, but we're reasonably optimistic that in the long run demand for our food and protein products is likely to be steady and growing," he said. "Over a longer period our prices will be a bit less volatile (than Australia) because we're geared into the growing middle-class in China rather than the infrastructure side."

More than a third of the value of the country's exports were dairy and meat products in the year ended Sept. 30, 2011, according to government statistics.

Mr. English added that this week's meetings had also raised the question of the world's central banks unwinding their positions after taking strong monetary easing measures in recent years.

"I don't think we really understand the unwinding of these extraordinary monetary measures. That's all out ahead of us," he said. "Demographics are going to be pushing a lot of people to cash in their assets. Baby boomers are going to be selling and so are the central banks and it may not be as politically straight forward as it looks now."

"We are pleased to be in an economy where those innovative monetary tools haven't been used," he said.

The New Zealand dollar has also gained on safe haven flows from investors fleeing turmoil in Europe, and looking for higher returns than in other developed countries where interest rates have dropped to historical lows.

Commenting on a possible reversal of safe-haven flows after a return of global investor confidence, Mr. English said: "That would help our rebalancing, which we need to do. That would be a good problem to have."

But he added that "there doesn't look to me to be a turning point in the near term."

title: INTERVIEW: N.Z. Fin Min:  Intervening  to Lower Exchange Rate Not a Solution
text:
LONDON--Recent moves by the world's largest central banks to stimulate their economies is driving up the New Zealand dollar and making life harder for the country's exporters, but intervening in the currency market to lower the exchange rate isn't a solution, New Zealand Finance Minister Bill English said Wednesday.

"We don't see a simple or easy way to manipulate the exchange rate," Mr. English said in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires. "Those countries that have set out to do so are either not succeeding or exposing themselves to pretty large risks."

Mr. English, who is in London to meet with U.K. Chancellor of the Exchequer George Osborne, international investors and rating agencies, said the Reserve Bank of New Zealand has authority to intervene in the currency market in specific circumstances--when there is extreme market disorder or to trim peaks and troughs in the exchange-rate cycle.

"It's up to them to decide whether those conditions apply, but we don't intend to create the expectation that somehow the N.Z. government can pick the exchange rate and push the market in that direction," he said.

The New Zealand dollar, which reached a post-float high of US$0.8841 in August 2011, is currently trading around US$0.8202.

Like Australia and emerging-market countries such as Brazil, New Zealand has seen its currency strengthen as result of moves by central banks in major economies--such as the Bank of Japan and the Federal Reserve--to ease their respective monetary policies. Investors are flocking to countries and assets that offer higher interest rates than the low rates offered in Japan, the U.S. and parts of Europe.

That, in turn, is prompting other central banks to employ their own measures to depreciate their currencies.

Mr. English, who is a lawmaker in the center-right National party that has governed since 2008, said rather than central bankintervention in the currency market, the government is trying to improve the competitiveness of exporters--a policy he conceded would take time to make an impact.

Mr. English criticized the monetary policy tool of quantitative easing--in which a central bank effectively prints more money to buy bonds--labelling it an "extreme measure".

"It's my view that while printing money has some shorter-term benefits, there is a lot of uncertainty about the longer-term damage that is being done," he said. "I'm pleased that we're not involved in that kind of process."

Mr. English said the most recent forecasts show the government is on track to achieve a budget surplus in the year to June 2015, but he said there were indications the economy had softened since then.

"We have a bit of headroom built into those last forecasts," he said, "but the way the world is changing, you take it one at a time."

Mr. English said an economic slowdown in China was a concern because of the impact it would have on Australia, which is New Zealand's largest market.

"How we do will depend more on impacts of the U.S. drought on dairy prices than whether China is up or down another percentage point," he said.

Mr. English said the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision Tuesday to cut its benchmark lending rate by 0.25 percentage point to 3.25%, was a reminder that Australia's once-in-a-hundred-year mining investment boom wouldn't last forever.

title: POLL-Aussie, NZ dlrs to dip only modestly in 2012
text:

By Cecile Lefort

SYDNEY, Feb 3 (Reuters) - The high-flying Australian and New Zealand dollars may pull back modestly in the coming months on global concerns, but will continue to be supported by their status as commodity currencies, a Reuters poll showed.

The median forecast of more than 50 analysts polled by Reuters showed the Australian dollar gradually slipping to $1.015 in early 2013, although still above parity.

On Friday, it was up at $1.0680, having risen 5 percent so far this year. The Aussie and the New Zealand dollar, which is up 7 percent this year, are among the best performing major currencies in that period. See and for polls.

"Residual eurozone uncertainties, including the outcome of Greek PSI negotiations, and the pace/magnitude of recent gains lead us to expect NZD/USD and AUD/USD to be modestly lower," said Hamish Pepper, an analyst at Barclays Capital in Singapore.

A survey of 46 analysts showed the New Zealand dollar was also expected to gently pull back to $0.78 mid-year, from $0.8300 where it currently stands.

The Antipodean currencies have been in demand since the U.S. Federal Reserve pledged to keep rates near zero out to late 2014 and triggered expectations of more easing. This is encouraging investors to borrow in dollars to fund carry trades in commodities and higher yielding assets.

Investors have been piling on long positions even though the Reserve Bank of Australia is almost certain to cut rates again next week partly because of global growth concerns as the European debt crisis drags on.

With a current cash rate at 4.25 percent, Australia has one of the highest rates in the developed world and has room to cut further should it need to stimulate growth, unlike many of its peers.

STRETCHED POSITIONS

Analysts warn, however, the Aussie bullish run could end abruptly.

"As these net long positions become increasingly stretched, at some stage there will be a downward correction to the Antipodeans currencies and these players will likely become forced sellers," said Annette Beacher, head of Asia-Pacific research at TD Securities in Singapore.

The kiwi has been a big favourite of momentum players and black box funds betting it can go a lot further yet, particularly as currencies like the yen and Swiss franc have been hemmed in by intervention.

Barclays' Pepper expected New Zealand to maintain its yield advantage over other G10 economies given a likely extended period of extremely low interest rates in the U.S. and eurozone.

He also forecast that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) will start hiking rates in the second half of 2012.

The RBNZ held its cash rate at a record-low equalling 2.5 percent last week because of global outlook concerns and modest domestic growth. A majority of analysts forecast the central bank will tighten its monetary policy late this year or early 2013.

(Reporting by Cecile Lefort; Editing by Ramya Venugopal)

title: FOREX -Euro consolidates with focus on US jobs, EU action
text:
* Markets awaiting U.S. non-farm payrolls data

* Euro seen consolidating in Asian session

* Next week's ECB, EU meets key to year-end sentiment

* Kiwi higher, fails to break above this week's high

By Antoni Slodkowski

TOKYO, Dec 2 (Reuters) - The euro struggled to make much headway on Friday, consolidating this week's gains as traders stuck to the sidelines ahead of a crucial U.S. jobs report and event-packed week that could prove decisive for the currency bloc.

The non-farm payrolls report is expected to show an increase of 122,000 jobs and a steady unemployment rate of 9.0 percent. A positive surprise would underpin a recent string of solid U.S. data and bolster risk sentiment, while a weaker-than-expected outcome may push investors to take more profits on recent gains.

The euro changed hands at $1.3460 against $1.3457 late in New York. It was off a one-week peak of $1.3534 hit on Wednesday after major central banks moved to ease a credit squeeze stemming from the crisis, sparking a rally.

"The move by the central banks simply eased liquidity worries for now. The big-bazooka solutions are coming next week and the euro's strength hinges on their feasibility," said Sumino Kamei, senior currency analyst at the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ in Tokyo.

French and German leaders are meeting next Monday to outline joint proposals to put to a Dec. 9 EU summit, seen as -- yet another -- make-or-break meeting for the 12-year-old currency bloc.

"EU leaders have disappointed in the past, so nobody is naive enough to simply pile into the euro on mere statements, especially since Europe faces serious economic headwinds anyway," Kamei said.

She added, however, that the currency may move another leg higher if the actions are strongly supported by the European Central Bank and even if the move up is not sustained, it may still prove an important chance to sell into a rally.

The central bank hinted on Thursday it was ready to move more aggressively to tackle the crisis if politicians agree on much tighter budget controls in the euro zone, though it stopped short of detailing what exact measures it would take.

Still, there is no agreement among EU policymakers regarding how such controls could be implemented and many other problems, including securing resources to leverage the euro zone's bailout fund, linger unresolved.

Economists expect the ECB to help banks and an economy on the verge of recession by cutting interest rates next week and announcing longer-term cheap liquidity tenders with easier collateral rules. Markets are pricing in a 25 basis point cut to 1.0 percent at the ECB's Dec. 8. policy meeting.

Decent stop-loss euro bids were spotted in the $1.3520-25 area, while offers were lurking near $1.3500. One possible resistance point for the currency lies near $1.3525, the bottom of the weekly Ichimoku cloud.

"Our economists believe that a satisfactory fiscal compact agreed upon at the summit next week should open the door to ECB quantitative easing, which we expect could come as soon as Q1 2012," wrote analysts at BNP Paribas.

But analysts at Societe Generale warned a lack of progress on the root causes of the euro zone crisis will translate into wider bond yield spreads and a weaker euro in January.

With the euro on the front foot for now, the dollar index

slipped 0.1 percent to 78.310. Against the yen, the dollar was mildly bid at 77.77, still hemmed in a 77-78 range with investors wary of more massive intervention by Japan.

The New Zealand dollar tested this week's high set on Wednesday at $0.7824 for the third time in three straight sessions, but came slightly short of it, last changing hands at 0.7806. It has risen nearly 4 percent this week.

Support for the kiwi is seen around $0.7730, while the 55-day moving average at $0.7900 is likely to cap the topside.

The Australian dollar stood at $1.0221, not far off a three-week peak of $1.0335 set earlier in the week.

Key resistance is seen around $1.0337, a level representing a 61.8 percent retracement of the November decline.

title: DJ INTERVIEW: NZ Opposition Pins Long-Shot Hopes On Opposing State Asset Sales
text:
-- NZ Labour Party's Trevor Mallard vows to fight Prime Minister Key on proposed government asset sales

-- Hiving off high-returning assets is "bloody silly;" public warming to capital-gains tax, Mallard says

-- The government should consider changing the RBNZ's mandate to fight the "too high" Kiwi dollar, he says 


 
   By William Mallard 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

AUCKLAND (Dow Jones)-New Zealand's opposition is staking its long-shot election hopes on tarring Prime Minister John Key's government with an unpopular plan to sell stakes in state-owned companies, a leading Labour Party official said.

Labour's shadow leader in the House, Trevor Mallard, who held various Cabinet posts between 1999 and 2005, vowed to make inroads by focusing attention on Key's plan to sell stakes of companies such as Air New Zealand Ltd. (AIR.NZ) and electric-power utilities, while offering as an alternative Labour's proposal to introduce a capital-gains tax.

Key is "an enormous asset" for his center-right National Party, Mallard told Dow Jones in an interview Friday. But the prime minister is "much more popular than his party."

The plan to raise up to NZ$7 billion in asset sales in unpopular. Both main parties agree on the goal of returning the budget to surplus over the next four years, but Mallard said the asset sales are a "bloody silly" idea because the companies have generated 17% average annual returns for the past five years. Labour's internal polls show its tax plan gaining popularity on the grounds of fairness in the months since the party began discussing it, he said.

Mallard insisted Labour form a coalition after the Nov. 26 election if it picks up 5-6 points and the Greens hold steady. "The odds are such that you wouldn't bet the house," but they're better than Samoa's chances when it faced mighty Australia in a July rugby match, he said.

Samoa beat the Wallabies 32-23 in a huge upset.

A survey Thursday in The New Zealand Herald showed the National Party with support of 53.8%, on track to form a government by itself, with Labour at 29.5%.

Mallard, Labour's associate finance spokesman, said the "too high" New Zealand dollar is "doing enormous damage to our export industries" and that the government should consider altering the central bank's mandate to help curb the currency.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has almost never intervened since the Kiwi was floated in 1985, and Mallard agreed that intervention is "not a real long-term strategy." But he said the government needs to "give serious consideration to other tools," such as the RBNZ's inflation target or measures of money supply.

The New Zealand dollar, which hit a nearly 30-year high last month above 84 U.S. cents, is trading Monday at US$0.8188.

 TOKYO  Aug 19 (Reuters) - The euro and commodity currencies such as the Australian dollar came under pressure on Friday after a raft of weak U.S. economic data and concerns about European banks sent skittish investors piling into U.S. Treasuries and away from stocks.

 Mounting fears of global recession sent Asian bourses down after the Nasdaq plunged more than 5 percent and European stocks dropped sharply, dragged lower by banks, while safe-haven gold

posted record highs above $1.840 per ounce.

 The fall in the Aussie, however, was limited as it held above its 200-day moving average, with traders citing support from fund and exporter selling of the dollar against Asian currencies.

 "I'm really surprised by how quiet the market is today, compared to stocks. Investors are awaiting more developments in Europe and the U.S. as we enjoy some lukewarm pre-weekend trading in Asia," said a trader for a major Japanese bank who did not want to be identified by name.

  The euro fell 0.2 percent to $1.4310, after slipping 0.8 percent to $1.4303 as an unnamed euro zone bank borrowed $500 million in one-week from the European Central Bank.

 That sent interbank lending rates soaring with the USD Libor/OIS spread blowing out to 19 basis points, the highest level in 12 months. Three-month Libor also struck four-month highs at 2.9778 percent.

 "In this situation where we are becoming more concerned about funding, it is natural that the U.S. dollar does well," said Robert Rennie, chief currency strategist at Westpac. 

"We are still within a very well rehearsed range of $1.41-$1.45," he added.

 The dollar was also up 0.1 percent against the New Zealand dollar, which was at $0.8218 after at one point dropping nearly 2 percent to $0.8196. The Aussie was down 0.1 percent at $1.0359 after skidding to $1.0338 from this week's high above $1.0600.

 "Investors are parking funds in dollars as global economic concerns heighten after weak U.S. data the previous day and as a lack of clarity about Europe's debt problems spreads to banks in the euro zone," said Tsutomu Soma, senior manager at Okasan Securities.

 Recent data heightened concerns that the United States will head back into recession at the same time the country's rising debt load and record deficit leave the Federal Reserve with fewer options to stimulate growth.     

 The data sparked a frenzy of safe-haven buying with 10-year Treasury yields hitting a deep low of 1.97 percent. They were last at 2.033 percent.

 Investors refrained from shifting into traditional safe havens such as the Swiss franc and the yen due to fears of intervention.

 Market players were reminded about the looming intervention after the dollar briefly spiked against the yen hitting as high as 77 yen on stop-loss buying with talk of buying from a British bank.

 STAYING ON GUARD

 Japanese authorities also warned traders to keep their guard up after Switzerland's central bank intervened in the forward market earlier this week and as it engineers negative interest rates. 

 "Dollar/yen is expected to be supported, but gains will be limited at 77 yen. It should gradually test downside below a record low 76.25," Okasan's Soma said.

 Soma's views echo those of other Tokyo traders who warn that as the Japanese return from their summer holidays next week, exporters will likely sell dollar/yen in end-of-the-month transactions, heightening the risk of intervention.

 "Of course the high dollar is difficult for our exporters, we would much prefer the dollar to be lower," Bill English said in reply to a question in parliament.

 "But there is no obvious monetary policy tool that could achieve that."

 The New Zealand dollar fell sharply against the U.S. dollar on Thursday, tracking the yen down after the Bank of Japan bought the greenback to weaken the Japanese currency.

 It last traded around $0.8535 after falling from $0.8640 when the Bank of Japan intervened to curb the strength of the Japanese yen. For more see 

 "We would prefer a lower exchange rate, the world's not delivering that to us, so we have to get on and build a competitive economy," English added.

 The kiwi's fall was given added momentum when English separately told the Dow Jones Newswires that a high local currency was a headwind for the economy.

 English repeated any potential intervention in markets to bring down the New Zealand dollar would be up to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, but said the experience of other central banks in intervening had been less than successful.

 Tim Kelleher, CBA's vice president of institutional banking and markets, said the Japanese intervention also triggered some stop-loss selling in the kiwi.

 "The main driver was the Japanese buying (U.S. dollar)," Kelleher said.

 The New Zealand dollar is up almost 10 percent so far this year, denting the competitiveness of the country's exports.

 Earlier this week, Prime Minister John Key, a former head of foreign exchange dealing at Merrill Lynch, said intervention by the RBNZ was unlikely to be successful because it had not worked overseas and the New Zealand economy continued to be seen as more attractive than the US economy.

title: FOREX -Euro at record low vs safe haven Swiss franc
text:
* Euro under pressure as Greek debt saga rolls on

* Hits record low vs Swiss franc <EURCHF=> in thin trade

* Large option structures vulnerable at 1.2000 francs

(Adds details, updates prices)

By Anirban Nag and Neal Armstrong

LONDON, June 13 (Reuters) - The euro hit a record low against the Swiss franc on Monday, as worries over attempts to deal with the Greek debt crisis made investors shy away from the common currency and seek relative safety in the franc.

Volumes were on the lower side with many centres in Europe closed for a holiday. The cost of insuring peripheral euro zone bonds against default hit a record high, while a general lack of appetite towards riskier assets dented euro sentiment.

The euro fell to as low as 1.2004 francs <EURCHF=> on trading platform EBS. Traders said stop-loss orders were triggered after it fell through 1.2050, and system-related selling pushed it towards 1.2000 francs in thin liquidity.

They highlighted large option structures at 1.2000, with a break below expected to trigger more euro selling. Euro/Swiss last traded around 1.2025, down around 0.6 percent for the day.

The euro <EUR=> also skidded to a one-week low in Asia of $1.4285 before some central bank demand helped it pare losses. It was last trading with slight gains on the day at $1.4383.

Resistance was at the 55-day moving average at $1.4398 and a concentration of former support levels around $1.4430/50, which includes previous intraday peaks in May and a 38.2 percent retracement of the May-to-June rise.

"What the euro needs is a resolution to the Greek crisis and the politicians and the central bankers do not appear to be close to finding one," said Kit Juckes, currency strategist at Societe Generale. "That uncertainty is weighing on the euro and I expect it to be stuck in a $1.40-$1.47 range."

European policymakers appeared deadlocked on how private investors could be involved in some form of restructuring of Greek debt. The European Central Bank is opposed to German proposals for a bond swap, arguing that it would trigger market turmoil.

Bundesbank head Jens Weidmann in comments released at the weekend said he was against extending the maturities of Greek bonds held by the ECB in any "soft" restructuring.

German and French banks were leaning towards contributing to a Greek rescue, even as it remained unclear how they could do so without triggering a default or credit default swap contracts. [ID:nLDE75A065]

Investors also see less risk of repeated euro zone rate hikes in the months ahead. Even as ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet signalled a rate hike is on the way in July, the ECB left inflation forecasts for 2012 little changed, prompting traders to slash expectations for higher policy rates.

The euro's uncertain outlook saw implied volatilities rise with risk reversals also widening, suggesting more downside risks for the single currency. <EURVOL=ICAP>

SAFE HAVEN FLOWS

The euro's woes have been compounded by a drop in global stocks that has prompted some market players to unwind carry trades funded with the U.S. dollar, the yen and the Swiss franc. World stocks slumped to a 12-week low on Monday. <.MIWD00000PUS>

The rush towards safe-haven assets boosted the Swiss franc and kept the dollar pinned near record lows hit last week. The dollar was last down 0.7 percent at 0.8374 <CHF=>.

"The Swiss franc remains the global barometer for risk and the fresh euro zone jitters have given renewed confidence to investors to push it higher," said Lena Komileva, head of G-10 currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman.

The Swiss National Bank meets this week for a rate decision, and is unlikely to signal any risk of intervention to cap the franc's strength.

The New Zealand dollar tumbled after a series of powerful earthquakes shook Christchurch, four months after the city was badly damaged by a 6.3 magnitude quake. The kiwi dropped 1 percent to trade at $0.8125 <NZD=D4>.

(Editing by Catherine Evans)

title: DJ 2nd UPDATE: RBNZ Stands Pat; No Rate Hike Tipped Until March
text:
-- RBNZ keeps its key rate at 2.5%, cites post-quake uncertainties

-- Gov. Bollard says the current rate looks "appropriate for some time"

-- Bollard says high oil prices, Kiwi dollar unwelcome

-- RBNZ tips on-year inflation easing back into target band after tax impact drops out

(Recasts lead, adds context and analysis throughout, snap poll in fourth paragraph, updates New Zealand dollar reaction in 12th paragraph.) 


 
  By Rebecca Howard 
  Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand's central bank left interest rates unchanged Thursday and, despite rising inflation, indicated it won't tighten policy for some time as the economy fights to recover from a devastating earthquake.

The head of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand also expressed concern about the strength of the local dollar, but economists say that unlike its counterparts in much of Asia, the RBNZ almost certainly won't intervene to weaken the currency.

"The outlook for the New Zealand economy remains very uncertain following February's Christchurch earthquake," Reserve Bank of New Zealand Gov. Alan Bollard said in a statement after the central bank left its Official Cash Rate at 2.5%. "Given the outlook for core inflation and continued economic disruption stemming from the earthquakes, the current level of the OCR is likely to remain appropriate for some time."

The median forecast for the RBNZ to raise rates, in a Dow Jones survey of economists after the central bank decision, is for March, unchanged from a poll a few days ago. Thursday's 14 forecast dates for a rate increase range from December to the second quarter of 2012. The central bank's last policy change was a half-percentage-point cut in March in response to the magnitude-6.3 quake.

"The RBNZ acknowledged some signs of improvement, but appears in no hurry to remove policy support," said Goldman Sachs economist Philip Borkin. "Given contained underlying inflation, a steep yield curve and the current profile of mortgage borrowers, we believe the RBNZ will remain more patient when it comes to tightening than it has possibly shown in the past."

The Feb. 22 quake, which killed more than 160 people, destroyed much of the country's second-largest city, just six months after another big quake in Christchurch.

Even as the economy suffers from the aftermath of the disasters, inflation is getting uncomfortably high. Consumer prices rose 4.5% from a year earlier in the first quarter, above the RBNZ's 1%-3% target band.

But this was largely due to an October increase in the goods-and-services tax and recent tobacco and cigarette tax hikes. Bollard said New Zealand's "annual inflation is expected to settle comfortably within the target band once these tax increases drop out of the annual rate."

ASB economist Jane Turner said the central bank "remains very comfortable on the inflation outlook," as "underlying inflation pressures are currently very subdued, allowing the RBNZ plenty of breathing room over the next year."

The central bank chief said growth among New Zealand's trading partners remains robust, elevating prices for the country's commodity exports, but that higher oil prices and the elevated level of the New Zealand dollar are unwelcome and "they will have some dampening effect on economic activity."

The New Zealand dollar fell to US$0.8007 from US$0.8078 in the 20 minutes after Bollard's statement before rebounding on a broad slide in the U.S. currency. At 0132 GMT the Kiwi dollar was at US$0.8053.

Although Bollard is displeased with the New Zealand dollar's rise to three-year highs against the greenback, "the conditions for intervention are definitely not there," said ANZ Bank senior economist Khoon Goh. The Kiwi isn't reaching near-term highs on a trade-weighted index, he said.

"Part of the driver for the higher Kiwi is a rampant Aussie and generalized U.S. dollar weakness, and there is not really a lot that the Reserve Bank can do about that," Goh said. "It is a very risky strategy to undertake unilateral intervention in the current environment anyway."

New Zealand's economic growth in the first quarter is expected to be very weak, given the extensive damage to infrastructure, buildings and residences in the Christchurch area on the country's South Island. Government officials have said about a quarter of the buildings in the city center will likely have to be demolished and thousands of homes may need to be rebuilt. In March, the Treasury estimated the quake will cut about 1.5 percentage points off this year's growth rate.

Bollard reiterated that business confidence, consumer spending and tourism all declined sharply following the earthquake but he was cautiously optimistic about activity outside the Christchurch area.

While many businesses and households in Christchurch remain affected, in the rest of the country confidence and consumer spending have shown some signs of recovery, he said, adding that housing market turnover and business investment are beginning to increase.

By Rebecca Howard, Dow Jones Newswires; 64-4-471-5990; rebecca.howard@dowjones.com

(END) Dow Jones Newswires
