title: CORRECT: NZ Agricultural Export Prices Likely To Remain Strong
text:
("UPDATE: NZ Agricultural Export Prices Likely To Remain Strong," at 0112 GMT, misquoted a Barclays Capital note in the 6th paragraph. The correct version follows:)


 
   By Rebecca Howard and Lucy Craymer 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand's agricultural export prices are likely to remain strong for some time, delivering benefits to the New Zealand economy, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said in a statement released Tuesday.

According to the statement, Reserve Bank of New Zealand Gov. Alan Bollard told a farming group, The Grasshoppers, late Monday that the bank expects the higher terms of trade to continue to be reflected in the exchange rate, as it is currently.

"The exchange rate would deliver the benefits of the rising terms of trade to the community at large--through higher wealth and cheaper imports," Bollard said.

Currency strategists see these comments as quashing the possibility that the central bank would look at intervening in the New Zealand dollar as it trades around a five-month high.

Barclays Capital said in an analyst note that intervention could be contemplated by New Zealand's central bank as the weak economic situation currently being confronted is quite different to situations of the past.

"In our opinion, the current environment is such that FX market intervention can be contemplated in a manner that is credible, consistent with the RBNZ's monetary policy objectives and not injurious to the central bank's balance sheet," it said.

But Bank of New Zealandcurrency strategist Mike Jones said his bank's view is that RBNZ intervention to lower the New Zealand dollar was "very unlikely" and this was supported by Bollard's comments that the exchange rate would deliver the benefits of the rising terms of trade to the community at large.

"It's also hard to argue the New Zealand dollar is unjustified relative to fundamentals," Jones said. "NZ's current account is still in deficit, but not by nearly the same extent as when the RBNZ last intervened."

Bollard added in his speech that monetary policy will remain focused on any medium-term inflationary pressures that arise, rather than the shift in the terms of trade itself.

However, "if households and firms use the income boost from higher commodity prices and exchange rates to bring forward consumption and investment, or increase borrowing, then pressure on resources in New Zealand would lead to more inflationary pressure," he said.

"Monetary policy would need to counteract any rise in inflation expectations," Bollard added.

Bollard's comments have been interpreted as slightly hawkish, with the swaps markets adding 11 basis points to where it expects to see the official cash rate in 12 months' time, said TD Securities Senior Strategist Roland Randall.

"The market made a more hawkish interpretation of Dr. Bollard's comments than we think is warranted," Randall said.

The New Zealand economy has remained sluggish and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand cut the official cash rate by 50 basis points on March 10 in an effort to boost confidence and increase spending following the devastating Feb. 22 earthquake.

The central bank Tuesday simultaneously released analysis, in a report entitled "The Outlook For Commodity Prices And Implications For New Zealand Monetary Policy." The report looks at what the boom in the terms of trade should mean to New Zealand's economy and in turn the central bank's rate policy.

"Monetary policy should remain focused on the medium-term objective of price stability," the report said. It added that while focusing on medium-term inflation, policy makers will need to be cautious that the boom doesn't lead to increases in inflation expectations.

"Should households and firms decide the income boost from higher commodity prices and exchange rates enables them to bring forward consumption and investment or increase borrowing, it is possible an internal demand shock will arise," the report said.

"Consequent pressure on resources within New Zealand would lead to more inflationary pressure and monetary policy would counteract any rise in inflation expectations," it said.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is required to maintain inflation within a band of 1.0% to 3.0%, although it looks through one-off price rises such as those related to the government's decision to increase the goods and services tax to 15% from 12.5% on Oct. 1 last year.

-By Rebecca Howard and Lucy Craymer, Dow Jones Newswires; 64-4-471-5990; lucy.craymer@dowjones.com [ 12-04-11 0248GMT ]

At 0330 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was trading at US$0.7664, compared with US$0.7539 late Friday. It touched a high of US$0.7672.

"There is a truckload of event risk" that is likely to buffet the currency, with a string of policy meetings by other central banks through the week, Mike Symonds, manager of foreign exchange sales at BNZ, said.

A lot of attention will focus on the Reserve Bank of Australia Tuesday, which is expected to keep interest rates on hold.

But Symonds said the central bank has recently been in the habit of surprising financial markets.

Market pricing for a hike in Australia is around 20%, but Symonds says this is too low with the actual risk closer to 50%.

The RBA could easily choose to hike, moving preemptively to head off inflationary pressures next year. Even if the central bank holds its cash rate target at 4.5%, there is very little risk it will back away from its intention to eventually increase rates.

HIFX senior trader Stuart Ive said that strong manufacturing data from China gave further support to the New Zealand dollar through the day.

Even a small pullback following rumors of intervention by the Japanese authorities to sell yen against the U.S. dollar only resulted in new attractive levels to buy the Kiwi. A Japanese government official said Monday that the yen's moves have been "excessive" recently, but declined to comment on whether Tokyo intervened in the currency market.

"The New Zealand dollar is very resilient right now," Ive said.

But clear direction won't be restored until the "design and extent" of U.S. quantitative easing measures are announced, he said.

New Zealand government bonds were lower in price over the day in extremely thin trade, tracking moves in the swap rates curve.

title: UPDATE: Asian Shares Mostly Higher; Techs Lead In Tokyo, Seoul
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates/adds market levels)

By Shri Navaratnam and Ga-Woon Philip Vahn

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian stock markets were mostly higher Friday with technology plays leading gains in Tokyo and Seoul, while weakness in China's banking stocks dragged the Shanghai market lower.

Investors were encouraged by a third-straight session of gains on Wall Street on Thursday, as well an unexpected increase in U.S. pending-home sales. However, buying was tempered by caution ahead of the U.S. non-farm payrolls report for August due later Friday.

"U.S. economic data have been surprising, more than less, on the upside this week," said Philip Wee at DBS Group Research in Singapore. That could be because of "U.S. double-dip worries injecting more-than-usual bearishness into the consensus forecasts."

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average was up 0.4% while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.2%, South Korea's Kospi Composite gained 0.1% and India's Sensex was 0.2% higher.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was flat, Taiwan's main index gained 1.1% and the Shanghai Composite index was down 0.2%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were two points lower in screen trade.

The Tokyo market was cheered by Wall Street's rise, with tech stocks outperforming after the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.1% Thursday.

However, the market's "gains may be limited since the yen's strength, which is our biggest concern, shows no signs of receding," said Kazuhiro Takahashi, general manager at Daiwa Securities Capital Markets. "We'd like to see how the dollar moves against the yen after U.S. jobs data later today," he said.

Elpida Memory rose 3.2%, Toshiba advanced 1.3% and Sony tacked on 1.7%. Automakers were also rising, with Toyota Motor up 1.4% and Nissan Motor 0.6% higher.

In Seoul, shares were supported by the positive sentiment in markets.

"The U.S. market has turned around from the short-term lows after the ISM (manufacturing) data Wednesday, so the domestic market's moving quickly in line as well," said Hyundai Securities analyst Bae Sung-young.

Tech stocks were broadly higher, aided by an easing of concerns about global growth prospects. LG Electronics rose 3.2%, Hynix Semiconductor added 2.8% and LG Display advanced 3.1%.

Shinhan Financial fell 2.0% on worries about the company's internal governance as the board took steps to remove President and Chief Executive Shin Sang-hoon from his posts.

Shinhan Bank, a unit of Shinhan Financial, said on Thursday it filed a complaint with prosecutors against Shin Sang-hoon and six others and accused them of breach of trust as well as embezzlement.

Banks were struggling in Shanghai after the China Securities Journal said, citing its own statistics, that four of China's five biggest banks reported increases in special-mention loans in the second quarter from the preceding quarter, offering fresh evidence of potentially high credit risk in the local banking system. Bank of China fell 0.6% and China Merchants Bank lost 0.8%.

Special-mention loans refer to loans that have a potential weakness or pose an unwarranted financial risk that, if not corrected, could weaken the asset and lead to higher risks.

China Vanke rose 0.9% after the company said its property sales in August more than doubled from a year earlier to CNY11.99 billion, a record monthly performance for a Chinese property developer.

The Sydney market was led higher by gains in materials, industrials and consumer staples.

Rio Tinto was up 0.4% and BHP Billiton rose 0.3%. Bank stocks were mostly lower, capping the market's gains. ANZ bank was off 0.7%, Westpac was off 1.0% and National Australia Bank fell 1.1%.

Nufarm fell 3.1% after Standard & Poor's placed the company's BB long-term corporate debt rating on negative credit watch, on concerns about liquidity and its ability to improve profitability in fiscal 2011.

In Hong Kong, Sino Land rose 2.3% after the blue-chip property developer said Thursday its net profit for the 12 months ended June 30 rose 63% to HK$6.09 billion, helped by revaluation gains in its investment properties.

Cement shares were leading gains in Thailand on hopes that construction activity will pick up after a Thai court Thursday allowed the resumption of almost all the projects at a controversial industrial estate, almost a year after they were suspended. Siam Cement rose 5.0%, Banpu gained 1.6% and PTT Chemical added 3.4%.

Elsewhere, Malaysian shares were down 0.5%, Singapore's Straits Times Index fell 0.1%, New Zealand's NZX-50 was up 0.6% and Indonesia's share market was 0.9% higher. Vietnam markets were shut for a public holiday.

In foreign exchange markets, the U.S. dollar traded in tight ranges against the euro and the yen as traders waited for the U.S. non-farm payrolls data.

The euro was at $1.2815, from $1.2821 late Thursday in New York, and at Y107.99 against the yen, from Y107.96. The dollar was fetching Y84.26, compared with Y84.21.

"With investors still on edge about the chance of a double-dip U.S. recession, we suspect any disappointment (on the U.S. jobs data) would scupper the recent bond market sell-off, providing headwinds for the U.S. dollar," said Mike Jones, currency strategist at the Bank of New Zealand.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened in the foreign exchange market Friday after the Singapore dollar hit an all-time high against the greenback, a person familiar with the central bank's thinking said.

The person told Dow Jones Newswires that the MAS "went in to smooth the U.S. dollar's fall around S$1.3435."

The Singapore dollar hit a record high late Thursday, with the U.S. dollar sliding to S$1.3425. The previous record was S$1.3438 to the greenback in July 2008. The U.S. dollar last traded at S$1.3471.

Lead September Japanese government bond futures were down 0.01 at 142.20 points, weighed by the Nikkei's gains and Thursday's weakness in U.S. Treasurys. The 10-year cash JGB yield was 0.5 basis point lower at 1.105%.

Spot gold was at $1,249.50 per troy ounce, down $1.80 from late New York Thursday. October Nymex crude oil futures were down 26 cents at $74.76 per barrel on Globex.

title: SNAP ANALYSIS-Yen hits 14-year high but no  intervention  expected
text:
TOKYO, Nov 26 (Reuters) - The yen climbed to a 14-year peak against the dollar on Thursday but the market does not believe Japanese authorities will intervene anytime soon because the move reflects broad dollar weakness, not yen strength.

JAPANESE INTERVENTION UNLIKELY

Although the yen has risen on the crosses on Thursday, the market sees the appreciation as a result of the falling dollar and the prospect that U.S. interest rates will stay low for a while.

Traders and analysts think Japan would need cooperation from the United States and Europe if it wanted to step in to buy dollars. This seems unlikely, particularly as the Federal Reserve described the dollar's recent drop as "orderly". [ID:nN24313828]

Market participants say the United States has little incentive to intervene when Treasuries continue to draw global funds and it is pressing for global trade to be rebalanced -- something analysts say means the dollar has to weaken.

Japan's Deputy Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda also believes the moves reflect dollar weakness and told Reuters the Ministry of Finance is not considering intervention. [ID:nT371315]

Officials say they must act appropriately against "abnormal" moves but one-month dollar/yen implied volatility, a measure of expected fluctuations, has jumped. It is still below 16 percent, where it has been since April, which suggests market moves are not disorderly.

INTERVENTION AT SOME STAGE?

The government said this month that Japan has returned to deflation. With the Nikkei share average <.N225> underperforming other markets, some analysts say the odds are rising that Japan could alter its "benign neglect" of yen strength and launch policies to deal with the economy.

In trade-weighted terms, the yen has risen much more modestly, as this graphic shows: http://r.reuters.com/zus63g("http://r.reuters.com/zus63g")

Its real effective exchange rate -- a trade-weighted, inflation-adjusted measure of its broad value calculated once a month by the Bank of Japan -- was 117.8 in October, roughly 9 percent below an eight-year high of 128.9 hit in January. <JPYEEXR=J>

But the yen has started to gain on the Australian and New Zealand dollars, making traders more circumspect about the possibility of intervention further down the line.

WHAT WOULD TRIGGER INTERVENTION?

Speed. If the dollar's fall accelerates against the yen and implied volatility rises above 20 percent -- which would signal a disorderly move -- market players would begin to see a serious chance of coordinated intervention.

Analysts say the market would grow warier of intervention risk if the dollar falls to 85.00 yen, 80.00 yen or its record low of 79.75 yen. But speculators tend to use round figures as targets at which to take profits, which tends to slow the rise. title: RPT-INTERVIEW-UPDATE 2-NZ dlr should reflect fundamentals-finmin
text:
* NZ's English says wishes NZD reflects economy, not flows

* Sees China playing greater FDI role in country

(Recasts with Reuters interview, adds details)

By Eric Burroughs

HONG KONG, Oct 5 (Reuters) - New Zealand Finance Minister Bill English said on Monday that he wished the country's strong currency reflected its economic fundamentals rather than currency market flows.

English also said that the government was trying to help the economy by getting its finances into shape.

"I wish it would reflect economic fundamentals rather than trade currents in the forex market," English told Reuters in an interview on Monday when asked about the currency.

The New Zealand dollar <NZD=D4> has soared 23 percent to a 14-month high against the U.S. dollar this year despite the country suffering its deepest recession on record, getting a boost from investor demand for higher-yielding, commodity-linked currencies as the world economy recovers.

The government and policymakers have repeatedly said the strong kiwi is not helpful for the country's exports but partly reflects the U.S. currency's broad slide.

English said that New Zealand's exporters have had to get by with a stronger currency for much of the past four years but that the government can best help by getting its finances into shape. The country's central bank is in charge of currency intervention.

New Zealand emerged from its longest recession on record in the second quarter but growth was a meagre 0.1 percent.

"We are realistic about how testing this recovery could be," English said.

English also said New Zealand's interest rates were likely to remain low when compared with neighbouring Australia.

"Our interest rates are likely to be lower for longer than for instance Australia," English told CNBC television earlier in the day.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has slashed rates to a record low 2.50 percent and pledged to keep them there or lower until the latter part of 2010 to help the economy.

The RBNZ is expected to leave rates unchanged at its next review on Oct. 29, according to a Reuters poll, with investors eyeing a first rate hike early in 2010. [NZ/POLL]

The Australian central bank holds its October policy meeting on Tuesday and most analysts expect it to keep rates at 3.0 percent [AU/INT], though two influential economic columnists say the central bank is likely to raise rates to 3.25 percent. [ID:nSYD44556]

English is meeting investors in Hong Kong and London to promote New Zealand, which relies heavily on foreign borrowing to fund its current account deficit -- totalling nearly 100 percent of the country's economy -- due to low levels of household savings.

The current account gap is a vulnerability, and the country's need to attract foreign capital may mean that China plays a greater role in providing foreign direct investment, English said.

"They are a likely to become more significant investors in New Zealand," he said.

English also said that Asian central banks diversifying their reserves and making a small increase in Australasian bonds was making a "big difference" for New Zealand as it tries to lure foreign investors to finance its deficit. (Additional reporting by Mantik Kusjanto in Wellington) (Editing by Kim Coghill)

title: MARKET SIGNALS-Asia at forefront of exit strategies, RBNZ lags
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 7 (Reuters) - The G20 went out of its way to make clear stimulus would not be removed too quickly and it's a little early to start talking exit strategies. Not that surprising and fine for the G8 world, where economic conditions are only just starting to turn the corner.

In the other G12, comprising Asia's biggest economies besides Japan, central banks are at the forefront of exit strategies as Australian Treasurer Wayne Swan flagged in remarks last week, despite other cautious remarks sticking to the G20 line in London.

The Bank of Korea, which meets this week, is up there with counterparts in Australia, China and India among Asian central banks that are the closest to pulling the trigger or taking other monetary measures.

Then there is the frustrated Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ). It also meets this week and has kept threatening further rate cuts to offset tightening in financial conditions via higher rates and a stronger currency.

RBNZ BETWEEN ROCK AND HARD PLACE

For a graphic on RBNZ rates and the New Zealand dollar's trade-weighted index: http://r.reuters.com/tuk25d

For the RBNZ, despite the threats, it's hard to see what a rate cut would achieve. New Zealand financial conditions are only partially determined by policy rates.

New Zealand's plight is not much different from that of other small and open economies in Asia: a central bank only has so much influence. In theory, they could print New Zealand dollars <NZD=D4> to try to stymie the currency strength.

But market players have argued the trade-weighted NZD <=NZD> is not at levels to justify intervention, noting that its 2007 kiwi-selling intervention had little sustained impact.

The New Zealand dollar has been one of the main currencies held hostage to equity markets via the risky asset correlation trade. That risk-correlation trade is showing signs of weakening, but only just, suggesting that the RBNZ probably has to sit tight and keep talking tough.

BOK CLOSER TO TIGHTENING

For a graphic comparing different short-term swap curves in Asia: http://r.reuters.com/bam25d

For the BOK, the short-end of the swap curve has been telling. The one-year/three-year swap curve has seen a notable flattening and the timing of a first hike has become clearer. By contrast, the New Zealand curve is holding near its steepest levels on record because a RBNZ shift on policy is expected to start a year out or further.

For the Bank of Korea (BOK), asset prices are a worry.

The KOSPI <.KS11> has been at the forefront of Asia's equity surge this year on the rapid recovery in manufacturing and tech, making it among the first indexes to reach the 61.8 percent retracement of its entire 2007-08 sell-off.

By contrast, the U.S. S&P 500 <.SPX> has only just reached a 38.2 percent retracement.

After S.Korea's Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) tightened mortgage lending rules on Friday, the BOK is likely to keep talking tough on asset prices.

But a rate hike -- rather than regulatory tinkering -- is only a matter of time. As with the Reserve Bank of Australia, the timing for a BOK move is seen most likely in the final months of the year.

U.S. ECONOMY HEALING, FAR FROM HEALTHY

For a graphic comparing the ISM indexes and continuing jobless claims: http://r.reuters.com/vum25d("http://r.reuters.com/vum25d")

Still, as many economists have repeatedly warned, the U.S. economy is just starting to heal. Job cuts are slowing, manufacturing has rebounded very quickly and the slide in corporate earnings has bottomed out.

But the U.S. economy has a long way to go on the road to recovery. Looking at the spread between the ISM non-manufacturing PMI and the manufacturing one, the underperformance of the services sector -- some 80-85 percent of the economy these days -- is striking.

That spread is near its most negative levels since the services PMI began in 1997. The total number of continuing jobless claims gives a glimpse of how many people are out of work.

The recession is almost certainly over. But U.S. growth in coming quarters should be spotty and noisy as the stimulus effects kick in.

Until the U.S. economic recovery solidifies and is less dependent on stimulus, Asia will tread carefully in tightening policy. (Editing by Neil Fullick)

title: NZ dollar holds near 9-month highs, bonds firmer
text:
* Kiwi stays near nine-month highs on rising equities

* Ignores another government warning on strong currency

* Swaps steady, bonds firmer

WELLINGTON, July 23 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> held near nine-month highs on Thursday as firmer stock markets supported appetite for higher-yielding currencies, while another government warning against a strong currency had little impact.

The kiwi settled around S0.6600/02 at 0515 GMT, compared with $0.6554/59 late on Wednesday. It hit a high of $0.6632 <NZD=D2> in overseas trading, the strongest since the first week of October last year, before retreating.

Asian equity markets were higher, including Hong Kong and Japan, which rose over 1 percent, pointing to solid risk appetite.

"Equities futures are up at the moment and the kiwi is pushing higher," said HSBC Treasury chief manager Daniel Brdanovic. "We need follow through from equities to give kiwi the momentum".

The New Zealand currency also benefited from a weak U.S. dollar, which hovered close to a seven-week low on Thursday.

Finance Minister Bill English said New Zealand needed a weaker currency to bolster exports and should consume less and save more if it is to shake off recession and correct economic imbalances. [ID:nWEL481934]

His comments echoed those he made last week in Sydney that the kiwi should be lower based on fundamentals, though he added then that policy makers were not considering market intervention to make that happen.

So far this year the New Zealand dollar has risen around 13 percent, and is nearly 35 percent above the six-year lows it fell to in March.

"These recent moves higher for the New Zealand dollar are far from favourable for an economy that requires rebalancing," said ANZ-National markets economist Philip Borkin.

With little on the domestic agenda this week, investors are already looking ahead to the central bank's interest rate review next week, with expectations for no change to the 2.5 percent cash rate [ID:nWEL57452].

Interest rate swaps were little changed, with two-year <NZDSM3NB2Y=> swaps bid at 3.91 percent, and five-year <NZDSM3NB5Y=> at 5.35 percent.

New Zealand government bonds were firmer, with yields on the benchmark NZ 10-year bond <NZ10YT=RR> 6 basis points lower at 5.75 percent, recouping previous' day losses. (Reporting by Mantik Kusjanto; Editing by James Thornhill)

title: UPDATE 3-New Zealand c.bank chief says long-term rates too high
text:
* NZ central bank says jump in wholesale rates unjustified

* C.bank says expects to keep its rates low for some time

* NZ dollar and market interest rates fall sharply (Adds comment, market reaction, background)

By Mantik Kusjanto

WELLINGTON, April 1 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank chief intervened on Wednesday to halt a rise in long-term interest rates, saying benchmark rates would stay low for much longer.

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Alan Bollard said the rise in wholesale rates was at odds with the bank's expectations for a slow recovery of the recession-hit economy, with risks to the downside, and with its policy of cutting benchmark rates.

"In these circumstances we believe the rise in longer-term interest rates is unwarranted and inconsistent with the monetary policy outlook," he said in a statement that sent the New zealand dollar lower and debt yields tumbling.

Last month, Bollard said rates would likely be cut further, but cautioned that they would not go as low as some were expecting because they needed to remain attractive to investors so the country could fund its big current account deficit.

That prompted investors to expect an end to the easing cycle and sparked a rush to seize low rates, sending swap and mortgage rates sharply higher and forcing the RBNZ to talk things down.

"It was an appropriate response given the irrationality we have seen in the market," said ANZ-National Bank chief economist Cameron Bagrie.

The verbal intervention sent the New Zealand dollar down more than 2 percent to a low of $0.5558, from around $0.5700. Bank bill futures rose sharply and the yields on government bonds settled around 8 basis points lower along the curve.

Five-year interest rate swaps, which had leaped more than 50 basis points in the past week, sank to 4.755/4.835 percent from 5.07/15 percent.

WILD SWINGS

The swaps market has seen wild swings over the past two weeks as banks rushed to hedge a wave of households renewing their expiring home loans at cheaper fixed rates.

At one point, five-year swap rates notched up their biggest weekly rise since 1994, while two-year swaps had their largest weekly increase since 1998.

The jump in yields in turn added to upward pressure on the kiwi dollar, making exports less competitive at a time when global trade is already reeling.

Bollard said if the distortion in rates and the currency continued it would put needless pressure on companies' and households' borrowing costs.

"As indicated in our March statement, we are projecting interest rates to remain at relatively low levels for an extended period," he said.

The RBNZ has cut interest rates to a record-low 3 percent from a high of 8.25 percent since last July, and signalled in its March 12 monetary statement that it expected rates to go to around 2.5 percent, and possibly as low as 2 percent if global conditions justified it.

A Reuters poll has analysts expecting the RBNZ cutting its cash rate by at least 25 basis points at its April 30 review, with a similar-sized cut in June.

OPTIONS

Some analysts have suggested the RBNZ could take more exotic action such as follow the lead of the U.S. Treasury and buy back long-dated government debt to pump money into the system.

Bank of New Zealandcurrency strategist Danica Hampton said quantitative easing was one option for the bank but also cautioned that the impact may be limited by the lack of scope and depth of New Zealand's capital market.

"If New Zealand were to launch a U.S.-style quantitative easing programme, what assets would the RBNZ or NZ Treasury buy?" she said, adding that the central bank could enter the swap market directly to stabilise rates.

David Troy, an interest rate strategist at ANZ, said the volatility was likely to be temporary and would pass, making it important for the RBNZ to hold to its strategy.

"There is a limit to how low the OCR (official cash rate) can go. However, there is no limit to how long it can stay low."

"With the economy yet to trough, market pricing of higher rates and a turn in the cycle is misplaced." (Editing by Jan Dahinten)

title: =DJ FOCUS: Rampant Rise In NZ Dlr, Rates May Spur RBNZ To Action
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--A sharp bounce in the New Zealand dollar and a spike in market interest rates have dramatically tightened monetary conditions in what may force a Reserve Bank of New Zealand response as radical as intervention in the interest rate swaps market.

The sudden reversal in market conditions could tighten the noose on businesses and consumers already suffering from the country's worst recession in decades and has likely caught the central bank off guard. As recently as its March 12 quarterly review of economic and monetary conditions, the RBNZ signaled that the Official Cash Rate, at 3%, could trough at 2.5% midyear and then rise quite steeply in 2010.

That view was based on expectations that a plunge in the New Zealand dollar over the past year coupled with a series of deep rate cuts since July would eventually spur a recovery.

But last week's move by the U.S. Federal Reserve to escalate its quantitative easing program has altered the landscape. The New Zealand dollar has surged 17% since March 10, a sizable part of this rally spurred by the Fed's drastic move to print money to help ease liquidity. At the same time, 10-year New Zealand dollar swap rates reversed a yearlong precipitous plunge, rising to 5.80% from 4.80%, driven by corporate demand for credit and international influences, prompting banks to raise mortgage lending rates.

'The RBNZ is on notice here,' said ANZ National Bank chief economist Cameron Bagrie. 'They are going to have to flag here that rates are going to have to remain low here for an extended period.'

New Zealand has been in recession for more than a year, and recent data show the downturn has deepened as the global economic slump has combined with a domestic-led housing slowdown to crunch consumption. Businesses continue to battle falling profits and job losses are expected to mount this year.

Warren Potter, fixed-interest portfolio manager with AMP Capital Investors, said the Kiwi dollar's rebound to around 57 U.S. cents and possible further gains, in conjunction with rising mortgage rates despite the RBNZ's 50 basis-point rate cut March 12, threatens to prolong the recession.


       Jawbone Rates Lower 
  Potter said the RBNZ first ought to 'jawbone' rates lower, starting before the central bank's next rate review April 30. 'That would have the effect of lowering front-end rates, and maybe reduce pressure for banks to continue to lift their mortgage rates,' he said. 
  If that fails, then the bank, which has already slashed the cash rate 525 basis points since July, ought to consider cutting its cash rate April 30 by more than the 25 basis points the market now anticipates. 
  'That would result in a dramatic move down in front-end rates,' said Potter. 
  Bagrie said the game has changed since the move by the Fed, which apart from escalating its quantitative easing also flagged its lending rates would remain near zero for an extended period. 
  'At the moment the local market is expecting rates to rise in 2010,' Bagrie said. 
  'That is just la-la stuff given the underlying state of this economy and given the nuances out of the Fed that they are going to keep rates low for an extended period,' he said. 'It defies logic in my mind why U.S. rates are going to remain low and we expect New Zealand rates to move up in 2010. It just ain't going to happen.' 
  The simple solution to relieve upward pressure on the currency and rates is for the RBNZ to clearly state that domestic rates will remain low for an extended duration, Bagrie said. Whether it needs to do that before its next formal review of the OCR is a moot point. 
  RBNZ Gov. Alan Bollard made it clear at the March review that there is a limit to how low he wants the OCR to go because as it approaches zero, interest-rate cuts have less impact. As well, with New Zealand running a huge external deficit - equivalent to 8.9% of gross domestic product - the country needs high rates to attract foreign capital, he said. 
       Unorthodox Measures 


The RBNZ may have to contemplate unorthodox measures to keep wholesale rates down, Potter said.

Currency intervention to weaken the New Zealand dollar is not an option because the RBNZ has clearly stated moves to influence the Kiwi's direction are unlikely to stick unless it is near what the bank considers an extremity of its band.

The Kiwi fell from a record peak above 82 U.S. cents in March 2008 to below 48 U.S. cents this month, helping to keep New Zealand exports steady despite the global recession.

Instead, the bank might take a leaf out of the Fed's new operations book and buy securities, Potter said. But rather than buy bonds it might become a receiver in the swaps market as swaps in New Zealand are the basis for mortgage rates.

The RBNZ has never intervened in the interest-rate swap market and such a move would likely cause a stir, as when it first intervened in the currency market in June 2007 - sending the Kiwi plunging about 3 U.S. cents.

New Zealand swap rates underwent a massive slump in the last year - the 10-year rate fell from 7.8% a year ago to 4.37% early last month - before their sharp reversal.

Mortgage rates, which didn't match the decline in IRS rates, are now headed higher, against the wishes of the RBNZ.

ASB Bank Thursday hiked its three-year mortgage lending rate to 6.5%, its second hike in as many weeks. ANZ National Bank this week lifted its three-year rate to 6.15% from 5.99% to match similar moves by Westpac and ASB last week.

While receiving swaps could add to the RBNZ's burgeoning balance-sheet risk, 'it would be pretty definitive and hard for the market to back up too much,' Potter said.

Bagrie said the idea of going down the quantitative-easing route would be 'a real stretch' because New Zealand lacks the benefit of scale, nor is it a global benchmark in the allocation of capital.

Bagrie said Friday's fourth-quarter GDP data may be so poor that they act as a wake-up to markets, spurring a reversal of the alarming upward trend in interest rates and the currency. If markets respond, that may ease pressure on the central bank to act quickly.

ANZ forecasts a a 1.2% fall in GDP on quarter, worse than the RBNZ's projection of a 0.8% contraction. The median forecast of 13 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires is for a 1.0% fall - the biggest GDP decline in almost 20 years.

'I think that might give the market digestive problems later in the week,' Bagrie said. -By Simon Louisson, Dow Jones Newswires; 64-4-471-5990; simon.louisson@dowjones.com

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand dollar rallied to a one-month peak Friday as a confluence of positive factors attracted buyers as global equities, led by Wall Street, surged on improved sentiment.

Bonds eased but losses were contained by a strong auction of NZ$150 million of government paper, while swap rates continued to push higher following on from Thursday's less dovish central bank policy stance.

The dramatic intervention overnight by the Swiss National Bank to stem the rise in the Swiss franc was the main focus in currency markets. The SNB decision also shifted attention to the Bank of Japan, which is facing similar problems with deflation and a strong currency.

Talk the Bank of Japan may intervene lifted the Kiwi/Yen, while the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's comment Thursday that it wanted to maintain a yield advantage also boosted this cross rate, traders said. The Kiwi rose to a two-month high against the yen of Y51.10, and a five-week peak against the Swiss franc of CHF0.6198.

"All this positive news of rallying markets and a less dovish statement from the RBNZ has helped the Kiwi. And we have a weakening U.S. dollar, which is supporting the currency," said Daniel Brdanovic, a dealer with HSBC in Auckland. The New Zealand dollar surged to a high of US$0.5225 in late morning trade - the highest level since Feb. 16.

Despite data earlier Friday showing New Zealand retail sales for January falling sharply, Brdanovic said the Kiwi has a raft of factors supporting it.

A sustained rally on Wall Street may allow the Kiwi to target Fibonacchi resistance at US$0.5235, he said. Overnight, U.S. stocks got a boost from strong performance in financial stocks, which fed into broad-based gains in Asia.

The New Zealand dollar got a strong boost from the RBNZ on Thursday, which indicated it was nearing the end of its easing cycle and that further cuts would be small.

The central bank cut the Official Cash Rate 50 basis points to an all-time low of 3.0% but said it's aggressive rate cuts will substantially slow.

RBNZ Governor Alan Bollard reiterated this message Friday in an interview with Radio New Zealand. He said that if rates are too low it will hurt the economy as depositors will be affected, which will in turn hurt some of the funding avenues.

"In addition we do rely on funding from overseas and that simply isn't going to come here if there isn't a reasonable rate for it. So we don't think that the model of interest rates going to near zero is actually appropriate for us."

In the debt market, bonds eased only slightly as the government's bond tender went solidly, with a strong bid-to-cover ratio. "we can't say precisely why the demand was so strong but it looks like a bit of offshore interest. It was quite a surprise because we didn't expect this tender to go that well based on recent ones," said one trader.

Swap rates continued to move higher on paying interest as the RBNZ's more conservative approach to easing policy rates kept receivers at bay.

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand dollar was weaker late Friday, hammered by persistent weakness in global stock markets.

Early in the session, the Kiwi touched a six-year low of US$0.5193 as investors bailed out of high yielding, risky currencies in favor of safe-haven assets.

It recovered slightly later in the day, helped by some profit-taking and a stronger Australian dollar after the Reserve Bank of Australia said it had been intervening to "provide liquidity" to the currency markets.

Traders said, however, that the bias for the Kiwi is definitely down.

The markets are being driven by "panic and fear" and "it's tough to see where any upside is going to come from," said OzForex dealer Jim Vrondas.

Early in the day, local traders said there were some rumors that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand was watching rates, and may be ready to intervene to defend the Kiwi, although there was no concrete evidence.

HIFX trading director Mike Hollows said it was possible that the central bank could intervene to "slow things down a bit" rather than defend the currency.

Hollows added, however, that the Reserve Bank would only act if it viewed the fall in the Kiwi as disorderly, something he said wasn't the case Friday.

While the focus was offshore, the New Zealand dollar was undermined also by news that dairy giant Fonterra had cut its forecast payout for the current season ending May 31 to NZ$6.00 per kilogram of milk solids from the NZ$6.60/kg it forecast just two months ago. Economists estimate the unscheduled cut will slice NZ$1 billion directly out of the economy.

Weak October credit card billings data, showing a 1.1% fall on month, was another reminder that consumer spending remains in the doldrums.

Traders said, however, that while the grim news added to the overall negative picture, the impact was relatively minor with the main driver being offshore markets.

"What happens in the local economy doesn't seem to matter too much at this stage," said Vrondas.

Government bonds yields and interest rate swaps also fell sharply, tracking offshore moves.

"Its been one-way traffic, following international moves and global sentiment," one local trader said.

Traders said the flow was light in New Zealand, with buyers thin on the ground. The news from Fonterra and the weak credit card billings had little impact given the global moves but added to the grim outlook and the pressure on yields.

title: 4th UPDATE: Asian Shares Slump On US Woes; Nikkei Falls 6.9%
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates/adds market levels)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian share markets fell Thursday - some of them to multiyear lows - after a late-day slump on Wall Street, with the health of the banking and auto sectors still cause for much concern.

"We haven't seen bargain hunting because nobody knows whether anything is a bargain anymore - value is disappearing overnight," said Najeeb Jarhom, senior vice president of research at AmFraser in Singapore.

Falls accelerated as the day wore on: Australia's S&P/ASX 200 ended down 4.2% at its lowest level since early 2004, with Japan's Nikkei shedding 6.9%, hurt in part by a surprise trade deficit in October; Korea's Kospi ended with a 6.7% decline with Taiwan's market down 4.5% at a more than six-year trough.

Margin lenders "are flat out with their margin calls," said Chris Blair, head of retail at Patersons Securities in Sydney; analysts elsewhere noted some redemption activity, though others said the continued slide in markets might prove attractive for braver, longer-term investors.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was recently down 6.2% with India's Sensex off 5.1%.

Light trading volume showed the level of caution among investors; "the market continues to trade on fear. Fundamentals are going to take a back seat for a while. It's like (watching) a terminal patient," said broker David Price of Forsyth Barr in New Zealand.

Japan's yen was notably higher with central banks intervening in several markets in Asia to keep a lid on the U.S. dollar; risk aversion was showing up in wider credit spreads while crude oil futures came in for some selling on demand-related concerns.

U.S. stock futures were down 1%-1.5% in screen trade and European spreadbetting firms were calling stocks there to fall; CMC Markets tipped London's FTSE-100 to drop 93 points.

Asia's declines came after the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed under 8000 for the first time in more than five-and-a-half years as investors worried about the future of U.S. auto makers and banks; it declined 5.1% while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 6.5%.

There were ongoing concerns about the U.S. economy with poor data Wednesday on the housing market and gloomy minutes from the recent meeting of the Federal Open Markets Committee.

Some were starting to talk about the risk of a global deflationary spiral: "Faced with this prospect, central banks (in Asia, ex Japan) are loosening monetary conditions and will continue to do so well into 2009," said analysts at Standard Chartered.

Technology stocks suffered with the Semiconductor Industry Association forecasting global chip sales for 2009 to decline 5.6%; Hynix Semi shed 15% in Seoul with Powerchip Semi down 6.9% in Taiwan and Elpida Memory off 3.7% in Tokyo.

"As dramatic declines in consumer and industrial confidence began developing in late summer, order cancellations began to grow and in many cases, slowing orders degenerated into a complete stop in orders as players across the supply chain moved to extremely cautious positions," said iSuppli senior vice president, market intelligence services, Dale Ford.

Shipping stocks were hit with Divay Goel, director and head of operations for Drewry Maritime Services, telling Dow Jones Newswires Wednesday he expected around 20% of orders for building new dry bulk shipping vessels may be canceled in 2009; Korea's Hyundai Heavy Industries sank 14.4%.

Japan's main index traded under 8000 for the first time since Oct. 29; banks were hit with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial tumbling 10% and Nomura Holdings 11% while insurer Tokio Marine Holdings shed 15% after reporting poor first half results and terminating its plan for a share buyback.

Miners and financials fell in Australia with BHP Billiton down 9.1% and Rio Tinto down 13%; ANZ Bank lost 5.9% with Commonwealth Bank 5.2%.

Hong Kong property stocks were hit with that subindex down 7% and Cheung Kong down 5.9%; HSBC fell 4.2% on worries about the outlook for business in Europe and the U.S.

The Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.6% after a 6.1% rally Wednesday; Singapore's Straits Times Index was down 4.1% with Malaysia's main index falling 2.0%, Indonesian shares 3.5% and Thai shares 4.0%.

New Zealand's NZX-50 closed with a 2.3% fall to its lowest level since June 2004, while Philippine shares ended down 3.5% decline.

In currency markets, the U.S. dollar fell to Y95.15 with the euro at Y118.80; the euro was around $1.2490 while the Australian dollar slipped back to US$0.6346.

Asian currencies were active: The U.S. dollar rose above S$1.53 against the Singapore dollar and against the Korean won it hit its highest level since March 1998, while it reached a 2008 high against the Malaysian ringgit; against the Thai baht, it touched its best level since March 2007.

The Philippine central bank was suspected of selling U.S. dollars to support the peso, with intervention also spotted in Indonesia, Korea and India; in Hong Kong, authorities again sold Hong Kong dollars to preserve the currency peg.

"Though valuations might look cheap for some currencies, this is typically not the time that investors take on more risk. Given how brutal this year has proved for many investors, we sense this adage may hold particularly true this year," said analysts at Morgan Stanley.

Japanese government bonds rose with futures adding 0.49 to 139.32; credit default swaps widened with the iTraxx Japan Series 10 index at 330 basis points from 290 basis points Wednesday.

Toyota CDS were at 170 basis points, from 135 basis points on Nov. 18 and 55 basis points on Oct. 2; "pretty wide, huh? Toyota used to trade almost the same level as sovereign" CDS, said a credit trader at a Western bank in Tokyo, adding "autos are just taking it on the chin - everyone's keeping an eye on what's happening with the Big Three in Detroit."

The cost of protection in Asia ex-Japan widened, too, with the five-year iTraxx investment grade index quoted at 425-470 basis points versus a 420 basis-point midspread close Wednesday.

U.S. Treasurys nudged up in Tokyo after strong U.S. gains with the 10-year note up 7/32 at 103 14/32, yielding 3.342%; players were betting on a further Fed rate cut in December.

Spot gold was at $735.20, up 30 cents from New York; front-month Nymex crude was down 93 cents at $52.69 a barrel on Globex - a 22-month low - after declining 77 cents in New York.

title: NZ dollar off lows on Aussie  intervention ; debt firm
text:
WELLINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> picked itself up from a two-week low on Thursday, buoyed by intervention by the Australian central bank, but remained under pressure amid growing risk aversion.

The kiwi had fallen more than 4 percent against the U.S. dollar to $0.5555, its lowest point since Oct. 29, in the offshore session, after U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson backed away from using a $700 billion bailout fund to clean up bank balance sheets.

But kiwi found a base in the onshore session as investors booked some profits after the yen's strong rise, and then benefited from a lift in the neighbouring Aussie dollar.

"The NZ dollar found a base in line with the Aussie following confirmation of the Reserve Bank of Australia's intervention," said RBC Capital Marketscurrency strategist Sue Trinh.

At 0400 GMT the kiwi was at $0.5611/21 compared with $0.5759/62 in late local trade on Wednesday. It ranged between $0.5545 and 0.5640 through the local session.

Australia's central bank earlier said it had intervened to support the Aussie currency in an illiquid market [nSYD366201].

However, sentiment towards the kiwi was not helped by local data that showed a pessimistic view of the current and future outlook for the New Zealand economy.

Data showed retail sales volumes 0.9 percent in the three months to Sept. 30, the third consecutive quarterly decline, backing views the recession has deepened. See [nWEL347218].

The latest real estate industry survey showed house sales were flat but prices rose slightly in October [nWEL000787], while manufacturing activity fell to a record low in the Business NZ latest perfomance of manufacturing index [nWEL996].

New Zealand's economic outlook also looked gloomier after the Treasury updated its pre-election forecasts showing larger government deficits, higher debt, and lower growth. See [nSYD354756].

"It was a very weak data flow -- consistent with our view the RBNZ will cut by at least 100 basis points in December, they are behind the curve in regards to the global slowdown," said RBC's Trinh.

New Zealand debt rallied for a third session with local bills <0#NBB:> now fully pricing in a 100 basis point rate cut at the RBNZ's Dec. 4 monetary statement.

The yield on the benchmark 90 day bank bill <NZ90DBB=RNZL>, which moves inversely to prices, was 23 basis points lower.

An auction of NZ$125 million of NZ government bonds was three times covered <NZDMO04>.

Bonds held their gains of previous days, with the benchmark 10-year bond <NZ10YT=RR> steady at 5.89 percent. (Reporting by Gyles Beckford)

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand dollar rose to a two-week peak Monday, carrying strong momentum into 2008, as its U.S. counterpart continued to suffer from the U.S. subprime crisis that has shaken financial markets this year.   

Traders say the Kiwi's immediate prospects appear favorable against a backdrop of weak U.S. economic data, amplified by a report Friday showing U.S. new home sales for November posting its biggest on-year drop in nearly 17 years.   

"The U.S. housing data continue to surprise on the downside. This credit crisis may have more to play out next year so it will be quite a difficult time for markets," said Daniel Brdanovic, a senior trader at  HSBC in Wellington.   

Brdanovic said the Kiwi's fortunes could go in either direction next year, adding that global uncertainty has clouded the outlook.   

The Kiwi, which rose to a two-week peak of US$0.7768 during morning trade, has advanced by around 10.3% against the U.S. dollar this year, after closing 2006 around US$0.7043. The gains have come despite the unprecedented intervention by the nation's central bank in the currency markets in the middle of this year, aimed at capping the high-flying Kiwi.   

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand intervened June 11 by selling the New Zealand dollar for the first time since the currency was floated in 1985.   

The June 11 intervention sent the New Zealand dollar down by nearly 2% from around US$0.7630. Since then, traders say the central bank had apparently intervened at least twice to kneecap the local currency with little success.   

The currency rose to a fresh 25-year peak of US$0.8110 in July before the U.S. subprime crisis knocked it back.   

Brdanovic said that despite a slowing domestic economy, rising inflation pressures will likely keep interest rates high in New Zealand and underpin the Kiwi's yield appeal.   

Economic prospects in the U.S., which appear poor at this stage, are also set to keep buyers interested in the Kiwi, he said.   

Against the yen, the Kiwi was at Y86.52 versus Y87.39 Friday.   

ANZ Bank senior dealer Alex Sinton said the New Zealand dollar's near term outlook favors more gains. "The overriding issues are weak data in the U.S. and a weak U.S. currency, and given that they favor a strong euro, the Kiwi will look to test 78 (US) cents," Sinton said.   

Thin trading conditions are likely to exaggerate some of the currency movements, he said, adding that most traders in global markets won't be back for another two weeks.   

Government bonds finished down in an extremely subdued session, with the market closing at midday for the holiday period.   

A local trader said some receiving in swaps and selling of bonds may have impacted trading. However, "I won't read too much into today's prices...it could be a bit of end-of-year wash-up going on," he said.   

Given a shortened trading week, the trader expects a quiet period for the rest of this week. "We can't really talk about the trends in the market until next week."   

New Zealand markets will be closed Tuesday and Wednesday for the New Year public holidays.

title: UPDATE 1-NZ cenbank sold net NZ$702 mln in June
text:
(Adds analyst comment)   

 WELLINGTON, Aug 6 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) sold NZ$702 million ($536 million) of New Zealand dollars on a net basis on the spot foreign exchange market during June, central bank data released on Monday showed.   

 The RBNZ was believed to have intervened at least three times on foreign exchange markets in June to sell the New Zealand dollar as part of its strategy to limit the rise in the kiwi.   

 The June currency dealings compared with a net NZ$58 million bought in May, and a monthly average of NZ$65.6 million bought for the previous 12 months.   

 It is not a direct and complete indication of the amount spent on intervention and includes liabilities of the New Zealand government's Debt Management Office. The full data is available on the Reserve Bank of NZ's Web site,   www.rbnz.govt.nz  ("http://www.rbnz.govt.nz")

 Analysts said the figure was similar to what the market had expected. They also suspected the central bank had continued to intervene in July.   

 "We expect the Reserve Bank to continue to actively go short the currency over the next few months," said Shamubeel Eaqub, director of investment research at  Goldman Sachs JBWere.

 "We think the central bank intervention tends to have only a short-term impact and we don't think this will be the catalyst for a sustained depreciation in the currency."   

 In June, the kiwi traded in a $0.7368 to $0.7687 range, according to Reuters data. It hit a post-float 22 year high of $0.8110 <NZD=D4> on July 24.   

 The currency was little moved by the data, trading around $0.7580. So far this year it has gained around 7.5 percent.   

 In July, the RBNZ said it would refine its foreign exchangeintervention strategy, with some of its actions becoming more passive as it left a portion of its reserves unhedged, allowing it to more effectively respond to any sharp falls in the New Zealand dollar.   

 The changes have been seen by analysts as bringing the RBNZ closer into line with broader market practice and similar to the way the Reserve Bank of Australia operates.   

 The RBNZ can spend as much as it wants in selling the kiwi dollar, but can only book losses of up to NZ$1 billion under an agreement with the government. Analysts have estimated that it might have as much as NZ$10 billion available for such interventions.   

 The central bank has said it will intervene when the value of the currency is at unjustifiable and exceptional levels given economic fundamentals, when it has a reasonable chance of success, and if it was consistent with its monetary policy aim of price stability.  ($1=NZ$1.31)

title: UPDATE 4-New Zealand ups rates, sees no further tightening
text:
(Updates New Zealand dollar in paragraph 6)   

WELLINGTON, July 26 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank raised interest rates on Thursday by a quarter point to 8.25 percent to quell inflation, but indicated it would stay put for a while on signs of an easing in domestic borrowing.   

The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> fell from 22-year highs after Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Alan Bollard said the central bank's four consecutive rate rises would be sufficient to contain price pressures.   

"The tone of the short statement was clearly more dovish than the market had been expecting. While maintaining a tightening bias, the RBNZ looks to be on hold," said Su-Lin Ong, senior economist at  RBC Capital Markets.

A Reuters poll of 15 economists after the decision showed all saw a cash rate of 8.25 percent as the peak and most expected it to remain there at least until June next year. [nWEL235517].   

"It is clear that the RBNZ would prefer not to lift rates any further largely due to its concern over the soaring New Zealand dollar," Ong said.   

The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> immediately lost ground after the decision and fell as low as $0.7962, down half a cent compared with before the central bank decision, before recovering slightly. [nWEL267425]   

The yield on 90-day bank bill <NZ90DBB=RNZL> rose 5 basis points to 8.54 percent.   

Worried about inflationary pressures from the tight labour market and rising oil and food prices, the central bank raised the official cash rate to a record 8.25 percent -- the highest since it was introduced at 4.5 percent in 1999.   

"New Zealanders have been showing early signs of moderating their borrowing," Bollard said. "Provided they keep up, and the pressures on resources continue to ease, we think the four successive increases we have delivered will be sufficient to contain inflation."   

CURRENCY CONCERNS   

Analysts said the central bank may have based its comments on anecdotal evidence or unpublished figures, because the data so far did not suggest an easing in domestic borrowing.   

Bollard told Reuters in an interview in June that he would not relax monetary policy until he saw clear evidence of a slowdown in consumer demand and house price inflation.   

The central bank raised interest rates by 25 basis points in March, April and June, but is starting the get worried about the strong New Zealand dollar, or kiwi.   

Bollard reiterated on Thursday the New Zealand dollar was hurting the export sector and that its current high level was not sustainable in the medium term.   

Investors have been pouring funds into the kiwi in carry trades, where they borrow in low-yielding currencies, such as the yen, to invest in high-yielding ones.   

The central bank has intervened at least three times since June 11 to moderate the pace of the New Zealand dollar's rise, the first intervention since the currency was floated 22 years ago.   

However, the currency has risen more than 6 percent since the bank unexpectedly raised rates to 8 percent on June 7.   

Yield-hungry investors could start favouring the neighbouring Australian dollar <AUD=> on expectations the Reserve Bank of Australia will raise rates to 6.5 percent as early as August, some analysts said.   

In contrast with Bollard, Reserve Bank of Australia chief Glenn Stevens said last week he was not surprised by the strength in the Australian dollar -- a signal markets took as meaning the Australian central bank was in no hurry to intervene to cap the Aussie's rise to 18-year highs.   

Others cautioned it was too early to conclude the RBNZ had finished tightening.   

"We are not yet convinced that the job is done," said  Westpac chief economic Brendan O'Donovan. "We are still a long way from the RBNZ taking further rate hikes completely off the table."

title: ANALYSIS-High Aussie dlr keeps inflation at bay ... for now
text:
SYDNEY, July 24 (Reuters) - A surge in the Australian dollar to an 18-year high is keeping a lid on import prices, lessening the chance of near-term rises in interest rates.   

 Strong domestic demand and a tight labour market could fuel inflation, but analysts cite the Aussie's strength as a text book case of how a floating exchange rate can help insulate an economy from upward price pressures.   

 "By crimping growth and working to reduce import prices, the Aussie's uptrend increasingly is limiting inflation pressures and weakening the case for any near-term RBA tightening," said Rory Robertson, interest rate strategist at  Macquarie Bank.

 The litmus test is on Wednesday with the release of the quarterly consumer inflation report -- a key number that guides the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) in its rate decisions.   

 A Reuters poll forecasts second-quarter headline consumer prices rising 1 percent, while the annual pace should slow to 1.9 percent from 2.4 percent in the March quarter. [ID:nSYA22609].   

 "The strong Aussie has had some impact on inflation,"  Westpac chief currency strategist Robert Rennie said. "The last couple of quarters of inflation have been very well behaved."   

 Known six years ago as the "Pacific Peso" and the "Little Aussie Bleeder," the Aussie has made a remarkable turnaround.   

 A combination of firm commodity prices, demand from booming China for Australia's minerals, a strong outlook for global growth, domestic economic reforms, Australia's interest rate differential, and a frail U.S. dollar have all helped the Aussie.   

 The Aussie rose to $0.8863 on Tuesday, its highest level since February 1989 and a gain of 12 percent so far this year. It was trading at below $0.4800 as recently as 2001.   

 NO WORRIES   

 The commodities boom, in particular, has justified the currency's gains in the eyes of the central bank. RBA Governor Glenn Stevens last week said he was not surprised by its strength, which the market took as a sign the bank was in no hurry to intervene.   

 That stands in stark contrast with Australia's Pacific neighbour New Zealand, where the central bank has intervened several times to stem an export-damaging rise in the kiwi <NZD=>.   

 The RBA's equanimity reflects the role a strong currency plays in keeping down import prices, important for a country where imports equal almost a quarter of the economy.   

 On Friday, domestic data showed only a slight 0.1 percent rise in import prices in the second-quarter even including a hefty 12.8 percent jump in fuel costs. Most other import prices fell, dragged down by the currency.   

 The Aussie also helped to hold back producer prices in the second quarter. Annual growth in prices slowed to a three-year low of 2.3 percent.   

 "While stronger domestic prices are a concern, lower yearly inflation gives the RBA more time to evaluate the impact of activity data on the broader inflation outlook," said Joshua Williamson, senior currency strategist at TD Securities.   

    TEMPORARY REPRIEVE   

 There are caveats.   

 Stevens has noted strong demand for services eventually puts more pressure on prices and wages and that the rise of the Aussie is a temporary reprieve.   

 "Nor can we assume that a rising exchange rate will exert a consistent dampening force on inflation of traded goods and services over the longer term, since exchange rates do not keep rising indefinitely," Stevens told a conference last month.   

 Inflation is likely to rise in 2008, he warned, leading the financial markets to price in an eventual rate rise.   

 Most analysts expect the RBA to keep rates at 6.25 percent in August for the ninth straight month. The 30-day interbank futures market <0#YIB:> has priced a 60 percent chance of a November rate rise, down from 80 percent two weeks ago. That risk moves up to 74 percent in December.   

 "(The) strong Australian economy suggests that a rate hike over the next six to 12 months can't be ruled out," said John Kyriakopoulis, currency strategist at nabCapital.

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--Few believe Finance Minister Michael Cullen will override the New Zealand central bank's focus on inflation in a bid to stem the surging Kiwi dollar, but analysts say his recent comments on the subject undermine the credibility of the country's monetary policy framework.   

Persistently high underlying inflation has raised market expectations of another interest rate increase by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand at next week's policy meeting.   

But Cullen has rattled sections of the domestic market who worry that his remarks on the Policy Targets Agreement, or PTA, damages the standing of the RBNZ and its single-minded pursuit of monetary stability.   

"If the bank doesn't hike next week, and even if the reasons for (staying on hold) are the central bank's views on the economy, then people may wonder if there's been political interference," said  Deutsche Bank chief economist Darren Gibbs.   

"So I think it's wholly unhelpful that these suggestions are being made or at least not being refuted by the finance minister," he added.   

While any action by the government to change the way interest rates are set by the RBNZ is likely to cause alarm bells in financial markets, it hasn't stopped Cullen from engaging lawmakers on the topic.   

Answering questions in Parliament over the last three days, the finance minister repeatedly referred to section 12 of the RBNZ Act, which gives the government the power to suspend the central bank's inflation focus by amending the PTA.   

Under the PTA, the RBNZ sets monetary policy to keep annual inflation inside a 1%-3% band over the medium term.   

Cullen, who is also deputy prime minister, has refused to rule out the possibility of the government instructing the RBNZ to pursue a different objective. On Thursday, after being grilled by the opposition, the minister again warned speculators in the New Zealand dollar that section 12 could be invoked under the RBNZ Act.   

However, he stopped short of saying he would consider intervening under the act.   

The New Zealand Herald newspaper quoted the minister as saying in its Thursday edition: "Section 12 is clearly there for a good reason. I would certainly not rule out its use."   


 
   Stubborn Inflation Pressures Force Rates, NZ Dollar Up 
    

The country's high interest rates have lured offshore investors seeking high returns, with yen funded carry trades boosting the New Zealand dollar to record heights. Carry trades refer to borrowing in low interest rate currencies such as the yen to buy higher-yielding currencies like the Kiwi dollar, and British pound.   

Stubborn domestic inflation pressures have forced RBNZ Governor Alan Bollard to raise interest rates in three quick moves this year, taking the Official Cash Rate to a record 8.00% - the highest policy rate in the developed world after Iceland.   

And nine of 15 economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires expect Bollard to tighten again at next week's rate-setting meeting, potentially giving another leg up to the New Zealand dollar, which tapped a fresh 25-year peak of US$0.7948 in overnight trade.   

The New Zealand dollar's strength has hobbled the country's export economy, prompting a storm of criticism against the government with opposition parties charging that the ruling Labour Party's high- spending ways of the past few years have complicated the central bank's fight against inflation.   

Some export businesses have also called for some form of action to kneecap the New Zealand dollar.   

If section 12 is invoked, the government can direct the RBNZ to use monetary policy for a different economic objective for a 12-month period, and make this change public by negotiating a new interim PTA with the governor.   

ANZ Bank chief economist Cameron Bagrie said that Cullen's comments on the PTA show "that there is considerable heat emerging over where the New Zealand dollar resides."   

Bagrie doesn't expect Cullen to alter the PTA but said the minister's view underscores the fact that the government has ultimate authority over the functions of the RBNZ.   

"While the Reserve Bank has independence, it is merely operational independence, and its continuation resides with the discretion of the government," he added.   

New Zealand's inflation eased to 2% on year in the second quarter, inside the RBNZ's target band, but domestic inflation - which excludes import prices - remains at an uncomfortable 4.1%.   

Ruling Labour Trail Opposition In Polls   

The anti-New Zealand dollar rhetoric by Cullen may partly reflect the Labour Party-led coalition's poor showing in polls,  Deutsche Bank's Gibbs said. With an election due late in 2008, the main opposition National Party has galloped ahead of Labour in recent polls.   

While politically it may make sense for the Labour Party to be seen as taking action against the high local currency, Gibbs thinks the finance minister's comments were mere "bluster."   

"It would be an extremely stupid move (changing the objective of PTA) and I don't see him doing it," he said. The powers of section 12 in the RBNZ Act were intended for use only during a major economic upheaval or crisis, Gibbs added.   

Currency traders say the New Zealand dollar is likely to head north of US$0.8000 over the short-term due to a broadly weaker U.S. dollar, and rising domestic interest rates.   

They note that the unprecedented intervention in the foreign exchange market by the RBNZ on June 11 - the first such action since the currency was floated in 1985 - had failed to knock back the New Zealand dollar.   

"We continue to view the persistent verbal intervention from the NZ government and actual intervention from the RBNZ as opportunities to buy NZD/USD on dips," said Sue Trinh, currency strategist at  RBC Capital Markets.

The New Zealand dollar was trading at US$0.7917 at 0457 GMT, off an intraday peak of US$0.7938

title: NZ Fin Min Brings Focus Back To RBNZ's Mandate As NZD Surges
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen appears to be causing ripples in local financial markets after telling Parliament Tuesday that the government has the capacity to suspend the central bank's single focus on inflation.   

Persistently high domestic inflation has forced Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Alan Bollard to raise interest rates in three quick moves this year, taking the Official Cash Rate to a record 8.00% - the highest policy rate in the developed world after Iceland. The consequent rush by offshore investors to buy into New Zealand dollar-denominated assets has driven the country's currency to record highs.   

Cullen's comments on the government's Policy Targets Agreement, or PTA, with the RBNZ came after the minister labeled the local currency "significantly overvalued."   

The New Zealand dollar reached a fresh 25-year peak of US$0.7941 Tuesday, prompting renewing debate in political circles on the negative implications for the local economy, and the RBNZ's inflation targeting regime.   

Even the central bank's unprecedented intervention in the foreign-exchange market June 11 - the first since the currency was floated in March 1985 - has failed to stop the New Zealand dollar's surge.   

According to dealers, the bank apparently intervened on at least two more occasions with little success.   

Bank of New Zealand currency strategist Danica Hampton said Wednesday's media coverage of Cullen's views may have caused a little doubt in the market about whether the RBNZ would hike interest rates again next week.   

"The press has been highlighting the Cullen comments on the PTA act...this could be causing a little bit of doubt to creep in on a hike," she said.   

The New Zealand dollar's modest pullback in early Wednesday trade may be partially linked to these comments, she said. The Kiwi, which fell to a low of US$0.7886 in morning trade from US$0.7916, has since recovered to US$0.7906 around 2345 GMT.   

In answer to a question in Parliament Tuesday, Cullen said the RBNZ act gives the government the power to override the central bank's objective of price stability.   

Cullen could instruct the RBNZ to change its objective, but that would require a new PTA to be signed. According to the Dominion Post newspaper, the minister later said he was merely pointing out that the capacity existed to alter the PTA's objectives, rather than signaling any intention to do so.   

Critics Say PTA Has Narrow Focus   

Under the existing PTA, the central bank chief is required to maintain annual inflation within a 1%-3% target band over the medium term.   

Critics charge that the bank's narrow focus on inflation has led to unnecessary interest rate increases, and sharp gains in the New Zealand dollar.   

Headline inflation in New Zealand eased to 2% on year in the second quarter, within the RBNZ's target band, but domestic inflation - which excludes import prices - remains at an uncomfortably high 4.1%.   

A slim majority of economists expect Bollard to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point to 8.25% at next week's policy meeting.   

Currency traders and economists say the New Zealand dollar could rise above US$0.8000 as long as inflation remains strong, putting pressure on the RBNZ to tighten policy.   

Westpac Bank chief economist Brendan O'Donovan said in a report that Bollard's "nightmare scenario" is that he will have to raise interest rates again next week, and watch the local currency soar above US$0.8000.   

He said Westpac is taking the RBNZ at its word when it said last month that foreign-exchange intervention "does not prejudge the future direction of monetary policy."

title: UPDATE: NZ Ctrl Bk Plans To Hold Some Unhedged  FX  Reserves
text:
(Adds detail, analyst comments) 
 
   By Symon Ross 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
    

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand said Friday it will hold some foreign reserves on an unhedged basis in future to better enable it defend any sharp falls in the New Zealand dollar.   

The central bank's latest stance is in contrast to its position over the past 20 years, where foreign currency assets have been fully matched by foreign currency liabilities. The central bank practice would also bring it in line with what its counterparts around the world do.   

A part of the Reserve Bank's foreign reserves portfolio will now be funded in New Zealand dollars rather than in foreign currencies.   

"In crisis situations it is of paramount importance that the Bank retains access to foreign currency reserves. With a portion of our reserves no longer borrowed from abroad, but funded internally, we will become less dependent on international capital markets in times of crisis," RBNZ Governor Alan Bollard said.   

Bollard said the move to a "more conventional approach" to foreign exchange management would give the bank a more effective means of responding to crisis situations involving sharp falls in the New Zealand dollar.   

The governor said the use of unhedged reserves would be less costly and cause less risk than using hedged reserves.   

"Unhedged foreign reserves provide a more effective form of insurance against a currency crisis," Bollard said.   

The RBNZ confirmed that it had intervened in the forex market on June 11 to sell New Zealand dollars for the first time since the currency was floated in 1985. It has been rumored to have intervened on a number of occasions since then to cap the Kiwi's gains, but the central bank didn't confirm this.   

Since June 11 the New Zealand dollar has hit a series of new post-float highs and touched US$0.7881 last week.   

The local unit had slipped to US$0.7834 by 0400 GMT from US$0.7864 prior to the release of the RBNZ's statement. Dealers attributed the weakness to the bank saying it still plans to intervene if the currency reaches excessive levels.   


 
   No Change To Intervention Criteria 
    

Greg Gibbs, currency strategist at ABN AMRO, said the announcement didn't mean a great deal as the RBNZ didn't change its criteria for intervention.   

"This is just about how they account for intervention. They are now doing it just like every other central bank, by running up reserve and FX forwards when they sell New Zealand dollars and running them down when they buy New Zealand dollars," Gibbs said.   

"This statement has no implications for rate decisions or the timing of intervention."   

Bank of New Zealand head of market economics Stephen Toplis said the announcement made sense, but shouldn't move the market much.   

"Clearly if you're going to intervene to try and move a currency around or build up reserves, it doesn't make an awful lot of sense to hedge them, because you're giving an opposite transaction that defeats the purpose," Toplis said.   

The statement did, however, substantiate the view that the bank prefers to build up reserves in foreign currency assets at a time when the currency is unusually high, rather than intervening to force it to a particular level, he said.   

The RBNZ said in its statement that overt intervention intended to affect the exchange rate directly may still occur but that it will also more gradually accumulate or reduce its foreign exchange position when the exchange rate is at extreme and unjustified levels.   

Bollard said he didn't expect the bank's more passive transactions to affect the exchange rate directly, but these would continue to be used to give "concrete signals" when the RBNZ thinks the exchange rate is overvalued or undervalued.   

"That may indirectly affect the exchange rate by discouraging speculators from pushing the currency to extreme levels," Bollard said.   

The central bank also expects greater variability in its net income from its more open foreign exchange position as a result of foreign exchange gains and losses.
