title: UPDATE 2-NZ retail sales jump in May, kiwi rises
text:
(Adds analyst's comment, updates market reaction)   

WELLINGTON, July 13 (Reuters) - New Zealand retail sales surged in May, data showed on Friday, reinforcing the central bank's hawkish anti-inflation policy and sending the currency to within a whisker of a 22-year post float high.   

Seasonally adjusted sales rose 1.2 percent in May, driven by higher car and supermarket sales, following a 1.2 percent fall in April. Economists in a Reuters poll had forecast sales to gain 0.4 percent on the previous month.   

"It keeps things boiling along, so there's still a tangible risk of another rate hike later this month," said  UBS senior economist Robin Clements.   

All eyes would be on second-quarter inflation data, due on Monday, which could be the catalyst for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to lift interest rates to 8.25 percent at its next review on July 26, analysts said.   

The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> surged on the sales data to gain more than a quarter of a cent to around NZ$0.7879, just shy of a 22-year post float high of $0.7881 reached earlier in the month. Bank bills were sold off, with the yield on the September contract <NBBU7> rising six basis points to 8.44 percent.   

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has raised its official cash rate by a total of 75 basis points this year to 8 percent on concerns over strong domestic spending, robust housing market and rising payouts to dairy farmers.   

RBNZ Governor Alan Bollard told Reuters in an interview in June that the central bank will not ease monetary policy until it sees a clear slowdown in consumer demand and house price inflation.   

Rising interest rates have been the main driver behind the rise in the New Zealand dollar. The central bank has been intervening to moderate the pace of the currency's rise.   

FOCUS ON INFLATION DATA   

Statistics New Zealand said May retail sales were driven higher by rises in motor vehicle and supermarket retailing, which gained 4.4 percent and 1.9 percent respectively.   

Core sales, which exclude car and fuel sales, rose 0.8 percent in May, following a 0.9 percent fall in the previous month and compared with a forecast for 0.3 percent rise.   

On a year ago, actual sales also rose a more-than-expected 6.7 percent.   

The market currently sees about a 45 percent chance of a another rate hike later in the month, up sharply from around 23 percent on Thursday.   

Analysts said the Monday's consumer price index, which is forecast to show a rise of 0.8 percent on the previous quarter, would be deciding factor for central bank.   

The RBNZ forecast in June the CPI to rise 0.7 percent in the second quarter, up from 0.5 percent gain the March quarter.   

"All eyes are on Monday's CPI and that will determine whether they go or not in July," said Khoon Goh, senior economist at ANZ-National Bank.   

Fourteen of 17 analysts in the latest Reuters poll expect the central bank to keep rates on hold at its next review on July 26.   

Latest data from government agency Quotable Value showed the annual pace of house value growth accelerated for the fifth straight month in June, rising 12.2 percent from a year earlier.

title: ANALYSIS- Bank of Canada may let C$, not rates, cool growth
text:
OTTAWA, July 10 (Reuters) - The  Bank of Canada is unlikely to implement a long series of interest rate hikes following its rate rise on Tuesday, and is seen relying instead on the soaring Canadian dollar to cool economic growth and inflation.   

The central bank came off the sidelines on Tuesday after holding rates steady for more than a year, and lifted its key overnight lending target by one-quarter point to 4.50 percent. It said "some modest further increase" in the rate may be needed.   

But reading between the lines in its statement there was a dovish undertone to the hawkish headline, leaving analysts with the clear impression the bank is not quite ready to commit to more than one more rate increase in the near term.   

"The stronger Canadian dollar is putting a little bit of a damper on the extent of the tightening that might be required, and that is what the bank is basically telling people," said Marc Levesque, chief market strategist at TD Securities.   

After the central bank made its rate announcement on Tuesday, the Canadian dollar dropped as low as C$1.0542 to the U.S. dollar, or 94.86 U.S. cents, from C$1.0496, or 95.27 U.S. cents, at Monday's close. At midafternoon on Tuesday it was at C$1.0516, or 95.09 U.S. cents.   

The bank revealed nothing of its analysis of the reasons for the Canadian dollar's meteoric rise to 30-year highs in recent weeks. It did say, however, that the higher trading range for the currency, combined with higher interest rates across the yield curve, would dull economic growth in 2008 and 2009. The higher Canadian dollar could keep the inflation rate below the bank's estimate, it also said.   

"Those things suggest they're going to be keeping their eye closely on the Canadian dollar, see how it performs between now and September before they make a decision as to what they're going to do in September," said Ted Carmichael of  J.P. Morgan Canada.

J.P. Morgan and TD Securities both expect just one more rate hike on Sept. 5 followed by another pause.   

Bank Governor David Dodge said last month that the gains in the currency since April had been faster than past experience would suggest but he was unclear on whether that would influence interest rates.   

While the bank has no target for the foreign exchange rate, it does react to any sharp currency movements that are out of line with economic pressures. Some economists say the recent gains have been of the undesirable variety, or so-called Type 2 -- fueled by market expectations of a rate hike, rather than by strong demand for commodities.   

"Citing the strong loonie as a key downside risk is a new development and is a mild hint that the bank views some of the currency's gain as Type 2," said Doug Porter, deputy chief economist at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note.   

Stewart Hall, market strategist at  HSBC, suggests that the  Bank of Canada was deliberately vague on the details of future rate hikes to put the brakes on the Canadian dollar. "The breadth and timing of the cycle is uncertain, and it is this uncertainty that will spare the  Bank of Canada from the challenges currently confronting the Reserve Bank of New Zealand," he said.   

New Zealand's central bank has intervened twice in the market to weaken its currency in the last several weeks   

Several economists noted that the bank's use of the word "modest" when referring to further rate hikes has been used in the past to signal just one more hike in a cycle.   

But the bank also has to fend off pesky inflation pressures that will not go away. Economists expect core inflation to climb to nearly 3 percent later this year as the effects of a June 2006 sales tax cut will no longer have the effect of reducing the 12-month figures.   

"It would be very difficult for the bank to see an inflation rate that's that much above their 2 percent target and not do at least one more rate hike," Carmichael said.

title: NZ dollar advances to 22-year highs on yield buying
text:
WELLINGTON, July 2 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> strengthened to 22-year post-float highs on Monday, lifted by steady buying by Japanese investors seeking high yielding currencies.   

The kiwi touched $0.7760 <NZD=D>, its highest level since it was floated in 1985, and traders said the risks were pointed to the upside given the possibility the central bank could raise interest rates again.   

"We see risks NZD will test $0.80 sooner rather than later," said  RBC Capital Markets senior currency strategist Sue Trinh.   

At 0525 GMT the kiwi was at $0.7752/62 from $0.7691/01 in late local trade on Friday.   

Traders said buying related to Japanese investment trusts was a key driver for the kiwi's rise, sending the currency up to a 20-year peak of 95.55 yen <NZDJPY=R>.   

The yen slipped after the Bank of Japan's key business sentiment tankan survey came in line with economists' forecast, suggesting the country's relatively low interest rates would rise only gradually.   

On a trade-weighted basis, the New Zealand dollar also hit an all-time high of 75.19 <=NZD>.   

With no significant local data due until NZ Institute of Economic Research's quarterly survey of business opinion on July 10, the kiwi's short-term direction will likely be determined by offshore factors.   

Traders speculate the Reserve Bank of New Zealand could intervene to curb the New Zealand dollar's strength, although the impact was likely to be limited.   

"RBNZ's intervention efforts are increasingly seen as futile, and the market is seriously underestimating the risk of further RBNZ tightening this cycle," said Trinh.   

The central bank has stepped in to sell the kiwi on three occasions since June 11, when it intervened for the first time since the currency was floated.   

Some players think the central bank could intervene on Wednesday when U.S. markets will be closed for a public holiday. The RBNZ has chosen to enter the market at times when it has been in a slow trading period, such as market holidays.   

Most economists in a Reuters poll think the RBNZ will not raise interest rates further after lifting them by a total of 75 basis points this year, with a median risk for a rise to 8.25 percent at its next review put at around 30 percent.

title: UPDATE 1-RBNZ says  forex intervention  aims to moderate peaks
text:
(Adds analyst comment, prices, details)   

WELLINGTON, June 27 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank said on Wednesday its currency intervention was aimed at moderating the rise in the New Zealand dollar and not to defend a certain foreign exchange level.   

In an article written for media, Reserve Bank of New Zealand Deputy Governor Grant Spencer said the strong kiwi dollar was hurting the country's exporters and current levels could not be sustained given the country's large current account deficit.   

"It does not attempt to defend a particular level of the exchange rate. Rather it sends a signal that, in the bank's view, the exchange rate is out of alignment with the economic fundamentals," Spencer said.   

The RBNZ has intervened to sell the New Zealand dollar three times since June 11, when it stepped in for the first time since the currency was floated in 1985.   

Spencer said intervention was an ongoing process and the central bank would not confirm specific activities. The RBNZ confirmed its first intervention, but has not commented on its subsequent forays.   

The New Zealand dollar showed little reaction to Spencer's comments, trading around $0.7645 <NZD=>, about half a U.S. cent below a 22-year post-float high of $0.7695 hit the previous day.   

Analysts said there was nothing surprising in the article and the central bank was likely to continue intervening when trading volumes were most light to maximise the impact.   

"What they are going to do now is be selective in terms of intervention and probably try to time it when they can get bigger impact for their buck." said ANZ-National Bank senior economist Khoon Goh.   

The currency has risen around 10 percent since March, lifted by demand for carry trades, where investors raise money in low yielding currencies to invest in high yielding ones.   

On Tuesday, Japanese Finance Minister Koji Omi warned investors to be wary of the risks of one-way bets against the yen, in an apparent reference to carry trades.   

Foreign exchange officials from South Korea and New Zealand also expressed concern over the yen's weakness at a meeting in Seoul, and agreed a potential unwinding of yen carry trades was a big threat to financial markets.   

They also agreed that potentially-affected countries needed to deal with the issue in a pre-emptive manner.   

Spencer reiterated that intervention did not signal a change in the direction of monetary policy, which was dependent on how inflation pressures evolve over the months ahead.   

"Evidence that inflation pressures are abating will be an important step in seeing the exchange rate return to more sustainable levels," he added.   

On June 7, the central bank unexpectedly raised interest rates to 8 percent -- the highest in the industrialised world -- because of concerns over the strength in consumer spending and a rampant housing market.

title: UPDATE:  Intervention  To Sell NZD Is An Ongoing Process -RBNZ
text:
(Adds details, context and NZD level.) 
    

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Wednesday said that its recent unprecedented intervention in the foreign exchange market to sell the local currency didn't run counter to the bank's monetary policy objectives.   

The RBNZ, which intervened June 11 to cap the high-flying New Zealand dollar for the first time since the currency was floated in 1985, said that intervention is an "ongoing process."   

The bank said in a statement that it won't comment publicly on specific intervention activities, but added that it will only intervene when it considers the New Zealand dollar at exceptional levels and unjustified by economic fundamentals.   

"Intervention operates at the margin, affecting the balance of demand and supply for the New Zealand dollar; it can have an immediate downward impact on the exchange rate as it did on June 11," the central bank said.   

The June 11 intervention sent the New Zealand dollar down by nearly 2% from around US$0.7630. Since then, traders say the central bank had apparently intervened twice to kneecap the local currency with little success.   

The currency rose to a fresh 25-year peak of US$0.7692 in the overnight session, and was quoted at US$0.7652 at 0340 GMT.   

The RBNZ said its action to sell the Kiwi wasn't an attempt to defend a particular level of the exchange rate.   

"Rather it sends a signal that, in the bank's view, the exchange rate is out of alignment with the economic fundamentals.   

"Those speculating in the New Zealand dollar need to be aware that the exchange rate isn't a one-way bet; they need to be cautious," the central bank said.   

New Zealand's interest rates - the second highest in the developed world after Iceland - have attracted inflows in carry trade, when investors borrow in low-yielding currencies, such as the yen, to invest in high-yielding ones.   

The central bank said its attempts to lower the New Zealand dollar don't run counter to its monetary policy objectives.   

"Intervention is about seeking to moderate the trend in the exchange rate and rebalancing monetary policy pressure.   

"It does not fundamentally alter monetary policy and does not signal a future easing of conditions," the bank said.   

Many economists had questioned the bank's June 11 intervention at a time when it was raising interest rates, saying that the RBNZ was sending mixed signals to the market.   

However, in its statement, the RBNZ reiterated that the outlook for interest rates will depend on how inflation pressures evolve over coming months. "Evidence that inflation pressures are abating will be an important step in seeing the exchange rate return to more sustainable levels," the bank said.   

The RBNZ raised the Official Cash Rate by a quarter percentage point each in March, April and June to a record high 8.00%, aiming to knock back demand pressures and cool persistently strong inflation.

title: ANALYSIS-Market wary but not intimidated by NZ  intervention
text:
WELLINGTON, June 22 (Reuters) - Raids by New Zealand's central bank on currency markets have failed to stop the high-flying kiwi dollar from hitting fresh 22-year highs and left it with a dilemma - when to strike again for maximum impact at minimal cost.   

 On each of the past two Mondays -- when offshore markets were closed and trading volumes thin -- the Reserve Bank of New Zealand stepped in to cap the rise in the kiwi dollar, which has rallied to its highest levels since it was floated in 1985.   

 "You'd have to be a little bit more wary on a Monday for the next few weeks because that is the time when intervention is most likely to have impact," said Anthony Byett, managing director at a forex advisory firm fxmatters.co.nz.   

 But keeping to such timing would be predictable, undermining the effectiveness of the intervention.   

 "As we've seen this Monday, interbank dealers will be more prepared now," he said.   

 The New Zealand dollar plunged nearly 2 percent after the central bank intervened on June 11, the first time it had done so since the New Zealand dollar was released from a fixed-rate policy to trade freely on international markets.   

 But the second intervention had a limited and short-lived impact.   

 The RBNZ, which has said it was concerned the high exchange rate could damage the export sector, confirmed its first intervention, but not the second.   

 A central bank interest rate of 8 percent -- the highest in the industrial world -- has made the New Zealand dollar a major investment target.   

 Many investors fund their purchases of New Zealand assets by borrowing in a low-yielding currency, such as the yen. Central bank rates in Japan are just 0.5 percent.   

 The kiwi rose as far as $0.7660 <NZD=> <NZD=D2> on Thursday, a fresh post-float peak and an all-time high on a trade-weighted basis <=NZD>.   

 TREND NOT A FRIEND   

 While the intervention has made some investors more cautious about buying the currency, some analysts think the central bank cannot fight the trend of global demand for higher-yielding currencies.   

 "I think they misread what the psychology was even before the intervention," said Westpac Bank currency strategist Michael Gordon.   

 Investors have remained wary but not put off by reports several times last week that the central bank was inquiring about prices in the foreign exchange market.   

 Masaaki Saito, assistant vice president of Gaitame.com, Japan's biggest currency margin-trading broker, said retail investors believe New Zealand's attractive yield difference outweighs the risk of central bank intervention.   

 "Japan's interest rate is only 0.5 percent while New Zealand is at 8 percent. In the end, it's that yield difference that individual investors are attracted to," he said.   

 Reflecting global demand for yield, the New Zealand dollar is not the only high-flying currency.   

 In recent months, the British pound <GBP=> has scaled a 26-year high, the Canadian dollar <CAD=> a 30-year peak, and the Australian dollar an 18-year high <AUD=>.   

 Both RBNZ Governor Alan Bollard and Bank of Canada Governor David Dodge have said the strength in their currencies can not be explained by domestic economic fundamentals.   

 So far, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has been far more relaxed about its currency, in part because its strength helps keep down import prices and so restrains inflationary pressures.   

 The RBA has also been more subtle in its currencyoperations, quietly selling the Australian dollars it bought between 1997 and 2001 when it was openly intervening to support the currency.   

 The selling has been routine since 2002 but was stepped up in the first four months of the year to reach over A$1 billion. Dealers suspect more has been offloaded since then.   

 The central bank tends to play down this selling as an effort to rebuild reserves, but really it is intervention by any other name, analysts say. By keeping it quiet, the RBA avoids becoming a target for speculators while retaining the ability to inject some two-way risk into the market.   

 Byett said the Australian central bank may also step up its presence in the currency market.   

 "At some stage soon, I think you'll see the RBA intervene in a more explicit manner than they've done to date this year," he said.   

 Byett said the RBNZ would be more effective if it adopted an RBA style of intervention.   

 The RBNZ can spend as much as it wants in kiwi-selling intervention but it can only book currency losses up to NZ$1 billion under an agreement with the government.   

 Given the constraint, analysts estimate the RBNZ could spend around NZ$10 billion on intervention -- just a fraction of the 35 trillion yen ($283 billion) the Japanese authorities sold in 2003 and 2004 to try to prevent a rapid rise in the yen from damaging a fragile economy.  (Additional reporting by Wayne Cole in SYDNEY)

title: NZ dollar trades tight range on Japanese buying
text:
WELLINGTON, June 22 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> held a tight range around $0.7630 on Friday as a steady stream of buying from Japanese investors seeking high yielding currencies underpinned the kiwi.   

There was no sign of intervention from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, despite the kiwi hitting a post-float high of $0.7660 in Asian trade on Thursday.   

"There's more demand coming out of Japan, which is not just going into kiwi," Westpac currency strategist Michael Gordon said.   

The kiwi has been a beneficiary of the carry trade -- where investors borrow a low yielder such as the yen to invest in the high yielding kiwi. New Zealand interest rates are 8 percent, the highest in the industrialised world.   

The Australian and New Zealand dollars have long been favourites of Japanese investors and are used for carry trades.   

A trader at a Japanese trust bank said he saw constant flows from investment trusts buying the euro and currencies of emerging markets that have become popular recently.   

The yen hit a 20-year low against the kiwi, a four and a half year low against the U.S. dollar and a 16-year low against the Australian dollar.   

At 0500 GMT the kiwi was at $0.7637/47, up from $0.7626/29 in late local trade on Wednesday, having traded a $0.7629 to $0.7645 range. It hit a high of 94.71 against the yen <NZDJPY=R>.   

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has twice intervened over the past two weeks to lower the kiwi, but traders say the bank is wary of trying to take on the market by defending a set level.   

The interventions have come on the past two Mondays, when closure in offshore markets meant maximum impact, but market-watchers say intervening on the third Monday in a row would be too predictable.   

The NZ dollar trade weighted index (TWI) <=NZD>, the central bank's preferred currency measure, was at 74.40, after hitting a record high of 74.62 on Thursday.   

New Zealand credit card billing rose a seasonally adjusted 0.5 percent in May, compared with the previous months 0.9 percent fall.   

Next week sees a host of important data, including gross domestic product, trade and current account figures.   

New Zealand bonds firmed, as U.S. Treasuries held steady, with yields falling two basis points.

title: RPT- FOREX -Low yield keeps yen near 4-1/2-yr trough vs dollar
text:
TOKYO, June 21 (Reuters) - The yen hung near a 4-1/2-year low versus the dollar on Thursday, weighed down as investors continued to use the currency to buy higher-yielding units such as the New Zealand dollar in carry trades.   

The kiwi was also closing in on a 22-year peak of $0.7640 hit earlier in the month and near the levels when the New Zealand central bank first confirmed it had intervened to sell the currency last week.   

The market is testing the central bank's will to step in and stem the currency's rise, and although intervention fears may slow the pace of the kiwi's ascent, the country's high interest rates are expected to keep it strengthening, traders said.   

The New Zealand dollar was up 0.4 percent at $0.7620.   

The yen drifted away from a record low against the euro but traders said it was only a matter of time before the single currency scaled a new high against the Japanese currency.   

"The basic trend of currencies with prospects of rising interest rates strengthening remains intact," said Nobuo Ibaraki, a forex manager at Nomura Trust and Banking.   

The Bank of Japan is expected to boost interest rates as early as August, but the interest rate differential with other countries is still wide enough to feed Japanese investor appetite for higher-yielding foreign assets, he said.   

"Because the yen's slide has been rapid, the market is expected to move sideways for now given a lack of major data or events. The yen's weakening trend will likely continue as there appears to be no clear bottom," Ibaraki said.   

The dollar was up 0.15 percent at 123.63 yen and just off a peak of 123.76 yen struck earlier in the week on electronic trading platform EBS, the highest since December 2002.   

The yen has lost about 2 percent against the dollar in about two weeks. Traders said a break above 124 yen may take some time but support at 123 yen looked firm.   

The euro was little changed at 165.58 yen moving away from the all-time high of 166.12 yen hit on EBS earlier in the week.   

The single European currency inched down 0.1 percent to $1.3390.   

Minutes from a Bank of England policy meeting in June released on Wednesday showed that BoE Governor Mervyn King and three other Monetary Policy Committee members opposed keeping interest rates steady at 5.5 percent but were outvoted by the remaining five members.   

Market players took that to suggest the BoE could raise interest rates as early as next month.   

Sterling rose across the board, hitting a fresh 15-year high against the yen.   

"The market remains focused on the direction of interest rates, with investors favouring currencies with an outlook of monetary tightening, such as sterling," said a trader at a big Japanese bank.   

The pound was at $1.9914 and 246.15 yen.

title: CENTRAL BANK  WATCH: RBNZ  Intervention  Muddies Rate Outlook
text:
By Rachel Pannett 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
    

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The actions of New Zealand's central bank in the past two weeks have sent a strong signal to foreign-exchange traders about its willingness to intervene in currency markets, but left interest-rate traders in a fog.   

By selling the country's currency for the first time since the New Zealand dollar was floated in 1985, on June 11 and again on Monday, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand made clear that it won't tolerate further sharp appreciation in the currency.   

Intervention by a central bank to weaken a currency would normally indicate that it has an easing bias as a weaker currency boosts exports and the overall economy.   

But the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is unlikely to want to encourage expectations of looser policy given that domestic inflation is forecast to return to the upper end of the central bank's target zone and the country's housing sector and credit growth remain overheated.   

With the RBNZ not set to meet again until July 26, investors face a long wait before the central bank's governor, Alan Bollard, provides more clarity on what currency intervention means for monetary policy.   

So far, financial market pricing indicates that investors have lowered their expectations of a further rise in New Zealand's official cash rate, which the RBNZ raised to 8.0% in June.   

Financial futures prices put the chance of a rate rise in July at around 19%, down from 50% just before the central bank first intervened in the currency market a little over week ago.   

"Clearly the RBNZ is uncomfortable with both the strength of the domestic economy and the strength of the currency. However, a lack of a clear and consistent view may ultimately undermine any attempts to ease pressure on either (the economy or the currency)," Macquarie analyst Hayden Atkins said.   

RBNZ Executes Another "Communications Clanger"   

Bank of New Zealand's head of market economics, Stephen Toplis, said the RBNZ's decision to intervene in currency markets was "another communications clanger".   

"If Alan Bollard wanted to ease monetary policy... that is certainly what he achieved," Toplis said.   

This isn't the first time Bollard's actions have confused markets.   

In March, financial markets pounced on the governor's comments that the RBNZ was assessing alternative measures to slow the housing market aside from raising the official cash rate.   

Market participants took those comments as a sign that the March hike would be the last this cycle but the RBNZ went on to lift rates at each of the next two reviews.   

The central bank said last week that the currency market intervention "doesn't prejudge the future direction of monetary policy, which as always will remain dependent on emerging market trends".   

But the fact that the RBNZ felt comfortable intervening suggests "it has no intention to raise rates further", Toplis said, although he puts the probability of further tightening in July at 40%.   

"We still think there's a very strong probability that the domestic data will prove much more inflationary than the bank currently has built into its forecasts. As such, strong currency or no, rates will need to rise," he said.   

Michael Gordon, a Wellington-based market strategist for  Westpac Banking Corp., agreed that if anything, successful intervention to push down the currency "increases the likelihood of another rate hike".   

With inflation threatening to return to the upper end of the RBNZ's 1% to 3% target band in the second half of calendar 2008, the bank can't afford to add to net demand, either via the domestic or export sectors, Gordon said.   

"Any boost to the export sector will have to be offset by an even greater slowdown in the domestic sector - which means more rate hikes," he said.   

Of course, any further rate hikes would make the New Zealand dollar even more attractive and offset the impact of last week's intervention.   

New Zealand's high official cash rate - currently the second highest in the developed world after Iceland - underpins the currency's yield appeal.   

Traders note that persistent demand from Asian speculative investors, as well as real money demand out of Japan - as people look for high-yielding homes for their summer bonuses, is preventing the New Zealand dollar from a significant break below US$0.7500.   

In trading Wednesday, the currency touched US$0.7601, its highest level since the RBNZ first intervened on June 11.

title: CENTRAL BANK  WATCH: RBNZ  Intervention  Muddies Rate Outlook
text:
By Rachel Pannett 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
    

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The actions of New Zealand's central bank in the past two weeks have sent a strong signal to foreign-exchange traders about its willingness to intervene in currency markets, but left interest-rate traders in a fog.

Intervention by a central bank to weaken a currency would normally indicate that it has an easing bias as a weaker currency boosts exports and the overall economy.   

But the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is unlikely to want to encourage expectations of looser policy given that domestic inflation is forecast to return to the upper end of the central bank's target zone and the country's housing sector and credit growth remain overheated.

So far, financial market pricing indicates that investors have lowered their expectations of a further rise in New Zealand's official cash rate, which the RBNZ raised to 8.0% in June.

"Clearly the RBNZ is uncomfortable with both the strength of the domestic economy and the strength of the currency. However, a lack of a clear and consistent view may ultimately undermine any attempts to ease pressure on either (the economy or the currency)," Macquarie analyst Hayden Atkins said.

This isn't the first time Bollard's actions have confused markets.

With inflation threatening to return to the upper end of the RBNZ's 1% to 3% target band in the second half of calendar 2008, the bank can't afford to add to net demand, either via the domestic or export sectors, Gordon said.   

"Any boost to the export sector will have to be offset by an even greater slowdown in the domestic sector - which means more rate hikes," he said.   

Of course, any further rate hikes would make the New Zealand dollar even more attractive and offset the impact of last week's intervention.

title: Aussie dlr near 18-yr highs, aided by carry trades
text:
SYDNEY, June 20 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar consolidated just near 18-year peaks against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday, drawing support from the insatiable appetite among investors for high-yielding currencies.   

The Aussie struck fresh 16-year highs against the yen, rising as high as 104.52 yen. Carry trades showed no signs of any let up as minutes from the Bank of Japan policy meeting suggested that interest rates there were unlikely to rise in a hurry.   

"Carry trades are here to stay and the view from Japan is rates are unlikely to rise," said Robert Rennie, chief currency strategist at  Westpac Banking Corp.

"For carry trades to be unwound, it would need coordinated verbal intervention from central banks globally. In an environment where is risk is very much favoured, any pullback by the Aussie is a good buying opportunity."   

In carry trades, investors borrow in the low-yielding Japanese yen to buy the higher yielding Aussie or kiwi. New Zealand's central bank intervened last week to drive down its currency, but the kiwi recovered, helped mainly by carry trades.   

At 4:00 p.m. (0600 GMT), the Aussie was quoted at $0.8466/71 against the U.S. dollar, up from $0.8434/39 here late on Tuesday. It had risen to a near two-week high of $0.8474 during the day, just off its 18-year peak of $0.8477 hit on June 7.   

The U.S. dollar slipped as investors unwound positions in dollar-denominated fixed income assets after U.S. bond yields continued to fall from five-year highs struck last week.   

U.S. Treasuries rallied on Tuesday after weak housing data reinforced a view that the housing sector would remain a drag on the U.S. economy.   

The spread between two-year Australian and U.S. government debt expanded to 145 basis points, from 136 points at the end of last week, as yields on U.S. Treasuries fell at a faster pace than their Aussie counterparts.   

Analysts said attractive Aussie rates, which were amongst the highest in the industrialised world, would continue to draw investment flows, especially from Japanese retail investors seeking higher returns.   

"Investment flows and extended gains for the Aussie against the yen have underpinned the Aussie. We are yet to see the catalyst for a break lower for the Aussie as global and domestic growth remains robust," said Tony Morriss, senior currency strategist at ANZ.   

Although Australia's central bank has kept the cash rate unchanged at 6.25 percent in the past seven months, financial markets are pricing in a rate hike by October, a move which could boost the Aussie.

title: NZ dollar hovers near $0.76, RBNZ  intervention  eyed
text:
WELLINGTON, June 19 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> held near nine-day highs on Wednesday, as wary investors looked for any sign that the central bank might be ready for another bout of intervention.   

The kiwi spent much of the session just below $0.7600, a level regarded by some as likely to set off alarm bells at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and possibly trigger intervention.   

"In light of the recent RBNZ intervention, market participants are still reluctant to chase the NZD higher," said Bank of New Zealand currency strategist Danica Hampton.   

At 0500 GMT the kiwi was at $0.7588/98 from $0.7552/55 in late local trading on Tuesday. It briefly touched a local session high of $0.7600 but traded no lower $0.7577.   

The central bank intervened on June 11 for the first time since the currency was floated 22 years ago and was seen in the foreign exchange market again last Monday.   

The first intervention sent the currency around 2 percent lower from a high of $0.7640, while the second foray at around $0.7550 sent the kiwi half a cent lower.   

The kiwi followed trends in the broader market, where the U.S dollar slipped after a pull back in bond yields which had been boosting the currency, and the yen was at multi-year lows on increased carry trades to take advantage of its low yield.   

The kiwi has been a beneficiary of the carry trade, where investors borrow a low yielder such as the yen to invest in a high yielder.   

"While there has been a steady stream of Japanese retail demand, leverage and momentum funds out of Asia have also been noted buyers," Hampton said.   

Investors were also watching the NZ dollar trade weighted index (TWI) <=NZD>, the central bank's preferred currency measure. On that basis 74, is seen as a possible trigger point for the RBNZ.   

The NZ dollar TWI was at 73.90, up 0.4 percent on the day. The index's life-time high is 74.54 reached in December 2005.   

The currency was unmoved by data showing a net seasonally adjusted gain of 360 long term and permanent migrants in May, nearly double the gain in April. The annual gain of 10,680 was up 4 percent on a year ago.   

Immigration gains were running at about half the RBNZ's forecast rate, which would help reduce domestic demand.   

"The easing in net migration may give the Reserve Bank some comfort on the housing front although the raft of key housing data remains far too strong," said  RBC Capital Markets senior economist Su-Lin Ong, adding that the central bank could afford to watch and wait.   

A warning by Finance Minister Michael Cullen that the property market might undergo a sharp correction also passed without effect.   

Next week's first quarter gross domestic product reading is the significant piece of data.   

New Zealand bonds were firmer as U.S. Treasuries drifted sideways after a three-day rally as weak housing data reinforced the view that U.S. interest rates will stay on hold.   

The yield on benchmark NZ December 2017 bond <NZG1217=RNZL> closed three basis points lower at 6.76 percent.

title: POLL-NZ dollar seen near peak, to ease in 2008
text:
WELLINGTON, June 19 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> is seen peaking in the next few months before gradually easing in 2008 as domestic spending softens and the central bank looks to start easing its tight monetary policy, a Reuters poll showed on Tuesday.   

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is widely expected to intervene again to stem the rise in the kiwi dollar after two such moves in the past week, but analysts say it was unlikely to have a significant impact on the market.   

"We expect the currency will peak in the next two or three month but I don't think (intervention) will necessarily be the driver that pushes it back," said Danica Hampton, currency strategist at Bank of New Zealand.   

"Intervention is one of those things that affect sentiment rather than materially impacting the real economy."   

The Reuters poll of 10 analysts has a median forecast for the kiwi of US$0.73 at the end of September and $0.72 at the end of December, before it is seen easing to $0.6720 by the end of June next year.   

As of Tuesday, the New Zealand dollar was trading at $0.7545/55, about one U.S. cent the below a 22-year post float high struck on June 8 after the RBNZ unexpectedly raised interest rates to 8 percent.   

In the previous poll taken before the June rate review, analysts expected the kiwi to stand at $0.73 at the end of September and $0.65 in June next year.   

On the RBNZ's preferred trade-weighted basis <=NZD>, the New Zealand dollar is seen at 71.4 at the end of September, easing to 70.6 and 66.6 in December and June, respectively. The RBNZ forecast the trade-weighted index to average 72 in the second half of 2007 and 71.6 in the first half of 2008.   

On June 11, the central bank intervened for the first since the currency was floated in 1985, and sold what it said was an exceptionally and unjustifiably high kiwi dollar.   

Market sources said the RBNZ stepped in again on Monday, although on a smaller scale, which briefly pushed the New Zealand dollar down about half a U.S. cent.   

Analysts said the long-term direction would be set by the strength in the economy and interest rates.   

Bank of New Zealand's Hampton said she expected to see the New Zealand dollar ease towards the end of the year, but it could hold up longer if consumer spending does not cool.   

The poll also showed 13 of 16 forecasters do not expect the central bank to raise interest again, after lifting them for the third straight time on June 7 [nWEL270282].

title: 3rd UPDATE: RBNZ Apparent Action To Sell NZD Under Fire
text:
(Adds closing levels for NZ dollar and bonds as well as analysts' comments.)   


 
    By Shri Navaratnam 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
    

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's apparent intervention in the foreign exchange market to sell the local currency for the second time in a week appears to have had little lasting impact, although the threat of further central bank action looms.   

Some analysts say the RBNZ is fighting a losing battle.   

Earlier Monday a government official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Dow Jones Newswires that the central bank had sold the Kiwi to cap any momentum in the currency toward 76 U.S. cents.   

"I can confirm that the central bank intervened this morning - it was modest intervention if you like - the (RBNZ) wants to hurt any rallies toward 76 (U.S.) cents," the official said.   

A central bank spokesman declined to say whether the RBNZ had intervened in the market, but dealers said it had.   

"They (RBNZ) were in the market earlier (Monday), offering around the 75.50 (U.S.) cent level," said Danica Hampton, currency strategist at Bank of New Zealand said.   

Hampton said that according to market talk, the RBNZ may have sold up to NZ$350 million. However, the reported local currency selling appears to have lost its impact beyond the initial selloff.   

The New Zealand dollar slipped to a low of US$0.7504 from as high as US$0.7554 this morning, but had recovered most of its losses and closed the domestic session at US$0.7547 at 0500 GMT.   

The reported selling of the New Zealand dollar comes after last week's unprecedented central bank intervention - the first since the currency was floated in March 1985.   

"Financial markets, particularly currency markets, are far bigger than any one player," said Clifford Bennett, chief economist at FxMax. "The RBNZ is a relatively small bank, and its attempt to cap the New Zealand dollar bull trend is a mistake. "The carry trade will continue to dominate, and it is the RBNZ's own policy that has made them a carry trade target," Bennett said.   

"Expect their intervention, waves of selling to have decreasing effect, until finally the market runs dramatically higher," he said.   


 
    RBNZ Says Kiwi Unjustifiably High 
    

Following last week's RBNZ action, currency dealers and analysts have said the central bank is likely to intervene again if the local currency, which hit a post-float high of US$0.7640 earlier this month, continues to rise.   

The RBNZ last week said it sold the currency because the Kiwi had reached an exceptionally high level that wasn't justified by economic fundamentals.   

The pair had since been trapped in an 80-point range, trading between US$0.7460 to US$0.7540 as traders were reluctant to push the currency too high.   

However, with the Bank of Japan leaving interest rates unchanged Friday, renewed demand for carry trades saw the New Zealand dollar pushed higher over the weekend.   

New Zealand's benchmark policy rate of 8.00% - the highest in the developed world after Iceland - has attracted inflows from carry trades, where investors borrow in low-yielding currencies to invest in higher-yielding currencies.   

The RBNZ has said it will intervene when the currency is unjustifiably high and when the conditions are right. According to the central bank, the intervention, when carried out, would also have to meet its policy target agreement.   

The agreement obliges the RBNZ to maintain price stability while avoiding unnecessary volatility in output, interest rates and the exchange rate.   

The government source said the RBNZ isn't eyeing specific levels to determine intervention but it wants to knock back any renewed upward momentum in the local currency.   

"There is no set policy on this (intervention), but they seem to be very uncomfortable with any indication the market may resume the currency rally," he said.   

The source said that at this stage the central bank appears to be more comfortable with the local currency trading close to US$0.7500.   

An  ANZ Bank dealer said it will be "very difficult" for the RBNZ to fight global trends toward higher-yielding currencies. As long as New Zealand interest rates remain attractive, the Kiwi will continue to encourage speculative investors, he said.   

The central bank last week said its intervention doesn't prejudice the future direction of monetary policy.   

RBNZ Governor Alan Bollard surprised markets earlier this month by raising the Official Cash Rate by a quarter percentage point to a record high to knock back resilient domestic demand pressures.   

It was the third consecutive rate increase this year, and economists say the risks of another tightening remain high due to broadly solid data and continuing inflationary pressures.   

There was muted reaction in the debt markets Monday to the reported RBNZ intervention. Bond prices rose but underperformed their U.S. counterparts as the market continues to price in about a 50% chance of another rate hike in New Zealand by September.   

Bond prices are expected to remain trapped in a range, with bias to sell on rallies. The New Zealand dollar should probably stay capped below US$0.7600, dealers said.

The central bank didn't confirm it had intervened in the market, but dealers said the bank was in the market selling the New Zealand dollar. The action from the RBNZ comes after last week's unprecedented intervention by the central bank - the first since the currency was floated in 1985.   

"They (RBNZ) were in the market earlier, offering around the 75.50 (US) cent level," said Danica Hampton, currency strategist at Bank of New Zealand said.

The RBNZ last week said it sold the currency because the Kiwi was exceptionally high and was unjustified by economic fundamentals.   

The pair had since been trapped in a 80 point range, trading between US$0.7460 to US$0.7540 as traders were reluctant to push the currency too high.   

However, with the Bank Of Japan leaving interest rates unchanged Friday, renewed demand for carry trade saw the Kiwi pushed over the weekend.   

New Zealand's interest rates - the second highest in the developed world after Iceland - have attracted inflows in carry trade, when investors borrow in low-yielding currencies, such as the yen, to invest in high-yielding ones.   

The RBNZ has said that it will intervene when the currency is unjustifiably high and when conditions are opportune. The intervention, when carried out, would also have to meet its inflation targeting regime.

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand intervened in the foreign exchange market Monday to sell the local currency, dealers said.   

The apparent action from the RBNZ comes after last week's unprecedented intervention by the central bank - the first since the currency was floated in 1985.   

"They (RBNZ) were in the market earlier, offering around the 75.50 (US) cent level," said Danica Hampton, currency strategist at Bank of New Zealand.   

The New Zealand dollar has eased off to US$0.7523 from around US$0.7550 earlier this morning.   

Another dealer at HSBC said the RBNZ was seen offering in the high 75 U.S. cent area.   

He said the RBNZ appears determined to lean against any sustained uptrend in the Kiwi.   

The RBNZ last week said it sold the currency because the Kiwi was at unjustifiably high levels.

title: Aussie at 16-yr peak vs yen, carry trades favoured
text:
SYDNEY, June 18 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar leapt to a 16-year high against a broadly weaker Japanese yen on Monday, underpinned by rising stock markets that reinforced a growing appetite for risky carry trades.   

The soft U.S. dollar, which retreated against the euro after tame inflation data and weak consumer sentiment reduced prospects of an interest rate increase from the Federal Reserve, also bolstered the Aussie.   

"All the positives and the renewed appetite for risk just stacked up for the Aussie dollar," said Robert Rennie chief currency strategist at  Westpac Banking Corp. "I would be surprised if the Aussie does not rise to $0.8450 this week."   

At 4:00 p.m. the Aussie <AUD=> was quoted at $0.8425/30, up from $0.8367/70 here late on Friday. It had fallen to a 10-day low of $0.8333 on Thursday after the central bank governor quashed hopes of an early domestic rate rise.   

Against the yen, the Aussie rose to 104.12/104.22 yen <AUDJPY=R>, up from Friday's 102.90/103 yen. It struck a 16-year peak of 104.24 yen, its highest since October 1991, benefiting from increased demand for carry trades after the Bank of Japan last week indicated it was in no hurry to raise rates.   

In carry trades investors borrow in the low-yielding Japanese yen to buy the higher yielding Aussie or the New Zealand dollar <NZD=>. The New Zealand kiwi weathered a bout of suspected intervention by its central bank, recovering from its losses as investors searched for higher yields.   

The Aussie also drew support from firm gold and base metal prices. Australia is a big exporter of commodities and has been riding a resources boom as it enters its 17th year of expansion.   

The robust pace of growth had led to speculation about a rate hike in the next few months, boosting the Aussie to an 18-year high of $0.8477 against the U.S. dollar on June 7. But central bank Governor Glenn Stevens last week poured cold water on those expections.   

Stevens said a lower short-term inflation outlook gave the bank more time to assess the need for higher rates. As a result, financial markets are pricing in a slim chance of a rate rise next month.   

"Support for the Aussie will come from the RBA still being in play, even through an imminent rate hike is next to no chance," said John Kyriakopoulos, currency strategist at nabCapital. "Governor Stevens acknowledged that strong economic growth and a tight labour market left the central bank more confident of their forecast for a rise in inflation next year."

title: NZ dollar falls as RBNZ  intervenes  again
text:
WELLINGTON, June 18 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> fell nearly half a cent early on Monday after the central bank intervened to sell the currency for the second time in a week.   

* Kiwi started local session around $0.7540/50 and touched a high of $0.7551 before the Reserve Bank of New Zealand intervened and knocked it back to around $0.7500.   

* RBNZ action seen as pre-emptive to stop the currency moving through technical levels towards $0.7600.   

* It had gained on Friday as its yield appeal attracted support, and had been bolstered offshore as the U.S. dollar slipped on tame inflation data and as the Bank of Japan left rates unchanged.   

* Large stop-loss orders at $0.7555/65 seen capping any kiwi rally in near term, with worries that RBNZ may intervene again keeping $0.7600 as a distant target in the meantime.   

* NZ data calendar light this week with only migration on Wednesday and credit card data on Friday the items of any note. Finance Minister Michael Cullen appears before parliamentary committee on Wednesday on last month's budget statement.   

* RBNZ reported by local media to have made submissions to a parliamentary committee recommending a capital gains tax on property investment and limits on immigration as two methods to lower demand and inflationary pressures. The central bank has made such recommendations previously.

title: UPDATE 4-Suspected  intervention  leaves NZ dollar little changed
text:
(Updates with latest market prices)   

WELLINGTON, June 18 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank intervened for the second time in a week on Monday to push down its high-yielding currency <NZD=>, traders said, but that did little to depress demand and most of the losses were quickly recovered.   

A spokeswoman at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) declined to say whether it had intervened again -- after last week's first intervention since the New Zealand dollar was floated in 1985 -- but traders said it had sold the currency.   

The RBNZ said last week it had intervened because the kiwi was at unjustifiably high, exceptional levels. It is concerned the high exchange rate could add to the pressure on some export sectors and push up the huge current account deficit.   

The kiwi dollar initially fell half a cent to a low of around $0.75, but it had recovered to around $0.7541/45 by 0400 GMT.   

"The market is getting its head around the fact that the RBNZ is not trying to get the massive shift lower in the currency, but just keeping it pinned on the top side," said Sue Trinh, senior currency strategist at  RBC Capital Markets.

The New Zealand dollar also fell half a yen to around 92.60 yen in the wake of the reported intervention but here, too, the effect was short-lived and it rallied to 93.09/25 yen <NZDJPY=R>, in sight of a 20-year high of 93.25 yen hit on Friday.   

On the central bank's preferred trade-weighted basis, the kiwi was at 73.57 <=NZD> after sliding as low as 73.20. The central bank forecast this month the trade-weighted index would average 70.2 in the first half of 2007 and 72 in the second half.   

The central bank had stepped in on June 11 after the currency hit a post-float high of $0.7640 following a surprise New Zealand interest rate rise to 8 percent on June 7.   

CONTINUED ACTION SEEN   

New Zealand's interest rates -- the highest in the industrial world -- have attracted inflows in the so-called carry trade, when investors borrow in low-yielding currencies, such as the yen, to invest in high-yielding ones.   

Over the past year, the kiwi has risen nearly 20 percent against the U.S. dollar while the Australian dollar <AUD=>, which earlier in the month hit an 18-year high on expectations of higher interest rates, has gained around 12.5 percent.   

Traders said Monday's intervention was about half of the suspected NZ$300-NZ$500 million ($225 million-$376 million) the Reserve Bank sold last week.   

The kiwi dollar spent much of last week in a range from $0.7450-$0.7510 after the intervention, but it resumed its move higher on Friday after the Bank of Japan kept interest rates steady and U.S. data showed benign inflation pressures.   

"I think one of the key lessons out of this is that the market shouldn't get too hung up about there being some sort of line in the sand that the Reserve Bank is trying to defend," said Nick Tuffley, chief economist at ASB Bank.   

"It's giving us the signal that they are prepared to come in every now and then when there is a bit of a lift in the New Zealand dollar for reasons that are not much to do with New Zealand."   

The Reserve Bank can spend as much as it wants in kiwi-selling intervention but it can only book losses up to NZ$1 billion on the foreign exchange market under an agreement with the government.   

Given the constraint, analysts estimate the RBNZ could spend around NZ$10 billion on intervention -- just a fraction of the 35 trillion yen ($283 billion) the Japanese authorities sold in 2003 and 2004 when trying to prevent a rapid rise in the yen from damaging a fragile economy.   

It has previously said it would step in if the currency was at exceptional levels not justified by economic fundamentals, if the intervention could be expected to succeed and if it was consistent with its goal of achieving price stability.   

It has also said it would not try to go against the market trend and would be more likely to intervene in times when there was a disorderly market. ($1=NZ$1.33) ($1=123.5 yen)

title: NZ Shares End Higher; Cautious Trade As NZD, Rates Weigh
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand shares closed higher on light volume Friday in a cautious response to rallying offshore markets, although brokers say the local bourse will struggle to make further gains from here as the country's high interest rates and strong New Zealand dollar continue to weigh.   

"A lot of investors are saying the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is going to win this battle (against domestic inflation pressures)... which will lead to a slowdown in the economy and won't be good for most companies," Hamilton Hindin Greene partner Grant Williamson said.   

The central bank raised rates three times and by a combined 75 basis points between March and June to the current 8.00%. The country's high yields have in turn supported a strong New Zealand dollar exchange rate, which, despite RBNZ intervention to sell down the unit earlier this week, is still trading around US$0.7500, just shy of recent 25 year peaks.   

The NZX-50 closed up 19 points, or 0.5%, at 4212.46 on modest volume valued at NZ$83 million.   

ABN AMRO Craigs adviser Alexandra Dalzell said the high interest rates and currency, along with signs of a slowdown in retail sales, are likely to keep investors on the sidelines near term.   

"There's not a lot of new money coming into the market at the moment," Dalzell said.   

Among the gainers, Auckland International Airport rose 3% to NZ$2.82 as  Macquarie Airports' sale of its stake in Rome-based Aeroporti di Roma refreshed talk the Australian airport investor may be considering a takeover play for Auckland Airport.   

Brokers said the deal may have trouble getting past Auckland Airport's local government majority shareholder, however.   

Defensive play  Contact Energy rose 0.6% to NZ$8.82, though it is still well off recent highs.   

Discount retailer The Warehouse rose 0.2% to NZ$5.98 after Australian grocer  Woolworths Ltd. lodged an appeal against a ruling by New Zealand's competition regulator barring it from bidding for Warehouse.   

Hamilton Hindin Greene's Williamson expects rival supermarket operator Foodstuffs Ltd. to follow suit, keeping the prospect of a contested bidding process alive. Still, he thinks Friday's move was widely anticipated by the market, so it is unlikely to boost the stock beyond current levels near term - especially given the high court appeal will be a "drawn out" affair.   

Bellwether Telecom Corp. closed steady at NZ$4.62 as it awaits an announcement on a successor for Chief Executive Theresa Gattung, who will leave the company June 30.   

Exporters Pumpkin Patch and Rakon gave back some of their recent gains on profit-taking, closing down 0.3% at NZ$3.70 and 0.6% at NZ$5.22, respectively.   

-By Rachel Pannett, Dow Jones Newswires; 64-4-471-5990; rachel.pannett@dowjones.com [ 15-06-07 0517GMT ]

title: NZ dollar gains on renewed demand for yield
text:
WELLINGTON, June 15 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> firmed on Friday as a rebound in global share markets lifted investors' risk appetite, sparking fresh demand for high-yielding currencies.   

The klwi shrugged off data suggesting the housing market -- the main inflationary concern for the central bank -- was showing signs of cooling down following interest rate rises by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. For story, click on [nWEL89185].   

Some analysts said the latest survey by the Real Estate Institute of New Zealand (REINZ) supported expectations that the central bank will not raise rates again, but others said it was still to rule out the possibility of a further tightening.   

"It is perhaps too early to expect strong evidence of a turn in the housing market in response to higher interest rates delivered in March and April, and is inconclusive for the Reserve Bank," analysts at ANZ-National Bank said in a note to clients.   

At 0510 GMT the kiwi was at $0.7514/24, up from $0.7507/10 in late local trading on Thursday.   

Against the yen, it was also firmer at 92.41/55 yen <NZDJPY=R> against 92.10/22. The Bank of Japan kept interest rates on hold at 0.5 percent as expected on Friday.   

The market remained cautious of pushing the New Zealand dollar too far up after the RBNZ's surprise intervention on Monday.   

Many players expect the central bank to step in again if the the kiwi, which the bank described as being exceptionally and unjustifiably high, firms towards its pre-intervention peaks.   

The New Zealand dollar was trading just below a post float 22-year high of $0.7640 when the RBNZ intervened.   

Other data showed New Zealand manufacturing sales rebounded a seasonally adjusted 0.8 percent in the first quarter, supporting views the economy likely grew at a faster pace during the quarter.   

The manufacturing data is seen as the last piece of relevant data before gross domestic product for the first quarter is released on June 29.   

A Reuters poll preliminary median forecast is for GDP growth of 1 percent on the previous quarter.   

The benchmark NZ December 2017 bond <NZG1217=RNZL> ended flat at 6.84 percent, but outperformed U.S. and Australian bonds which both saw yields rise ahead of U.S. inflation data.

title: CHARTING ASIA: NZ  Currency  May Resume Fall Vs Dollar
text:
By Jerry Tan 
 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
    

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's unprecedented intervention Monday, which knocked the New Zealand dollar from its post-float high, has triggered negative signals for the currency's technical outlook.   

The kiwi, as the currency is known, could fall to US$0.7363 and possibly US$0.7236 in the near term, the charts indicate.   

At 0258 GMT Thursday, the New Zealand dollar was quoted at US$0.7500, having drifted between US$0.7451 and US$0.7540 since the intervention and below its post-float high of US$0.7638 set last Friday.   

Adding to the deteriorating outlook, data issued earlier Thursday showed a surprise 1.2% fall in retail sales in April, which is the steepest monthly decline in more than three years.   

The weak data could encourage expectations that the central bank may stop tightening monetary policy. New Zealand's high interest rates and, in particular, the large gap between these rates and interest rates elsewhere, has been the main factor for the currency's gains over the past 12 months. The central bank hiked its official cash rate to a high of 8.00% on June 7.   

The threat of further central bank intervention has discouraged market participants from buying the kiwi, as the currency is known.   

On the daily Kiwi-dollar chart, the currency pair is trading within a flag formation between US$0.7451 and US$0.7540.   

The flag, which is a continuation pattern and usually marks the halfway point of a sharp move, warns of risk to the downside after the current consolidation ends.   

Adding the negative kiwi-dollar outlook is the slow stochastic indicator, which is bearish and falling from an overbought level. Since it is still far from oversold, there is room for the kiwi to fall further against the dollar near-term.   

The Moving Average Convergence/Divergence, or MACD, indicator is still in bullish mode. But the positive MACD histogram bars are contracting, which points to waning upward momentum of the short-term kiwi-dollar uptrend which started from the May 25 low of US$0.7236.   

The immediate target for the bearish kiwi-dollar outlook is US$0.7363, which is the measured objective of the flag formation. Any extension of the fall would target US$0.7236, the May 25 low.   

Any violation of the US$0.7638 resistance would abort the negative kiwi outlook.

title: NZ manufacturing activity growth speeds up in May
text:
WELLINGTON, June 14 (Reuters) - New Zealand manufacturing activity accelerated in May as new orders remained strong and offset the negative impact from a strong local currency, a survey showed on Thursday.   

The seasonally adjusted Business NZ Performance of Manufacturing Index (PMI) rose to 56.8 last month from 54.4 in April, but was down from 58.1 in May last year.   

A figure over 50 indicates manufacturing is expanding, while under 50 indicates contraction.   

"The high dollar is still the hot issue, but the continued growth in new orders augurs well for future growth prospects," Business NZ economist John Pask said in a statement.   

Four of the PMI's five sub-indices rose on the previous month, with product and finished stocks showing the strongest gains. Deliveries was the only measure to decline from April.   

Pask said the strength of the New Zealand dollar was the most-mentioned negative factor facing manufacturers, but rising interest rates were also singled out along with signs of slowing demand, and a shortage of skilled labour.   

The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> hit a 22-year post-float high of $0.7640 last Friday, supported by New Zealand's high interest rates.   

However, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand intervened in the foreign exchange market on Monday for the first time since the currency floated in 1985 to bring down what it regarded as an unjustifiably high NZ dollar.   

The kiwi has settled lower at around $0.7500 since the intervention.   

A rise in the currency makes New Zealand's exports less competitive on world markets, although it also lowers the price of imported raw materials.   

The central bank last week unexpectedly raised its official cash rate to 8 percent to curb medium-term inflation pressures generated by a hot housing market and resilient domestic consumption.   

A Reuters poll has only three of 16 forecasters expecting a further rate rise, although the median risk of a rise in July was put at 40 percent.

title: NZ dollar claws back after slipping on soft data
text:
WELLINGTON, June 14 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> hovered around $0.75 on Thursday, recovering earlier losses suffered on weaker-than-expected retail sales data, though the market remained wary of further intervention by the central bank.   

The kiwi dropped nearly half a U.S. cent after data showed retail sales fell 1.2 percent in April, the biggest monthly drop in over three years, cooling expectations the central bank would raise interest rates again.   

But the currency regained its footing and gradually ground higher, supported by strength against the Aussie dollar.   

Analysts said the main focus of the market remained on the possibility of another intervention by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand after the central bank stepped into the market for the first time in over two decades on Monday.   

"I don't expect the RBNZ to be looking at intervening imminently again," said Sue Trinh, senior currency strategist at  RBC Capital Markets.

"But if the exchange rate starts creeping higher, then we'd be urging a bit of caution."   

Trinh said the RBNZ could intervene if the kiwi's trade weighted index (TWI) rose to around 74.00/25 <=NZD>, a level where it intervened on Monday.   

At 0510 GMT the kiwi was at $0.7507/10 little changed from $0.7500/03 in late local trading on Wednesday.   

On a trade-weighted basis, the New Zealand dollar firmed to 73.35 from 73.22.   

Against the Aussie, it nudged up to A$0.8944/53 <NZDAUD=R> against A$0.8918/26 after comments from Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens dampened expectations for a near-term interest rate rise.   

Stevens said softer short-term price pressures provided time to assess the need for higher interest rates.   

Some traders said Business NZ data showing manufacturing activity accelerating slightly in May also offered the New Zealand dollar some support.   

The benchmark NZ December 2017 bond <NZG1217=RNZL> ended 2 basis points lower at 6.83 percent, but lagged their U.S. and Australian counterparts on lingering concerns of another rate lift by the RBNZ.

title: FOREX -Dollar rises vs euro for fifth straight session
text:
(Recasts; updates prices)   

NEW YORK (Reuters) - The dollar rallied against the euro for the fifth consecutive session Tuesday to an 11-week high, according to Reuters data, as rising U.S. Treasury yields lured investors.   

With few major U.S. economic indicators on Tuesday, dealers stuck to buying dollars based on the recent advantage of U.S. government bond yields over other government debt, a trade some analysts said could be close to running its course even as the benchmark U.S. Treasury yield climbed to a five-year high.   

"The dollar's getting support from Treasury yields," said Ron Simpson, director of currency research at Action Economics in Tampa, Florida. "But we're waiting for U.S. retail sales, CPI and PPI later in the week which may determine the dollar's direction."   

In late afternoon trading, the euro was down 0.4 percent from late Monday at $1.3311, near its session low of 1.3309 -- the pair's lowest level since March 30.   

Against the Japanese yen, the dollar was little changed at 121.70 yen, near a 4-1/2-year high around 122.20 yen hit in January.   

The greenback also hit a 3-1/2-month high at 1.2431 Swiss francs while the dollar index touched a two-month peak.   

Expectations of a near-term cut in U.S. interest rates have faded, sending bond yields higher.   

This, coupled with continued concerns about inflationary pressures voiced by Federal Reserve policy-makers, has supported the dollar.   

Some analysts cautioned that views on the dollar could change, depending on what information is gleaned on Wednesday from the U.S. retail sales report for May. The U.S. producer price index for May will be released on Thursday, with the U.S. consumer price index for May released on Friday.   

Investors will also be watching the U.S. Treasury's semiannual Report on International Economic and Exchange Rate Policies on Wednesday, for any comments on China's yuan.   

The yuan on Tuesday posted its largest gain against the dollar since its July 2005 revaluation, rebounding from a three-day slide after the central bank set a much higher reference rate for the Chinese currency.   

U.S. policy-makers have argued that China's managed currency policy artificially weakens the yuan, favors Chinese exports and widens the U.S. trade gap. While the Treasury report is not expected to label China a currency manipulator, investors may remain cautious ahead of the report.   

Investors will also closely monitor the unveiling of a bill in the Senate on Wednesday that would allow the U.S. to impose penalties on countries setting their currencies artificially low.   

PLAYING SAFE WITH KIWI   

The New Zealand dollar was down 0.1 percent against the U.S. dollar after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand intervened in the market and weakened its currency for the first time since the kiwi was floated in 1985.   

The RBNZ's intervention has not dented investor focus on reaching for higher yields and rewarding currencies where interest rates are likely headed higher.   

Monday's RBNZ selling helped to drive the New Zealand dollar down as much as 2 percent to a low of $0.7461. On Tuesday, the New Zealand dollar was at US$0.7506, still up 6.6 percent in the year-to-date.   

With the focus on yields, sterling rose broadly after Bank of England Governor Mervyn King said UK rates may need to rise again if capacity pressures, pricing intentions and inflation expectations remain elevated. But the pound's gains were capped by slightly softer-than-expected May inflation data.   

The British pound edged up 0.3 percent to $1.9750 .

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand dollar closed slightly lower Tuesday, consolidating in a tight range as the market digested the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's intervention in the currency market Monday.   

The Kiwi fell to a low of US$0.7466 in overnight trading from US$0.7627 just before the RBNZ moved to weaken the currency.   

But it traded steadily just above US$0.7500 Tuesday.   

Sue Trinh, currency strategist at  RBC Capital Markets, tipped the Kiwi to trade sideways against the greenback overnight, noting there is little U.S. data due that could alter the current picture.   

She pegs initial support at US$0.7490, with the topside likely limited at US$0.7550 near term.   

"Having said that I wouldn't rule out a push to fresh technical highs eventually, not today or tomorrow but in coming weeks, especially with the risk the RBNZ has to tighten again," said Trinh.   

Dealers said there is a good chance of further intervention should the Kiwi approach its post-float high of US$0.7640, touched Friday.   

"A one-off move is definitely not going to stem the tide," said HSBC senior dealer Daniel Brdanovic, who added however that there is "quite a large risk" speculators will challenge the RBNZ over further intervention.   

A government policy adviser told Dow Jones Newswires the central bank sees US$0.7600 as an area of concern, with anything above that at this stage in the current economic cycle as grounds for intervention.   

Dealers generally didn't think the RBNZ intended to trigger a sharp downside move and had achieved its goal of ironing out a peak in the currency cycle.   

"They've managed to get the currency down on a trade-weighted index basis. I think it has stabilized things and put some of the crosses back into the middle of recent ranges," said Mike Hollows, director of trading at HIFX.   

He noted the Kiwi pulled back from A$0.9050 against its Australian counterpart to "more realistic" levels near A$0.8900.   

The New Zealand dollar closed at Y91.65, down from Y91.70 Monday, with good demand on dips still evident, dealers said.   

Government bonds rallied at the short end, while the interest rate swap market was also stronger.   

"This intervention has probably caused some uncertainty in terms of future rate moves. It's made people less confident there's going to be another hike and maybe happier to buy fixed interest, either to receive on the swaps or buy bonds," said one trader.   

Another trader said the market was correcting last week's selloff after the RBNZ raised the Official Cash Rate to 8.0%, and would now wait for second-quarter data before any more big moves.

title: NZ Shares End Up As Exporters Benefit From RBNZ  Intervention
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand shares closed higher on modest volume Tuesday as investors gave a cautious show of approval to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's decision to weaken the soaring New Zealand dollar exchange rate.   

Currency-sensitive exporters like manufacturers Fisher & Paykel Healthcare and Rakon, and children's clothing retailer Pumpkin Patch led the market gains, buoyed by the central bank's decision to sell down the currency late Monday, pushing the New Zealand dollar from around US$0.7620 to an overnight low of US$0.7466.   

But ABN AMRO Craigs adviser Jennifer Moreton said the positive response from the equities market was tentative, with investors not yet convinced the RBNZ action will have a lasting impact.   

With the New Zealand dollar still trading above US$0.7500, investors will likely remain on the sidelines near term, to see if the RBNZ acts again, she said.   

"I think it's a conscious decision to watch the market and wait for opportunities," Moreton said. She also noted the bank's decision to act in the currency market by selling the Kiwi dollar was somewhat at odds with its tightening track on interest rates, keeping investors in "wait and see" mode.   

The NZX-50 closed up 22 points, or 0.5%, at 4227.56 on light volume valued at just NZ$86 million.   

Medical equipment maker Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, which generates around 60% of its sales in U.S. dollars, closed up 1.7% at NZ$3.53.   

GPS parts manufacturer Rakon rose 2.5% to NZ$5.33, and Pumpkin Patch, which on Friday warned the strong New Zealand dollar exchange rate and high interest rates will dent fiscal 2007 earnings, rallied 3% to NZ$3.75.   

Rural services firm PGG Wrightson, another beneficiary of a lower New Zealand dollar, rose 1.2% to NZ$1.76.   

In contrast, pay television operator Sky Network Television, which pays for much of its programing in U.S. dollars, fell 0.9% intraday but closed flat at NZ$5.64.   

Discount retailer The Warehouse continued to regain ground after being sold heavily in the wake of a Commerce Commission decision to knock back rival takeover bids by supermarket operators Woolworths and Foodstuffs.   

The stock closed up 0.8% at NZ$6.12 on talk the pair may appeal the decision, or that an alternative privatization plan might surface involving majority shareholder and founder Stephen Tindall.

title: NZ dollar holds near 75 cents, RBNZ and data eyed
text:
WELLINGTON, June 13 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> settled in a modest range against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday as investors remained wary of possible central bank intervention and waited for data that might influence future rate rises.   

The currency has stayed within a moderate range around $0.7500 since the Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised on Monday in an unprecedented intervention to sell what it regarded as an overvalued currency.   

"The kiwi's not been allowed to stray too far, with bargain hunters looking to buy when it dips and people a shade nervous about going too high because the RBNZ may reappear," said a dealer.   

At 0515 GMT the kiwi was at $0.7500/03 from $0.7516/25 in late local trading on Tuesday. The currency traded a $0.7480-0.7513 range.   

The currency has found $0.7470/80 a solid support level so far, but has been seen as capped at $0.7540/50 in the near term.   

The kiwi was up around 0.6 percent against the yen <NZDJPY=R> as it benefited from a move higher by the U.S. dollar, which has been buoyed by a rise in bond yields.   

The kiwi and the neighbouring Aussie have gained as investors covered short positions after a drop in Asian stock markets failed to spark an unwind of carry trades.   

The currencies have been major beneficiaries of carry trades, where investors borrow in low yield currencies such as the yen to invest in high yielders.   

New Zealand retail sales data is due on Thursday, with expectations in a Reuters poll of a flat outcome for the month of April, with core sales excluding motor vehicles sales and services also expected to be flat. March month sales surprised with a seasonally adjusted 1.3 percent rise.   

The strength of domestic consumption has been a factor in the RBNZ raising rates, which in turn has spurred the kiwi's appreciation.   

"The data covers the after the first two cash rate hikes, and so may yield the first indications of a softening in household consumption," said BNZ strategist Danica Hampton.   

Data on Wednesday showed New Zealand food prices rose 0.3 percent in May.   

New Zealand debt was weaker along the yield curve by as much as seven basis points as U.S. Treasuries recovered from an early slide that had sent yields up to a five-year high as upbeat economic data squashed expectations of a Federal Reserve rate cut.   

The benchmark NZ December 2017 bond <NZG1217=RNZL> ended seven basis points higher at 6.86 percent, but still outperformed U.S. and Australian counterparts on expectations that New Zealand rate rises may have come to an end.
