title: ANALYSIS-NZ  central bank  to  intervene  again - but lightly
text:
WELLINGTON, June 12 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank is expected to intervene again to weaken the kiwi dollar, but not risk an all-out war against speculators because of its shoestring budget.   

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ), which on Monday used its intervention powers for the first time since the currency was floated in 1985, is unlikely to draw a line and to defend a set level, a method previously used by the Bank of Japan, analysts said.   

"Having declared war on the New Zealand dollar foreign exchange markets, the RBNZ now has to play a smart 'hit-and-run' tactic to keep the markets guessing and make their attacks effective," said Roger Kerr, director of Asia-Pacific Risk Management.   

It's a juggling act because the central bank's main task -- reining in inflation -- has prompted it to raise interest rates to 8 percent, the highest in the industrialised world.   

Monday's intervention signals the central bank thinks rates have peaked, some analysts believe, although the authority hasn't spelled that out.   

Even without further hikes, the yield on the kiwi is big enough to keep attracting so-called carry trade, where investors borrow low-yielding currencies, such as the yen, to fund the purchase of high-yielding assets, such as the New Zealand dollar.   

It's tough to stem that flow, certainly with the central bank's limited intervention budget, analysts said.   

LIMITS   

Westpac Bank currency strategist Michael Gordon estimates the central bank could spend around NZ$10 billion on intervention, just a fraction of the 35 trillion yen ($288 billion) the BOJ sold in 2003 and 2004 in trying to prevent the rapid rise in the yen from damaging the then-fragile economy.   

"If a George Soros look-alike wanted to take the RBNZ on, they just keep buying NZDs until the RBNZ runs out of selling resources," Kerr said.   

Soros is a hedge fund manager who pocketed more than $1 billion after he out-muscled the Bank of England in its defence of a weakening sterling.   

Traders speculate the RBNZ sold around NZ$300-NZ$500 million ($225-$376 million) against the U.S. dollar and possibly the yen, which sent the currency tumbling as much as 2 percent from just below the 22-year post float high of $0.7640.   

The Reserve Bank can only book losses up to NZ$1 billion on the foreign exchange market under an agreement with the government.   

The New Zealand dollar has so far stabilised around $0.75 <NZD=>, down over one U.S. cent from a 22-year peak on Friday, but still up more than 19 percent from a year earlier.   

CARRY TRADE   

Some economists think the RBNZ will aim to smooth the currency's rise, in a similar way to the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA).   

The RBA has not officially intervened since 2001, when it supported the Aussie dollar when it fell to 50 U.S. cents <AUD=>. But it regularly buys and sells the currency -- it has sold over A$1 billion during the first four months of this year.   

But even a flexible approach could prove to be in vain given the power of the carry trade.   

"If the economy remains strong and they continue to tighten policy in response, and commodity prices continue to rise, it's difficult to see why the currency won't go higher," said  Deutsche Bank chief economist Darren Gibbs.   

Many analysts had expected any intervention by the central bank to come after it had finished raising rates because it had previously said it would not try to go against the market trend when intervening.   

On Monday, the Reserve Bank said the intervention did not prejudge the future direction of monetary policy, but analysts said the action diluted the central bank's message that it was still worried about inflation.   

"The market's conclusion after yesterday was that, if the bank is intervening in the currency, then presumably we're close to the top in rates, if not at the top," Deutsche's Gibbs said.

title: RPT-RBNZ battles Japan  FX  day-traders post- intervention
text:
TOKYO, June 12 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank faces a tough opponent after having intervened in currency markets on Monday to weaken the high-flying New Zealand dollar: Japanese FX traders eager to buy the high-yielding "kiwi" currency.   

Japanese day traders and other individual traders nearly doubled their bets on a stronger New Zealand dollar on Monday after the selling by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand in its first intervention since the NZ dollar was allowed to trade freely in 1985.   

Data from the Tokyo Financial Exchange showed that Japanese margin traders -- who use borrowed funds to boost the size of their bets -- raised their positions in the New Zealand dollar to $347 million from $180 million the previous day.   

While the positions at the TFX are not large relative to the overall market, analysts said they typify the trading style of Japanese investors: selling higher-yielding foreign currencies when they strike peaks against the yen, but then buying when they tumble.   

"Japanese retail investors were not discouraged by the authority's action," said Masafumi Yamamoto, currency strategist at Nikko  Citigroup in Tokyo. "It is likely that Japanese retail investors will continue to increase their foreign currency exposure, especially that of high yielding currencies like NZD."   

The NZ dollar rose nearly half a percent to 91.65 yen <NZDJPY=R> on Tuesday, up from Monday's low near 90.80 yen but off the 17-year high near 93.00 yen struck late last week. The kiwi has steadily risen over the past seven years against the yen, more than doubling in value from its lows in late 2000.   

FX margin trading has boomed in the past few years as individuals look for ways to make money in higher-yielding currencies.   

The Financial Futures Association of Japan, which tracks FX margin activity, estimates that trading volume surged to 109.2 trillion yen ($898.2 billion) in the January-March quarter, up 40 percent from the previous quarter.   

Japanese investors have flocked to online FX trading and mutual funds featuring foreign assets for better returns, with short-term domestic rates still just 0.5 percent compared with New Zealand's 8 percent or 5.25 percent in the United States.   

Such Japanese demand for foreign currencies and assets has helped to spur the carry trade, in which the low-yielding currency is used by investors as a cheap source of funds to buy higher-yielding assts.   

New Zealand authorities have previously tried to tackle the Japanese hunger for their currency, especially uridashi bonds denominated in the New Zealand dollar and sold directly to Japanese households.   

Officials from New Zealand's Treasury and central bank visited banks and securities houses in Tokyo about a year and a half ago, saying investors needed to be warned of the risks of a potential sharp fall in the NZ dollar.   

But Japanese investors have been undeterred, and the New Zealand currency remains among the most popular for uridashi bonds. ($1=121.58 Yen)

title: RPT- FOREX -Dollar firm, rising U.S. yields eyed for support
text:
TOKYO, June 12 (Reuters) - The dollar was steady against the yen and euro on Tuesday as investors focused on rising U.S. bond yields, while the New Zealand dollar inched up a day after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand intervened to weaken the currency.   

The market was closely watching whether benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yields would re-test last week's near five-year peak of 5.25 percent to determine how much further the U.S. currency could advance.   

Treasury yields have surged on diminishing expectations for Federal Reserve rate cuts and worries about more central bank monetary tightening around the world to combat inflation pressures, helping lift the dollar to a two-month high versus the euro.   

"There is a risk for yields to ease back after a rapid rise, but if upcoming data is strong, yields will likely come under upward pressure while the dollar may be supported," said Masafumi Yamamoto, currency strategist at Nikko  Citigroup.

The dollar was little changed around 121.65 yen hovering near the 4-1/2-year high of 122.20 yen struck in January.   

The euro was steady around $1.3363 near a two-month low around $1.3320 touched on Friday as the 10-year Treasury yield surged to match the Fed's target overnight rate of 5.25 percent. The euro edged up slightly to 162.60 yen   

The pound edged up after Bank of England Governor Mervyn King said late on Monday that British interest rates may need to rise again from the current 5.5 percent if signs of price pressures and capacity constraints stay high.   

Sterling was up 0.1 percent against the dollar at $1.9715   

With inflation concerns rising, analysts said they will be closely watching inflation data for Britain and the United States due out this week.   

British consumer price figures will be released at 0830 GMT on Tuesday. Core consumer prices are forecast to have risen 0.4 percent in May from the previous month and 3.3 percent year-on-year.   

"The dollar will be supported as long as the market sees rising interest rates reflecting firmness in the U.S. economy," said Masashi Kurabe, a senior manager of forex trading at  Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ.   

"But if inflation picks up to push interest rates higher, that may end up causing a triple fall in stocks, bonds and the dollar," Kurabe said.   

LITTLE IMPACT ON CARRY   

The New Zealand central bank's intervention to sell its currency after the kiwi hit a 22-year high versus the U.S. dollar last week has done little to cool carry trades, in which investors use low-yielding currencies such as the yen to pick up assets in high-yielding ones, traders said.   

Monday's RBNZ selling helped to drive the New Zealand dollar down as much as 2 percent to a low of $0.7467 The kiwi was up 0.1 percent at $0.7510, against $0.7640 on Friday -- the highest since the currency was allowed to trade freely in 1985.   

New Zealand's action was seen as an isolated move with little overall market impact, as it ran counter to the trend of global monetary tightening in line with a solid global economy, traders said.   

The RBNZ raised rates to 8.0 percent last week, the highest in the industrialised world.   

"It was contradictory to sell the New Zealand dollar while tightening credit the previous week," Kurabe said. "But I see the intervention as part of its smoothing operation. The RBNZ has no intention of pushing the kiwi further down but may raise rates again due to inflation concerns." (Additional reporting by Tetsushi Kajimoto)

title: Dairy payouts cloud inflation battle - RBNZ's Bollard
text:
WELLINGTON, June 12 (Reuters) - An increase in New Zealand dairy farmer incomes and spending will make it more difficult to keep inflation under control, the central bank governor said on Tuesday.   

Alan Bollard said higher commodity prices, particularly for the dairy industry, was fundamentally good news for the New Zealand economy, but how the higher incomes were spent might add further pressures to an already stretched economy.   

"But to the extent that some of it is spent, it may make it harder to achieve our medium-term inflation target," Bollard said in speech notes to an agricultural group.   

Bollard made no mention of the current level of the New Zealand dollar, which the Reserve Bank of New Zealand has described as unjustifiable and exceptional.   

On Monday, the central bank intervened and sold New Zealand dollars because of the currency's high level, triggering a fall of over 1.5 percent. It was the RBNZ's first intervention in the foreign exchange market since the kiwi was floated in 1985.   

The central bank last week raised its official cash rate to 8 percent, the highest in the industrialised world, because of strong inflation pressures.   

The RBNZ said a factor behind the rate rise was a forecast 27 percent lift in payouts to the country's approximate 12,000 dairy farmers, which would add around NZ$2 billion to the economy and risked stoking demand and inflation.   

"This effect could be compounded even further if these higher incomes become reflected in higher rural land prices," Bollard said.   

He said the inflationary impact of the higher dairy payouts would be partly offset by the strong exchange rate.   

"The high New Zealand dollar will dampen medium-term inflation pressures by suppressing activity in exporting sectors not lucky enough to be receiving high commodity returns," Bollard said.   

The central bank is required to keep inflation between 1 percent to 3 percent on average over the medium-term. Inflation in the year to March 31 was 2.5 percent, although it remained outside the target range between mid-2005 and mid-2006.   

The dairy industry is New Zealand's single biggest export earner, accounting for around 20 percent of exports and generating around 7 percent of gross domestic product.   

Bollard said a combination of high demand and constrained supply was behind the strong rise in world dairy prices, which were likely to stay at high levels in the short term.   

Higher world commodity prices would usually be associated with a higher exchange rate, which had dampened dairy farmer incomes but given consumers gains through lower import prices.

title: DJ Dollar In Ranges As  Forex  Mkts Focus On New Zealand
text:
NEW YORK, Jun 11, 2007 (DJCS via Comtex) --   

By Dan Molinski
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES
   

The dollar is in tight ranges against its top rivals early Monday, with currency markets focused on New Zealand after its central bank stepped in overnight to curb the meteoric rise of its currency.   

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand confirmed in a statement that it intervened in the foreign exchange market to sell the New Zealand dollar, the first time it's done so since it free-floated its currency in 1985.   

"We regard current levels of the exchange rate as exceptional and unjustified in terms of the economic fundamentals," Reserve Bank Governor Alan Bollard said.   

The bank did not say how much it sold, though several traders said it appears the bank sold up to NZ$1.5 billion. The move knocked the New Zealand dollar to $0.7503 recently after it reached a 25-year high of about $0.7640 late Friday.   

In other currencies early Monday, the euro was trading at $1.3348 from $1.3364 late Friday, while the dollar was at Y121.73 compared with Y121.75, according to EBS. The euro was at Y162.44 compared with Y162.67 late Friday. The dollar was at CHF1.2386 compared with CHF1.2359, while the U.K. pound traded at $1.9668 from $1.9678 late Friday.   

After the intervention by New Zealand's central bank, analysts are wondering who else may follow suit. Several currencies are currently trading at multi-year highs against the generally weak U.S. dollar.   

Such intervention also raises questions about the profit-potential for carry trades, where investors borrow currency that offer low interest rates, such as the yen, to buy those that pay high yields, such as the New Zealand dollar. Perhaps, analysts said, the trend by New Zealand and other high-yielding currencies to keep offering even-higher rates will end.   

"Markets may well read [Monday's] move as the RBNZ showing a surprising degree of uncertainty, if not reluctance, to hike again," said analysts at Credit Suisse in an email. "A continuation of intervention would be clearly inconsistent with further rate hikes."   

The news out of New Zealand has shifted focus away from the U.S. dollar, which hit a two-month high against the euro on Friday after a sharp rise in U.S. bond yields boosted demand for the greenback.   

The rise in bond yields comes as investors continue to price out the now slim odds that the Federal Reserve will cut interest rates anytime this year. Improved U.S. economic data has swayed many economists away from the idea that rate cuts would be needed to help kick-start an economy that remains sluggish, partly due to a housing crunch.   

Overnight, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Sandra Pianalto said housing price adjustments have slowed U.S. economic growth, but said there has been no spill-over into the consumer sector yet.   

Still, she said at a conference in Dublin, a contagion effect remains a risk. "We are watching that very closely," she said.   

The dollar reacted little to Pianalto's comments, however, and stayed in tight ranges against the euro and yen.   

There is no important U.S. data report out Monday, and traders said the dollar is likely to trade mostly sideways ahead of a raft of U.S. economic data that will be released starting on Tuesday. Friday's consumer price inflation data will be a key report.   

-By Dan Molinski, Dow Jones Newswires; 201-938-2245; dan.molinski@dowjones.com   

(Shri Navaratnam in Wellington and Quentin Fottrell in Dublin contributed to this report.)   

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: RPT-UPDATE 2-NZ  central bank intervenes , sending kiwi sliding
text:
(Adds more analyst comment, background)   

WELLINGTON, June 11 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank intervened on Monday for the first time in more than two decades to cap a soaring New Zealand dollar, spurring a 2 percent fall in the currency.   

Saying the kiwi dollar was unjustifiably high, the central bank entered the market to rein in a currency that had jumped 28 percent in the last year to hit a 22-year peak on Friday.   

"As stated in our June monetary policy statement, we regard current levels of the exchange rate as exceptional and unjustified in terms of the economic fundamentals," Alan Bollard, governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, said in a statement.   

The kiwi slid to a session low of $0.7486 after the intervention, down from Friday's high of $0.7640. The neighbouring Australian dollar also fell.   

The central bank's first intervention since the currency was floated in 1985 came after a surprise interest rate hike to 8 percent last week to rein in inflation and the reappointment of Bollard for a second five-year term two weeks ago.   

New Zealand's high rates -- the highest in the industrial world -- have attracted inflows in the so-called carry trade, when investors borrow in low-yielding currencies, such as the yen, to invest in high-yielding ones.   

The inflows helped push up the currency 3.5 percent in the last month alone but analysts said the intervention was unlikely to turn the currency around.   

"Today's action shows they've lost patience with the currency. It's not going to send the currency into a bearish mode. What they are trying to do is cut off the peaks of the currency," said Khoon Goh, senior economist at ANZ-National Bank.   

"All they're doing is avoiding sending the currency to the 78 U.S. cent level, which it looked destined for."   

CARRY TRADES   

The New Zealand dollar also fell around 2 percent against the yen <NZDJPY=R> to about 91.13 yen, down from a 17-year high near 93 yen struck on Friday.   

"For the NZ dollar, it's all negative short term. But in the end, economic fundamentals will win the day," said Stephen Toplis, head of research at Bank of New Zealand. "If domestic growth fails to wane and the central bank remains up against it on the inflation front, the NZ dollar will remain well-supported."   

The Reserve Bank of NZ has had the power to intervene in the foreign exchange market since the currency was floated in March 1985, but it had never used the power until Monday.   

The neighbouring Australian dollar <AUD=>, also a high-yielding currency, was caught in the sell-off and fell to a low around $0.8395 from $0.8430, before rebounding slightly. Australian financial markets were closed for a public holiday.   

"I do not think this will prompt a reversal of carry trades, although it will likely moderate the pace at which the currency appreciates. The currency will keep on its firm trend and may even renew its high (against the yen)," said Masaki Fukui, senior market economist,  Mizuho Corporate Bank in Tokyo.   

"The same goes for other high-yielding currencies, although the Australian dollar was dragged down as well today ... The basic trend (of yen carry trades) has not changed.   

KIWI STILL BULLISH   

The central bank had previously said it would only step in if the currency was at exceptional levels not justified by economic fundamentals, if the intervention could be expected to succeed, and if it was consistent with the central bank's role of achieving price stability.   

It has also said it would not try to go against the market trend and would be more likely to intervene in times when there was a disorderly market.   

"Without historical precedent, it will be difficult to judge how long the RBNZ will be in the market to weaken the NZD, and how much weaker NZD could go," said Sue Trinh, senior currency strategist,  RBC Capital Markets in Sydney,   

"But the international evidence on successful currency intervention is mixed, and intervention is a distraction from the RBNZ's core policy objective, which is to contain medium-term inflation within 1-3 percent, where the most potent instrument is the official cash rate."   

Bollard has described the currency as being exceptionally and unjustifiably high in the central bank's past two policy statements.   

Asked by Reuters on Friday if the comments were deliberately used to raise intervention as an issue, Bollard said: "We just want to be quite transparent about our view about the currency, and those are our views."   

In the same interview, he said some of the kiwi's rise was justified by high commodity prices and expressed doubt that the RBNZ's own rate rises were to blame.   

The RBNZ forecast in its June monetary policy statement the trade-weighted New Zealand dollar <=NZD> would average 68.6 in the first half of 2007 and 68.3 in the latter half.   

As of Monday it was at 73.45, below an all-time high of 74.54 reached in December 2005. (Additional reporting by Tokyo bureau)

NEW YORK, June 11 (Reuters) - The dollar rallied to a 3-1/2 month high against the Swiss franc on Monday, with U.S. 10-year Treasury yields over 5 percent and investors largely ignoring the New Zealand central bank's first market intervention in 22 years.   

The New Zealand dollar posted its largest decline in 15 months at one point after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand sold its own currency, but there was only limited impact on carry trades in which investors buy high-yielding currencies like the New Zealand dollar funded by borrowing low-cost currencies such as the Swiss france or the Japanese yen.   

"Have the conditions for the carry trade altered? No," said Joe Trevisani, chief market analyst at FX Solutions, in Saddle River, New Jersey. "Everyone is looking over their shoulder but for now we are still close enough to highs on the kiwi that if things calm down, it will go higher."   

The U.S. dollar briefly peaked just above 1.2400 Swiss francs <CHF=>, before settling at 1.2380 francs, up 0.3 percent from late Friday.   

The New Zealand dollar fell 1.7 percent to US$0.7510 <NZD=>, well off highs of US$0.7640 reached on Friday, the strongest level since the currency was floated in 1985.   

The U.S. dollar climbed for the fourth consecutive session against the euro, with the euro down 0.1 percent at $1.3354 <EUR=>.   

The RBNZ intervention to curb the New Zealand dollar came four days after the central bank surprised markets by raising its key interest rate to 8 percent, the highest benchmark rate in the industrialized world.   

Central bank intervention is one of the biggest risks to carry trades, but the modest impact on the broader market showed the resilience of the seemingly ubiquitous trading strategy.   

"After months of warning, the action (by the RBNZ) backs up the central bank's stance," Camilla Sutton, currency strategist with Scotia Capital in Toronto, wrote in a note.   

"Fall-on effects on carry have been evident, but remain somewhat muted. We would expect today's news to benefit the Australian dollar/New Zealand dollar cross ... ," she said.   

Against the yen, the New Zealand dollar tumbled 1.6 percent to 91.47 yen <NZDJPY=R>. The dollar was little changed against the yen at 121.74 yen <JPY=>.   

The spread of the implied benchmark U.S. interest rate in December 2008 over the euro zone equivalent was near its widest in three months, with fixed-income markets reflecting low implied chances that the Federal Reserve would have to loosen monetary policy this year or next.   

"We think that as a result of the repricing of the U.S. yield curve here and the capitulation in terms of U.S. growth deceleration ... the dollar deterioration is likely to pause over the very short term," Jack Malvey, chief global fixed income strategist with  Lehman Brothers, said at the Reuters Investment Outlook Summit.   

"But in a 12- to 18-month period we still envision the dollar to weaken particularly against Asian currencies."   

With no major U.S. economic data on Monday, dealers kept liquid currencies, other than the New Zealand dollar, in narrow ranges, waiting for the May U.S. retail sales report on Wednesday.   

Dealers said robust risk appetite, supported by gains in global equity markets, could mean buyers dip their toe back into the New Zealand dollar market later this week, barring any further action from the central bank.   

The Australian dollar slipped 0.2 percent versus the U.S. dollar <AUD=> to US$0.8435, but it jumped 1.5 percent against the New Zealand dollar to NZ$1.1219 <AUDNZD=>.

title: Aussie dlr supported by rate outlook, eyes cenbank
text:
SYDNEY, June 12 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar nudged up on Tuesday, benefiting from speculation that domestic interest rates could rise in coming months, as well as firm commodity prices and a shift out of the New Zealand currency.   

 Fresh merger and acquisition news also underpinned the Aussie, which last week scaled a 18-year high of $0.8476 against the U.S. dollar.   

 Late on Monday, Canada's  Brookfield Asset Management Inc.  offered to buy construction and property firm  Multiplex Group  in a deal worth A$4.2 billion.   

 "In the short term, the M&A story, rising stock markets and commodities will continue to be supportive of the Aussie," said Robert Rennie, chief currency strategist at  Westpac Banking Corp.

 "But all eyes are on the Reserve Bank chief as it has been a while since we have heard something from the central bank."   

 Governor Glenn Stevens speaks at a conference on Thursday and is expected to sound a hawkish note after a slew of strong economic data last week reignited concerns about price pressures. That could give a lift to the Aussie, analysts said.   

 Financial markets are pricing in a 24 percent chance Australia's central bank would lift rates here next month. That risk increases to 54 percent in August and 72 percent by September.   

 At 4:00 p.m. (0600 GMT) the Aussie dollar <AUD=> was quoted at $0.8434/37, compared with $0.8421/26 here late on Friday, and after having eased a low of $0.8405 in offshore trade.   

 It also rose against the New Zealand dollar <AUDNZD=R>, trading around $1.1208/19, rising from $1.1031 on Friday.   

 The Aussie eased in the kiwi dollar's wake on Monday after New Zealand's central bank intervened to weaken the currency -- the first time it has taken such action since the kiwi was floated in 1985.   

 However, analysts said if the Reserve Bank of New Zealand steps in again to curb the kiwi's strength it could see yield-hungry investors switch into the Aussie.   

 "In an environment where carry trades are very much alive, and where the kiwi would have generally outperformed, the intervention adds a two-sided risk in the short term," said John Kyriakopoulos, currency strategist at National Australia Bank.   

 "The Aussie would benefit from this as we have already seen some of the switch happen from the kiwi to the Aussie."   

 The Aussie as well as the New Zealand dollar have both benefited from carry trades, where investors borrow in the low yielding Japanese yen to buy an asset bearing a higher return.   

 The kiwi <NZD=> steadied on Tuesday after falling nearly 2 percent on Monday's intervention, which traders speculated was worth between NZ$300 million and NZ$500 million.

title: NZ dlr recovers some losses made on  intervention
text:
(Adds analyst comments, updates price)   

WELLINGTON, June 12 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> recouped some of its losses on Tuesday, steadying after an unprecedented intervention by the central bank the previous day had had sent it tumbling around 2 percent.   

The currency was little moved after a closely-watched speech by Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Alan Bollard to an agricultural group provided few surprises.   

"Some of the Asian accounts are starting to doubt whether or not the Reserve Bank has got any muscle, but I think it's more about a signalling effect than the weight of money behind the intervention," said Danica Hampton, currency strategist at Bank of New Zealand.   

At 0559 GMT the kiwi was at $0.7516/25, having traded a relatively narrow $0.7504-0.7527 range.   

The currency fell as low as $0.7465 in post-New Zealand trade on Monday, pushed down also by a stronger U.S. dollar. It had been trading slightly below $0.7640, a 22-year post high hit on Friday, when the central bank intervened.   

The RBNZ said it stepped into the market on Monday, for the first since the currency was floated in 1985, because the currency was at unjustifiable and exceptional levels.   

Traders speculate the RBNZ sold around NZ$300-NZ$500 million ($225-$376 million) of kiwi dollars against the U.S. dollar, and possibly the yen, halting the kiwi's meteoric rise following last week's interest rate rise.   

In his speech, Bollard made no mention of the level of the kiwi dollar but did warn that higher payouts to dairy farmers, fuelled by strong commodity prices, might add to an already-stretched economy.

title: RPT-ANALYSTS VIEW 5-NZ dlr tumbles on RBNZ selling  intervention
text:
TOKYO, June 11 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar tumbled as much as 1.8 percent from near a 22-year peak against the U.S. dollar on Monday as New Zealand's central bank intervened to sell the currency, calling its value exceptionally and unjustifiably high.   

The kiwi initially plunged on rumours of intervention that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand later confirmed, the first such intervention since the central bank allowed the currency to trade freely in 1985. For the RBNZ's statement, click on [ID:nNZF000394].   

MARKET REACTION   

- The NZ dollar fell 1.8 percent to a low of $0.7497 and was last at $0.7500 <NZD=D4> compared with $0.7635 in late U.S. trade on Friday. The kiwi also fell more than 1 percent against the euro <EURNZD=R> and yen <NZDJPY=R>.   

- The kiwi jumped to a post-float peak of $0.7640 last Friday after the RBNZ surprised markets by raising interest rates last week to 8.0 percent, the highest in the industrialised world.   

- The Australian dollar shed 0.5 percent to $0.8416 <AUD=D4> on the kiwi's drop, but other major currencies were stable. The euro slipped 0.15 percent to $1.3352 <EUR=> from late U.S. trade Friday.   

COMMENTS   

(Following comments were made after RBNZ confirmation)   

ROBIN CLEMENTS, SENIOR ECONOMIST,  UBS NZ, CHRISTCHURCH   

"The currency intervention capacity was described as adding another instrument to the monetary policy tool kit. Now the RBNZ has actually used it. But will the intervention have a meaningful impact on the exchange rate? That is, was it opportune?   

"Presumably the RBNZ thought the intervention today could be effective. As it stands the NZ dollar is down over 1 percent against the U.S. dollar, so the jury is out. Time will tell."   

- - - -   

KHOON GOH, SENIOR ECONOMIST, ANZ-NATIONAL BANK, WELLINGTON   

"Today's action shows they've lost patience with the currency.   

"It's not going to the send the currency into a bearish mode. I think what they (Reserve Bank) are trying to do is cut off the peaks of the currency. All they're doing is avoiding sending the currency to the 78 U.S. cent level, which it looked destined for.   

"They will probably stop if they feel that the New Zealand dollar has fallen to a level where they feel comfortable with. If not, they will continue."   

- - - -   

STEPHEN TOPLIS, HEAD OF RESEARCH, BANK OF NEW ZEALAND, WELLINGTON   

"For the NZ dollar, it's all negative short term. But in the end, economic fundamentals will win the day. If domestic growth fails to wane and the central bank remains up against it on the inflation front, the NZ dollar will remain well-supported.   

"Even after today's correction, it should be noted that the NZ dollar is not far different from where it as immediately after the RBNZ's monetary policy statement."   

- - - -   

SUE TRINH, SENIOR CURRENCY STRATEGIST, RBC CAPITAL MARKETS, SYDNEY   

"We have been surprised by this intervention since the RBNZ has previously outlined four necessary conditions for intervention, and of the four conditions, there is one factor that put the odds of intervention by the RBNZ as very low -- intervention to weaken the currency would have to be consistent with Policy Targets Agreement (PTA) (i.e. the RBNZ's monetary policy objectives).   

"The RBNZ needs a high currency given non-tradable inflation pressure, and any intervention to weaken the currency risks causing a negative inflationary impact, which would be contrary to the PTA.   

"Late Friday, RBNZ's Governor Bollard said that New Zealand still had medium-term inflation to deal with.   

"This is the first time in the post float era that the RBNZ has intervened in the currency markets. Without historical precedent, it will be difficult to judge how long the RBNZ will be in the market to weaken the NZD, and how much weaker NZD could go.   

"But the international evidence on successful currency intervention is mixed, and intervention is a distraction from the RBNZ's core policy objective, which is to contain medium-term inflation within 1-3 percent, where the most potent instrument is the OCR.   

"Lastly, the RBNZ has limited capital to play with (the RBNZ was given an additional NZ$1 billion for the specific purposes of intervening in 2004, and to absorb marked-to-market losses).   

"For these reasons, a cyclical top in NZD has yet to be put in place as long as the USD is weak, and the RBNZ is tightening. NZD/USD faces support at 0.7495. Below there is more sturdy support at 0.7405."   

- - - -   

MASAKI FUKUI, SENIOR MARKET ECONOMIST, MIZUHO CORPORATE BANK, TOKYO   

"I do not think this will prompt a reversal of carry trades, although it will likely moderate the pace at which the currency appreciates. The currency will keep on its firm trend and may even renew its high (against the yen).   

"The same goes for other high-yielding currencies, although the Australian dollar was dragged down as well today ... The basic trend (of yen carry trades) has not changed.   

"That has much to do with Japanese investors buying higher-yielding currencies, while foreign investors may bear in mind the need to reduce their carry trade positions amid growing uncertainty over equity markets and the global economy."   

- - - -   

(Following comments were made before RBNZ confirmation)   

KOJI FUKAYA, SENIOR CURRENCY STRATEGIST, DEUTSCHE BANK, TOKYO   

"It would not surprise me if there was an intervention, given that the central bank had made cautious comments on appreciation of the currency.   

"It may impact other high-yielding currencies by unnerving investors conducting carry trade who have become wary about rising intererst rates worldwide.   

"That would prompt those investors to cover yen short positions against cross currencies such as the euro, rather than the dollar.   

"But such an adjustment will unlikely last long, as long as global economies stay in the current sound conditions.   

"Still, if an adjustment of overextended positions among investors drags on, the yen would appreciate, pushing euro/yen as low as 157-158 yen and dollar-yen to below 120 yen." - - - -   

MAGNUS PRIM, CHIEF ASIA CURRENCY STRATEGIST, SEB, SINGAPORE   

"They are taking steps obviously. They are a bit concerned about the development we have seen for some time in the New Zealand dollar. But having said that, it's very hard for intervention like this to turn the trend. The aim is not to turn the trend, the aim is to slow down the development we have seen."   

He did not expect the move to have any major impact on other currencies.   

- - - -   

TOMOKO FUJII, HEAD OF ECONOMICS AND STRATEGY JAPAN, BANK OF AMERICA, TOKYO   

"There had been comments saying that the currency levels (of the New Zealand dollar) can't be justified by fundamentals. So it's not a big surprise that such rumours have emerged.   

"At the moment, it's an issue specific to the New Zealand dollar, although there could be some spillover.   

"I don't think there will be a direct impact on investor risk appetite just from what happened with the New Zealand dollar.   

"With regard to the yen, there will be a focus on investor risk appetite and on Chinese economic data due this week.   

"The situation seems alright but if equities fall more than investors can bear, there would be a risk of a steeper-than-expected reversal of yen carry trades."   

- - - -   

BACKGROUND   

- In the past two RBNZ policy statements, the central bank has said the NZ dollar was exceptionally and unjustifiably high based on medium-term fundamentals, which some analysts had seen as signalling the potential risk of intervention.   

- In an interview with Reuters last week, RBNZ Governor Alan Bollard said the kiwi was "high and hurting" and that he was not convinced New Zealand's steep short-term rates were pushing up the currency. For interview highlights, click on [ID:nWEL14507]

title: UPDATE 2-NZ  central bank intervenes , sending kiwi sliding
text:
(Adds more analyst comment, background)   

WELLINGTON, June 11 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank intervened on Monday for the first time in more than two decades to cap a soaring New Zealand dollar, spurring a 2 percent fall in the currency.   

Saying the kiwi dollar was unjustifiably high, the central bank entered the market to rein in a currency that had jumped 28 percent in the last year to hit a 22-year peak on Friday.   

"As stated in our June monetary policy statement, we regard current levels of the exchange rate as exceptional and unjustified in terms of the economic fundamentals," Alan Bollard, governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, said in a statement.   

The kiwi slid to a session low of $0.7486 after the intervention, down from Friday's high of $0.7640. The neighbouring Australian dollar also fell.   

The central bank's first intervention since the currency was floated in 1985 came after a surprise interest rate hike to 8 percent last week to rein in inflation and the reappointment of Bollard for a second five-year term two weeks ago.   

New Zealand's high rates -- the highest in the industrial world -- have attracted inflows in the so-called carry trade, when investors borrow in low-yielding currencies, such as the yen, to invest in high-yielding ones.   

The inflows helped push up the currency 3.5 percent in the last month alone but analysts said the intervention was unlikely to turn the currency around.   

"Today's action shows they've lost patience with the currency. It's not going to send the currency into a bearish mode. What they are trying to do is cut off the peaks of the currency," said Khoon Goh, senior economist at ANZ-National Bank.   

"All they're doing is avoiding sending the currency to the 78 U.S. cent level, which it looked destined for."   

CARRY TRADES   

The New Zealand dollar also fell around 2 percent against the yen <NZDJPY=R> to about 91.13 yen, down from a 17-year high near 93 yen struck on Friday.   

"For the NZ dollar, it's all negative short term. But in the end, economic fundamentals will win the day," said Stephen Toplis, head of research at Bank of New Zealand. "If domestic growth fails to wane and the central bank remains up against it on the inflation front, the NZ dollar will remain well-supported."   

The Reserve Bank of NZ has had the power to intervene in the foreign exchange market since the currency was floated in March 1985, but it had never used the power until Monday.   

The neighbouring Australian dollar <AUD=>, also a high-yielding currency, was caught in the sell-off and fell to a low around $0.8395 from $0.8430, before rebounding slightly. Australian financial markets were closed for a public holiday.   

"I do not think this will prompt a reversal of carry trades, although it will likely moderate the pace at which the currency appreciates. The currency will keep on its firm trend and may even renew its high (against the yen)," said Masaki Fukui, senior market economist,  Mizuho Corporate Bank in Tokyo.   

"The same goes for other high-yielding currencies, although the Australian dollar was dragged down as well today ... The basic trend (of yen carry trades) has not changed.   

KIWI STILL BULLISH   

The central bank had previously said it would only step in if the currency was at exceptional levels not justified by economic fundamentals, if the intervention could be expected to succeed, and if it was consistent with the central bank's role of achieving price stability.   

It has also said it would not try to go against the market trend and would be more likely to intervene in times when there was a disorderly market.   

"Without historical precedent, it will be difficult to judge how long the RBNZ will be in the market to weaken the NZD, and how much weaker NZD could go," said Sue Trinh, senior currency strategist,  RBC Capital Markets in Sydney,   

"But the international evidence on successful currency intervention is mixed, and intervention is a distraction from the RBNZ's core policy objective, which is to contain medium-term inflation within 1-3 percent, where the most potent instrument is the official cash rate."   

Bollard has described the currency as being exceptionally and unjustifiably high in the central bank's past two policy statements.   

Asked by Reuters on Friday if the comments were deliberately used to raise intervention as an issue, Bollard said: "We just want to be quite transparent about our view about the currency, and those are our views."   

In the same interview, he said some of the kiwi's rise was justified by high commodity prices and expressed doubt that the RBNZ's own rate rises were to blame.   

The RBNZ forecast in its June monetary policy statement the trade-weighted New Zealand dollar <=NZD> would average 68.6 in the first half of 2007 and 68.3 in the latter half.   

As of Monday it was at 73.45, below an all-time high of 74.54 reached in December 2005. (Additional reporting by Tokyo bureau)

title: UPDATE:  New Zealand  Dollar Reverses Run On  Intervention
text:
By Wanfeng Zhou   

NEW YORK (Dow Jones) -- Less than a week after surprising the market with an interest-rate hike that boosted New Zealand's dollar to 22-year highs, the country's central bank now find itself in a position to dampen the currency's rise.   

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand confirmed Monday that it had intervened in the foreign-exchange market by selling the New Zealand dollar to weaken it. It is the first time the Reserve Bank of New Zealand has intervened since the country's currency was floated in 1985.   

"As stated in our June Monetary Policy Statement, we regard current levels of the exchange rate as exceptional and unjustified in terms of the economic fundamentals," Reserve Bank Governor Alan Bollard said in a statement posted on the central bank's web site.   

The New Zealand dollar, or the kiwi, tumbled on Monday, falling 2% against the U.S. currency, 1.7% against the Australian dollar, and 1.9% against the yen.   

"The unprecedented intervention...caught the market completely wrong-footed after last week's surprise rate hike," said Marc Chandler, global head of currency strategy at  Brown Brothers Harriman. "The intervention effectively reversed last [week]'s strong gains."   

The intervention came after the kiwi surged to its strongest level in 22 years against the greenback last Thursday following the central bank's unexpected move to raise its interest rate by a quarter-point to a record 8% -- the highest among major economies.   

The rising global interest in carry trades -- in which investors borrow low-yielding currencies, such as the yen, and reinvest in higher-yielding currencies -- has boosted demand for the New Zealand dollar in recent years.   

The New Zealand dollar has appreciated about 20% against the dollar and 30% against the yen in the past 12 months.   

A fight on its hands   

The rise in the value of the New Zealand dollar has led to worries that currency strength would hurt economic growth by making exports more expensive. Earlier this year, Bollard indicated that the level of the kiwi dollar was unjustified based on fundamentals.   

"If today's action by the [central bank] is a statement of intent, then the bank may well have a fight on its hands," said Simon Derrick, currency strategist at  The Bank of New York. "Whilst wanting to offer some protection for the export sector, Bollard has made clear that he wishes to maintain a tight monetary policy."   

Masafumi Yamamoto, analyst at  Citigroup, said if the kiwi dollar does not stop appreciating, "it might be natural to assume that the bank may intervene again."   

But Kathy Lien, chief strategist at DailyFX.com, said while further intervention is not out of the question, any further move "could be limited by the fact that New Zealand does not have much money to spend."   

The special fund that they have set up for intervention only has approximately 7 billion New Zealand dollars or US$5.3 billion. "Their intervention war chest is small," she said.   

Sue Trinh, senior currency strategist at  RBC Capital Markets, said the surprise intervention could be a "distraction" from the central bank's core policy objective, which is to fight inflation.   

The central bank said after its June rate hike that "a sustained period of slower growth in domestic activity will be required" to alleviate inflation pressures. "This further increase in the [official cash rate] is to ensure that inflation outcomes remain consistent with achieving the target of 1 to 3% inflation on average over the medium term."   

Still, "without historical precedent, it will be difficult to judge how long [it] will be in the market to weaken the New Zealand dollar, and how much weaker currency could go."   

Follow suit   

The unusual policy action by New Zealand's central bank has greater implications for risk appetite and carry trades, analysts say. It also sparked speculation whether other central banks may follow suit.   

For instance, the Bank of Japan has come under intense political pressure from its trade partners for the low level of the yen. Should Japanese officials follow suit and intervene, investors' tolerate of risk may be upset and the market may see a sharp unwinding of carry trades, analysts say.   

Bank of New York's Derrick said New Zealand's intervention could help shift the Group of Seven leading countries' stance on currency intervention. The G7 nations, in the past, have been aiming at prompting currency flexibility, as a way to pressure China to make its yuan more flexible.   

"How long will the governments and central banks of the "developed" world be prepared to continue with a policy of non-interventionism when other nations continue to "manage" their currencies seemingly to their own advantage and show little interest in changing these policies in the near future?" he said, in a note to clients. " As far as New Zealand is concerned the answer would appear to be: 'no longer.'"   

"This summer could mark a significant turning point for political thinking within G7 and beyond on the issue of currency market intervention," he said.   

Remains attractive   

Despite Monday's decline, expectations for further rate hikes and a weak dollar will likely continue to support the New Zealand dollar, analysts said.   

"Ultimately Bollard is wrong. The New Zealand dollar is not at exceptional levels nor are they unjustified," Chandler said. "The market, which votes with its money, says the interest rate differential - 7.5% over Japan overnight rates, for example, trumps New Zealand's trade and current account deficits and the decline in the competitiveness of its manufacturing sector."   

"Unless the [Reserve Bank of New Zealand] plans on continuing to intervene, market forces will likely continue to favor the kiwi," he said, in a note. "Indeed the intervention may be seen as offering a new buying opportunity."   

Citigroup's Yamamoto said New Zealand's currency "remains attractive for mid-to long-term investors like many Japanese investors," as the levels of the interest rates in New Zealand are the highest among major countries and further tightening is expected.   

"However, those who aim for a short-term currency gain should be discouraged by the RBNZ's move," he said.   

But Daragh Maher, strategist at French Bank Calyon, said he's "wary" of the outlook for the kiwi dollar.   

The central bank's move "has introduced another downside risk that will have to be taken on board by those keen to buy the New Zealand dollar at such overvalued levels. "Policymakers have made it clear that they see limits to the currency's upside."   

"The limits to the downside, by contrast, are some way distant." [ 06-11-07 1648ET ]

title: NZ Fin Min: RBNZ Clearly Felt Criteria For  Intervention  Met
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen said Monday that the central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market earlier in the day because it felt all criteria for such action had been met.   

Cullen also cautioned that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's intervention is a reminder to investors to desist from overinvesting in the local currency.

title: NZ dollar slips after cenbank warning
text:
WELLINGTON, April 27 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar slipped on Friday, after the central bank's warning on the currency the previous day sparked speculation among some traders of possible currency intervention.   

But most analysts think the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is unlikely to intervene given the kiwi's current strength is partly due to weakness in the U.S. dollar and as a weaker currency would have an inflationary impact on imported goods.   

"Currency markets were a little spooked by the comment that the level of exchange rate was 'unjustified' relative to medium-term fundamentals," said Danica Hampton, currency strategist at Bank of New Zealand.   

"At this stage, we don't think intervention is a real threat, and we view (Governor Alan) Bollard's comments on the NZD as simply a clever way of taking the sting out of the currency following the rate hike."   

By 0510 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was trading around $0.74 <NZD=>, compared with $0.7480/82 in late local trade on Thursday and a 22-year post-float high of $0.7493 <NZD=D2> reached last week.   

The RBNZ raised interest rates to 7.75 percent on Thursday but did not mention whether a further tightening would be necessary as it did in previous statements.   

Many traders expect the central bank to remain vigilant over inflation pressures which will likely support the kiwi.   

"Until markets become convinced the RBNZ's actions are slowing growth, robust domestic demand is likely to keep the NZD/USD well supported on dips," Hampton said.   

Data showed on Friday electronic retail card spending fell for the first time in eight months in March, but analysts said it still pointed to solid consumer demand which will likely keep interest rates elevated into next year.   

Government bonds rebounded, with yields slipping around 2 basis points along the curve.

title: UPDATE 1-RBNZ's Bollard says  forex intervention  an option
text:
(Adds market reaction, details)  

WELLINGTON, Dec 8 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand could intervene in the foreign exchange market if it considered the currency to be "exceptionally and unjustifiably high", Governor Alan Bollard was quoted as saying on Friday.  

"If we think it's exceptionally and unjustifiably high and we think that intervention is an option for us, then we've got the tools to do that. So we'll always consider that," Bollard told TVOne. The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> dropped about a quarter of a cent to around $0.6870 following Bollard's comments, pulling back from a 10-½ month high of $0.6922 reached on Thursday.  

On Thursday, the RBNZ held interest rates at 7.25 percent -- the highest in the industrialised world -- but warned it may have to raise them again due to a stronger-than-expected domestic economy, sparking a rally in the currency and short-term yields.  

The Reserve Bank has always had the power to intervene in the foreign exchange market, by directly selling the New Zealand dollar, but has not done so since the New Zealand dollar was floated in 1985.  

In 2004, the RBNZ received a NZ$1 billion capital injection to bolster its reserves in case it needed to buy or sell the New Zealand dollar, prompting speculation the central bank was going to be more interventionist.  

The bank has said it will step in only if the currency is at exceptional levels not justified by economic fundamentals, the intervention can be expected to be successful, and it is consistent with the bank's role of achieving price stability.  

Speculation of a possible RBNZ intervention was rekindled last year after Bollard described the currency as being "exceptionally high".  

In Thursday's monetary policy statement, Bollard warned that sustained strength in the New Zealand dollar could threaten the ongoing re-balancing of the economy.  

The strong kiwi dollar has been partly blamed for New Zealand's annual current account deficit swelling to a record high NZ$15.15 billion ($10.45 billion), or 9.7 percent of gross domestic product, as of the September quarter. ($1=NZ$1.45)

title: UPDATE 1-RBNZ to keep OCR, ready for  forex intervention
text:
(Adds detail, quotes, background)  

WELLINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank said on Friday it will keep its official cash rate as its main monetary policy tool, and is ready to intervene if a global flu pandemic disrupts trading on foreign exchange markets.  

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Alan Bollard said the official cash rate, a benchmark rate at which the central bank trades with retail banks, would remain as its main method of keeping inflation in check, despite losing some of its effectiveness.  

"We're quite clear the OCR will remain the core tool of monetary policy for the forseeable future," Bollard said at a briefing on the bank's financial stability report.  

Last week, the RBNZ and the Treasury said they were looking at new tools to lessen reliance on the official cash rate.  

"But they may amount to nothing at all, (and) they're never likely to be more than ancillary," Bollard said.  

The cash rate, instituted in 1999, has lost potency with more borrowers taking up fixed-term loans, which have delayed and lessened the impact of any moves in cash rates.  

The RBNZ last month resumed its tightening cycle, raising the cash rate to 7 percent -- the highest in the developed world -- to counter stubborn inflationary pressures from the hot housing market and high oil prices.  

A Reuters poll has all 15 forecasters surveyed expecting the cash rate to be raised again on Dec. 8 by a quarter point.  

READY FOR PANDEMIC  

Bollard refused to comment on how monetary policy might be conducted if there was a global bird flu pandemic, but said the RBNZ was planning to ensure key financial systems would keep operating.  

Deputy governor Adrain Orr said the RBNZ was ready to intervene in the foreign exchange market if birdflu hit.  

"We'll be making sure ... that our foreign reserves will be poised and ready if the foreign exchange markets become dysfunctional and we have to be providing some type of price making role through that," Orr said.  

The RBNZ had been speaking to other central banks on the issue, but there was little concern at this stage.  

The financial stability report echoed the comments in the May report about unprecedented levels of household debt, with some borrowers likely to be at risk in the event of a sharp downturn.  

The risks to New Zealand's financial system were growing, with the economy imbalanced after years of strong growth. It was well placed to weather any slowdown, although it might be tested if there was a sharp downturn.  

"All in all, the risk conditions facing the financial system over the next six months could be more testing than during the past six months," Bollard said in the six-monthly report.  

"We do not see those strains as spilling over to the financial system on a scale that would undermine its overall stability -- though specific stresses cannot be ruled out."  

The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> foreign exchange market had been functioning well, although turnover was expected to decrease as the economy slows and New Zealand's interest rate advantage over other countries narrows.

title: RPT-ANALYSIS-NZ cenbank's hands seen tied on  FX intervention
text:
WELLINGTON, Nov 14 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank is caught in a conundrum: how to engineer an export-boosting fall in its currency when such a fall would likely stoke inflation and force a currency-boosting rise in interest rates.  

Faced with a record current account deficit, Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Alan Bollard has railed against what he sees as an unjustifiably high Kiwi dollar.  

But with almost the same breath he warns that a drop in the currency would further aggravate inflation and could lead to a rise in interest rates -- already the highest in the industrialised world at 7.0 percent.  

The central bank could always intervene directly to sell New Zealand dollars. Recently Bollard referred to the currency as being "exceptionally high," a term used by the RBNZ to describe one of its conditions for intervention.  

The New Zealand dollar <NZD=> has eased from a 23-year high against the U.S. dollar, but on a trade-weighted basis <=NZD>, the central bank's preferred measure, it remains near record peaks.  

"All this sounds like a central bank which has the mindset where it will intervene," said Greg Gibbs, senior currency strategist at RBC Capital Markets.  

Gibbs said a rise in the trade-weighted index (TWI) to new highs and the New Zealand dollar's climb above its recent peak against the Australian dollar <AUDNZD=R>, the currency of its biggest trading parter, could prompt the Reserve Bank to intervene.  

The high exchange rate has ravaged the country's export sector. The annual current account deficit hit 8 percent of gross domestic product in the second quarter and is still widening.  

CONDITIONS NOT MET  

The Reserve Bank has always had the power to intervene in the foreign exchange market, but has not done so since the New Zealand dollar was floated in 1985.  

Last year, the RBNZ received a NZ$1 billion capital injection to bolster reserves in the event it needed to buy and sell the New Zealand dollar, prompting analysts to think the central bank was going to be more interventionist.  

But many analysts think the chances Bollard will act on his warnings are slim because the conditions spelt out by the RBNZ for intervention have not all been met and, given current circumstances, are actually contradictory.  

The bank has said it will step in only if the currency is at exceptional levels not justified by economic fundamentals; the intervention can be expected to be successful and is consistent with the bank's role of achieving price stability.  

The first condition is considered fulfilled given the relative high exchange rate and a slowing economy.  

But analysts doubt intervention would depress the kiwi dollar for long given foreign appetite for the kiwi's high yield has seen a record NZ$21 billion ($14.4 billion) of eurobond issuance this year.  

More fundamentally, weakening the currency would also put upward pressure on imported inflation and thus work against the central bank's tight monetary policy.  

Annual inflation rose to a five-year high of 3.4 percent in the third quarter, breaking above the central bank's target band of 1.0 to 3.0 percent. And strong wage and employment data out last week, point to further pressure ahead.  

"They would probably take the view that if we are still in a situation to raise interest rates, we shouldn't be trying to weaken the currency," said Darren Gibbs, senior economist at Deutsche Bank.

title: RBNZ Ratcheting Up Inflation Rhetoric, Keeps Hike Threat
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is trying hard to talk down persistent inflationary pressures, warning that consumption demand needs to moderate in order to avoid further rate hikes and a painful slowdown in economic growth.  

In hard-hitting comments over the past 24 hours aimed at curbing resilient domestic activity, Reserve Bank Governor Alan Bollard said that housing and consumption growth isn't slowing enough to contain rising inflation pressures.  

Translation: More rate increases will be needed if domestic consumption doesn't abate sufficiently enough to comfort the central bank, which isn't shying away from its hawkish language despite eight tightening steps since January 2004.  

On Wednesday, Bollard told the Employers and Manufactures Association in Auckland that New Zealanders' "love affair with housing leaves us very exposed to a property slump."  

The governor repeated this message in an interview with Radio New Zealand early Thursday, saying that the current rate of annual house price inflation of 14% can't continue unabated. "Anybody who thinks that house price inflation can continue at 14% is living in a cloud cuckoo land - it can't," he said.  

"We see that having some quite significant effects in our imports, and that's driving the export sector into quite hard times," he said  

John McDermott, chief economist at ANZ Bank, says the Reserve Bank seem to be on a "campaign of clearly articulating their worries about the problems facing this economy."  

"As unpalatable as it is, the only medicine the Reserve Bank has to offer is higher interest rates," McDermott said.  

More Hikes In The Cards  

ANZ Bank now expects Bollard to follow last week's quarter percentage point increase to the Official Cash Rate with another one at the Dec. 8 Monetary Policy Statement.  

That would raise the cash rate to 7.25% from the current 7.00%, already the highest in the developed world, and much higher than the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy rate of 4.00%. In all, four of 12 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires expect rates in New Zealand to rise next month.  

Bollard last week left the door open for a further tightening after raising the cash rate to 7.00%, saying the central bank remains concerned that inflation isn't abating sufficiently to achieve the RBNZ's medium-term target of 1%-3% annual growth in the consumer price index.  

Bollard warned that borrowers and lenders alike need to recognize the consequences of debt accumulation, and that its effects on saving and the current account deficit are unsustainable. A correction requires a slowdown in the housing market, credit growth and domestic spending, he said.  

The problem confronting Bollard is a resilient domestic economy, especially led by the stubborn strength in housing market demand, and a weak external sector which is struggling to cope with a high New Zealand dollar. Adding to this is the cyclical inflation pressures caused by a surge in gasoline prices.  

The domestic economy is operating at full capacity, and therefore wage and price pressures remain harder to combat - and persistently high gasoline bills may give businesses a compelling argument for raising their product prices.  

"The Reserve Bank appears to be increasingly nervous about the imbalances in the economy," Tim Bowring, economist at Macquarie Bank. "On one hand the governor indicates the bank is continuing to look at inflation over the medium term, on the other hand Bollard suggests the sooner domestic demand eases the better," Bowring said.  

NZD Under Attack  

"At this stage we believe the case for a further rate rise is unconvincing, but based on the RBNZ governor's comments, it would appear that a hike is certainly on the cards," Bowring said.  

In Wednesday's speech, Bollard said the strong domestic demand is further widening the current account gap, which is being exacerbated by demand from offshore investors attracted to the high New Zealand interest rates, and New Zealand-dollar returns.  

The country's current account deficit reached 8% of gross domestic product in the second quarter.  

In a veiled warning that central bank may be prepared to intervene in the foreign exchange market, Bollard said the New Zealand dollar is currently at unsustainable, and in some respects, unjustifiable, levels.  

Just over two years ago, the bank was given specific powers to intervene in the foreign exchange market if the New Zealand dollar was considered unsustainably and unjustifiably high or low.  

Bollard said the central bank "won't stand in the way" of a New Zealand dollar fall.  

The New Zealand dollar rose to US$0.7465 against its U.S. counterpart - a 22-year post-float high. The pair has since come back to around US$0.6930, but is still above the post-float average of US$0.5800.  

Bollard said the correction in economic imbalances will occur only through a slowing in domestic demand, which will reduce inflation to the central bank's target zone by 2007.  

"This, however, comes at a cost to slowing growth," Bollard said.  

"But it's important to recognize that such an adjustment needs to happen - the sooner it happens, the less costly it will be," the governor said.  

Annual inflation in the third quarter rose to 3.4% - above the central bank's threshold.  

-By Shri Navaratnam, Dow Jones Newswires; 64-4-471-5990; shri.navaratnam@dowjones.com. [ 03-11-05 0013GMT ]

title: NZD Ends Down After Fed Hike, RBNZ Comments; Bonds Weak
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand dollar closed lower Wednesday after its U.S. counterpart was bolstered by the Federal Reserve's 12th consecutive interest rate hike overnight.  

The Kiwi shrugged off the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's veiled warning of potential intervention to dent the high-flying local currency.  

However, some dealers said the Reserve Bank's expectations for the Kiwi to fall over time may have weighed on the U.S. dollar/New Zealand dollar.  

Government bond prices closed slightly lower, but the short end of the curve pared its losses as some in the market interpreted Bollard's comments as a warning of a sharp slowing in economic growth.  

The Kiwi finished at US$0.6968, down from Tuesday's close of US$0.7005 after trading in a local range of US$0.6962-US$0.6889.  

Against the Australian dollar, the New Zealand currency ended at A$0.9378 from A$0.9388 Tuesday.  

HSBC Treasurer Trevor Pye said the U.S. dollar's overnight strength, especially against the euro, was dented slightly in the Asian session on profit-taking. But the positive sentiment toward the U.S. dollar in the wake of the Fed's quarter-percentage-point hike to the federal funds rate to 4.00% continued to weigh on the majors.  

"The Kiwi has failed to go anywhere today. It's remained top heavy," Pye said.  

Reserve Bank Governor Alan Bollard in a speech Wednesday said that the Kiwi was at an unsustainable, and in some respects, unjustifiable level.  

Bollard said the currency will eventually fall as the economy continues to slow from its red-hot pace of growth of the past few years.  

Bollard's comments on the Kiwi was interesting as the central bank has previously said it will intervene only if the New Zealand dollar was at an unjustifiable and unsustainable high or low.  

Deutsche Bank Senior Economist Darren Gibbs said the central bank would also need to be certain that any intervention would be a success and that it would be in line with the Policy Targets Agreement.  

Gibbs said these criteria may not be met in the near term, but added that intervention remains a possibility in the middle of next year.  

The PTA is an agreement between Bollard and the government that, among other things, requires the governor to ensure central bank actions don't disrupt the markets. The Kiwi is expected to remain supported above US$0.6950, while resistance was pegged at US$0.7010. [ 02-11-05 0504GMT ]  

Government bond prices closed slightly weaker, especially in the long end.  

"(Bollard's speech) perhaps made some feel that the economy could enter a sharp slowdown," said a trader. "It probably helped the short end pare some of its losses."  

Short-dated bond yields, led by the July 2008 paper, closed up 1.5 basis points after being 3 basis points higher before Bollard's speech.  

Traders said the market remains heavy due to expectations the Reserve Bank will hike rates again in December. The bank raised the cash rate by a quarter percentage point to 7.00% last week, the eighth increase since the tightening cycle started in January 2004.  

"The market is still expecting a rate hike in December and that's why you didn't see a big rally in the short end of the curve," the trader said.  

The bank bill futures market rallied after Bollard's speech. Traders said some players were spooked by the possibility of a recession.

title: RBNZ Bollard: Housing, Consumption Keeps Pressure On CPI
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Alan Bollard Wednesday said that strong housing market activity and consumption is driving inflation higher, and warned the country risks a property slump as the economy slows down.  

In a speech to the local Employers and Manufacturer's Association, Bollard said that while there are signs of a slowdown in domestic spending, housing and spending need to moderate further to contain rising inflationary pressures.  

Bollard also criticized comments made by the property industry that housing activity can continue at current levels, saying such comments are "self-serving and unhelpful to those that will be caught up and damaged by a property market correction."  

He said that past interest rate increases have slowed housing price growth, but noted that it is still growing at an annual rate of 14% and driving unsustainable levels of consumer spending. [ 02-11-05 0313GMT ]  

"The danger of this is it means our love affair with housing leaves us very exposed to a property slump," Bollard said.  

The governor also repeated recent warnings that the government's fiscal promises, which were made ahead of the Sept. 17 election that was narrowly won by the center-left Labour Party, could fuel the strong domestic economy further.  

"And the big oil price rise is already increasing headline consumer price index, while second round effects could drive inflation further," Bollard said.  

Bollard last week raised the Official Cash Rate by a quarter percentage point to 7.00%, and left the door open for a further tightening, saying the central bank remains concerned that inflation isn't abating sufficiently to achieve the RBNZ's medium-term target of 1%-3% annual growth in the consumer price index.  

The quarter-percentage-point increase was the eighth hike since the Reserve Bank began its current tightening phase in January 2004, resulting in the highest rate since the bank adopted its six-weekly OCR review in 1999.  

Bollard warned in last week's statement that borrowers and lenders alike need to recognize the consequences of debt accumulation, and that its effects on saving and the current account deficit are unsustainable. A correction requires a slowdown in the housing market, credit growth and domestic spending, he said.  

"The prospect of further tightening may only be ruled out once a noticeable moderation in housing and consumer spending is observed," Bollard said.  

Annual inflation was 3.4% in the third quarter, driven by a surge in fuel prices and higher construction costs.  

In Wednesday's speech, Bollard said the strong domestic demand is further widening the current account gap, which is being exacerbated by demand from offshore investors attracted to the high New Zealand interest rates, and New Zealand-dollar returns.  

Bollard said the New Zealand dollar needs to fall if the current account deficit is to improve, and added that the currency will eventually ease as the economy slows.  

The country's current account deficit reached 8% of gross domestic product in the second quarter.  

In a veiled warning that central bank may be prepared to intervene in the foreign exchange market, Bollard said the New Zealand dollar is currently at unsustainable, and in some respects, unjustifiable, levels.  

Just over two years ago, the bank was given specific powers to intervene in the foreign exchange market if the New Zealand dollar was considered unsustainably and unjustifiably high or low.  

Bollard said the central bank "won't stand in the way" of a New Zealand dollar fall.  

The New Zealand dollar rose to US$0.7465 against its U.S. counterpart - a 22-year post-float high. The pair has since come back to around US$0.6970, but is still above the post-float average of US$0.5800.

title: NZ VOTE:National Would Remove RBNZ  FX Intervention  Power
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand's central bank will lose its right to independently intervene in foreign exchange markets if the country's main opposition party wins power at the general elections this month.  

John Key, finance spokesman for the center-right National Party, said that if his party is elected to government, he will reverse a law which allows the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to intervene and influence the local currency when it is at "unjustifiably" high or low levels.  

"I don't think currency intervention achieves anything," Key told Dow Jones Newswires.  

"In recent times we've had the New Zealand dollar at post-float highs and the bank hasn't come in, and rightly so," he said. "In a sense they're never going to."  

New Zealand's current Labour-led government last year handed the central bank the right to intervene independently in foreign exchange markets, breaking with a near-20-year policy of not intervening.  

Previously, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand had been able to intervene at the direction of the country's treasurer, which would likely only happen in exceptional circumstances.  

The law change came as the New Zealand dollar was hitting historical highs against its U.S. counterpart, and there was widespread concern that export incomes would suffer and cause a slowdown in the New Zealand economy.  

The New Zealand dollar was floated in 1985 and has gained strongly since reaching a post-float low of US$0.3898 in October 2000. It gained 25% in each of 2002 and 2003, and earlier this year hit a post-float high of US$0.7465.  

Following the change in law, the central bank said it didn't anticipate intervening very often, although there could be a small benefit from intervention.  

The central bank hasn't used its new power despite the recent highs in the New Zealand dollar.  

"For all the hassle and cost, I'm opposed to it (intervention)," Key said.  

Key said that the National Party, if elected, will remove an additional NZ$700 million of funding the current government has earmarked to give the central bank over the next two fiscal years to help strengthen its balance sheet.  

He said foreign exchange market players can work out roughly what size the central bank's reserves are, and "that's dwarfed by massive hedge funds."  

"Most of the hedge funds have more in their back pocket than New Zealand has in reserves," said Key, a former head of global foreign exchange for investment bank Merrill Lynch.  

Key said he remains comfortable with the bank's right to intervene at the direction of the treasurer in a catastrophic situation, and would keep that law in place.  

The New Zealand dollar has in recent months pulled back from its historical highs, but remains well above its post-float average of about US$0.5800. Around 0145 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was at US$0.6953, up from US$0.6949 at the open of Thursday's local session.  

The National and Labour parties are locked in a close race ahead of the Sept. 17 vote. Several polls earlier this year have indicated a neck-and-neck battle, with the latest 3 News/TNS poll showing that the National Party is slightly ahead.
