title: RBNZ: Any  FX Intervention  Likely To Be Aggressive, Public
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand's central bank says that if exercises its recently granted intervention power in the foreign exchange market it will intervene aggressively and quickly make public its actions.  

In an article published in the latest Reserve Bank of New Zealand Bulletin late last week, the bank reiterates its intervention policy and reveals how it would carry out any foreign exchange market dealings.  

"The style of execution will be relatively aggressive. The Bank will ask market participants to quote it a price and would deal on those prices, thereby forcing transactions into the market," the Reserve Bank said.  

"This approach is more likely to result in the bank's counterparts quickly acting to pass on the bank's deals to others, creating ongoing transaction activity in the direction the bank desires, maximizing the impact on the exchange rate."  

The Reserve Bank states that "often, intervention will be very open and public."  

"In these cases, the Bank will issue a press release shortly after having intervened, noting it has intervened and the rationale for the intervention."  

The bank said it will comment on intervention "if it thinks such commentary is useful in enhancing the effectiveness of the operation."  

"Sometimes, though, the Bank may wish to intervene covertly, which will mean that there will be no comment from the Bank at the time of intervention."  

Last year the Reserve Bank was given the means to intervene in the New Zealand dollar market when the local currency is "exceptionally" high or low, relative to the level that economic fundamentals suggest it should be at. Before that mandate, the Reserve Bank was allowed to intervene only during a financial crisis.  

Despite the Kiwi, as the New Zealand dollar is known, rising to a 22-year high of US$0.7465 last month, the Reserve Bank doesn't yet appear to have intervened in the market  

In the article by Kelly Eckhold of the Reserve Bank's Financial Stability Department and Chris Hunt of the bank's Economics Department, the Reserve Bank reiterates its intervention policy of not trying to fight market trends.  


 
   RBNZ Would Probably Intervene In NZD/USD 
   

Instead, the Reserve Bank will wait until market participants become less sure about the currency's direction, the balance of capital flows shifts toward pushing the exchange rate back toward equilibrium and there is a relative absence of capital flows that might offset intervention.  

The Reserve Bank also revealed how it is likely to carry out any actual intervention.  

It will usually intervene in the New Zealand dollar/US dollar currency pair, because it is the most liquid and because most other currency pairs are derived with reference to that exchange rate.  

Transaction actions will generally be with wholesale market participants and would typically be of a similar size as the standard market parcel of NZ$10 million or more.  

"To maximize the strength of the intervention signal the Bank is likely to transact with a number of market makers simultaneously," the Reserve Bank said.  

Usually, when the Reserve Bank transacts in the foreign exchange market, it tries to minimize the impact.  

"The execution approach in intervention situations will be quite the opposite, as the aim of the operation would be to maximize the exchange rate impact," the Reserve Bank said.  

"This implies that the Bank would look to intervene at times when there is relatively little interest by other market participants to trade against it."  

The Reserve Bank said it will use the opposite approach when unwinding any currency positions gained as a result of intervention.  

"The associated transactions will be performed in a manner consistent with minimizing the impact on the exchange rate," the bank said.  

"For example, the Bank will pick times when there are a number of other investors interested in trading in the opposite direction, and its execution style will be very passive."  

- By Christopher Niesche, Dow Jones Newswires; 64-4-471-5990; christopher.niesche@dowjones.com [ 04-04-05 0226GMT ]

title: UPDATE: RBNZ Bollard Says NZ Dollar Echoing Commodities
text:
(Adds details, economist comment)  

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--Reserve Bank of New Zealand governor Alan Bollard said Wednesday that domestic interest rates aren't the major factor influencing the level of the New Zealand dollar, and reiterated his view that the local unit isn't out of line with world commodity prices.  

The Official Cash Rate "can have an impact" on the level of the New Zealand dollar, Bollard told New Zealand Parliament's Finance & Expenditure Select Committee, "but it's one of a number of things, and not the major" factor that drives the currency's movements.  

The U.S. dollar and export commodity prices have more effect, Bollard added.  

The RBNZ last week raised the Official Cash Rate by 25 basis points to 6.75% in an effort to stifle persistent inflation.  

The New Zealand dollar responded by temporarily jumping to US$0.7449, its highest level since it became a free-floating currency 20 years ago, although it has since pulled back to be trading at US$0.7407 at 2230 GMT.  

Bollard told the committee that the central bank was mindful in making its latest rate increase decision that the rise "shouldn't have much effect" on the level of the New Zealand dollar.  

He added that the rate rise didn't have "much effect" on the local currency 24 hours after the rise.  

Bollard reiterated his view that the New Zealand dollar is maintaining its historical relativity to commodity prices, which have also been "very high."  

"If you plot some of the indices of commodity prices against the New Zealand dollar, you'll find that they move in sequence very closely," Bollard told the committee.  

"On that measure you'd say the New Zealand dollar is not right out of bounds - it's keeping that same relativity that it has historically."  

Asked if the central bank is considering intervening in foreign exchange markets to bring down the high New Zealand dollar, Bollard was tight-lipped.  

He described intervention as "a very limited sort of tool," and said it is a "very limited option under the specific circumstances."  

The Reserve Bank was given the power last year to intervene if it believes the New Zealand dollar is "exceptionally and unjustifiably" high or low.  


 
   Consequences Of Wrong Monetary Policy Decision Higher Than Before 
   

Deutsche Bank chief economist Ulf Schoefisch said Bollard's comments showed he is "uncomfortable with the currency where it is, but he doesn't seem to think he can do much about it."  

"That's not a very comfortable position to be in as far as the current account deficit developments are concerned," Schoefisch added.  

New Zealand's current account deficit hit 5.8% of gross domestic product in the third quarter of last year, up from 4.8% in the second quarter, according to official data released late last year.  

Fourth-quarter figures are due next week, but Bollard faced questions about the central bank's latest Monetary Policy Statement, which forecasts the current account deficit will expand to measure 6.5% of GDP in 2005 and 2006, and 6.75% in 2007.  

Bollard described the present current account level as "an undesirable feature" of the New Zealand economy, and said the forecast increase will take it to "quite a significant level."  

But he noted that financial markets haven't shown any particular concern about the current account deficit level to date.  

Bollard told the committee that the consequences of making a wrong decision on monetary policy now are greater than previously because the economy is reaching a turning point.  

He added that "there's a possibility of a harder landing than we are forecasting,", but added "we don't expect that to happen."  

When he raised rates last week, Bollard said he decided that the risk that another rate increase would slow the economy too much was outweighed by the risk that the bank might have to raise rates even more later to contain inflation if it didn't move now.  

Bollard said he is keeping a "very close" eye on labor cost indicators, and whether labor shortages are being rewarded "where appropriate" with pay increases.  

"But we wouldn't want to see that spilling over into areas where it didn't need to spill over," he added.  

The Reserve Bank has forecast the gross domestic product to grow by 4.5% to the end of the first quarter of this year and to grow by 3% to the end of the first quarter of 2006.

title: UPDATE 2-NZ sounds alarm bells over  currency  strength.
text:
MELBOURNE, March 9 (Reuters) - New Zealand sounded alarm bells on Wednesday over the rise in the country's currency to 22-year highs above 74 U.S. cents, concerned it could damage the country's trade position.  

The New Zealand dollar, known as the kiwi in currency markets, rose to a high of 74.06 U.S. cents ahead of a central bank meeting on Thursday to review interest rates.  

"Let's see whether that's temporary or not, whether it's a blip in advance of a Reserve Bank announcement, which you sometimes see," Finance Minister Michael Cullen told Reuters.  

"Clearly, at that level, it does start to become a very real concern," he said, after speaking at a financial conference in Melbourne.  

The kiwi fell after Cullen's comments to a low of 73.58 U.S. cents before recovering to last trade at 73.69/79 U.S. cents.  

A near 90 percent rise in the currency since October 2000 has cut into the earnings of exporters, such as forestry company Carter Holt Harvey, and was cited this week for putting two sawmills and a wood processing plant out of business.  

Exports generate the equivalent of one third of gross domestic product. The country's primary products, such as dairy and meat, account for about 40 percent of annual exports worth NZ$31 billion ($23 billion).  

Record commodity prices have helped insulate farmers from the brunt of the currency's strength, which makes imports cheaper.  

"But it tends to keep driving the current account deficit, which is getting uncomfortably high," Cullen said.  

New Zealand accumulated a trade deficit of NZ$3.9 billion ($2.9 billion) in the year through January, just below the record NZ$4.2 billion in the year through December.  

The current account deficit ballooned to 5.8 percent of gross domestic product in the third quarter from a low of 2.5 percent at the end of 2001.  

HIGH, BUT FOR HOW LONG?  

Bob Walters, the chief executive of Export New Zealand, which represents around 4,000 exporters, said the New Zealand dollar's strength could soon become more of a problem for its members.  

"I guess the real concern of most of our members is how long is it going to continue at these relatively high levels - I would think a lot of them are getting very close to the end of hedging," he said.  

Dairy exporter Fonterra Co-operative Group Ltd., New Zealand's largest company, has said the currency's lofty heights will depress payouts to its 13,000 farmer suppliers in the 2005/06 season, when commodity prices are expected to ease from record levels.  

World prices for 13 New Zealand commodities measured by ANZ Bank rose to a record high in February. The value of the products in local currency terms fell 0.3 percent from a month earlier, but were still 9.3 percent higher than a year earlier.  

Cullen said there was little the government could do about the dollar's level, but the Reserve Bank had certain limited resources it could use where it saw a risk to systemic stability.  

"If the level of the dollar creates some sort of systemic problem within the economy or within the financial system the bank now has the capacity to engage in limited action," he said.  

"The bank makes that determination and I don't comment on that at all."  

Last year, the government expanded the powers of the central bank to intervene in the foreign exchange market.  

Most analysts expect the New Zealand dollar to fall in value later in the year as economic growth slows.  

But a run of stronger-than-expected data has raised the risk that New Zealand might raise interest rates, already the highest in the industrialised world, again on Thursday.  

A Reuters poll narrowly expected the central bank to leave the official cash rate at 6.5 percent, estimating the risk of a rate hike at 45 percent.  

Reserve Bank of New Zealand governor Alan Bollard will issue a monetary policy statement on Thursday at 9 a.m. (2000 GMT Wednesday).

title: UPDATE 1-NZ's Cullen says not comfortable with high NZD.
text:
WELLINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen said on Wednesday he was not comfortable with the high level of the New Zealand dollar , although exporter confidence remained at high levels.    

 Cullen said: "I am not entirely comfortable with that" when asked at a parliamentary committee whether he had concerns about the New Zealand dollar's level against the U.S. dollar.    

 "But luckily we do have high commodity prices, and it's muting the effect of the high oil prices," Cullen said.    

 Exporter confidence was surprisingly high despite the exchange rate, Cullen said.    

 The kiwi fell about 15 ticks to $0.6835 after Cullen's comments, but later recouped the losses and last traded at $0.6860, near its local opening level.    

 The kiwi has risen about 6 percent so far this year, but remains below the near-7 year highs of $0.71 posted in mid-February. It hit a trough for the year of $0.5910 in late May.    

 New Zealand's strong economy and high interest rates have been credited as reasons for the currency's strength.    

 Asked if the currency's level would justify Reserve Bank of New Zealandintervention, Cullen said it was entirely up to the central bank to decide if and when it might intervene.    

 "Their intervention rules are around systemic instability within the markets, I think you'd be pushing to say we were at that point."    

 Cullen, who was appearing before the committee to discuss the government accounts for the past year, ruled out any likelihood of tax cuts or changes to tax thresholds, despite posting a large budget surplus last year and the forecast of another in the current year.    

 Asked if national carrier Air New Zealand Ltd. (AIR.NZ) would need extra capital after the collapse of the planned alliance with Australia's Qantas Airways Ltd. (QAN.AX), Cullen reaffirmed a long standing commitment for NZ$150 million ($104 million) if the airline needed it.    

 "I have no advice at all that we would be called upon for any more than that for the foreseeable future," Cullen said.    

 The airline was bailed out by a NZ$885 million government rescue package in 2002, which resulted in the government acquiring an 82 percent stake.

title: NZ Dlr Ends Up Despite Fin Min Comments; Bonds Steady
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand dollar gained against its U.S. counterpart Wednesday, despite the finance minister's comments that he is uncomfortable with the high level of the local unit, while government bonds closed barely changed.  

The New Zealand dollar traded a local range of US$0.6840-US$0.6865 and closed at US$0.6858, up from US$0.6836 Tuesday.  

Against its Australian counterpart, the New Zealand dollar closed at A$0.9437, edging down from Tuesday's close of A$0.9442.  

As it has recently, the Kiwi - as the New Zealand dollar is known - made its gains overnight against a broadly weaker U.S. dollar.  

In what was an otherwise uneventful local session, the market's attention was captured by comments by Finance Minister Michael Cullen about the high level of the Kiwi.  

"I'm not entirely comfortable with the position at the present time," Cullen told Parliament's Finance & Expenditure Select Committee.  

Asked whether the Reserve Bank of New Zealand should use the means it was recently granted to intervene in the foreign exchange market, Cullen said, "It's entirely up to the Reserve Bank if and when they intervene."  

The New Zealand dollar fell to US$0.6840 after Cullen's comments, from US$0.6858 before the comments were reported.  

Bank of New Zealand currency strategist Sue Trinh said the comments were nothing new, and the dip was more a knee-jerk reaction.  

Indeed, Cullen has previously said the Kiwi's rise has been causing "pain" for the export sector.  

Westpac head of spot foreign exchange Basil Payn said Cullen's comments "had no lasting impact at all."  

"We bounced back pretty quickly," he said.  

The day's trade saw more buying of the Kiwi from Asia due to continued issuance of New Zealand dollar-denominated uridashi bonds.  

Also, local importers continued to take advantage of the relatively high level of the local unit to sell it and buy foreign currencies.  

"The buyers and sellers are continuing to net each other off," said Payn.  

Payn said he expects an overnight range in the Kiwi of US$0.6850-US$0.6900. [ 20-10-04 0513GMT ]  

Government bond prices were barely changed after what one trader described as another quiet day of trading.  

The 8% November 2006 bond yield closed at 6.08%, down just one basis point from Tuesday, while the 6% April 2015 bond closed at 6.04%, unchanged from Tuesday.  

"There's no flow or anything significant that's pushing the market one way or the other," said a trader at a local bank.  

The trader said investors might be unwilling to change their positions ahead of the central bank's next review of the official cash rate on Oct. 28.

title: Bollard Says RBNZ Could Hold  FX  Position 5 Yrs Or More
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand would take a medium- to long-term view when it intervenes in the foreign exchange market, potentially holding positions for five years or so, central bank Governor Alan Bollard said Wednesday.  

Bollard was speaking on National Radio after Tuesday's vote in New Zealand's Parliament ratifying a new funding agreement between the government and the central bank governor.  

The agreement, which provides balance sheet firepower for the RBNZ to intervene in the foreign exchange market, was passed by 84 votes to 35.  

The center-right National Party, led by Bollard's predecessor Don Brash, voted against ratification, as did the free-market Act Party.  

Bollard said the central bank would look to intervene when the New Zealand dollar, known colloquially as the Kiwi, was a long way from its average medium-term level and that level wasn't justified by economic fundamentals.  

"We have been looking at getting this intervention power for some time now. We see the opportunity to have a leveraged effect with a small real effect on the New Zealand dollar multiplying up to quite a significant effect across the economy," Bollard said.  

"I would expect other players to notice what we were doing and take similar action," he said.  

The RBNZ would intervene to smooth the peaks and lessen the troughs of the New Zealand dollar's cycle, he said.  

Bollard said he didn't expect to use the intervention power much at all. "I won't be unhappy if I go through my term and don't use it," he said.  

Bollard was appointed to a standard five-year term on Sept. 23, 2002.  

He expected the RBNZ's intervention practice would be nearest to the Australian model than to any other central bank model.  

"The Reserve Bank of Australia recently has had small success in taking the Australian dollar down from the top of its cycle and up from its bottom," Bollard said.  

The RBNZ wanted its own power to intervene rather than using the Minister of Finance's power to instruct the central bank to undertake intervention.  

Bollard said the RBNZ over the next few months would lay out a framework publicly for its intended intervention practice.  

He said lobbying from sector groups in the economy over when and whether to intervene to influence the Kiwi was to be expected.

title: NZ's parliament agrees to RBNZ funding changes.
text:
WELLINGTON, April 6 (Reuters) - New Zealand approved on Tuesday a beefing up of the central bank funding to allow it to intervene in the foreign exchange market.  

The parliament passed, 84 to 35, a government resolution varying the Reserve Bank of NZ's funding agreement, so that any losses incurred as a result of foreign exchange intervention would not be treated as expenditure and would not cause the bank to breach its maximum allowable expenditure.  

The measure was supported by all parties except the opposition National Party, headed by former RBNZ governor Don Brash and the right wing ACT Party.  

The RBNZ will get a NZ$1 billion capital injection to cover any unrealised losses it might suffer in buying and selling the New Zealand dollar.  

The bank will also increase foreign exchange reserves by NZ$1.9 billion to NZ$7 billion, to be used should financial markets become dysfunctional.  

The RBNZ has always had the power to intervene in foreign exchange markets, but has never done so since the New Zealand dollar was floated in early 1985.  

In March, the RBNZ asked the government for the capacity to intervene in foreign exchange markets at times when the New Zealand dollar reached extreme and unjustifiable levels.  

This would see the bank looking to smooth out the extremes - top and bottom - of a cycle, but which could also result in paper losses.  

Such losses were likely to be temporary, and reverse as the exchange rate cycle progressed, Finance Minister Michael Cullen said during the debate. "The bank is not expecting to intervene often, and is not promising that intervention will always succeed," Cullen said.  

"But it considers there will be opportunities to make a small but valuable difference, where that is consistent with the bank's price stability target."  

The bank has said it would enter markets only when the currency was at extreme levels not justified by economic fundamentals; intervene when there was a real chance of influencing the market; not target any particular level of the dollar; and not act against the long term trend of the exchange rate.  

The New Zealand dollar , which last traded at $0.6482/92, is about 20 percent higher against the U.S. dollar than a year ago, largely driven by the greenback's slide and New Zealand's 425 basis point interest rate advantage.

title: NZ Fin Min: RBNZ To Give  Forex Intervention  Cost Annually
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand will declare profits and losses from any foreign exchange intervention in its annual report, the finance minister told lawmakers Tuesday, in introducing amending legislation to boost the RBNZ's capacity to intervene in the currency market.  

The government is currently putting forward changes to the RBNZ's legislation aimed to enhance the central bank's ability to intervene in the foreign exchange market, through increases in the central bank's equity and in its holding of foreign currency reserves.  

"These measures will strengthen the bank's capacity to intervene in the foreign exchange market for two purposes," Finance Minister Michael Cullen said.  

"The first is to stabilize the market in periods of market dysfunction such as when the market is very illiquid," he said.  

"The second is to reduce exchange rate variability, by intervening in the market where the New Zealand dollar exchange rate is either severely over or undervalued relative to economic fundamentals," Cullen said.  

New Zealand's parliament is voting Tuesday on amendments to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989, including the funding agreement between the central bank and the government which sets the amount of income the central bank is allowed to retain to meet its operational expenses.  

Cullen said the main change to the funding agreement is that any market losses sustained by the Reserve Bank as a result of intervening in the foreign exchange market won't be treated as expenditure for the purpose of the funding agreement and won't cause the central bank to breach the maximum allowable expenditure under the agreement.  

Market losses on currency positions aren't part of the central bank's operational expenses, he said.  

"It is therefore appropriate that these expenses are not included in the funding agreement," Cullen said. "However, the bank will still be required to report any market losses in its statement of financial performance, in accordance with New Zealand accounting practice, and will still be accountable for all aspects of its financial performance and risk management."  

The Reserve Bank provides a statement of its financial performance in its annual report.  

However, it acknowledges that positions taken by the central bank to affect the value of the New Zealand dollar are likely to be inferred from the government's monthly accounts.  

Cullen said it had been the central bank's policy for a long time to be ready to intervene when the market for the New Zealand dollar is dysfunctional.  

"The government has agreed to a substantial increase in the bank's foreign currency reserves for that purpose giving the bank access to around NZ$7 billion in reserves for market stability purposes," Cullen said.  

The new policy is for the Reserve Bank to intervene to reduce the peaks and troughs of the exchange rate cycle, Cullen said.  

Since the New Zealand dollar was floated in March 1985, the Reserve Bank hasn't intervened in the market to influence the level of the exchange rate.  

Cullen said he has been advised by the Reserve Bank that a well-timed intervention in the foreign exchange market, when the exchange rate is markedly over or undervalued relative to economic fundamentals, can help to diminish the peaks and troughs in the exchange rate cycle.  

Cullen said the central bank isn't expecting to intervene often, and isn't promising that intervention will always succeed.  

The Reserve Bank is expected to say when it is intervening most but not all of the time.  

Cullen also said that as the central bank has itself made very clear, any intervention carries some element of financial risk. "The bank will almost inevitably carry market losses on its books from time to time, but these will generally be of an unrealized and non-permanent nature and are likely to reverse as the exchange rate cycle progresses."

title: INTERVIEW: NZD  Intervention  Policy May Have Short Life
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand's main opposition party, the center-right National, will deny the country's central bank the multiparty support it wants for a new foreign exchange intervention policy, and will consider removing the bank's power to intervene independently when it next becomes the government.  

National's associate finance spokesman, John Key, a former head of global foreign exchange for investment bank Merrill Lynch, said Wednesday the party would vote against a motion in Parliament to approve changes to the funding agreement between the government and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.  

Those changes will pave the way for foreign exchange reserves held for national emergencies - such as an outbreak of foot and mouth disease destroying confidence in the country's financial markets and making it impossible to trade the currency - to be increased by NZ$1.9 billion to NZ$7 billion over four years.  

More controversially, the amendments will allow the Reserve Bank to use an undisclosed amount of funds for intervention to trim the peaks and troughs of the exchange rate cycle, and will inject NZ$1 billion into the bank so its balance sheet can absorb marked-to-market losses on foreign exchange positions.  

Key said National supports emergency reserves being increased because the economy has grown significantly since the target level for reserves was last changed in 1998, but the party opposes New Zealand breaking with the clean float of its currency. The central bank hasn't intervened in the currency market since the local dollar was floated in March 1985.  

"We are not going to support" the change to the funding agreement when it is voted on in Parliament, Key told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. The date for the Parliament vote hasn't been announced.  

The Reserve Bank earlier this month appealed for multiparty support for the policy change, saying this would reduce the risk of a "policy u-turn" that could result in marked-to-market losses becoming real losses.  


 
              Policy Change Certain To Pass 
   

Despite the National Party's opposition, ratification by Parliament is assured because the left-wing Green Party has said it would vote with the minority Labour-led coalition, giving it a majority.  

The next National government would consider taking away the Reserve Bank's right to intervene in the currency market independently of the government if the central bank hasn't intervened by the time National is elected government, Key said.  

When the policy change is passed, the central bank would still need government approval to use its emergency reserves, but intervention to influence the level of the New Zealand dollar would be conducted independently of the government.  

National currently has a large lead over the Labour-led government in opinion polls, but the next election doesn't have to be held until late 2005.  

Key said if the central bank has intervened and still had open foreign exchange positions by the time National forms the government, the party won't force it to close those positions "because they could be under water" and to buy those positions back could produce "very significant" losses for the New Zealand taxpayer.  

"We are not going to cut off our nose to spite our face...If they haven't intervened at the time we come into office, then I guess we will take a fresh look at that (intervention policy) and will determine whether we want to take away from them the right" to intervene, he said.  

National opposes intervention in the New Zealand dollar market because the "likely returns are small and the risks are quite great," Key said.  

"We don't think it will actually do very much at all in terms of the exchange rate movement. The reality is that they will only get involved at the tops or bottoms of the cycle, which as the Treasury Department highlighted, is very difficult to do.  

"And it creates a huge amount of moral hazard. I think what will happen - inevitably, businesses will become more reliant on a belief that the government can actually change the exchange rate when the proven evidence is they can't," he said.

title: NZ dollar holds ground above $0.65 ahead of data.
text:
WELLINGTON, March 30 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar notched up its third day of gains on Tuesday, holding above 65 U.S. cents as the market awaited offshore data due later in the week.  

By 5:35 p.m. (0535 GMT) the kiwi was at $0.6533/41, compared with $0.6481/91 late on Monday.  

"The market's been firm, a little bit surprisingly I suppose given that the sentiment from offshore was pointing towards ongoing euro weakness," said Bancorp Treasury Services director Jon Clarke.  

The kiwi traded a 40-point range capped by $0.6545, and was likely to remain entrenched within a wider range between $0.6400 and $0.6550 for the meantime.  

"We're still following the lead provided by sentiment on the euro against the U.S. dollar, and that's picked up today, so we've picked up today and the Aussie picked up," Clarke said.  

The U.S. dollar has fallen to a near 3-1/2-year low against the yen since reports on Monday, since denied, that the Bank of Japan was scaling back its policy of intervention in the currency.  

The euro regained some form, having eased ahead of the interest rate-setting European Central Bank meeting on Thursday.  

"I think really the market's going to maintain itself somewhere around here until we get the ECB data on Friday morning (NZT), and then the non-farm payrolls from the States," he said.  

On Friday the U.S. March non-farm payrolls data will give an indication of the state of the labour market, the key lagging indicator in an otherwise improving U.S. economy.  

The kiwi was unmoved after Finance Minister Michael Cullen released details of the financial capacity the Reserve Bank of New Zealand will get for any intervention in currency markets.  

New Zealand foreign exchange reserves, for use when financial markets are in extreme crisis, would be increased by NZ$1.9 billion to NZ$7 billion.  

The central bank would also get an increase of NZ$1 billion in capital to cover temporary losses incurred if it intervenes to smooth out the highs and lows of the exchange rate cycle.  

New Zealand debt made minor gains at the short end but was unchanged further along the curve, despite the fourth straight day of price falls for U.S. Treasuries which have been hit by investor concerns of forthcoming data, especially the March jobs report.  

New Zealand has a quiet data week ahead, with the National Bank of NZ business confidence survey and building consents data on Wednesday the only items of note.  

Among the movements, February 2005 bond yields were two basis points lower at 5.35 percent, while there were no changes for November 2006s at 5.39 percent, July 2009s at 5.61 percent, and April 2013s at 5.78 percent.

title: UPDATE 1-RBNZ to get NZ$2.9 bln for  intervention -FinMin.
text:
WELLINGTON, March 30 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank is to get a NZ$1 billion ($650 million) capital injection as part of its plan to cope with the high flying currency, while the country's foreign exchange reserves will be increased by another NZ$1.9 billion, Finance Minister Michael Cullen said on Tuesday.   

 Earlier this month the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) asked the government for the capacity to intervene in foreign exchange markets at times when the New Zealand dollar reached extreme and unjustifiable levels.   

 The cash injection would allow the RBNZ to cover any losses incurred during intervention, Cullen said.   

 The increased foreign exchange reserves are earmarked for use only at times of crisis when markets are "dysfunctional".   

 "These measures should assist the economy by tempering exchange rate volatility," Cullen said in a statement.   

 In a letter to Cullen from the RBNZ, released at the same time, the bank repeated its approach to intervention.   

 This included entering markets only at times when the kiwi was at extreme levels not justified by economic fundamentals; intervening when there is a real chance of influencing the market; not targeting any particular level of the dollar and, not going against the long term trend of the exchange rate.   

 The New Zealand dollar was unmoved, sitting within its opening narrow range around $0.6510.   

 Deutsche Bank chief economist Ulf Schoefisch said the latest release added little to what was already known.   

 "We believe that the ongoing implications for foreign exchange markets will be relatively minor," he said.   

 The central bank has said several times since it unveiled its proposals that any intervention would be opportunistic and look only to trim the highs and lows of the exchange cycle.   

 The New Zealand dollar , known as the kiwi, has risen about 19 percent against the U.S. dollar over the past year, largely driven by the greenback's slide and New Zealand's 425 basis point interest rate advantage.   

 The RBNZ's overall foreign currency position would be limited, governor Alan Bollard said in the letter.   

 Over the medium term the bank would aim to maintain, on average, a net zero open foreign exchange position, and it would get out of the market when the exchange rate was not at "exceptional levels" and when they could "avoid influencing the exchange rate".   

 New Zealand's overall foreign exchange reserves currently stand at NZ$5.1 billion, including Debt Management Office holdings and International Monetary Fund special drawing rights.   

 The RBNZ's capital would be increased through raising its investment in government bonds.   

 The planned NZ$1.9 billion increase in foreign currency assets would be done over a four year period to lessen any impact on markets.   

 Cullen said a motion needed to ratify a change to the RBNZ's funding agreement has been introduced into the 120 seat parliament, where it has majority support.

title: NZD Up On Japanese Buying Interest; Bonds Little Changed
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand dollar finished higher Tuesday, helped by Japanese-based interest and a stronger euro and Australian dollar.  

Government bond prices ended almost flat after opening lower as investors avoided pushing yields too far either way ahead of crucial data from the U.S. this week.  

Traders said mid-curve bonds were slightly weaker but the rest of the curve came back better bid compared with the morning.  

The New Zealand dollar, or the Kiwi as it is colloquially known, closed at US$0.6535, up from US$0.6483 Monday, after trading a local range of US$0.6501-US$0.6542.  

Against its Australian counterpart, the Kiwi ended at A$0.8722, up from Monday's close at A$0.8693.  

The Kiwi spent the local session mostly nestled between US$0.6505 and US$0.6525 before offshore-based buying, led by Japanese interest, drove it higher, said Basil Payn, head of foreign exchange markets at Westpac Bank.  

"The currency had gotten a bit short after the comments about the forex reserves and we saw a short squeeze late in the day," he said.  

Earlier Tuesday, Finance Minister Michael Cullen said the central bank's foreign exchange reserves fund for stabilizing the local currency market will be raised by NZ$1.9 billion to NZ$7 billion and further funds will be approved for intervention to trim the peaks and troughs of the exchange rate cycle.  

Cullen also said the central bank's equity will be increased by about NZ$1 billion to help it cope with the risks associated with the new policy of intervening in the New Zealand dollar market. Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank asked the government for greater capacity to intervene in the foreign exchange market to temper the New Zealand dollar's rise.  

Payn said the Kiwi's fall Tuesday was brief as news about "raising the reserves isn't new."  

He said the Kiwi is likely to attempt a break higher in offshore trade, possibly closer to the US$0.6575 resistance level.  

However, others such as an ANZ Bank dealer said further gains in the Kiwi aren't likely to come easy as its ascent from recent three-and-a-half-month lows of US$0.6340 "hasn't been very convincing."  

He said the Kiwi was supported Tuesday by a stronger euro and Australian dollar, the latter of which was helped by an unexpected rise in domestic building approvals, which rose 3.2% on-month in February compared with expectations for a 3.0% fall.  

"The Kiwi is really doing a little bit of a range trade within a one to one and a half (U.S. cent) range, and I think we're unlikely to break much higher given recent trends," the dealer said.  

The local bond market remained range-bound through the session with the short end of the curve paring minor early losses to close unchanged.  

Long bonds such as the November 2011 bonds ended up 0.5 basis point, while the July 2009 bonds also ended up 0.5 basis point.  

A bond trader said the local market is looking ahead to price action in the U.S. ahead of key data out this week. "The market basically shuffled through in a very narrow range and was well-supported by the end of the day," he said.  

In the U.S., the Institute For Supply Management's manufacturing survey for March will be released Thursday, and the March employment report will follow on Friday.  

"I think the payrolls report is the crucial piece of data people are waiting for...the U.S. bonds have been a bit heavy of late and markets don't want to second-guess how the data will stack up," the trader said.  

Another trader said the unexpected rise in Australian building approvals led Australian bonds to weaken slightly before bouncing back, which had a neutral effect on New Zealand bonds.  

"The bonds here have performed well really, most are trading with the flows as there's nothing in the domestic market to push prices (either side) in a big way," he said.

title: 2nd UPDATE: NZ Central Bk's  Forex  Reserves To Be Boosted
text:
(Updates with comment from analyst, funding details)  

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen said Tuesday the central bank's foreign exchange reserves for stabilizing the currency market during periods of dysfunction will be raised by NZ$1.9 billion to NZ$7 billion and further undisclosed funds will be approved for intervention to trim the peaks and troughs of the exchange rate cycle.  

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand also released a raft of papers and correspondence between itself and the finance minister about intervention, but all references to the amount of money the central bank will have for intervention to trim the extremes of exchange rate cycle - the key information for markets - was removed from the documents.  

The papers indicate it could take up to four years for the central bank's emergency reserves to be increased to NZ$7 billion, or 2.45 billion Special Drawing Rights, a notional currency used by the International Monetary Fund.  

The necessary changes to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's funding agreement with the government will be voted on in parliament Tuesday. The legislature is expected to ratify the change in policy as the left-wing Green Party has said it will vote with the minority Labour-led government on the intervention issue.  

The finance minister also said the central bank's equity will be increased by about NZ$1 billion to help it cope with the financial risks associated with the new policy of intervening in the New Zealand dollar market.  

Deustche Bank Chief Economist Ulf Schoefisch said the change in intervention policy has generated considerable interest, but "we believe the ongoing implications for foreign exchange markets will be relatively minor."  

Recent comments by Reserve Bank Governor Alan Bollard that he wouldn't be surprised if no intervention occurred during his term as governor have underlined his intention to use the new intervention power only in "extreme" circumstances, said Schoefisch.  

Earlier this month the Reserve Bank asked the government for greater capacity to intervene in the foreign exchange market to temper the New Zealand dollar's rise.  

The central bank holds reserves to keep the New Zealand dollar market functioning in periods of market dysfunction but hasn't intervened since the local dollar was floated in 1985.  

Last month the New Zealand dollar hit a seven-year high of US$0.7102 against the U.S. dollar, which was a gain of 82% since its post 1985-float low of US$0.3898 which it hit in October 2000.  

Independent Operation Of Policy  

The new aspect of intervention policy gives the central bank the capacity to buy or sell the New Zealand dollar when it is either exceptionally low or high relative to the level that economic fundamentals suggest it should be at.  

This type of intervention will be carried out independently by the Reserve Bank using powers it has under Section 16 of the Reserve Bank Act.  

"These measures should assist the economy by tempering exchange rate volatility and will move New Zealand monetary management closer toward Australian practice," Cullen said.  

"They are strongly supported by the government as they are consistent with the changes we have introduced to monetary policy since taking office in 1999."  

In other changes, Cullen has given the Reserve Bank the power to use its emergency reserves without seeking the finance minister's permission.  

"In a period of market dysfunction, it is recognized that the bank may need to intervene very quickly," Cullen said in a memorandum to the bank dated March 25.  

Cullen has given the central bank a standing direction under Section 17 of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act to intervene using funds of up to 175 million SDRs when intervention is urgently required but the finance minister or his deputies can't be contacted quickly.  

The government will increase its gross debt over the next four years to fund the increase in the central bank's reserves, according to a Cabinet paper released Tuesday.  

"The increase in reserves will add to gross sovereign debt, although the precise impact depends on when the bank calls on the resources, and the detail of the transaction between the New Zealand Debt Management Office and the (central) bank," the paper said.  

The increase in gross debt would "reduce the extent to which the government is likely to overachieve" on its long-term objective of gross debt equaling 30% of gross domestic product on average. New Zealand's net debt would be "largely unchanged."

title: NZ To Borrow To Increase  Central Bank Forex  Reserves
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand government will increase its gross debt over the next four years to fund a significant increase in the central bank's foreign exchange reserves, making it more difficult for the government to beat its target of gross debt averaging 30% of the economy, according to a Cabinet paper released Tuesday.  

Release of the document follows Finance Minister Michael Cullen's announcement Tuesday that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's emergency foreign exchange reserves will be increased by NZ$1.9 billion to NZ$7 billion and the bank will also be given reserves, of an undisclosed amount, for intervention to temper peaks and troughs in the New Zealand dollar's exchange rate cycle.  

"The increase in foreign reserves for market stabilization purposes is likely to occur in phases over the four years, although it could be brought forward if the need arises," Cullen said in the Cabinet paper.  

The central bank will also need to build reserves for the new policy of intervening to influence the level of the New Zealand dollar, he said.  

"The increase in reserves will add to gross sovereign debt, although the precise impact depends on when the bank calls on the resources, and the detail of the transaction between the New Zealand Debt Management Office and the bank," the paper said.  

The increase in gross debt would "reduce the extent to which the government is likely to overachieve" on its long-term debt objective of gross debt equaling 30% of gross domestic product on average.  

New Zealand's net debt would be "largely unchanged" as the borrowed funds will be invested in foreign currency assets, Cullen said.  

The central bank is also to get an injection of NZ$1 billion of new equity to help its balance sheet cope with the financial risks of the new intervention policy.

title: UPDATE 1-RBNZ argues for NZD  intervention , ready to act.
text:
WELLINGTON, March 25 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand repeated on Thursday that it was ready to intervene in foreign exchange markets, saying it could be modestly effective as long as the timing was right.  

Since the central bank said two weeks ago it would seek authority to intervene, markets have been sceptical that the RBNZ could make much of a difference because its currency reserves standa at a modest NZ$3.5 billion ($2.3 billion).  

The New Zealand dollar, known as the kiwi, has surged about 19 percent against the U.S. dollar over the past year. The rise has been driven largely by the greenback's slide, as well as New Zealand's 425 basis point interest rate advantage.  

RBNZ Deputy governor Adrian Orr said that while intervention could not reverse bigger international trends, it could still could be effective.  

"The Bank would intervene at opportune times, not when the currency's direction is being dominated by strong international trends or consensus opinions," Orr said in a speech prepared for delivery to a meat industry conference.  

At best intervention would likely only soften the extreme tops and bottoms of a cycle, he said.  

Over the past three-and-a-half years the kiwi has touched a low of just below $0.39 in late 2000 and a high around $0.7100 in February.  

INCREASE RESERVES  

The RBNZ asked the government for the capacity to intervene in foreign exchange markets when the New Zealand dollar moved to extreme and unjustifiable levels out of touch with economic fundamentals.  

Orr said the RBNZ wanted to increase significantly its current foreign exchange reserves, which have stayed at about the same level since the currency was floated in 1985, and are earmarked for use in times of crisis when markets become "disorderly".  

The bank has also asked for a capital injection so it can absorb any temporary losses it might incur in any intervention.  

The plan to buy and sell New Zealand dollars made "good portfolio management sense" over the long term, Orr said.  

"On average over the medium term we anticipate having no exposure to foreign exchange swings."  

Orr said the proposed system should not attract speculators to "take the Bank on", and the RBNZ believed the risks were relatively small and manageable. ($1=NZ$1.54).

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand dollar closed lower Thursday following broad overnight gains by its U.S. counterpart, while government bond prices gave up early gains to end slightly lower on the back of a weaker Australian market.  

The New Zealand dollar, or the Kiwi as it is colloquially known, closed at US$0.6504, down from US$0.6576 Wednesday, after trading a local range of US$0.6480-US$0.6542.  

Against the Australian dollar, the Kiwi ended at A$0.8748, slightly down from Wednesday's close at A$0.8754.  

The Kiwi, which fell more than 1% overnight to a low of US$0.6507, declined further as sellers capped gains on rallies.  

The Kiwi got some support on Thursday's surprise narrowing of New Zealand's annual current account deficit in calendar 2003 to 4.5% of gross domestic product, from 4.6% in the 12 months to end-September. Economists had forecast the deficit to widen to 4.9% of GDP.  

New Zealand's monthly trade balance also moved into surplus in February for the first time in nine months after export growth outstripped the rise in imports. Data showed the trade balance for February was a surplus of NZ$136 million against expectations in a Dow Jones Newswires poll for a deficit of NZ$86 million.  

However, the run-up was short-lived and wasn't enough to push the Kiwi sufficiently higher to offset the impact of a broadly higher U.S. dollar, said Johnathan Bayley, strategist at Westpac Bank.  

Bayley also said comments from Reserve Bank of New Zealand Deputy Governor Adrian Orr that the bank would move to "significantly" increase foreign exchange reserves had little impact on the market.  

Orr said New Zealand's foreign exchange reserves need to be sufficient to ensure the central bank can cope with extremely volatile market conditions when they occur.  

He reiterated that the central bank also recently asked the government for greater capacity to intervene in the New Zealand dollar market when the local currency is exceptionally high or low.  

The comments saw the Kiwi fall about 15 points, but the currency recovered to trade near the US$0.6500 region.  

"On the whole, the Kiwi looks weak," Bayley said, adding that support is around US$0.6480 and below that is the key March lows of US$0.6400.  

Bank of New Zealand Currency Strategist Sue Trinh said the Kiwi failed to attract sufficient demand to support it above US$0.6500.  

"The Kiwi looks vulnerable at these levels and if we get further U.S. dollar strength, a deeper move down can't be ruled out," she said.  

She expects an overnight range of US$0.6480-US$0.6540, with the bias skewed to the downside.  

In the local bond market, prices reversed minor early strength after the Australian market weakened slightly, traders said.  

"The current account number was strong, but it really didn't have an effect on bonds...we basically followed the Australian market," one trader said.  

He said the mid-curve bonds were slightly better bid, but added that interest across the curve remained subdued.  

"There wasn't really anything domestically interesting enough for people to chase after," the trader said.  

A second trader said Friday's release of fourth quarter GDP growth numbers may have a greater influence on the market. "Although the data is basically historic, a number substantially off expectations may have an effect one way or the other," he said.  

Production-based GDP is expected to have expanded 0.9% from the third quarter and 3.5% in the 12 months ending December, according to the median forecast of 12 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires recently.  

The slope of the bond curve steepened slightly, with the yield gap between the 6.5% February 2006 bond and the April 2013 bond finishing at 37.5 basis points, up from 37 basis points Wednesday.

title: NZ Central Bk:  FX  Reserves To Be Increased Significantly
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--Reserve Bank of New Zealand Deputy Governor Adrian Orr said Thursday that the bank will move to "significantly" increase foreign exchange reserves after Finance Minister Michael Cullen agreed the central bank needs a greater capacity to intervene in the local currency market.  

Orr, in notes for a speech to Meat New Zealand's annual conference in Whangarei, said more reserves appear necessary because the global foreign exchange market has grown significantly since 1984 when the New Zealand dollar was floated.  

New Zealand's foreign exchange reserves need to be sufficient to ensure the central bank can cope with extremely volatile market conditions when they occur, he said. "The Minister of Finance has agreed with our advice and will be moving to increase significantly the level of foreign currency reserves the bank will manage for such insurance purposes." [ 25-03-04 0217GMT ]  

Orr reiterated that the central bank also recently asked the government for greater capacity to intervene in the New Zealand dollar market when the local currency is "exceptionally" high or low, relative to the level that economic fundamentals suggest it should be at.  

This type of intervention would be aimed at "trimming the extreme tops and bottoms" of the New Zealand dollar exchange rate cycle, he said.  

The central bank isn't recommending a Bank of Japan-style of intervention, Orr said, whereby Japanese policy-makers use significant funds with the aim of influencing the long-term trend of the yen or stand in the path of strong trends in the currency.  

"What we are recommending is intervening when the moment is justified and opportune," he said.

title: NZ dollar trundles after euro, trades tight range.

The kiwi dollar was however enjoying some "safe haven" support, while the markets awaited more fallout from news that Israel had killed the spiritual leader of the militant group, Hamas.

Cullen said the continued high level of the New Zealand dollar was worrying because it might discourage investment in the export sector and limit the country's ability to take advantage of the global upturn.

title: NZ Fin Min: Important To Ensure  Forex  Policy Independent
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen said Wednesday he wants the nation's central bank to independently operate a proposed policy for intervening to dampen the local dollar's strength.  

Intervention poses financial risks and it is important that the revised foreign exchange policy seeks to minimize those risks, the minister said in speech notes for a speech to a Deutsche Bank-organized investment conference in Auckland.  

"One important way this can be done is by ensuring the Reserve Bank Governor can operate this policy independently of day-to-day political pressures, that is, by keeping the focus on the medium term," said Cullen, who in the past few months has been trying to talk the New Zealand dollar down from its current high level.  

The government is considering proposals from the central bank for it to increase the foreign exchange reserves it maintains for intervention to calm volatility in the local dollar - but hasn't used in 20 years - and to establish separate reserves for a new intervention policy aimed at smoothing out peaks and troughs in the currency.  

Cullen said it is also important that the central bank's foremost consideration remains meeting its Policy Targets Agreement objective of keeping annual consumer price inflation in a 1% to 3% band.  

"Indeed any revised policy on intervention is unlikely to alter the Policy Targets Agreement. It is merely another tool to help the Governor achieve those targets in the least cost manner.  

"It is consistent with the requirement in the Policy Targets Agreement for the (central) bank to seek to avoid unnecessary instability in the exchange rate," the finance minister said.  

Cullen reiterated that there "may be some merit" in having a greater capacity to intervene in the New Zealand dollar market.  

This capacity would allow room for a policy that "aims to dampen the extreme peaks and troughs of an exchange rate cycle, that is, the three to five years swings from peak to trough in the exchange rate."  

The impact of any intervention is unlikely to be large, Cullen said. "Maybe a few cents at the peaks and troughs of the cycle, or alternatively helping the cycle to turn a little earlier than otherwise would happen."  

The New Zealand dollar last month hit a seven year high of US$0.7102, which represented a gain of 82% from its post-1985 float low of US$0.3898 hit in October 2000.  

Keeping the New Zealand dollar a floating currency will remain a key component of the nation's macroeconomic policy framework, Cullen said.

title: Asia Bonds-Deviant curves in Australia, NZ, Korea.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 17 (Reuters) - Kinks in Australian and New Zealand benchmark yield curves suggest expectations of lower interest rates while South Korean debt is pricing in a rate hike, but analysts say the markets are getting ahead of themselves.   

 Some signs of slowing domestic growth, currency appreciation, and global factors such as uncertainty over the U.S. economic recovery and last week's bombing in Spain were having an undue influence on bond markets, they said.   

 "What the market has done is it has taken away all prospects of tightening and is actually starting to angle towards some chance of an easing," said Peter Jolly, strategist at the National Bank of Australia.   

 Jolly was referring to the Australian bond yield curve , which shows an inversion. The curve is positively sloping until six months and then three-year yields slide to 4.99 percent, below the 5.25 percent cash rate.   

 The New Zealand curve  shows yields rising until six months, then falling progressively until the two-year tenor.   

 This inversion or dip is a sign markets expect rates to be lowered. Australia's curve has been inverted for some months.   

 Jolly said disappointment with some data in Australia and New Zealand and with the U.S. February jobs numbers had led to the view that rates would be cut. But he did not agree.   

 The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates in November and December, to moderate household borrowing. But it stayed pat in February and March as the currency  hit seven-year highs and retail spending cooled. Since then, consumer sentiment has deteriorated, housing loans have fallen and joblessness is up.   

 The Reserve Bank of New Zealand hiked rates in January but held the line this month and sought powers to intervene to rein in the New Zealand dollar .   

 FLATTER CURVES   

 Besides the shift in monetary expectations, analysts suspect bonds were sold as investors exited so-called carry trades, which involve buying assets in high-yielding currencies.   

 Still, interest rate swaps  in Australia have not inverted, but are just very flat. Spreads between five and two-year swaps are about 20 points, the tightest in 10 months.   

 "People haven't really focused on what's going on in Australia," said Peter Carpenter, director of global interest rate products at American Express Bank, Singapore.   

 "I don't think there is going to be any rate hike in the next two or three meetings, but certainly rates are at the bottom of the range of neutral policy."   

 For an economy expanding at four percent annually, rates could move up within the 5.0-6.25 percent neutral range the RBA has set, analysts say. Then the yield curve definitely needs to be flat or rising, not inverted.   

 "Even if the RBA is on hold, you have to have a positive curve. I think these rates are very artificial levels created by external factors and I don't think they will stay here very long," said Carpenter.   

 KOREA TOO STEEP   

 South Korean yields  have been falling after last week's impeachment of President Roh Moo-hyun and analysts expect rates will be kept at record lows until consumer spending picks up.   

 Still, the spread between the overnight rates , around 3.6-3.8 percent, and the one-year bond at 4.2 percent is too high, say analysts, making the curve steeper than the U.S. Treasury curve or other Asian bond curves.   

 But monetary policy expectations seem to have taken a backseat in Korea, analysts said.   

 Bert Gochet, strategist with UBS, said the heavy issuance of monetary stabilisation bonds (MSBs), which the central bank uses to soak up the won released in currency intervention, was the reason for the steep curve.   

 Also, local fund managers had been selling bonds to move their money into soaring Korean stocks  which hit nearly two-year peaks this month, he said.

title: UPDATE 1-RBNZ says no NZ dlr level in mind,  intervention  rare.
text:
WELLINGTON, March 17 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand will not target any particular level of exchange rate nor battle the market in the event it intervenes in the foreign exchange market, according to a background paper released on Wednesday.    

 The central bank surprised last week when it said it would ask the government for the "capacity" to intervene in the currency market if the kiwi dollar  reached unjustifiable levels that were not in tune with economic fundamentals.    

 The bank said in its background paper it would need a capital injection to give it the funds to be able to intervene.    

 Governor Alan Bollard later said any new funds should be kept separate from the current NZ$3.5 billion ($2.3 billion) foreign exchange reserves, which it wants kept in case of extreme cases when markets become "disorderly".    

 Asked at a parliamentary committee how much extra money the bank would need, Bollard refused to give a figure.    

 "We don't wish markets to take initial positions about what they think our ensuing positions might be," he said.    

 The New Zealand dollar has gained around a quarter of a cent since the comments to last trade at $0.6533/40. That compared with Tuesday's late local level of around $0.6485.    

 The kiwi dollar has gained around 19 percent against the greenback over the past year making it one of the best performers in the world, but also severely dented export earnings.    

 RARE AND OPPORTUNISTIC    

 Bank of New Zealand treasury economist Craig Ebert said neither the paper nor Bollard's appearance before the parliamentary committee added much to last week's announcement.    

 "Broadly speaking (they were) fire fighting what seemed to be misunderstandings, they were really clarifying what they are not going to do," Ebert said.    

 The RBNZ paper repeated previous comments that intervention would only occur when the currency was at extreme levels not justified by economic fundamentals.    

Intervention would be "rare" and "opportunistic", it said.    

 "We do not expect to intervene very often or to be able to alter the exchange rate by a sufficiently large amount to make this a substantial issue," it said.    

 "The Bank will not be attempting to stop the exchange rate moving when economic adjustment would be helped by that movement - we will not be targeting or defending any particular exchange rate."    

 The RBNZ already has the power to intervene when financial markets are "disorderly" - when a price is not being offered in the currency - but has never done so since the kiwi was floated in early 1985.    

 Ebert said a large number of the "mechanics" of how the RBNZ would increase its reserves and operate in the market had yet to be worked through.    

 "Even so I think the prospect of them intervening is quite low," Ebert said.    

 Bollard said no work had been done on whether the bank might have intervened at any time in the past.    

 Over the past three-and-a-half years the kiwi has touched a low of just below $0.39 in late 2000 and a high last month around $0.7100.    

 Any intervention policy could eventually be profitable for bank, the RBNZ said.    

 "There is likely to be a small benefit from intervention, enough to outweigh the comparatively small risks of implementing the policy."

text:
WELLINGTON, March 17 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand said it would not target any particular level of exchange rate nor battle the market in the event it ever intervenes in the foreign exchange market, according to a background paper released on Wednesday.   

The central bank surprised last week when it said it would ask the government for the "capacity" to intervene in foreign exchange markets if the kiwi dollar reached unjustifiable levels that were not in tune with economic fundamentals.   

The RBNZ said any intervention would occur only at the extremes of a exchange rate cycle and would be "opportunistic".   

The bank said it expected interventions to be infrequent.   

"We do not expect to intervene very often or to be able to alter the exchange rate by a sufficiently large amount to make this a substantial issue," the paper said.   

"The Bank will not be attempting to stop the exchange rate moving when economic adjustment would be helped by that movement - we will not be targeting or defending any particular exchange rate," the bank said.   

It said it would not be taking on the market when investors and traders generally were moving in a particular direction, nor would it seek to "smooth out" the daily, weekly or even yearly movements in the exchange rate.   

"Such volatility is clearly a nuisance, but business can and do deal with that by hedging their currency positions."   

However, it said intervention would be taken into account when it came to setting interest rates, which could see a "slightly smaller exchange rate cycle" offset by a "slightly greater inflation cycle or by a slightly greater interest rate cycle".   

The New Zealand dollar last traded at $0.6493 compared with Tuesday's late local level of around $0.6480/90.   

Since last week's intervention comments the kiwi has fallen more than nine percent on the intervention comments combined with the RBNZ decision to keep interest rates on hold.   

The RBNZ said it will need a capital injection and increase in foreign exchange reserves to be able to intervene and absorb any losses incurred, which is why it needs the approval of the parliament.   

The bank currently has around NZ$3.5 billion in foreign cash reserves.   

The RBNZ already has the power to intervene during times when financial markets are "disrupted" but has never done so since the New Zealand dollar was floated in early 1985.   

Bollard has said he did not see that the RBNZ would have intervened during the kiwi's most recent cycle which has seen it appreciate from just below 39 U.S. cents in late-2000 to a peak of just over 71 cents in last month.   

Finance Minister Michael Cullen has already thrown his backing behind the proposal.

title: UPDATE: NZ Central Bk Won't  Intervene  In  Forex  Mkt Often
text:
(Updates with details about proposed capital injection for Reserve Bank, Bollard's comments to parliament's finance committee, market reaction)  

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--Intervention in the New Zealand dollar market to "ameliorate" extremes in the currency could have significant benefits for the economy, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said Wednesday in a background paper on its intervention proposal.  

The Reserve Bank stunned markets last week by announcing it has asked Finance Minister Michael Cullen for greater capacity to intervene in the foreign exchange market when the New Zealand dollar is unjustifiably low or high. That news sparked a 3% fall in the currency against the U.S. dollar over 24 hours.  

The background paper said the New Zealand dollar varies across the economic cycle "to a far greater extent than the underlying economic situation warrants" and that the economic costs of such exchange rate distortions can be significant.  

"Successful intervention would only ameliorate these distortions to a limited extent, but the benefits from doing so might be considerable," the bank said.  

"Our view is that there is likely to be a small benefit from intervention aimed at dampening the exchange rate cycle, enough to outweigh the comparatively small risks of implementing the policy."  

The New Zealand dollar last month hit a seven-year high of US$0.7102, which was a gain of 82% from its post-1985 float low of US$0.3898 in October 2000.  

New Zealand hasn't intervened in its currency market since the local dollar was floated nearly 20 years ago and its foreign exchange reserves currently only total NZ$3.5 billion.  

The bank said selling New Zealand dollars when the currency is exceptionally high, or buying the currency at the other extreme, would "seem to" change monetary policy by altering the money supply, but added that any intervention would be "sterilized" in line with international practice.  

"We do not expect to intervene very often or be able to alter the exchange rate by a sufficiently large amount to make this (altering monetary policy) a substantial issue.  

"But to the extent that we are able to affect the path of the exchange rate through foreign exchange market intervention, that would be taken into account in our interest rate settings," the bank said.  

Intervention would give the central bank a "small amount" of additional capacity to fulfill its Policy Targets Agreement with the government, which requires the bank to avoid unnecessary instability in interest rates, economic output and the exchange rate.  

The New Zealand dollar rose to US$0.6508 from US$0.6486 before release of the background paper because the central bank's comments reassured investors that intervention isn't imminent.  

ANZ Bank director of foreign exchange markets John Body said the Reserve Bank has signaled "a very pragmatic intervention policy...it's going to be economically very valid and based on long analysis."  

Capital Injection Required  

The background paper reiterated last Thursday's statement by Reserve Bank Governor Alan Bollard in which he said intervention would be aimed at extremes in the currency and wouldn't be used to fight the New Zealand dollar's prevailing trend.  

"We will not be attempting to slow or reverse the exchange rate's movement when a large number of investors and traders are convinced that the exchange rate is going to continue to move in the same direction," the paper said.  

Nor will the bank be targeting any particular level of the New Zealand dollar and nor will it attempt to "smooth out" day-to-day or week-to-week volatility in the currency.  

"Intervention would be opportunistic, rather than a 'come what may' stand in the market against the odds," the bank said.  

The paper said intervention would expose the bank to changes in the value of the New Zealand dollar, but "the proposed strategy is in fact likely to be profitable to the Reserve Bank over the medium term, as long as the exchange rate continues to show a cyclical pattern."  

In the short to medium term it is probable there will be "substantial" unrealized gains and losses in foreign exchange trading," the paper said.  

"It would be desirable that any intervention strategy enjoyed multiparty support in Parliament, to minimize the risk that a policy u-turn might cause marked-to-market accounting losses to become real losses," the bank said.  

The left-wing Green party has said it will vote with the Labour-led minority coalition government on the issue of intervention, providing a majority in parliament for the policy change. Giving the central bank greater capacity to intervene only requires ratification in parliament, not a law change.  

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand will need a capital injection from the government to give it greater capacity to intervene.  

Bollard told parliament's finance and expenditure select committee Wednesday morning that increasing the central bank's foreign exchange reserves will take two forms.  

First, current reserves, which the bank can use to calm extremely volatile market conditions, will be increased to make the central bank more effective in that area, and these reserves will be ring-fenced from other reserves.  

Second, the capital injection will be used for reserves to implement the new intervention policy, to be operated under Section 16 of the Reserve Bank Act, which allows the bank to deal in foreign exchange independently of the government.  

Bollard said the central bank has given the government a proposal about what its reserves should be increased to, but declined to reveal the amount.

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--Intervention in the New Zealand dollar market to "ameliorate" extremes in the currency could have significant benefits for the economy, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said Wednesday in a background paper on its intervention proposal.  

The Reserve Bank stunned markets last week by announcing it has asked Finance Minister Michael Cullen for greater capacity to intervene in the foreign exchange market when the New Zealand dollar is unjustifiably low or high. That news sparked a 3% fall in the currency against the U.S. dollar over 24 hours.  

The background paper said the New Zealand dollar varies across the economic cycle "to a far greater extent than the underlying economic situation warrants" and that the economic costs of such exchange rate distortions can be significant.  

"Successful intervention would only ameliorate these distortions to a limited extent, but the benefits from doing so might be considerable," the bank said.  

"Our view is that there is likely to be a small benefit from intervention aimed at dampening the exchange rate cycle, enough to outweigh the comparatively small risks of implementing the policy."  

The New Zealand dollar last month hit a seven-year high of US$0.7102, which was a gain of 82% from its post-1985 float low of US$0.3898 in October 2000.  

New Zealand hasn't intervened in its currency market since the local dollar was floated nearly 20 years ago and its foreign exchange reserves currently only total NZ$3.5 billion.  

The bank said selling New Zealand dollars when the currency is exceptionally high, or buying the currency at the other extreme, would seem to change monetary policy by altering the money supply, but added that any intervention would be "sterilized" in line with international practice.  

"We do not expect to intervene very often or be able to alter the exchange rate by a sufficiently large amount to make this (altering monetary policy) a substantial issue.  

"But to the extent that we are able to affect the path of the exchange rate through foreign exchange market intervention, that would be taken into account in our interest rate settings," the bank said.  

Intervention would give the central bank a "small amount" of additional capacity to fulfil its Policy Targets Agreement with the government, which requires the bank to avoid unnecessary instability in interest rates, economic output and the exchange rate.  

The background paper reiterated last Thursday's statement by Reserve Bank Governor Alan Bollard in which he said intervention would be aimed at extremes in the currency and wouldn't be used to fight the New Zealand dollar's prevailing trend.  

"We will not be attempting to slow or reverse the exchange rate's movement when a large number of investors and traders are convinced that the exchange rate is going to continue to move in the same direction," the paper said.  

Nor will the bank be targeting any particular level of the New Zealand dollar and nor will it attempt to "smooth out" day-to-day or week-to-week volatility in the currency.  

"Intervention would be opportunistic, rather than a 'come what may' stand in the market against the odds," the bank said.  

The paper said intervention would expose the bank to changes in the value of the New Zealand dollar, but "the proposed strategy is in fact likely to be profitable to the Reserve Bank over the medium term, as long as the exchange rate continues to show a cyclical pattern."  

In the short to medium term it is probable there will be "substantial" unrealized gains and losses in foreign exchange trading," the paper said.  

The main risk for the central bank is that it fails to recognize a structural shift in the New Zealand dollar and tries to offset it unsuccessfully, sustaining losses.  

"It would be desirable that any intervention strategy enjoyed multiparty support in Parliament, to minimize the risk that a policy u-turn might cause marked-to-market accounting losses to become real losses," the bank said.  

The left-wing Green party has said it will vote with the Labour-led minority coalition government on the issue of intervention, providing a majority in parliament for the policy change.
