title: UPDATE 2 -NZ cenbank gov warns of  currency intervention , rate hikes might slow
text:
* RBNZ Gov says NZ$ over-valued and unsustainable

* RBNZ could sell NZ$ if currency does not weaken

* High currency factor may slow future rate rises   (Recasts, adds details, quotes, updates market reaction)

By Gyles Beckford

WELLINGTON, May 7 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank on Tuesday warned that it may have to intervene to weaken the country's high-flying currency, and suggested interest rate hikes might be slowed if the kiwi dollar remains elevated.

The forthright comments by Reserve Bank of New Zealand  governor Graeme Wheeler sent the New Zealand dollar -- the 10th most traded currency globally -- skidding nearly half a U.S. cent, as markets adjusted to the prospect of a less aggressive tightening cycle.

"If the currency remains high in the face of worsening fundamentals, such as a continued weakening in export prices, it would become more opportune for the Reserve Bank to intervene in the currency market to sell New Zealand dollars," Wheeler said in a speech to a dairy farming conference.

Wheeler said a stubbornly strong New Zealand dollar "will be a factor in our assessment of the extent and speed with which the Official Cash Rate needs to be raised."

Analysts were quick to note that the RBNZ has made similar intervention warnings in the past, but the implications for interest rates weren't lost on domestic markets.

"We do expect that sustained NZ dollar strength will slow the tightening cycle this year," said ASB Bank chief economist Nick Tuffley, who is picking another 25 basis point hike in June.  "But, beyond June, continued NZ dollar strength would reinforce our view that the RBNZ would pause until the end of the year."

Faced with rising inflation pressures in a booming economy, the RBNZ started its long-awaited rate-tightening cycle in March, becoming the first central bank in a developed economy to raise rates. Wheeler's latest comments suggest the bank may not apply the brakes too hard.

Another 25-basis-point hike at the June meeting would lift the cash rate to 3.25 percent, following similar-sized hikes in March and April, but a prolonged pause beyond that point would leave rates much lower than the RBNZ's implied projection of 4.25 percent by year-end.

Analysts expect the central bank to lower its projection on interest rates in June.

"Were the currency to hold at current levels, moving into the June MPS forecast round, there would be scope for inflation forecast downgrades, which should also cascade into the RBNZ's rate track," JP Morgan senior economist Ben Jarman said in a note to clients.

GLOBAL KIWI

The kiwi, one of the 10 most traded currencies globally, has been boosted by dairy export driven terms of trade at 40 year highs, and the central bank's resumption of rate rises boosting its yield attraction for investors in carry trades.

Currency carry traders borrow in countries with low interest costs to fund purchases in markets with higher yields. At 3.00 percent New Zealand's rates are well above the Fed fund's rate of 0.0 to 0.25 percent and even that of Australia which is at 2.50 percent.

The central bank's intervention arsenal is dwarfed by the massive global currency trade, with more than 100 billion New Zealand dollars traded daily -- meaning interest rates remain the biggest tool to manage the kiwi.

The RBNZ has talked intervention in the past and occasionally sold the currency in modest amounts, but Wheeler's comments were his most assertive piece of jawboning since he became governor in 2012.

"We are closer to intervention. It would not be a surprise if they were to do it one day," said Westpac senior currency strategist Imre Speizer.

"It's stronger rhetoric against the exchange rate than we have seen from this governor yet."

Wheeler said the kiwi, which hit a two-and-a half year high of $0.8779 on Tuesday, was overvalued and unsustainable at current levels

He said the currency could be expected to weaken if the Chinese economy were to slow, global dairy prices fall, financial market volatility was to return, and the U.S. economy improved.

The kiwi dropped to a low of $0.8700 from $0.8740. It last traded at $0.8690. So far this year it has risen about 5.8 percent against the U.S. dollar, and in March a visiting IMF team said it was overvalued by as much as 15 percent.

RBNZ POWERLESS

The RBNZ has regularly voiced its concern about the high currency, but has also admitted that it's largely powerless to affect the value other than at the margins, and that any intervention would be to remind investors that the currency was "not a one way bet".

A year ago, Wheeler made a similar sort of speech and disclosed the RBNZ had sold the currency for the first time in five years.

Dairy products provided about a third of the country's NZ$50 billion export earnings in the year to March, with China the biggest buyer. But prices have fallen more than 20 percent over the past two months, and the high currency remains a headwind to export earnings.

A Reuters poll of 17 economists shows all but one expect the RBNZ to raise rates to 3.25 percent in June, and though most economists anticipate rates to rise to 3.75 percent by the end of the year, Wheeler's comment puts the more aggressive market forecasts in perspective.

The "dairy price dynamics are now bringing the currency into sharper focus," JP Morgan's Jarman said, and that would feed into a more modest interest rate tightening track.        (Editing by Shri Navaratnam)

title: UPDATE 1 -NZ jobless holds at 5-yr low, cenbank seen hiking again in June
text:
* NZ jobless rate flat at 6 pct in Q4

* Jobless rate stays at lowest since Q2 2009

* Data bolsters expectations for RBNZ rate rise

By Naomi Tajitsu

WELLINGTON, May 7 (Reuters) - New Zealand's jobless rate remained at its lowest in five years in the first quarter and a record number were in the workforce, maintaining expectations for another interest rate increase next month.

The jobless rate was unchanged at 6.0 percent in the three months to March, Statistics New Zealand said on Wednesday. This was higher than economist forecasts for a 5.9 percent print, but the rate stayed at its lowest since the June 2009 quarter and points to a growing labour market as the economy strengthens.

Employment growth was driven by the jobs in the construction industry, helping to boost the labour participation rate to 69.3 percent, the highest on data going back to 1986. The number of people employed rose by a seasonally adjusted 22,000.

The New Zealand dollar slipped to $0.8693 after the data from around $0.8723 beforehand, as investors sold the currency on the slightly higher-than-expected jobless rate. The currency had earlier tumbled in early trade after Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor warned the bank may have to intervene to weaken the currency.

Wheeler said if the currency stayed high in the face of worsening fundamentals, such as continuing weakening in export prices, "it would become more opportune for the Reserve Bank to intervene in the currency market to sell NZ dollars."

Wheeler also said a high currency would contain tradable inflation pressures and would be a factor in its rate-raising decisions.

Still, Tuesday jobs report pointed to ongoing growth in the labour market, suggesting the RBNZ will raise official interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.25 percent at its next review in June, following two similar hikes in March and April.

"This is a pretty strong report and this is how the RBNZ will see it. For interest rates, it doesn't change the move to 4.5 percent by next year," said Annette Beacher, head of Asia-Pacific research at TD Securities in Sydney.

"I see the RBNZ tightening in June, then rest for a couple of months."

Annual inflation rose 1.5 percent in the first quarter, staying near the mid-point of the RBNZ's 1 percent-3 percent target range and keeping the central bank on its monetary tightening track after it began raising rates in March.

More New Zealanders are finding jobs as the country's $180 billion economy continues to grow at a solid pace on the back of earthquake reconstruction projects in the Canterbury region, a booming housing market and increasing dairy exports.

Employment gains were led by job opportunities in construction in the Canterbury region, along with retail and other services industries in Auckland, the country's largest city.

Private sector wages edged up 0.3 percent in the latest quarter, maintaining a rising trend albeit at a slower pace than economist forecasts for a 0.5 percent rise.

Some analysts said that a further slowing in wage growth as strong labour demand is met by increasing participation may quell overall inflation pressures, taking pressure off the RBNZ to raise rates down the line.

"Rising cyclical potential growth should ... go some way to containing inflationary pressure in forthcoming quarters," JPMorgan analysts said in a note.

"And the fact that wages grew a very benign 0.3 percent in Q1 underscores the point that measures of slack across the New Zealand are well behaved, and argue against the magnitude of tightening currently implicit in RBNZ forecasts."

A Reuters poll of 17 economists shows that all but one expect the RBNZ to raise rates to 3.25 percent in June, with most economists anticipating rates to rise to 3.75 percent by the end of the year.

(Reporting by Naomi Tajitsu; Editing by Shri Navaratnam)

title: New Zealand  Dollar Falls After  Central Bank  Talk of  Intervention
text:
WELLINGTON, New Zealand--The New Zealand dollar fell Wednesday after the country's central bank said it may intervene to weaken it, but the bank's plan to continue raising interest rates will make engineering a decline in the currency a challenge over the long term.

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Graeme Wheeler said the central bank may need to take action to weaken the currency, among the world's best-performing major currencies this year, to prevent its strength from choking off exports ranging from fruit to wine.

"If the currency remains high in the face of worsening fundamentals, such as a continued weakening in export prices, it would become more opportune for the Reserve Bank to intervene in the currency market to sell New Zealand dollars," he told a conference of dairy farmers.

The New Zealand dollar, known as the kiwi, dropped nearly half a cent against the U.S. dollar following his comments, to US$0.8702.

Keith Poore, head of investment strategy for AMP Capital New Zealand, which has more than 18.0 billion New Zealand dollars (US$15.6 billion) under management in the country, said Mr. Wheeler's comments added to rising risks facing the kiwi in the near term. Those risks include falling prices of milk, New Zealand's biggest export.

"At the current level there is definitely reason for the kiwi to move lower," said Mr. Poore, who has been a seller of the currency for the past month.

Still, the kiwi remains up nearly 4% this year against a basket of currencies that includes the U.S. dollar and British pound, partly due to record-high terms of trade as the New Zealand's agriculture-rich economy feeds Asia's growing appetite for dairy products. New Zealand's central bank has called it unsustainably high at current levels.

The New Zealand dollar has risen 1.0% over the same period against its counterpart in Australia, which was New Zealand's main trading partner until it was recently overtaken by China.

Further fueling the recent rally was the central bank's interest-rate increases in March and April, which were intended to tame inflation and cool a real-estate market at risk of overheating. The benchmark interest rate now stands at 3.0%, much higher than in other developed economies.

The interest-rate differential with neighboring Australia is particularly seen as bullish for the kiwi. On Tuesday, Australia's central bank held its policy rate at a record-low 2.5% for the eighth meeting in a row and signaled it would keep it at that level for some time to stoke an economy struggling with a fading mining boom.

New Zealand's central bank, meanwhile, has said it plans to raise interest rates by around two percentage points in the current tightening cycle, which it expects to last at least two years. Given that plan, any attempts at intervening to weaken the kiwi will have limited success, said ASB Economist Nick Tuffley.

Fergus McDonald, head of bonds and currencies for Tyndall Investment Management New Zealand LTD, which has around NZ$3.5 billion under management in New Zealand, also expects the kiwi to remain firm.

"If the RBNZ sticks to its guns and puts up interest rates and the rest of the world doesn't, it will continue to support the kiwi," he said.

New Zealand policy makers have acted to weaken the currency previously. In late 2012 and early 2013 the central bank sold the currency for the first time in nearly four years. The amount, however, was limited and prompted criticism that the central bank had misled markets over the extent of the intervention in an effort to "talk" the currency lower.

The central bank's latest talk of intervention also may reflect frustration at the currency's continued strength in the face of falling prices of dairy products, which account for around a third of exports. Milk prices fell a further 1.1% in the GlobalDairyTrade Auction overnight on Tuesday, bringing the total decline since mid-February to 23%.

In any case, David Croy, ANZ Bank's head of global markets research for New Zealand, said the central bank was unlikely to intervene quickly because there is no guarantee such a move would weaken the kiwi significantly.

Instead, Mr. Croy interpreted Mr. Wheeler's comments as a warning. They are a "reminder that the economy will start to come under pressure if commodity prices weaken further and the New Zealand dollar doesn't respond," he said.

title: UPDATE 2-China to allow direct yuan, NZ dollar trades
text:
(Adds comment, details)

BEIJING/WELLINGTON, March 19 (Reuters) - China has allowed direct domestic trading of the yuan against the New Zealand dollar to encourage such trading as it internationalises the Chinese currency.

The move, announced on Tuesday by the central bank during a visit by New Zealand Prime Minister John Key to Beijing, comes after China doubled the yuan's trading band over the weekend in a milestone step that gives investors more freedom to set the value of the tightly controlled currency.

China is New Zealand's largest export destination and a major buyer of dairy products produced in the South Pacific nation. The move was seen as promoting trade between the two countries, which rose 25.2 percent to NZ$18.2 billion ($15.71 billion) in 2013, and increase capital flows.

"Today's announcement will further reduce the costs of trade and investment transactions between New Zealand and China, increasing the ease of doing business for the benefit of businesspeople in both countries," New Zealand Prime Minister John Key said in a statement.

As part of China's sweeping plans to overhaul its maturing economy and let market forces drive a host of industries, the government wants to gradually relax its hold over the yuan and turn it into a global reserve currency that one day rivals the dollar.

The government's wish to promote international use of the yuan is partly driven by its concern that China is too vulnerable to the fluctuating value of the dollar.

China is home to the world's largest foreign exchange reserves, worth $3.82 trillion at the end of last year. About a third is invested in U.S. government bonds.

To promote international use of the yuan, China has signed a series of currency swaps with foreign governments in order to increase the overseas circulation of the Chinese currency.

Beijing has also allowed foreign exchange traders to directly trade a string of currency pairs within China to lower transaction costs. The New Zealand dollar is the 10th foreign currency that can be directly traded against the yuan in China.

And some data suggests China is making headway in its efforts to raise the yuan's profile.

Global transaction services organisation SWIFT said in December that the yuan overtook the euro in October to become the second-most used currency in trade finance.

But despite rising use of the yuan overseas and the apparent greater freedom that investors have in trading it, China's central bank still keeps the currency on a tight leash with traders reporting regular central bank intervention in the market. ($1 = 1.1587 New Zealand Dollars) (Reporting by Koh Gui Qing in Beijing, additional reporting by Naomi Tajitsu in Wellington; Editing by Robert Birsel and Keiron Henderson)

title: Australian dollar on the ropes after RBA; kiwi off recent lows
text:
* AUD near 3-mth low vs USD and euro, 3-yr low vs GBP

* Aussie hit by RBA intervention comment, upbeat US data

* AUD and NZD down 1.3 pct vs USD since Monday

By Naomi Tajitsu and Cecile Lefort

SYDNEY/WELLINGTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar licked its wounds on Friday after the head of the country's central bank said he was open to intervening to weaken the currency, while the New Zealand dollar bounced off lows as investors squared up short positions.

The Aussie skidded to a near three-month low of $0.9198 in offshore trade before edging back up to $0.9244.

It was also hard hit against the euro and the pound. The common currency climbed to a near three-month peak of A$1.4621 , bringing in sight the August high of A$1.5029. The pound surged to a three-year peak overnight with charts pointing to further upside. It was last at A$1.7520.

Much of the pressure for the Aussie came after Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens stepped up his rhetoric against the strength of the currency, which he has long argued was overvalued when judged against economic fundamentals.

While Stevens made clear that intervention was not without risks, markets were in the mood to sell the Aussie especially after a closely watched report showed China's factory sector grew at a slower pace in November.

Not helping was encouraging U.S. data that underpinned the U.S. dollar, as well as expectations the Federal Reserve will have to start tapering its asset buying at some point, whether December or March.

All that left the Aussie nursing hefty losses for the week. It was down 1.3 percent against the U.S. dollar since Monday and a clear break below $0.9200, the 61.8 percent of the August-October rally, would open the way to a test of a three-year low of $0.8848.

By contrast, the New Zealand dollar managed to pop up to a session high of $0.8245 following tame comments by a central bank official about kiwi strength.

Investors had expected a stronger complaint by Reserve Bank of New Zealand Assistant Governor John McDermott, who said that the currency was overvalued and that the RBNZ would like to see it lower.

The kiwi was broadly stronger, clocking an intraday high around 83.40 yen. It also shone against the Aussie , which slid to around NZ$1.1194, closing in on a two-month low around NZ$1.1192 hit earlier this week.

Expectations that the RBNZ will raise rates from a record-low 2.5 percent early next year also helped the kiwi .

Market participants said McDermott's comments were seen as part of the central bank's usual jaw-boning against currency strength, in contrast with the RBA's more aggressive effort to talk down the Aussie.

"There was no smoking gun in the speech. All it said was that the kiwi is overvalued, there was nothing new in it at all," said Tim Kelleher, head of institutional FX sales at ASB.

Traders had bought back the currency after it fell to a one-week low of $0.8175 on Thursday, tumbling in sympathy with losses in the Aussie. Yet, the kiwi was still down 1.3 percent since Monday.

Kelleher said that despite its slide the previous day, support had held at the kiwi's 200-day moving average of $0.8173, which also prompted demand. But he added that offers seen above $0.8250 would likely limit further gains for now.

New Zealand government bonds inched lower, nudging yields 1.5 basis points higher across the curve. Bonds remained on the back foot following relatively weak demand at an offer of inflation-linked bonds on Thursday.

Australian government bond futures were a touch softer with the long-end of the curve at 20-month lows. The three-year bond contract eased 1 tick to 96.820, while the 10-year contract fell as deep as 95.700, a level unseen since March 2012. A break below 95.600 would test the lowest in nearly three years. (Editing by Chris Gallagher)

title: RBNZ Assistant Governor McDermott: New Zealand's Exchange Rate Overvalued
text:
WELLINGTON, New Zealand--The historically high New Zealand dollar remains a significant headwind for the country's export sector but keeping interest rates low or intervening in the currency market would have little impact, Central Bank Assistant Governor John McDermott said in a speech Friday.

"The New Zealand dollar is overvalued from the standpoint of its effects on the economy and we would like to see a lower exchange rate," Mr. McDermott told lobby group Federated Farmers.

"The bank does intervene in the foreign exchange market from time-to-time. But evidence from the past, here and elsewhere, suggests foreign currency intervention is unlikely to have a sustained impact in lowering the exchange rate," he said.

Daily foreign currency transactions in New Zealand dollars "swamp any practical intervention capacity," as they average around 100 billion New Zealand dollars (US$82 billion) a day with more than 80% of transactions taking place offshore, Mr. McDermott said.

Instead, the solution lies in improved microeconomic policies, in particular those that promote greater competition, Mr. McDermott said. He also noted New Zealand's dependence on foreign funding "means that we have persistently needed interest rates above those in most developed economies," adding to pressure on the New Zealand dollar.

"Raising domestic savings relative to our investment needs appears the best way to sustainably lower New Zealand's real interest rates and take the pressure off the real exchange rate," Mr. McDermott said.

title: UPDATE 1-New Zealand central banker's comments boost "overvalued" NZ dollar
text:
(Adds comment, detail, background)

WELLINGTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - When Reserve Bank of New Zealand Assistant Governor John McDermott said on Friday the New Zealand dollar was overvalued and he would like to see it weaken, it did exactly the opposite and rose to a session high.

Speaking in Wellington, McDermott conceded the RBNZ was not inclined to actively weaken the currency as it prepares to raise interest rates next year, which markets took as little more than the central bank's usual jawboning against currency strength and drove it higher.

McDermott's comments appeared to acknowledge that the RBNZ was unwilling to enter the $4 trillion-a-day currency market to weaken the "kiwi" at the moment, given its limited resources to take on overseas players controlling roughly 90 percent of trade who have been buying the currency for its relatively higher yield.

The kiwi popped up to a session high of $0.8245 after the speech, as the absence of any signal that the RBNZ would try to weaken the currency spurred some buying.

McDermott said the New Zealand dollar was at historically high levels due the country's current high terms of trade, particularly booming dairy prices, and relatively strong economic performance.

"The Reserve Bank believes that, from a long-term perspective, the exchange rate is overvalued," he said.

"The high exchange rate is contributing to economic imbalances and the Reserve Bank would like to see it lower in order to promote more sustainable economic growth."

But he added that evidence in New Zealand and other countries suggested that foreign currency intervention was unlikely to have a sustained impact on lowering the exchange rate.

Expectations that the RBNZ will raise rates from a record low 2.5 percent early next year has boosted the kiwi, which hovers in range of a post-float high hit against a currency basket earlier this year after gaining nearly 5 percent so far this year.

Ongoing strength in the kiwi has been a headache for RBNZ Governor Graeme Wheeler, who said last week that he was concerned that a looming rise in interest rates would put upward pressure on the New Zealand dollar.

The RBNZ's tone on the currency's strength has been tempered compared with a speech by Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Glenn Stevens, who on Thursday said he was "open-minded" on whether to intervene to weaken the high Australian dollar, stepping up his rhetoric after long complaining of the currency's strength.

"Overall, in this episode so far, the bank has not been convinced that large-scale intervention clearly passed the test of effectiveness versus cost. But that doesn't mean we will always eschew intervention," Stevens told the Australian Business Economists' annual dinner.

ANZ currency strategist Sam Tuck said the RBA was taking a stronger position against the "Aussie" as it approaches the end of its monetary easing cycle -- which has done little to depreciate the currency -- while the RBNZ is widely expected to enter a monetary tightening cycle next year.

"The RBA can afford to be a bit more activist against the currency because there's no danger in the short term of their actions boosting the currency," Tuck said.

"The RBNZ has to be a little bit more pragmatic because they have to justify why strength in the currency isn't going to impede them from achieving their primary goal, which is to ensure price stability and make sure house price and construction inflation doesn't spill into the broader economy."

The RBNZ has said it expects to begin raising interest rates, which have been at a record low 2.5 percent since April 2011, sometime in 2014 to counter growing inflation pressures from a stronger economy.

Analysts polled by Reuters overwhelmingly expect the tightening cycle to start in March next year, with markets pricing in nearly 100 basis points tightening in a year's time .

text:
* Aussie up 2 pct so far in October, housing data surprisingly strong

* Kiwi off 6-wk lows after RBNZ signals rate rises next year

* C.bank says high NZD gives it more flexibility on when to hike

By Naomi Tajitsu and Cecile Lefort

SYDNEY/WELLINGTON, Oct 31 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar bounced on Thursday after surprisingly strong housing data showed record-low interest rates were helping the economy gain traction, lessening the need for further easing.

The New Zealand dollar also got a lift after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand disappointed doves by reiterating that higher rates would likely be needed next year.

The Aussie hopped up half a U.S. cent to $0.9504 as government data showed approvals to build new homes surged 14.4 percent in September, far above forecasts.

The number of approvals was the highest since March 2010 while their dollar value was the highest on record, a comfort to the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) which has been counting on home construction to underpin growth as mining cools.

"Housing is taking the baton from mining and will drive the economy over the next year," said Craig James, chief economist at CommSec.

"Multiplier effects from housing on the economy are significant, meaning many sectors will share in the gains of the building boom," he added. "The RBA is reluctant to cut rates again given the signs of firmer economic activity."

The central bank holds its November policy meeting next week and is thought almost certain to keep rates at 2.5 percent. Interbank futures <0#YIB:> imply only a 36 percent probability of any further cuts in rates.

In April, the RBNZ sold a net NZ$256 million, the largest intervention in five years, after the trade-weighted New Zealand dollar, the bank's preferred currency measure, hit its highest against a basket of five currencies since the kiwi was floated in 1985.

The May purchase of New Zealand dollars was the first since January, and the most since March 2011, when the bank bought a net NZ$525 million.

Earlier this month, the RBNZ said the kiwi dollar was still overvalued despite its recent fall.

RBNZ Governor Graham Wheeler has said the central bank will likely be more active in foreign exchange markets, and that it is ready to intervene where it thinks it has a good chance of influencing the exchange rate.

title: DJ  New Zealand Currency Intervention  Draws Criticism
text:
WELLINGTON--New Zealand's central bank sold much less of its local currency holdings last month than economists had been expecting, prompting charges it misled markets over the extent of the intervention in order to help drive down the soaring currency.

Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand forewarned that it had "intervened" in currency markets in April to help ease pressure on the country's exporters grappling with an elevated Kiwi, which has risen about 10% in the past year against a basket of currencies. The New Zealand dollar dropped nearly a cent against the U.S. dollar on that announcement.

While the central bank routinely buys and sells small amounts of the currency to support liquidity, the Reserve Bank's explicit reference to intervention was the first since 2007, leading some economists and strategists to believe the April sell-off would be significantly higher than the 256 million New Zealand dollar (US$208 million) figure subsequently announced Thursday. Some economists had expected a figure of as much as NZ$1 billion.

Earlier Thursday, Gov. Graeme Wheeler said the central bank was prepared to step up its intervention in the foreign-exchange market if circumstances demanded it, pushing the Kiwi lower by almost half a cent against the greenback.

Annette Beacher, Singapore-based head of Asia-Pacific research at TD Securities, said the final number for April fell "far short" of expectations.

"Does this confirm that all along that it is merely jawboning the currency lower?" she said. "We question the wisdom of such announcements of intervention by senior RBNZ staff when the evidence clearly shows a lack of resolve."

Alex Sinton, Auckland-based director of institutional foreign exchange at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group, was also critical.

"It was misleading, absolutely, the governor deliberately played it up," he said. "Clearly the amount was insignificant. What will be interesting will be May's numbers."

The central bank said it had no comment on the suggestion its use of the word intervention was misleading.

Central banks in Australia, New Zealand and parts of Asia have been stepping up moves to deal with an influx of international capital as investors scour the globe looking for higher returns in countries where interest rates remain relatively high following the global financial crisis. The inflows have kept currencies such as the Aussie and Kiwi strong, while complicating efforts to manage growth.

Australia's central bank has cut interest rates to a record low 2.75%--still above the U.S. and much of Europe--and at its monthly policy meetings frequently notes the stubborn strength of the Australian dollar. New Zealand's benchmark cash rate is at 2.5%, where it's been since March 2011 to help the economy recover from a series of devastating earthquakes.

Elsewhere, China is moving to curb bets on the rising yuan, while Thailand this month was looking at ways to deal with the strongest baht since the 1997 Asian financial crisis.

The last time New Zealand's central bank officially said it had intervened in the currency market was in 2007, when it was also seeking to bring down the currency. It sold nearly NZ$1.5 billion in June of that year and about NZ$1.6 billion between February and June 2008.

"The timid nature of this intervention suggests that the RBNZ doubts its effectiveness and is prepared to only act to counter spikes higher," said Greg Gibbs, a foreign-exchange strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland, who is based in Singapore. "This activity is much below the more aggressive actions undertaken in 2007-08."

title: DJ   New Zealand Central Bank  Open to More  Currency Intervention
text:
WELLINGTON--New Zealand's central bank ruled out raising interest rates any time soon to curb spiralling house prices, and said it was prepared to sell more local currency holdings to help rein in a soaring Kiwi that's hurting the nation's exporters.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has held the benchmark cash rate at a record low 2.5% since March 2011 to help jump-start an economy battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in Christchurch, driving house prices to all-time high this year. It's also been grappling with an elevated Kiwi--up around 10% in the past year against a basket of currencies--that's made it more difficult for companies in the mainly agriculture-exporting nation to compete globally.

The central bank has been selling New Zealand dollars in recent months to help ease the pain felt by the country's exporters. In December, it sold nearly NZ$200 million in the biggest sale of New Zealand dollars it had undertaken in almost four years. The pace of its Kiwi selling has slowed this year, however, with only NZ$28 million sold in the first three months combined.

The central bank is scheduled to release its latest foreign-currency-transaction data later Thursday. Earlier this month, Mr. Wheeler confirmed the Reserve Bank had sold more Kiwi holdings in April, without saying how much.

"The Reserve Bank has been responding to the rising exchange rate through two avenues-- maintaining the official cash rate at an historically low level and through a degree of currency intervention," central bank Gov. Graeme Wheeler said in a speech Thursday. "We are prepared to scale up our foreign exchange activities if we see opportunities to have greater influence."

The Kiwi fell to US$0.8098 from US$0.8138 just before the governor spoke as traders factored in a higher likelihood of future currency declines.

In his speech, the governor said the bank remained concerned over "risks" associated with the housing market as prices continued to track higher. While normally the bank would raise rates to dampen house prices, "this would carry significant risks of a further strengthening in the exchange rate," he said. The bank had other means to help bring down house prices such as tighter lending rules, said Mr. Wheeler.

He added that interest rates had more chance of staying lower for longer if house prices started to cool, and may even be cut if that happened while the exchange rate continued to rise.

New Zealand's home prices continue to hover near record highs, fueled also by growing demand for housing in the country's two largest cities, Auckland, where there is a rapidly expanding population, and Christchurch, where some 10,500 homes were destroyed in a series of earthquakes.

The latest data for April show house prices in Auckland jumped 13.3% on the year, while in the Canterbury-Westland region, where Christchurch is the major city, prices climbed 10%.

title: WSJ Blog:New Zealand  Central Bank  Seeks Clearing House for Trades
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's MoneyBeat blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/moneybeat/)

By Lucy Craymer

New Zealand's central bank is seeking a clearing house to handle its foreign exchange swaps and other financial trades, bringing it in line with new reforms in the U.S. and Europe which will force much of the global over-the-counter derivatives market to be cleared rather than conducted in private, bilateral trades.

It comes as Reserve Bank of New Zealand Gov. Graeme Wheeler admitted earlier this month the central bank had intervened in foreign currency markets by reducing its New Zealand dollar holdings, and would do so again if needed to contain a soaring local currency that's dragging on tourism and denting the competitiveness of the nation's agricultural exports.

Normally during an intervention the central bank would sell New Zealand dollars on the spot market, without using a clearing house. But a clearing house could handle foreign exchange swaps to balance the outflow after the intervention, traders said.

Tender documents seen by the Wall Street Journal show the central bank has requested proposals from clearing houses to manage on average a couple of foreign exchange swap, cross-currency basic swap and single currency interest-rate swap transactions a month valued at about $200 million each.

A clearing house acts as a facilitator for two parties that want to trade financial instruments such as stocks, bonds or derivatives, and like an insurer, it may be liable for the value of a trade if one of the parties defaults. A Reserve Bank spokeswoman said adopting a clearing house system would help the bank manage its risks.

In December, the central bank sold nearly 200 million New Zealand dollars (US$161 million) in the most significant sale in nearly four years, official data show. The pace of its sales slowed early this year, with the central bank selling only NZ$28 million in the first three months of the year combined. The Reserve Bank is due to release foreign currency transaction data for April later this month and some analysts say the intervention may have gathered pace again.

Parties interested in acting as the central bank's clearing agent have until July 1 to submit a proposal.

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand will disclose on Thursday the amount of New Zealand or "kiwi" dollars it sold in April, offering the first details of its low-level intervention operation that was initially revealed during a parliamentary committee hearing earlier this month.

Market participants expect the RBNZ offloaded around NZ$300 million to NZ$500 million ($242-404 million) in April. That is much less than the roughly NZ$1.5 billion the central bank sold in July 2007, during its last campaign to actively weaken the kiwi.

Since April, the kiwi has lost roughly 7 percent against the U.S. dollar, but analysts say the move has been driven by external factors.

Since taking the helm at the central bank in September, RBNZ Governor Graeme Wheeler has expressed his disdain of the kiwi's strength, which has tormented exporters in the agricultural economy.

But the kiwi is the 10th most traded currency in the $4 trillion global foreign exchange market, and central bank has limited firepower. Wheeler said in an early speech as governor that there were "clear limits to what monetary policy and exchange rate intervention can do to lower the New Zealand dollar".

title: New Zealand cenbank governor deploys tactical  currency  talk
text:
WELLINGTON, May 10 (Reuters) - In the global currency arena small player New Zealand probably deployed its last best tactic this week - a strategically timed disclosure.

The country's central bank governor, Graeme Wheeler, knocked around half a cent off the New Zealand dollar after divulging at a parliamentary committee that it had been active in currency markets.

The small South Pacific agricultural economy is grappling with a currency that has been driven to near-record levels in part by demand from investors with cheap money chasing New Zealand's comparatively high interest rates.

The elevated currency is helping to contain imported inflation but is undermining exporters.

Wheeler's comments revealed few details and he gave no idea whether it was full-blooded selling of the kiwi, of the likes seen in 2007, or more discreet and passive management of reserves, but he conceded that the latest actions were unlikely to have materially changed the exchange rate.

"We could potentially take the tops off rallies," Wheeler told the committee, as he conceded, yet again, that the bank can do little to combat a "significantly overvalued" currency.

That was small comfort for a tradables sector battling a currency that hit a 20-month high in mid-April and is in sight of the 28 year post-float high of $0.8842 touched in August 2011.

But the reality spelled out to the committee is that minnows, such as New Zealand, suffer the collateral damage from the loose money policies of the U.S. Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan, European Central Bank, and the Bank of England, which account for around two-thirds of the word's output.

"All those factors ... are pushing down interest rates and by the same token New Zealand is attracting very substantial capital flows that's putting pressure on the exchange rate, so it's a double-edged sword."

Analysts see the RBNZ's jawboning as little more than a token effort, given the resources at hand are like a peashooter, as the Finance Minister called it earlier in the year.

"It's impossible to move a market that turns over around $27 billion per day with a small amount of passive intervention"," said Sean Keane of Triple-T Consulting.

The New Zealand dollar, which is freely tradable, accounts for around 2 percent of global currency trading.

BLAME IT ON THE FED

So the New Zealand dollar's best bet would seem to lie in major central banks around the world, but most notably the Fed, paring back their money printing policies.

"The Fed's QE policies are currently adding around 10 cents onto the fair-value of the kiwi," said Bank of New Zealandcurrency strategist Mike Jones in a recent research report, which estimated the fair value at $0.7500 to $0.7900.

"So unless you think the Fed is about to halt or reverse QE; New Zealand commodity prices are about to fall off a cliff; or offshore risk appetite is about to dry up, there is little reason to expect the NZD/USD to head substantially lower anytime soon."

In such an environment Wheeler can be expected to engage in periodic bouts of jawboning but little else.

A little over a month into the job, last October, he made it clear he was not inclined to tilt at foreign exchange windmills, and that controlling inflation was his priority. It's a message he's repeated several times since.

The RBNZ has clear criteria for currency intervention, including whether it would work, whether the currency was exceptionally high, and whether the market conditions were right and it has a good chance of succeeding.

Arguably most of the conditions have been met, with the notable exception of the chances of success, where the waves of cheap money turned loose by the easy monetary policies of the major economies are looking for a high-yielding home.

With a housing market that is moving into record territory, an economy growing around 2.5-3 percent a year, inflation seen moving up to the middle of the RBNZ's target band, and elevated prices for key agricultural exports, the bank has all but ruled out cutting its overnight cash rate to lower the currency.

"If we reduced the OCR without sound reasons, the exchange rate might drop initially but rise later when the inflationary implications of the rate cut became clear," Wheeler said last year, a point reiterated in subsequent statements.

New Zealand's experience is mirrored in neighbouring Australia, where the central bank has been struggling with a painfully high currency of its own.

It tried some surreptitious intervention last year, selling Aussie dollars directly to central banks that wanted them rather than going through markets.

But again the amounts were modest and had no discernible impact on the currency overall.

Even cutting rates has had scant effect with the currency actually rising after reductions in October and December last year. Its frustration with the high currency was likely one reason it chose to cut again this week, taking its cash rate to an all time trough of 2.75 percent.

This time the Aussie eased, but only because the U.S. dollar surged against everything.

A Reuters poll of 47 analysts shows an expectation the kiwi will be $0.8430 until mid-year an $0.8200 in a year's time.

The most likely trigger for a fall in the New Zealand dollar is an end to the Federal Reserve's bond buying or a significant shock such as a slump in the global price of dairy products which make up around a quarter of exports, or a marked slowdown in China, the country's biggest export market.

In that environment New Zealand, like other currency small fry, has little choice but to grin and bear it, and every so often say or do something that reminds investors that a rising currency is "not a one-way bet".

title: Australia & NZ dlrs rally on rousing jobs news
text:
* Surge in jobs data triggers A$ & NZ$ short-covering

* Aussie & kiwi up 0.5 pct on the day vs USD

* Markets pare back chance of June rate cut in Australia

By Gyles Beckford and Cecile Lefort

SYDNEY/WELLINGTON, May 9 (Reuters) - The Australian and New Zealand dollars bounced on Thursday following stellar labour reports in both countries, prompting markets to pare back the risk of a June rate cut in Australia while reinforcing the outlook for steady to higher NZ rates.

The Australian dollar gained 0.6 percent on the day to $1.0240. Its recovery from a two-month low of $1.0155 hit twice this week caught many speculators short and forced them to buy back the Aussie.

The local dollar jumped as high as $1.0255 where it met heavy resistance. A break there would open the way to $1.0318, the 38.2 percent retracement of the April-May fall.

Australian employment surged by 50,100 in April to more than make up for a drop the previous month and nudge the jobless rate to 5.5 percent, a resoundingly upbeat report that contrasted with the central bank's decision to cut interest rates on Tuesday.

"While this survey is notoriously volatile, it does give us more confidence that the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) will stand pat, at least for now, after this week's cut," said Alvin Pontoh, a strategist at TD Securities in Singapore.

Interbank futures <0#YIB:> duly eased as the market tinkered with expectations of the timing of another cut. A move by July now looks more like a 50-50 bet than the sure thing priced in before the jobs news.

Still, the strength of the currency is one reason the RBA eased to a record low of 2.75 percent on Tuesday, so further gains would likely add to the case for another move in time.

"We suspect the Bank's easing bias isn't going anywhere while the AUD trades around $1.02-$1.05, as part of the RBA's apparent management of the currency," said Pontoh.

Yields on three-year government cash bonds bounced off six-month lows to last trade at 2.579 percent, from 2.481 percent.

Australian government bond futures followed suit with the three-year contract down 0.060 points to 97.440, some way off 97.530 set this week, the highest since October.

The 10-year contract eased 0.045 points to 96.830, with the yield curve flattening.

RBNZ INTERVENTION EFFORTS ERASED

The New Zealand dollar was propelled about 0.6 percent higher on the day to $0.8459.

It got its first lift of around half a cent after data showed New Zealand added a record 38,000 jobs in the first quarter, pushing the jobless rate down to a three-year low of 6.2 percent..

The rally was extended after Australia's jobs data, taking the kiwi as high as $0.8481. That recouped all the losses caused by Wednesday's news the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) had been quietly intervening to temper the currency.

"The markets liked it (the data), they were probably a bit short given the comments from the Reserve Bank (of NZ) yesterday, and it's back to where it was before then," said ASB Bank head of institutional sales Tim Kelleher.

"Locally it's been a bit of risk on, and following on from the positive equities in New York ... it will be a struggle to make Aussie and kiwi come off tonight."

Near term resistance was seen just below $0.8500, at the 20 day moving average, and above that Wednesday's high of $0.84524, with support at $0.84253.

The strength of the often volatile labour data was regarded with some suspicion and it was not considered convincing enough to alter the RBNZ's outlook for steady rates this year.

"This largely reflects the current backdrop of muted inflation out turns and expectations, together with the elevated level of the NZ dollar continuing to dampen down tradable inflation," said First NZ Capital's director of economics, Chris Green.

The RBNZ's concerns about a frothy house market would hardly have been assuaged by data showing national house prices rose 7.1 percent in the year to April to a record high.

New Zealand government bond yields rose as much as 7 basis points at the long end of the curve.

title: UPDATE: Strong New Zealand Jobs Figures Muddy Waters For  Central Bank
text:
--New Zealand dollar jumps on better-than-expected jobs data

--Employment rate at three-year low

--Labor market "much weaker" excluding Canterbury


 
   By Rebecca Howard 
 

WELLINGTON--New Zealand's unemployment rate has dropped to its lowest level in three years, highlighting the dilemma for the country's central bank as it juggles improving economic data and a high currency, and causing the Kiwi to erase losses made after Wednesday's intervention comments by the central bank governor.

The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell to 6.2% in the first quarter of the year from a revised 6.8% in the fourth quarter, data from Statistics New Zealand showed Thursday. The rate was the lowest since March 2010.

The New Zealand dollar jumped on the data and remained higher early afternoon, trading at US$0.8464 at 0221 GMT from US$0.8414 prior to the release. The currency had tumbled nearly a cent Wednesday after New Zealand's central bank said it had intervened in foreign currency markets and would do so again if needed to contain a soaring local currency.

The Kiwi's strength comes despite interest rates being held at a record low 2.5% since March 2011 as the Reserve Bank of New Zealand looks to support the economy through a tepid recovery in the wake of a series of devastating earthquakes in the South Island's Canterbury region.

Gains of around 10% in the currency over the past year on a trade-weighted index basis have heightened difficulties for companies in the mainly agriculture-exporting nation looking to compete in global markets.

The central bank has indicated rates will remain on hold this year, but has also said the outlook is "finely balanced." On the one hand, data show the economy growing at its fastest pace in three years in the final quarter of 2012, with increasing fears the housing market may be overheating. On the other, inflation remains extremely benign and the high dollar is acting as a significant headwind.

Just how much the latest data will influence thinking at the central bank is open to debate.

While acknowledging the data were stronger than expected, ANZ Bank Senior Economist Mark Smith cautioned that the survey tends to be volatile. He noted that "business sentiment surveys point to a continued willingness to take on more staff, but our job ads survey and anecdotes point to marked sector and regional differences, and do not suggest a smooth recovery."

As a result, he expects the OCR to "remain on hold for a while yet," and is penciling in a first increase for March.

In contrast, Alvin Pontoh, TD Securities Asia-Pacific Macro Strategist, notes that despite the currency's strength, "we continue to believe that a sustained improvement in the data combined with a hot housing market will force the RBNZ to lift the OCR rate from the current record low of 2.5%, in December. This is 3-6 months earlier than the consensus expects."

And while Diane Ramsay, industry and labor statistics manager at Statistics New Zealand, called the data a "strong turnaround," the statistics office also noted that part of the improvement was due to the rebuild in earthquake stricken Canterbury.

"Excluding Canterbury from the national estimates shows a much weaker labor market, with both the employment rate and labor force participation rate falling over the year," it said.

title: RPT- FX  COLUMN-RBNZ "peashooter" cannot keep the kiwi down
text:
(Repeat)

-- Neal Kimberley is an FX market analyst for Reuters. The opinions expressed are his own --

By Neal Kimberley

LONDON, May 8 (Reuters)- The New Zealand central bank should savour the success of its foreign exchange intervention on Wednesday to weaken its currency, commonly known as the kiwi, against the U.S. dollar as it may be short-lived.

The arguments for the New Zealand dollar, which hit a 20-month high of $0.8676 in April, to remain strong against the greenback are compelling and the central bank seems unwilling to bet the farm to weaken it.

The Reserve Bank confirmed on Wednesday selling the kiwi for only the second time since it was floated in 1985.

RBNZ Governor Graeme Wheeler confirmed the intervention to a parliamentary committee but acknowledged the move was not likely to "materially change" the exchange rate.

Whether Wheeler would have revealed the intervention without being asked by the committee is unknowable.

Data from the central bank's website indicates that previous bouts of intervention have not been that substantial.

In November 2012 the RBNZ sold a net 64 million New Zealand dollars while in December it sold the princely amount of 199 million kiwi.

Set against the multi-billion daily size of the New Zealand dollar forex market those volumes are peanuts, or perhaps more accurately peas.

"We'll be out in the war zone with a peashooter," said Finance Minister Bill English in February, playing down Wellington's will to curb the kiwi's strength.

"We have been pretty clear we are not willing to take the kind of huge risks involved in large scale speculation on the exchange rate with taxpayers' dollar," he said.

If the RBNZ is unwilling to intervene in strength, economic fundamentals still should underpin the New Zealand dollar.

Exports to China rose 32 percent in the 12 months to March as the world's second biggest economy displaced Australia as New Zealand's biggest export market.

And while some long-term investors see the commodity-linked kiwi, Australian and Canadian dollars declining due to economic slowdown in China, they say New Zealand's reliance on less cyclical agricultural exports may limit falls.

A surging housing market has triggered RBNZ warnings of inflation and financial stability risks that might even necessitate interest rate hikes from the current 2.5 percent record low.

And the $25 billion reconstruction of Christchurch following the 2011 earthquake remains a stimulus to the economy that should support the local dollar.

Asian central bankers looking to diversify the spread of their foreign exchange reserves, and conscious of New Zealand's trade relationships with Asia, are likely to buy the kiwi on dips in its price.

In truth, Wednesday's RBNZ intervention may have succeeded because the kiwi selling occurred when the broader forex market was holding New Zealand dollars and had to adjust positioning.

However, with the arguments in favour of holding the kiwi still solid, the sell off might merely encourage new buyers.

Unless the New Zealand central bank is prepared to swap its peashooter for a howitzer, the odds are that the kiwi bounces back from Wednesday's fall.

(Editing by Nigel Stephenson)

title: NZ  Central Bank  Leaves Cash Rate Unchanged At 5.25%
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held the Official Cash Rate steady at 5.25% Thursday, saying it still believes the slowing economy will eventually reduce inflation pressures, but that near-term inflation might prompt a small rate hike later this year.  

And in a surprise announcement, the Reserve Bank said it has asked Finance Minster Michael Cullen to be allowed to intervene in the foreign exchange markets to influence the New Zealand dollar exchange rate.  

Commenting on the reason for leaving the OCR unchanged, Reserve Bank governor Alan Bollard said "with tentative signs becoming more evident in recent weeks, it remains our view that this projected growth slowdown will occur and eventually will reduce the accumulated inflation pressures."  

Despite his forecast of a slowdown in the longer-term, Bollard said near-term inflation pressures remain and "the latest activity indicators remain quite robust."  

Under an agreement with the government, the Reserve Bank must keep annual inflation inside a 1% to 3% target band.  

"There are ongoing risks that the bottlenecks in the economy persist for some time yet," said Bollard in the March Monetary Policy Statement, or MPS.  

"Any persistence in the current inflation pressures could see actual inflation nearing the top of the bank's target range."  

"With this uncertainty, we judge it as appropriate at this stage to wait and watch the data, to see whether a further small increase in interest rates will be required this year."  

Also Thursday, Bollard said he the Reserve Bank has recommended to Finance Minister Michael Cullen that when the New Zealand dollar is "exceptionally and unjustifiably high" that the bank be allowed to intervene in the foreign exchange markets.  

Using New Zealand dollars to buy foreign currency "would put downward pressure on the exchange rate."  

When the New Zealand dollar is "exceptionally and unjustifiably low" the Reserve Bank wants to be allowed to buy New Zealand dollars.  

Seven of 13 economists in a Dow Jones Newswires poll before the decision expected the Official Cash Rate to be raised to 5.5% and most thought the cash rate wouldn't go higher than 5.5% in 2004.  

The Reserve Bank ended a cycle of interest rate cuts with a surprise 25 basis point rate hike in January to 5.25% to keep consumer price inflation in check following stronger-than-expected domestic economic growth.  

The bank said at the time that the January hike ensured that any future rate hikes would likely be moderate.  

Bollard said Thursday that January's hike was justified because New Zealand's sustained economic growth over recent years has increased inflation pressures in domestic industries, including housing and construction.  

Nonetheless, overall inflation has been "so far offset by weak imported inflation due to the rising NZ dollar," he said.  

The Consumer Price Index rose only 1.6% from a year earlier in the fourth quarter of 2003, well inside the Reserve Bank's inflation target.  

Bank Lowers Long-Term Growth Forecast  

In the March MPS, the Reserve Bank upped its near-term growth forecast, but lowered the longer-term forecasts.  

The bank is now projecting gross domestic product growth in the 12-months to the end of March at aroudn 3.5%, up from its December MPS estimate of 2.75%.  

Growth is then expected to slow to around 3% in 2005 year, unchanged from December's forecast. However in the 2006 year, growth is expected to have slowed considerably to 1.75%, down from its previous projection of 2.5%  

The bank also said that "significant inflation pressures have accumulated in parts of the domestic economy" despite signs of a slowdown in growth.  

The bank is now projecting annual inflation in the first half of 2004 to average around 2.25%, up from its December expectations of 1.5%. It is expected to remain around 2.5% in the second half of 2004 and the first half of 2005.

title: RBNZ seeks power to  intervene  in  currency  market.
text:
WELLINGTON, March 11 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand said on Thursday it wanted the power to intervene in the foreign exchange market to influence the level of the New Zealand dollar.  

The Reserve Bank's current stance is to use its foreign exchange reserves to intervene only if the foreign exchange market became "disorderly" but it has not done so since the currency was floated in early 1985.  

Reserve Bank Governor Alan Bollard said in a statement accompanying the bank's monetary policy statement that the central bank would recommend to the government that it be given the ability to use New Zealand dollars to buy foreign exchange, putting downward pressure on the exchange rate.  

"And, when the exchange rate is exceptionally and unjustifiably low, we would be able to sell foreign exchange to buy New Zealand dollars, putting upwards pressure on the exchange rate," he said.  

"By unjustifiable, we mean when the exchange rate has moved to a level in excess of that readily explained by the relevant economic fundamentals, which occurs only infrequently," Bollard said.  

Bollard said the process proposed is similar to that used by the Reserve Bank of Australia for some years.  

The New Zealand dollar has been one of the strongest performing currencies in the past year rising around 25 percent against the U.S. dollar. The RBNZ said the kiwi was around 15 percent above its long-term average on a trade weighted basis .  

He said the general aim would be to influence the exchange rate in a way consistent with maintaining price stability and that the bank would not seek to change the long-run exchange rate.  

"At best, we can influence the exchange rate only by a small amounts at the extremes of its cycle when it is a long way from economic fundamentals," he said.  

Bollard said more work and consultation was needed before final decisions could be made and procedures put in place.

title: NZ, Australia Should Unite On Any  FX Intervention  - HSBC
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--Any intervention in currency markets by the New Zealand and Australian central banks to drive their currencies down should be coordinated, according to a top economist.  

Investment bank HSBC's (HBC) chief economist in Australia, John Edwards, said in a research note Monday that New Zealand and Australia are small players on the world stage and could add to their firepower, authority and credibility by acting jointly.  

The recent appreciation of the U.S. dollar, which has given the Australian and New Zealand economies some respite from the continued strengthening of their currencies, means intervention isn't likely to be carried out "anytime soon" but it can't be ruled out if U.S. dollar depreciation resumes in a big way, Edwards said.  

The Australian and New Zealand dollars are "very highly correlated" and "it would be ridiculous for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to act alone. If the Reserve Bank of Australia and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand are not already talking about this possibility, they certainly should be," Edwards said.  

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's current foreign exchange reserve target is a range of 1.4 billion to 1.7 billion special drawing rights, a notional currency used by the International Monetary Fund. Actual reserves stand around 1.5 billion SDRs, which equates to NZ$3.6 billion.  

Australia's foreign exchange reserves are about A$35 billion.  

The potential for New Zealand to intervene in its currency market for the first time since the New Zealand dollar was floated in March 1985 has weighed on the local currency recently.  

New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen, in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires Feb. 19, gave his clearest hint yet that he is prepared to break with convention.  

"I wouldn't rest easy on the assumption that the settings for the last 20 years are going to remain unchanged," Cullen said in the interview. "I would be inclined to factor that into one's judgment."  

Edwards said that if the U.S. dollar resumed depreciating and the Australian dollar broke through US$0.81 and kept rising - it is currently around US$0.7750 - then the "timing and nature" of intervention would become the central issue.  

The same would apply if the New Zealand dollar, currently around US$0.6880, again broke through US$0.70 and kept on appreciating, he said. In February, the New Zealand dollar hit a seven-year high of US$0.7102.  

Intervention could be successful in limited circumstances, Edwards said.  

"There needs to be a widely shared sense that the currency has indeed overshot...the market conditions also need to be right. The perfect circumstance for interventions is when the market is very long and traders are overextended," he said.  

"In this circumstance, the central bank can cause a great deal of injury to long positions in Australia and New Zealand dollars at relatively little cost."  

-By Stephen Wright, Dow Jones Newswires; 64-4-471-5990; stephen.wright@dowjones.com

title: NZD Down As Fin Min Says May  Intervene ; Bonds Just Down
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--The New Zealand dollar closed sharply lower against the U.S. dollar Friday after the finance minister hinted the central bank might soon intervene to stem the local currency's rise, for the first time in nearly 20 years.  

New Zealand government bond prices closed just a touch lower as a slight overhang of supply and weak sentiment sent the local market in the opposite direction to overseas bonds.  

Yields closed on their intraday highs as the market took on an offered tone after the Kiwi - as the New Zealand Dollar is colloquially known - sank.  

After trading in a local range of US$0.6977 to US$0.7021, the New Zealand dollar closed at US$0.6977, down from Thursday's close of US$0.7016.  

Against the Australian dollar, the Kiwi, as the local unit is known, closed at A$0.8844, down from Thursday's close at A$0.8862.  

Finance Minister Michael Cullen said the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is concerned about the relatively low level of its foreign exchange reserves by international standards.  

"The Reserve Bank of New Zealand wants to build up its reserves, and it's reported to me along those lines," Cullen told Dow Jones Newswires.  

"(A)t the same time the bank and Treasury are finalizing advice on options for intervention in foreign exchange," he added, noting that a report is due from the Treasury in three to four weeks.  

To build up its foreign currency reserves, the RBNZ would have to buy them with New Zealand dollars. The local unit is expected to be pushed lower by the Kiwi selling or by sentiment from that selling.  

The Kiwi was little changed overnight and was supported by "reasonably good buying across the board" during the local session, said Basil Payn, Westpac head of spot foreign exchange.  

"Obviously those comments from Dr. Cullen knocked it down from US$0.7035 to US$0.6995," said Payn about 40 minutes before the local close.

title: Fin Min: RBNZ, Tsy Finalizing Advice On  FX Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen Friday gave his clearest indication that the central bank might soon intervene in currency markets for the first time in almost 20 years.  

The government is concerned that strength in the local unit, which is up almost 70% against the U.S. dollar over the past two years, will damp exports and the overall economy.  

Cullen said the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is concerned about the relatively low level of its foreign exchange reserves by international standards.  

"The Reserve Bank of New Zealand wants to build up its reserves, and its reported to me along those lines," said Cullen. "Its levels of reserves haven't changed since 1990, and I'm getting a final report back in three to four weeks time, and at the same time the bank and Treasury are finalizing advice on options for intervention in foreign exchange," he said in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires.  

At 0220 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was at US$0.7010, down from US$0.7035 just prior to Cullen's remarks.  

Cullen said that if the policy of nonintervention changes then the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's approach would be similar to that of its Australian counterpart.  

"The RBA has two different approaches, one is what it calls replenishing its reserves, and the second is where they intervene. I think it would be sensible that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand would operate in a similar fashion," he said, speaking on the phone from his office in Wellington, New Zealand.  

It seems, however, more a question of when rather than if the central bank shifts its approach.  

When asked whether intervention is likely in the coming months or this year, the minister said: "I wouldn't rest easy on the assumption that the settings for the last 20 years are going to remain unchanged, I would be inclined to factor that in to one's judgment."  

The finance minister said the central bank independently has been "concerned about the level of reserves being adequate to deal with market disruption."  

"We've been working for some time on that and we have come to the conclusion that by international standards our reserves are rather lower than would be expected," he said, referring to discussions with the central bank.  

The Reserve Bank's current foreign exchange reserve target is a range of 1.4 billion to 1.7 billion special drawing rights, a notional currency used by the International Monetary Fund. Actual reserves stand around 1.5 billion SDRs, which equates to NZ$3.6 billion.  

How the reserves are increased is crucial, said Cullen, adding that they could be upped either by borrowing offshore, or borrowing onshore and purchasing foreign currency.  

"What it would mean is one significant break in policy, which has been government policy for a considerable number of years, which is maintaining net zero foreign exposure," he said.  

Despite the possible shift in policy, Cullen emphasized that intervention isn't a cure-all.  

"Intervention can only have a limited effect in topping off the extremes in the currency, you can't affect the cycle itself or the direction of change, so even if the RBNZ had been intervening, we would have still seen a large appreciation in the Kiwi against the U.S. dollar over the past year," he said.  

The New Zealand currency is colloquially referred to as the Kiwi after the nation's flightless bird.  

Turning to the outlook for the economy, Cullen said exchange rates will be the major influence on forecasts for gross domestic product growth in coming years.  

"Most advisers would suspect that growth is continuing to run faster than forecast....but I think people are starting to think now that the dollar will have an impact on slowing the economy quicker toward the end of this year and running into 2005," he said.  

An Economic & Fiscal Update issued December forecast GDP growth of 2.8% for the year ending March 2005 - unchanged from a very conservative projection of growth through March 2004 - accelerating to 3.4% in 2005/06.  

When asked about possible revisions to the forecast for 2004/05 in the government budget to be issued May 27, he indicated it would be unchanged.  

"I think there are over and unders which are likely to even out on the 2.8% figure, (which) would be the best guess. Looking beyond that, it is going to depend on when the U.S. dollar starts to turn, or the New Zealand dollar starts to turn on its own," he said.

title: NZ WATCH: Fin Min May Be Serious About NZD  Intervention
text:
By Stephen Wright 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--Markets like to dismiss New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen's hints about intervening in the foreign exchange market as mere saber rattling. But his track record of fiddling with policy frameworks - and his skepticism of pure free market policies - suggest he's determined to act in some way.  

Cullen's latest outburst about the skyrocketing New Zealand dollar - which is now at seven-year highs around US$0.70 - was notable in that he broke with his previous refusal to provide specifics and gave some detail about his options for influencing the New Zealand dollar.  

"Increasing foreign exchange reserves may have an impact on the foreign exchange rate," he told Parliament's finance and expenditure select committee Wednesday.  

Cullen went on to say that he hasn't yet decided if he will instruct the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to increase its reserves. "I'm still discussing that with the Reserve Bank."  

The Reserve Bank's current foreign exchange reserve target is a range of 1.4 billion to 1.7 billion special drawing rights, a notional currency used by the International Monetary Fund. Actual reserves stand around 1.5 billion SDRs, which equates to NZ$3.6 billion.  

Cullen's comments suggest his talks with Treasury and central bank officials, first revealed late last year, have progressed significantly. His comments - which were most spooky for offshore players less familiar with the local scene - helped drag the New Zealand dollar down about 30 points Wednesday.  

One reason to dismiss Cullen's remarks as posturing is a broad-based local consensus that direct currency market intervention would have a minimal effect at best. Japan's heroic and expensive effort to block the yen's rise is frequently cited as an example of the futility of intervention.  

The New Zealand dollar's quick recovery from Wednesday's jawboning is seen as a perfect illustration that fundamental trends in currencies can't be defeated.  

"The overnight price action proved that this thing is a lot bigger than the finance minister. USD sentiment is what it's all about right now, and thus Greenspan's testimony revived the NZD," said Bank of New Zealand currency strategist Sue Trinh in a note Thursday.  

The local currency appreciated 25% against the U.S. dollar in 2003 and 26% in the previous year. So far this year, the New Zealand dollar has already appreciated by 6.4%.  

In the early stages of that appreciation, the currency was recovering from a clearly undervalued level - it hit a post-1985 float low of US$0.3898 in October 2000. But more recently, general U.S. dollar weakness has driven the Kiwi's ascent, resulting in it overshooting into overvalued territory according to some economic models.  

Another popular reason to dismiss Cullen is politics. The strength of the currency means the New Zealand economy risks a hard landing in 2005 - an election year - so it is in the government's interests to be perceived by voters as addressing the problem, even if it does nothing substantial.  

In some quarters, personal annoyance with the often prickly finance minister may play a part. One senior dealer said he wouldn't comment on the possibility of intervention as he didn't want to give Cullen the satisfaction of thinking he was being taken seriously.  

But Cullen, with his attacks on the Reserve Bank in the lead-up to 2002 general election, and his subsequent changes to the Policy Targets Agreement, which made for more flexible monetary policy, has shown he's not afraid to buck convention or disregard what markets think.  

In fact, with a whole range of other policy initiatives and decisions, Cullen and the Labour-led administration have shown a tendency to want to modify the free market orthodoxy that has prevailed in New Zealand since the mid-1980s.  

For example, in 2001 the government used taxpayer funds for a massive - by local standards - bailout of Air New Zealand (though it stopped short of renationalizing the carrier).  

With last year's reforms to the electricity market - which, due to New Zealand's dependence on hydroelectricity, periodically suffers supply shortages and massive price spikes - Cullen was instrumental in adding a layer of regulation and intervention to the industry, though he left free market fundamentals intact.  

Thus it would be entirely consistent for Cullen to steer clear of radical steps like capital controls or abandoning the floating exchange rate, but to direct the central bank to increase its foreign exchange reserves with the aim of slowing the New Zealand dollar's rise. Cullen might hope that such action would be the catalyst for a correction lower as soon as the current trend in global currency markets had run its course.  

Certainly the Reserve Bank has the expertise in money market operations to sterilize any extra liquidity generated in the process of selling New Zealand dollars to buy the U.S. dollar.  

Cullen's public comments about raising foreign reserves suggest he wouldn't hesitate to use direct and public methods in any effort to prevent New Zealand dollar appreciation.  

However, covert, unpublicized market intervention through local banks wouldn't be inconceivable. The Reserve Bank might also try to exert moral pressure by calling the dealing rooms of local price-making banks to discuss their positions, or by leaving offers at a certain level - anything to convince the market that New Zealand dollar appreciation was no longer an entirely safe bet.  

One market observer points out that Cullen is putting billions of dollars into an investment fund to help pay for part of the cost of universal pensions - so if he's prepared to bet on equity markets, he might not blanche at throwing a couple of billion at the currency market.  

And although Japan's intervention against the yen is cited by some as a failure, it's viewed by others as a success - the yen has appreciated much less steeply against the dollar than other major currencies have in the past couple of years, and this has helped protect Japanese exports.  

Most market participants remain reluctant to accept that New Zealand will break with its clean float and experiment with intervention - it's not known to have intervened once since the float.  

But the idea of the central bank trying to influence the New Zealand dollar isn't laughed off by dealers quite as quickly as it was just a few weeks ago - and that in itself is a significant shift in market sentiment.
