title: NZ govt eyes options on kiwi dlr - PM Clark.
text:
WELLINGTON, Jan 16 (Reuters) - New Zealand Prime Minister Helen Clark reiterated on Friday there was little the government could do to stem the kiwi dollar's rise, but it was mulling with Treasury whether there were options "on the margins".  

The central bank said in November it was reviewing the tools it could use to influence the resurgent kiwi dollar in the wake of comments from Finance Minister Michael Cullen that he had unspecified options to curb the kiwi's climb.  

The government is concerned at the impact of the currency's sharp rise on the exporters. The New Zealand dollar , one of the top performing developed currencies in 2003, scaled fresh six-and-a-half year highs this week, peaking at around 68.7 U.S. cents.  

"I think most people accept that our dollar's been driven up because of the U.S. dollar's weakness and no-one expects the government to perform a minor miracle over that," Clark told Radio New Zealand. "He (Cullen) and Treasury will obviously be looking at whether there's anything that one can do on the margins and he's the best person to talk to about that."  

"But when the U.S. dollar's in a dive everyone else is affected."  

Clark acknowledged exporters, particularly farmers battling dry weather conditions on the east coast of the South Island, were feeling the pain of the kiwi's 25 percent gain against the greenback last year.  

"I think it's the rate of change, the volatility, that most affects exporters," she said.  

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has never intervened in foreign exchange markets since the kiwi dollar was freely floated in 1985, but has always reserved the right to do so.  

RBNZ Governor Alan Bollard said last year the central bank would only consider intervention if finance markets were severely disrupted.

title: RBNZ non- intervention currency  stance holds-Bollard.
text:
WELLINGTON, Nov 27 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank is sticking by its policy of non-intervention in currency markets although it is reviewing what tools might be open to it, Governor Alan Bollard said on Thursday.   

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand would only consider intervention under conditions of severe market disruption, where a price was not being given for trades in New Zealand dollars, Bollard told a parliamentary committee.   

"That would much more likely be in a case where the New Zealand economy was either under severe stress or there were some big shocks coming through from abroad, and there were some concerns about the New Zealand dollar falling rapidly," Bollard said. The Minister of Finance recently said that he had options to bring down kiwi, which has risen 16 percent on a trade weighted basis and by 30 percent against the U.S. dollar over the past year.   

Bollard said the key influence on kiwi at present was financial markets' concern over the size of the United States current account and fiscal deficits, which the RBNZ could do nothing about.   

"That's not to say that what the bank does or says can't have an effect, we can under certain circumstances. But we're interested in all of this as the traded sector ought to be in the real exchange rate and the longer term aspects of it because that's what impacts through the New Zealand economy."   

However, the level of the exchange rate and the damage it could be causing the tradeable sector was one factor that shaped monetary policy, Bollard said.   

The RBNZ has previously cited the high level of the currency and its impact on exporters as one factor in either cutting or holding its official cash rate.   

The bank will issue a monetary policy statement on December 4, with money markets pricing in a 25 basis point rise, but a Reuters poll puts the chances of a hike at 40 percent.   

The central bank has kept rates steady at 5.0 percent since August, after three rapid fire cuts totalling 75 basis points between April and July.   

Most forecasters surveyed expect a hike in the first quarter next year saying that the strength of the New Zealand dollar - estimated at four percent above the RBNZ's forecast for the current period - is offsetting inflationary pressures from the strong domestic economy. Bollard said New Zealand exporters had adjusted much better to kiwi's current high level than in a previous period in the mid-1990s, when it reached $0.72, because they were more aware what tools finance markets were able to offer.   

Although he refused to answer questions that might directly relate to next week's monetary statement, Bollard said the strength of the housing sector reflected a "a stronger demographic" and increase in demand because of immigration.   

The level of household debt was not a problem for the stability of the financial system, although time would probably show that some of the investment had been misdirected, he said.

title: More upside seen for NZ dollar, despite Cullen.
text:
AUCKLAND, Nov 7 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar is expected to push higher, especially against the backdrop of a weaker U.S. dollar, but will fall short of post-float highs, economists said on Friday.   

Kiwi has been one of the stellar performers of the currency markets over the past 18 months as it has benefited from high interest rate differentials, strong economic fundamentals, and U.S. dollar weakness.   

Despite concern voiced at the size and speed of the appreciation - 29 percent over the past year against the greenback, and 14 percent on a trade weighted basis - kiwi is not seen as likely to correct any time soon.   

For the moment, economists are forecasting the kiwi to rise further, particularly if U.S. dollar weakness persists.   

Factors supporting the kiwi include prospects of higher rates after the Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates by 25 basis points to 5.0 percent on Wednesday.   

Deutsche Bank NZ expects the kiwi to hit 63 U.S. cents in 12 month's time - a forecast that is likely to be revised upward if U.S. dollar weakness persists.   

But the bank sees less upside for the currency's Trade Weighted Index if the central bank opts to keep rates at 5.0 percent while the RBA continues along a tightening path.   

National Bank of NZ (NBNZ) sees the kiwi at $0.6300-$0.6400 in the year ahead, but does not expect it to reach the peak of previous cycles - $0.7275 in June 1988, and $0.7170 in November 1996.   

Kiwi is currently sitting near year highs at $0.6138/48.   

"Our 12 month view of 63 U.S. cents is likely to be revised upward, but less upside is seen for the Trade-Weighted Index, particularly if the Reserve Bank of NZ remains on hold while the RBA continues to tighten," Deutsche Bank NZ senior economist Darren Gibbs said.   

JAWBONING   

Recent comments talk by the Finance Minister, Michael Cullen, about the currency, and possible government options to curb its rise have been largely dismissed as just talk.   

Cullen, who has in the past tried to talk down the value of the kiwi to soften the blow to New Zealand's currency-prone export sector, raised the spectre of intervention before parliament's finance and expenditure committee meeting this week.   

Questioned further in parliament, Cullen said: "My intention was to signal that the government is not without options. No specific conclusions can be drawn from that statement, and it would be most unwise to do so".   

Since floating in 1985 successive governments and the central bank have taken a hands-off approach to the New Zealand dollar, leaving the currency to find its own level.   

Over that period kiwi has traded a 38.95 to 72.75 U.S. cent range.   

Cullen has so far declined to elaborate on what the "options" might be, but his comment was nevertheless seen as a departure from the status quo.   

"Cullen is clearly trying to jawbone. He's been trying it now for months, using different tacks, now he's floating the idea of intervention," said Darren Gibbs, senior economist at Deutsche Bank NZ.   

Basil Payn, head of spot foreign exchange at Westpac Institutional Bank, said the market saw Cullen's comments as representing a slight change in tack.   

"It's a change of 'speak' but I don't think the market will see it as any change in policy," Payn said.   

There were other forms of intervention, other than selling kiwi, which could dampen the economy and the exchange rate, a such as a capital gains tax on property, Gibbs said.   

Such a tax, while difficult to enforce, could help slow the housing market, reducing the need for the high interest rates that have helped underpin the currency.

title: NZ WATCH: Fin Min Doesn't Like His Kiwi Overcooked
text:
By Stephen Wright 
 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--Finance Minister Michael Cullen's hint he could curb the New Zealand dollar's strength through intervention in the currency market has been greeted with skepticism, if not outright derision.  

"Saddam Hussein led the world to believe he had weapons of mass destruction...and Michael Cullen is trying to let the markets know he has weapons of currency suppression," said Tony Alexander, an economist at Bank of New Zealand, in a response that underlined the lack of credibility given to Cullen's remarks.  

The finance minister sparked a minor media sensation on Wednesday this week - but failed to move the currency one iota - with his response to a question on what he will do about the high New Zealand dollar, which is causing pain for exporters.  

"The government doesn't regard itself as entirely without options in this respect," he told Parliament's finance and expenditure select committee.  

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act enables the country's Treasurer - currently Cullen - to direct the monetary authorities to intervene in the foreign exchange market and also requires the bank to hold foreign exchange reserves for that purpose.  

But the Reserve Bank hasn't intervened in the foreign exchange market since the New Zealand dollar was floated in 1985.  

Cullen was next asked if he would use his "options" for dealing with the kiwi - a shy, flightless and near extinct native bird that the currency is named for.  

"That's a matter I would prefer not to comment on at this point," he told the committee. "I'm always considering doing all sorts of things. Whether I'm considering doing something in that area is for me to know."  

He was even less illuminating on the subject when asked in parliament the next day if he was signaling changes to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act, changes to the floating exchange rate, or intervention in the currency market.  

"My intention was to signal that the government isn't without options. No specific conclusions can be drawn from that statement and it would be most unwise to do so," Cullen said.  

His most obvious options for attempting to influence the currency, which has risen about 50% against the U.S. dollar since the beginning of last year, seem to be either directing the country's central bank to sell the kiwi, or imposing some form of controls on the flow of capital.  

But the first option would have at best a temporary impact as the New Zealand dollar is in an upward trend against the U.S. dollar and intervention can't defeat this trend, which is driven by economic fundamentals, said Westpac currency strategist Johnathan Bayley.  

If Japan's monetary authorities, which have accumulated years of experience at intervention, can't halt the rise of the yen against the U.S. dollar then New Zealand's central bank won't have any luck at stopping the Kiwi's rise against the dollar, he added.  

Another factor making intervention in the near to medium-term implausible is the fact the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is expected to raise interest rates in the first quarter of next year.  

It would look rather "incongruous" for the central bank to try and weaken the currency through intervention while at the same supporting the currency with higher official interest rate, said Deutsche Bank Economist Darren Gibbs.  

"Intervention normally does not work unless the market is about ready to move there anyway...when things are absolutely extended and the market is looking for a catalyst to turn, that is the time to intervene."  

With the Kiwi sitting around US$0.61 and potentially going much higher "you would be asking for trouble if you intervened," said Gibbs. "Hedge funds around the world would go 'great, money to be made in New Zealand'."  

However, Cullen may also have had in mind steps like a capital gains tax to take the heat out the country's housing market, said Gibbs. Such a tax could weaken the currency if the impact was interest rates not rising, or not rising as much as they would otherwise.  

The second major option - of imposing capital controls - seems an unthinkable, backward step in an open, deregulated economy like New Zealand.  

"Cullen is playing to a domestic audience with his comments...and I don't think he for one minute he seriously contemplates" capital controls, said Bank of New Zealand's Alexander.

"My intention was to signal that the government is not without options, but no specific conclusions can be drawn from that statement and it would be most unwise to do so," Cullen said.  

Pressed by Brash and other lawmakers to give more detail Cullen would only repeat the answer.  

The New Zealand dollar was trading a narrow range around $0.6160/65, near six year highs, as it kept track with the closely correlated Australian dollar .

title: NZ FinMin weighs options on resurgent kiwi dollar.
text:
WELLINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - New Zealand's Finance Minister said on Wednesday the government had options to influence the value of the kiwi dollar, which has soared to six year highs against the greenback, although he declined to give details.   

 Michael Cullen, who has repeatedly said the high level of the kiwi dollar is hurting exporters, was asked at a parliamentary committee if he intended to do anything about its value, New Zealand Press Association (NZPA) reported.   

 "The government doesn't regard itself as entirely without options in this respect, but those options have to be dealt with very carefully indeed," Cullen was quoted as saying.   

 He did not outline the options and declined to comment on any timeframe.   

 "I'm always considering all sorts of things. When I'm doing something in that area is probably only for me to know at the moment," Cullen added.   

 Neither the New Zealand government nor the central bank have intervened in foreign exchange markets to affect the value of the New Zealand dollar since the currency was floated in 1985.   

 However, Cullen has periodically commented on the high level of kiwi and the damage it has been inflicting on the external sector.   

 SELF CORRECT   

 Cullen predicted the New Zealand dollar, which has gained around 25 percent against the U.S. dollar over the past 12 months on the back of relatively high interest rates and a robust domestic economy, could correct of its own accord.   

 "Who knows, there might be a correction in the U.S. dollar value, though I think it is more likely looking out, that the New Zealand dollar will correct on its own, given the widening current account deficit," Cullen said.   

 Weaker exports and the SARS virus combined with the currency's climb pushed New Zealand's current account deficit to its highest annual level in three years at the end of the June quarter to NZ$5.89 billion ($3.59 billion) or 4.6 percent of gross domestic product.   

 It was not clear whether lowering New Zealand's official cash rate would automatically subdue the kiwi dollar as it sometimes encouraged people to put money into the country in the assumption that a cut would lead to higher economic growth, NZPA quoted Cullen as saying.   

 Cullen's comments came shortly before Australia's central bank raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point to 5.0 percent - the same level as New Zealand's benchmark lending rate.   

 In response, the Australian dollar  gained nearly one percent against the greenback before profit takers pegged it back to around $0.7090. Kiwi last traded around $0.6130, up from $0.6120 at the start of Wednesday's local session.

title: Fin Min Asks Agencies For NZD  Intervention  Ideas - Report
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen has asked the country's central bank and Treasury Department to report on ways to curb the rising New Zealand dollar, the Dominion Post newspaper reported Thursday without citing its source.  

The newspaper said it understands that Cullen is exploring how the two government agencies could use existing activities such as the issuing and timing of government bonds or currency trading to influence the New Zealand dollar.  

The report follows comments by Cullen to Parliament's finance and expenditure select committee Wednesday in which he hinted at the possibility of the government ordering intervention in the currency.  

Asked in the committee what he will do about the high New Zealand dollar, Cullen said "the government doesn't regard itself as entirely without options in this respect."  

The New Zealand dollar has gained about 50% against the U.S. dollar since the beginning of last year, denting export returns.  

The Dominion Post report quoted opposition National Party deputy finance spokesman John Key urging caution.  

"While there is concern about the impact that a rising exchange rate is having on our exporters, Dr. Cullen's options are very limited," he said.  

Key said the last intervention was in the mid-1990s when the Reserve Bank sold about NZ$200 million to smooth the exchange rate. It had "shock effect" but little long-term impact.  

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand, in a report on its Web site, said it maintains foreign exchange reserves so that it has the capability to intervene but hasn't done so since the New Zealand dollar was floated in 1985.

title: New Zealand's  central bank  joins Swiss-based BIS.
text:
WELLINGTON, Aug 19 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand said Friday it had joined the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the Switzerland-based bank and forum for central banks which provides emergency cash. 

 BIS currently has 49 member central banks, including those of Australia, China, Germany, France, Britain and the United States, plus the European Central Bank. 

 The RBNZ said it had paid NZ$100 million ($59 million) for a small shareholding in the Basel-based institution, which provides emergency funds to support the global monetary system when needed. 

 "The benefits to both the Reserve Bank and New Zealand include increased access to foreign currency funding, which in a crisis could enhance the bank's capabilities to intervene in markets to maintain stability," the bank said in a statement. 

 The Reserve Bank has not intervened in currency markets since the New Zealand dollar was floated nearly 20 years ago. 

 In the 1960s BIS helped support the Italian lira, French franc, and British pound, and more recently provided cash to help stabilise the economies of Mexico and Brazil.

title: NZ dollar ends above key support, bonds firm.
text:
AUCKLAND, Dec 5 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar ended above key support on Thursday as the market awaited the outcome of the Auckland City Council's decision on the possible sale of its one quarter stake in Auckland International Airport (AIA.NZ). 

 A decision to proceed with the sale, worth around NZ$400 million ($200 million) at current market prices, was likely to lend some support for the currency while a decision against could lead to a fall. 

 A dip below $0.5000 was seen as possible if the council decided against it or a rally over $0.5050 if it was approved, based on the possibility of NZ$400 million washing through the market. 

 But the focus generally was on the U.S. dollar versus the yen, particularly in light of Japan's weak yen policy. 

 "People seem to be taking on board the Bank of Japan's comments and getting short yen and long everything else," said one dealer. 

 Another key issue for the market was whether the European Central Bank opts to cut rates by the 50 basis points the market expects when it meets later on Thursday. 

 New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen's comments that the kiwi was at the top end of its "comfort zone" against the Australian dollar, but not overpriced against the U.S. dollar, stopped the kiwi's rally in its tracks at around $0.5030. 

 Cullen said New Zealand manufacturing exporters would be more comfortable if the kiwi  cross rate against the Aussie retreated at least five percent from near five-year highs around 89.5 Australian cents. 

 "It (NZD) still is very much at the top end of the comfort zone on the Australian cross rate," Cullen told Reuters in an interview. 

 But with New Zealand's policy of non-intervention in its exchange rate, Cullen's comments were largely dismissed as talk. 

 "It was a bit of a nothing comment at the end of the day," said one dealer. 

 "I guess there was some initial reaction to it but the market was actually struggling above the $0.5030 level when it came out anyway. There was limited topside at that point in time," he said. 

 The kiwi finished at $0.5013/23, up from Wednesday's close of $0.4985/95, and above key support at $0.5005. 

 In the corporate bond market, Transpower's 2006 bond issue went off at an eight basis point premium to the equivalent swap. In governments, the local yield curve ended flatter. 

 February 2005 bonds were unchanged at 5.79 percent while the November 2006s dropped a basis point to 5.95 percent.

title: UPDATE 1-INTERVIEW-NZD too high against Aussie dlr - NZ FinMin.
text:
WELLINGTON, Dec 5 (Reuters) - New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen said on Thursday the kiwi dollar was rising too far against the Australian dollar, but was not overpriced against the greenback. 

 Cullen said New Zealand manufacturing exporters would be more comfortable if the kiwi  retreated at least five percent from near five-year highs around 89.5 Australian cents. 

 "It (NZD) still is very much at the top end of the comfort zone on the Australian cross rate," Cullen told Reuters in an interview. 

 The comments blunted buying interest in the rising currency, taking kiwi off local session highs against both currencies. 

 "The kiwi was getting paid up to the low $0.5030s and as soon as the Cullen comments hit the wires it certainly took the sting out of the market and tempered buying interest," said Bank of New Zealand currency strategist Stuart Ritson. 

 However Cullen's influence on exchange rates is seen as limited to talk, Ritson said. New Zealand's independent central bank has never intervened in currency markets since the currency was floated in 1984. 

 FLYING KIWI 

 Kiwi has risen 20 percent against the greenback since the start of this year and is up nearly 10 percent against the Australian dollar, an appreciation which has cut incomes of New Zealand exporters. 

 "They (manufacturing exporters) would be happier if we were down more around that A$0.85 or a bit below zone," Cullen said. 

 Australia is New Zealand's largest trading partner, taking about a fifth of the country's NZ$32 billion of exports, while the United States takes about 15 percent. 

 But Cullen said kiwi's  current level against the greenback at around 50 U.S. cents did not seem to be an issue. 

 "That's not high...We are certainly not outside anything like the long-term equilibrium rate," he said. 

 WARM WELCOME 

 Cullen said he was satisfied with the performance of new Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Alan Bollard and his operation of monetary policy under new guidelines. 

 "I have every impression that he is going well. People have confidence in his judgment," he said. 

 The revised agreement specifies an inflation target of one-to-three percent on average over the medium term, from the previous zero-to-three percent range. 

 Bollard's first two interest rate reviews have left the official cash rate stable at 5.75 percent. 

 Cullen said official growth and fiscal forecasts would be revised higher in the December Economic and Fiscal Update due on December 19. 

 "The overall numbers will be stronger than the pre-election fiscal update," Cullen said, referring to official forecasts issued in June. 

 Cullen said it was possible gross domestic product would grow four percent in the year to March, compared with 3.1 percent forecast in June. 

 However the current account deficit, which has influenced the kiwi's strength, was forecast to grow from its current 2.5 percent of gross domestic product. 

 "It is certainly again getting towards the outer reach of what you might regard as the comfort zone," he said, adding that a deficit above five percent of GDP was not desirable.

title: NZ Dollar Down Early; Tracks A$, Euro; OCR Review Wed
text:

 At 2123 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was quoted at US$0.4872, down from US$0.4878 late Friday in Wellington.

 Dealers say the New Zealand dollar is likely to range-trade between the US$0.4800 and US$0.5000 region as offshore investors continue to rejigger their U.S. dollar positions amid forecasts of further depreciation for the greenback. 

 A second dealer said the Xerox blowup has yet again highlighted the problems wracking U.S. corporates. The office equipment concern said Friday it expects to restate revenues by about US$2 billion over a five-year period. 

 "The corporate news out of the U.S. just keeps getting  worse, and there are still concerns about the pace of U.S. economic growth," he said. "All this will keep the Kiwi on  the backfoot with  investors on a cautious footing." 

 He said factors which had driven the New Zealand dollar - interest rate differentials and a robust economy - will continue to underpin support for the currency in the medium term. 

 Johnathan Bayley, currency strategist at Westpac Bank, said the local currency will remain a "laggard" in the dollar-bloc due to the cautious tone in international markets.

title: NZ Dlr Lower Late; Profit-Taking After Cullen Comments
text:
WELLINGTON -(Dow Jones)- The New Zealand dollar was lower against the U.S. dollar late Friday in Wellington after a volatile session marked by profit-taking in the local unit after its recent strong gains. 

 At 0625 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was quoted at US$0.4680, down from US$0.4730 late Thursday in Wellington and down also from a 23-month high at US$0.4765 traded in New York prior to the open. 

 A Wellington bank dealer said the pair traded a very wide range of about US$0.4660 and US$0.4735 Friday. 

 Comments by Finance Minister Michael Cullen early in the session - in which he expressed concern about the potential economic implications should the recent strong run in the currency continue indefinitely - sparked an initial selloff in the New Zealand dollar down to about US$0.4680 compared with US$0.4725 prior to his comments, the dealer said. 

 The dealer said it was speculative accounts which had recently become long in the New Zealand dollar who availed the opportunity of Cullen's comments to sell-down the currency at a profit. 

 Cullen said in interviews with newswire services that the recent strength in the local currency would be of concern to him if the trend were to continue, although economists and market-watchers were quick to note that in New Zealand the government doesn't have anything to do with setting the level of the currency. 

 The central bank, moreover, hasn't intervened in the foreign exchange market since the New Zealand dollar became a free-floating currency in the mid 1980s. 

 Almost everyone expects the currency to resume its appreciating trend as the year progresses, if for no other reason than interest rate differentials, which strongly favor the New Zealand dollar over other currencies. 

 Dealers said overnight they expect buying interest will lend a base of support to the New Zealand dollar on any dip toward US$0.4650. Selling interest will cap any gains toward US$0.4720. 

 One dealer said any breach of US$0.4650, however, could see a quick march down to US$0.4600. 

 Statistics New Zealand will Monday publish its provisional April merchandise trade report. 

 According to a Dow Jones Newswires poll of economists, the economy recorded a merchandise trade surplus of around NZ$275.5 million in April compared with a surplus of NZ$456 million in March.

 In his comments Friday, Cullen noted the cross rate. Any sustained rise in the cross toward A$0.8500 would likely cause concern to local exporters, the minister told Dow Jones Newswires. 

 Despite the easing in the cross rate Friday, it remains up about 1.6% from A$0.8310 at the start of May.

title: New Zealand's Nonintervention In  Forex  Market Served Econ Well-Report
text:
WELLINGTON -(Dow Jones)- The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's long-standing policy of not intervening in the foreign exchange market has served the economy well, according to a research report published in the central bank's quarterly Bulletin Friday. 

 "Inflation targeting and a policy of nonintervention in foreign currency markets have so far proved effective in maintaining price stability and avoiding currency crises," the report said. 

 The Reserve Bank has since the late 1980s directed monetary policy with an aim to maintaining stability in the general level of prices. The New Zealand dollar became a free-floating currency in 1985. 

 This dual approach has provided appropriate incentives to the private sector to hedge their foreign currency risks and the central bank can be "happy" with its approach, the report said. 

 The report was written by Nils Bjorksten and Anne-Marie Brook, analysts at the central bank's Economics Department. 

 The authors also said, however, that there is a developing view among international academics that free-floating exchange rates don't deliver as many benefits as some had anticipated in the 1980s. 

 The report also examines the potential benefits and drawbacks of New Zealand abandoning its independently floating currency in favor of either joining a larger monetary union or alternatively adopting the U.S. dollar.

title: Can$ snaps winning streak as tech worries weigh.
text:
LONDON, June 12 (Reuters) - The Canadian dollar broke a week-long winning streak against the greenback on Tuesday, as a raft of earnings warnings in the semiconductor sector stoked concern over Canada's economy. 

 The Canadian dollar retreated almost a cent from the previous day's four-month highs around C$1.5150 , underperforming its commodity-currency peers. 

 Recent optimism over Canada's growth outlook waned late on Monday after an analyst cut estimates for technology bellwether Nortel Networks Corp and fresh earnings warnings from two U.S. semiconductor firms. Toronto stocks closed down 1.45 percent. 

 "The Canadian dollar is being hurt by its vulnerability to the U.S. economy and losses in tech stocks," said Jim Webber, chief economist at Toronto Dominion Securities in London. 

 "This is coming at a time when there is growing confidence that Australian and New Zealand economies are on a recovery track." 

 Around 80 percent of Canada's exports go to the United States. Canada's economy and its stock market are heavily exposed to the high-tech sector. 

 Meanwhile, the Australian dollar - which had survived a test of US$0.52 in the Asian session - gained over half a percent against the U.S. dollar, supported by the euro's rebound amid persistent wariness of euro-supportive central bank intervention. 

 The New Zealand dollar also tracked the Aussie higher, coming within firing range of US$0.42 , a key near-term chart barrier. 

 "Recent Australian and New Zealand economic data have surprised on the upside," said Jane Foley, currency economist at Barclays Capital. "Both the Aussie and the Kiwi dollars have also gained from the bounce in euro/dollar, while the Canadian dollar has been left struggling."

title: A$ rebounds from record low vs US dollar in Europe.
text:
LONDON, Oct 6 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar rebounded in Europe on Friday from record lows it set against the U.S. dollar earlier in Sydney, helped by the euro's recovery against the U.S. unit amid concerns of further Group of Seven intervention. 

 The New Zealand dollar outperformed the Australian dollar and held above record lows around US$0.3990 it had hit against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday. 

 The latest push down in the Aussie to record lows around US$0.5280 in Friday's Sydney comes after the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision earlier in the week to leave its interests on hold despite market expectations of a quarter point tightening. 

 The renewed selling in the Aussie dollar coincided with a downturn in the euro after the European Central Bank surprised markets by raising interest rates on Thursday, raising concerns over euro zone growth prospects. 

 However, the euro's rebound across the board in Europe on Friday helped lift the Aussie dollar, traders said. 

 "There has been a link between the euro and the Australian dollar," said Andrew Baxter, head of foreign exchange at the Commonwealth Bank of Australia in London. 

 "The RBA passed a rate hike this week. Also important to look at is the reserves positions - while the ECB has a large warchest, the RBA does not and that is why the Aussie dollar is open to a speculative attack. So it has been a proxy hedge for the euro because people think that the Aussie won't get that much help from the intervention in the euro." 

 The Aussie rose as far as US$0.5338 by 1012 GMT according to Reuters data, up about 1/2 a cent from earlier record lows around US$0.5280, as euro/dollar firmed . 

 KIWI DOLLAR OUTPERFORMS AUSSIE DOLLAR 

 Against the kiwi dollar, the Aussie fell to new session lows around NZ$1.3230 . 

 The New Zealand dollar also recovered to day's highs around US$0.4030, up more than a quarter cent from the day's lows, which were just above Wednesday's record lows around US$0.3990. 

 Traders said the kiwi dollar outperformed the Australian dollar mainly because the US$0.40 level was seen as a psychologically important level which the market was reluctant to break below. 

 The market's focus was now shifting to the U.S. payrolls report due out at 1230 GMT, particularly after the U.S. Federal Reserve warned this week that a tight labour market was an inflationary threat. 

 Chartists said if the Australian dollar could fall to US$0.50 if it broke below the US$0.5280 record lows. 

 "The unit has lower to go and ideally for now US$0.5340 will cap the upside for a test of US$0.5250," said Rahul Badhwar, senior marketing manager at HSBC, Bombay.

WELLINGTON -(Dow Jones)- New Zealand Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash said Thursday the New Zealand dollar's fall to historic lows this week was due to a mix of factors, but that much of the fall was a reversal of the currency's overvaluation in the late 1990s. 

 In a speech entitled "The fall of the New Zealand dollar: What has happened and what does it mean," delivered to a meeting of the American Chamber of Commerce in Auckland, Brash said that there was no quick or easy way to reverse the New Zealand dollar's decline. 


Brash said no one could tell whether the New Zealand dollar would fall
further in the short term but over the long term he expected it to
strengthen.
- - 05/10/00 00-19G



In large part, the fall in the local currency is due to the strength
of the U.S. dollar.



The weak dollar also reflects New Zealand's large current account
deficit, the fact New Zealand is viewed as an old-style economy, that
New Zealand interest rates are comparable to those in major capital
markets and some nervousness - whether warranted or not - about the
policy direction of the Labour Party/Alliance Party coalition
government, he said.



The New Zealand dollar fell to an all-time low of US$0.3992 Wednesday.



"There is no single, simple explanation for the fall in the New
Zealand dollar over the last two years," Brash said.



Since it hit a peak of US$0.7100 in November 1996, the New Zealand
dollar has fallen 44%, he said. On its trade-weighted index, the dollar
has fallen 32% from 69.00 in late April 1997 to around 47.00 this month,
he said.



"A significant part of the depreciation since early 1997 had been the
reversal of an overvalued currency," he said.



There appears to be little risk the fall in the exchange rate will
adversely impact New Zealand's financial system, he said.



And Brash also noted there could be positive outcomes from the
currency's fall.



The low New Zealand dollar is likely to significantly reduce the
current account deficit and shift economic activity into exports.



"It may well lead to a somewhat faster rate of growth in the medium
term," he said.
- - 05/10/00 00-29G



If the low New Zealand dollar results in upward pressure on prices,
the Reserve Bank would tighten, thereby increasing unemployment, and
slowing growth temporarily, he said.



However, failure to tighten if inflation took hold would likely cause
the currency to fall further, he said.



Brash said the central bank would only intervene in the foreign
exchange market if trading in the New Zealand dollar was disorderly, but
that isn't the case at present.

title: Aussie dollar pulls back in Europe, eyes euro.
text:
LONDON, Sept 26 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar backed off early highs against the U.S. dollar in Europe on Tuesday, disappointed by the euro's inability to extend gains after last week's bounce on concerted Group of Seven intervention. 

 A dearth of domestic economic indicators in Australia this week meant the market continued to focus on the euro, which the Aussie dollar has been tracking for some time. And so far the single currency was struggling to make headway after Friday's spike up in reaction to G7 intervention, traders said. 

 Until U.S. businesses and securities loose lustre in the eyes of global investors, gains in the euro and dollar bloc currencies were likely to be tentative despite the risk of central bank intervention, analysts said. 

 "I think both the Australian and New Zealand dollars will just continue to be disadvantaged versus the U.S. dollar unless there's a key change in U.S. fundamentals," said Jane Foley, currency strategist at Barclays Capital in London. 

 "Trends are a function of capital flows and capital flows are a function of where investors want to invest their money, and that in turn is a function of fundamentals. Central bank intervention by itself cannot change trends." 

 Foley expected the Australian dollar to continue gyrating in line with euro/dollar's swings in the near term, given the nervousness about euro intervention. 

 The Australian dollar pulled back below US$0.5470 by 1005 GMT after briefly rising above US$0.55 in Sydney trading. It was now about a cent off peaks it hit immediately after the euro intervention on Friday and back within 1-1/2 cents of record lows around US$0.5360 set last week. 

 "There are a lot of people who went long the Aussie dollar after the intervention (in the euro), and they may have to be shaken out before we can get through these levels above US$0.55," said a Japanese bank dealer in London. 

 The New Zealand dollar was also on the retreat, fading toward US$0.4120 from early highs above US$0.4155 to mirror its Australian counterpart. 

 Earlier in the day, August trade data released by Statistics New Zealand showed a monthly trade deficit of NZ$345 million, in line with market expectations. 

 While crude oil imports were a major reason for the deficit and the figures were in line with economists' forecasts, traders said the data were a reminder of New Zealand's bulging current account imbalance and certainly not helping mend sentiment on the kiwi dollar. 

 The Canadian dollar was trapped in a tight C$1.4863-1.4880 range, near the middle of its two-week trading band.

title: NZ's PM Clark Says NZ Dollar Undervalued
text:
CANBERRA -(Dow Jones)- New Zealand Prime Minister Helen Clark said Tuesday that the country's currency is undervalued but coordinated intervention by central banks last week to support the euro has helped the New Zealand dollar. 

 "The money has flooded into the greenback and the yen," she said during an interview with Australian Broadcasting Corp. radio. "The Aussie, the Kiwi, the euro, we are all struggling in its wake." 

 "The best we can do is say yes, our currencies are undervalued but we are going to get out there and boost our exporting and our tourism like crazy to take advantage of that in the mean time," she said. 

 At 0642 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was quoted at US$0.4147, up from US$0.4111 late Monday in Wellington and up also from its local open at around US$0.4130. 

 Clark said the coordinated intervention by the world's major central banks last Friday to support the euro has helped the New Zealand dollar but should be followed up with further intervention. 

 Asked whether the intervention will be effective, she said "it will be if they do it a number more times but to date it has helped our dollar a bit." 

 Clark, who was speaking from Auckland, is heading to Australia for talks with Australian Prime Minister John Howard. The talks are scheduled for Thursday. 

 She also said that a common currency for Australia and New Zealand is inevitable because of a global trend toward larger and larger population groupings. 

 Asked whether a common currency is part of the formal agenda for her talks with Howard, she said there is "nothing formal but it is obviously something that has been batted about." 

 Clark said New Zealand's government has "got to look at (a common currency) to see whether there are advantages for New Zealanders. If it helps us maintain prosperity we would be crazy to say no." 

 "I am of the view myself that the way the world is going, we are looking for larger and larger critical mass," she said. New Zealand is a small country with a population of 3.8 million and Australia, with a population of nearly 19 million "isn't a very big country either," Clark said. 

 "So we are all looking at how we can increase the mass in which we work," she added. 

 Australian Treasurer Peter Costello has said Australia would only consider a currency union where New Zealand takes on the Australian dollar and wouldn't consider a common currency. 

 "We take a rather different view," Clark said. "The proposals that have been batted around by the economists in New Zealand have talked about a merger and a common central bank." 

 "I think the Australian government, like our own government, really hasn't given it serious consideration," she said. 

 "Personally, I think becoming part of larger critical masses is inevitable," Clark said. "Our stock markets are looking at merging, there is this issue over the currency and of course the New Zealand and Australian economies are very, very closely integrated." 

 -By Iain McDonald, Dow Jones Newswires; 61-2-6208-0901; iain.mcdonald@dowjones.com

title: NZ Dlr Up Late On Euro  Intervention ; Resistance US$0.415

 At 0545 GMT, the New Zealand dollar was trading at US$0.4115, up from US$0.4085 late Friday in Wellington but below its session high of US$0.4155, dealers said.

 A second bank dealer said the local market is wary about further central bank intervention to support the euro, adding that this can be expected to lend support for the local currency on any dips toward US$0.4090 after the local close. 

 A third dealer said while the outlook for the New Zealand dollar has brightened thanks to the coordinated action to bolster the euro, it is important that the New Zealand dollar remains above US$0.4070 for this brighter outlook to remain valid. 

 Selling interest toward US$0.4150 is expected to offer initial resistance overnight. Further resistance is reported around US$0.4180, dealers said.

 WELLINGTON, Sept 21 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar bounced back from its new record low set overnight following the plunge in the euro and the Australian dollar . 

 While momentarily flirting with its record low level in early Thursday morning trade, the kiwi was hanging around $0.4070 level by 9 a.m. (2100 GMT), after its record low of $0.4050. 

 "It's totally flow driven if someone comes in and sells it, there's no reason we can't go lower and if someone comes in and buys it, there's no reason we won't go higher," one currency trader said. 

 "The market is purely at the hands of transactional flows." 

 Dealers said the kiwi dollar was basically coattailing Australian dollar and the euro. 

 The euro/dollar emerged from its record low below 84.40 cents by late New York trading after U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said the U.S. dollar policy was unchanged and the U.S. was watching forex developments closely. 

 "It's really out of our hands whether we go up or down. The market is quite thin and volatile," the trader said. 

 The Australian dollar's move was seen dictating the kiwi's direction in local trade, and some picked retracement from losses in the Australasian currencies on fears of intervention by the Reserve Bank of Australia. 

 "There's still that perception that that's the risk, so therefore it gives it a slightly bit of bid tone, unless we see fresh selling. Without fresh selling, Aussie will be bid," the trader said. 

 "At this stage, I would say there is some risk to both kiwi and Aussie just spiking up quickly. But having said that, if it gets up to the 41 figure level, at this stage, you'll have to say it's probably sell." 

 On the cross, the kiwi was quoted at $0.7543/63 at 9 a.m. (2100 GMT) against $0.7580/00 on Wednesday. 

 Another currency trader said the Group of Seven finance ministers' meeting scheduled for the coming weekend was keeping the market on its toes. 

 "They will be talking about the euro, what has to be done, strong dollar policy, whether or not intervention will be recommended. International Monetary Fund has recommended intervention into the euro market and whether or not the G7 will go along with it, we'll wait and see," he said. 

 "There has to be a reasonable chance that we'll see that come, come Monday morning." 

 IMF Managing Director Horst Koehler said on Wednesday the euro was "heavily undervalued" and that central bank intervention should not be seen as taboo. 

 Domestically, Statistics New Zealand will announce its June quarter balance of payments data on Friday at 10.45 a.m. (2245 GMT). New Zealand's large current account deficit is seen as another factor capping any kiwi rally. 

 The current account deficit for the March year had previously been at 8.2 percent of the GDP, but has recently been revised down to 7.1 percent. 

 "If the current dismal state of the currency is in part attributable to external account comparisons, then there should be reason for change," ANZ said in its commentary. 

 Economists polled by Reuters on average see June quarter balance of payments at NZ$1.353 billion deficit and June year deficit at NZ$7.485 billion, or 7.1 percent of GDP.

title: RBA wins battered Australian dollar no respite.
text:
LONDON, Sept 7 (Reuters) - The Australian dollar fell to within sight of its record lows against the U.S. dollar on Thursday, crashing through the levels at which London traders had spotted the Reserve Bank of Australia buying the currency. 

 London traders said on Thursday they saw the RBA buying Australian dollars for U.S. dollars below US$0.5600. An RBA official in London declined to comment. 

 However, the size of the central bank's purchases were said to be small and the Australian currency was back on the slide as soon as the central bank disappeared from view. 

 "The market is not particularly rational now but it could remain that way for quite some time, so to call a turning point for these currencies is extremely dangerous," said Jim Webber, chief economist at Toronto Dominion Securities in London. 

 The Australian dollar fell as far as US$0.5535, its lowest level since August 1998 and within sights of record lows around US$0.5530. 

 "It's interesting that they (the RBA) were asking prices yesterday and today they have been intervening, buying small amounts," said at a trader at a Australian bank in London. "But people are getting used to them being around and it was only small amounts and I still expect it to go to US$0.5330 in the next 24 hours or so." 

 Traders said in an environment where the U.S. dollar remained the market's favourite currency, the Australian dollar would struggle to find few friends even though economic data remains relatively robust. 

 "It's a function of very, very bad sentiment because the economic data has not been very bad. It's been the same story that international investors would rather hold U.S. dollars than the euro, the Aussie dollar and just about everything else," said Jane Foley, currency strategist at Barclays Capital. 

 "Our forecast is that the Aussie dollar will go down to US$0.50 in three-months." 

 There was little respite for the Australian dollar from any front and it fell to its lowest in more than five years against the yen as the Japanese currency soared across the board, hitting record highs against the euro. 

 The Australian central bank's credibility was not being called into question despite its failure to support its currency on Thursday, with traders saying it had little chance of turning sentiment on its own given current market conditions. 

 "It's disastrous because the interbank market went long when the RBA came in because they expected it to hold the Aussie up and soon as RBA disappeared as they went home, all the bids disappeared. When you have have got markets of this nature you can't stop it," said a trader at a German bank in London. 

 "The only way the Aussie dollar and the Kiwi dollar could get back is if we get the European Central Bank intervening in euro/dollar. And if ECB come in they will not come alone and they will come with the Bank of Japan intervening the dollar/yen or euro/yen and the RBA would sort out its own currency." 

 Traders said they did not expect the U.S. Federal Reserve or the Bank of England to join in in any intervention. 

 Meanwhile, the New Zealand dollar dropped to fresh record lows around US$0.4165 against the U.S. dollar. 

 Traders said the Kiwi dollar would also continue to fall, not only because of the weakness in Aussie dollar but also because its own poor domestic fundamentals. 

 "The Kiwi dollar has got even more problems and it is going to continue to underperform and we expect it to fall to US$0.37 in three months," said Foley from Barclays.

title: WRAP: NZ Fin Min Tries To Counter Negative Perceptions
text:
SYDNEY -(Dow Jones)- New Zealand Finance Minister Michael Cullen tried to counter negative perceptions of his government's economic policies Wednesday in his first address to Australian business leaders and economists. 

 He also used the opportunity to say the New Zealand dollar is undervalued and gave the mildest of hints that interest rates should remain on hold for a while. 

 Cullen told the Trans-Tasman Business Circle that New Zealand has simply moved to the center under the Labour-Alliance coalition. 

 "Far from lurching to the left, we have made a modest move to the center," Cullen said, adding that Australia, in his view, remains more interventionist and less orthodox than New Zealand. 

 Cullen said his government aims for "greater consistency between Australian and New Zealand law," although he said he has little interest in a unified currency. 

 "He tried to deflect a lot of concerns of international investors. He is battling the perceptions of his government," said Macquarie Bank Fixed-Income Analyst David Bassanese. 

 Bassanese said international investors aren't aware of the "intricacies" of the policy changes by the New Zealand government, elected last year, and this had caused an erosion of business and consumer confidence. 

 Cullen said he has been "disturbed" by comments filtering back to New Zealand that the government has changed its attitude toward foreign investment, and much of his speech was spent assuring that his government is seeking to create a better environment for overseas investors. 

 "There has been no anti-investment policy switch, and if anything the new government is pending more, not less, to attract foreign investment," Cullen said. 

 He tried to allay fears over the review of how the Reserve Bank of New Zealand conducts monetary policy, saying the review aimed to see what tools the central bank needs to be more effective. 

 "The independence of the bank and its primary focus on price stability aren't open for review. We just want to improve operations if that is possible," Cullen said. 


           Hints Rates Shouldn't Rise Further



In questions later with journalists, Cullen hinted that the Reserve
Bank should be more cautious in raising interest rates over the next few
months as economic growth in New Zealand is being led by exports, which
is less inflationary.



"We'll wait and see, it depends on (Reserve Bank of New Zealand
Governor Don) Brash's assumptions on growth and whether that is export
led," Cullen said.



New Zealand's official cash rate is 6.5%, and the central bank's last
statement was interpreted as pointing toward further rate rises in the
second half of the year.



Macquarie's Bassanese said if rates are put on hold, it will be good
news for the New Zealand economy.



"The Reserve Bank (of New Zealand) has been too aggressive in raising
rates," he said.



Despite the higher interest rates, the New Zealand dollar has suffered
as investors took the view the tight monetary policy will harm growth.



The New Zealand currency has dropped 11% against the U.S. dollar since
the beginning of the year to trade at US$0.4597 Wednesday. Its
performance has been worse than its trans-Tasman neighbor, the
Australian dollar, which has fallen about 9.3% this year to trade
currently around US$0.5880.



Both currencies are undervalued, Cullen said. "Clearly the Australian
dollar and the New Zealand dollar are undervalued. That's a reflection
of market sentiment, and eventually market sentiment will change," he
said.



-By Clyde Russell, Dow Jones Newswires, 612 8235-2958

Bond spreads widened as yields adopted their familiar pattern of underperforming U.S. rallies.

Traders expected an overnight range around US$0.4720-90, depending on the levels achieved by the Australian dollar . Bond spreads widened as local maturities retained their pattern of outperforming U.S. weakness and underperforming U.S. rallies, dealers said.

title: Cash rate best monetary tool currently in NZ-Brash.
text:
WELLINGTON, May 9 (Reuters) - The governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said on Tuesday that the central bank's official cash rate (OCR) was the best monetary policy tool currently used. 

 However Brash told a media briefing on a government review of monetary policy operation that it was worth reviewing the tool. 

 "Let's have an expert make a judgement," Brash said. 

 He pointed that the cash rate mechanism had only been introduced recently - in March last year. 

 It was worthwhile asking if this was a "sensible evolution" in monetary policy operation. 

 Brash said that international experience did not suggest that foreign exchange intervention was an effective method of determining a monetary policy stance. 

 This was also taken up by Finance Minister Michael Cullen, who is implementing the review. 

 Cullen said it would take an awful lot of convincing for him to back intervention in the New Zealand dollar. 

 Earlier, Cullen announced that the monetary policy review will consider how the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) interprets and applies its inflation target and whether it has an adequate range of instruments to effectively manage monetary conditions. 

 He said the review will consider the following: 

 - The way the Reserve bank interprets and applies the inflation target set out in the Policy Targets Agreement with a view to ensuring that this approach to achieving medium term price stability is consistent with avoiding undesirable instability in output; 

 - Whether the Reserve Bank has an adequate range of instruments and is using its current instruments effectively in altering monetary conditions in the desired direction; 

 - The range of sources, availability, type and timeliness of data, and the impact of these variables on forecasting and decision making; 

 - Whether the policy decision making process and accountability structures promote the best outcomes possible; 

 - The co-ordination of monetary policy with other elements of the economic policy framework, including an evaluation of the relationship between monetary policy operations and other Reserve Bank functions such as prudential oversight of financial institutions; 

 - Whether the Reserve Bank's communication of monetary policy decisions to the public and financial markets is as simple, clear and effective as possible. 

 Cullen said the total cost of the review, including the cost of using existing resources, is expected to be between NZ$200,000 and NZ$500,000. 

 It would be carried out by a reviewer from outside New Zealand, he said. 

 "Recommendations arising from the review will be discussed with the Reserve Bank Governor, Dr Don Brash, before the Government makes any decisions on how to proceed," Cullen said in speech notes for an address to a business audience in Wellington.

title: NZ Cullen, Brash Repeat Opposition To  Forex Intervention
text:
WELLINGTON -(Dow Jones)- New Zealand Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash and Finance Minister Michael Cullen Tuesday reiterated their belief that intervention in the currency market isn't very useful. 

 Brash told reporters the international experience suggests that it isn't very useful for central banks to directly intervene in foreign exchange markets, but there can't be any harm in the monetary authority offering its views on the issue. 

 The Reserve Bank of New Zealand hasn't used its reserves to intervene in foreign exchange markets since 1985, and the country's political parties also oppose the idea of the central bank intervening in currency markets. 

 Cullen, speaking to reporters with Brash after announcing details of a review of the operation of monetary policy, reiterated that viewpoint. 

 "I would be very surprised if the reviewer would have in mind to recommend that we went into direct intervention in foreign exchange markets and it would take an awful lot of convincing of me to suggest that we ought to be doing that," Cullen said.

title: NZ's Brash Says Monetary Inquiry Is Useful, Appropriate
text:
WELLINGTON -(Dow Jones)- Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash said Tuesday a government-sponsored inquiry into monetary policy is an appropriate way of assessing if there are ways to improve either his central bank's governance structure, or its operational procedures. 

 "I am keen to cooperate fully with the review because I think it is a useful thing to do a decade down the track and if we can find ways of improving the performance of the bank I would certainly welcome that," Brash told reporters. 

 The central bank's operational independence and legal requirement to aim monetary policy at the maintenance of price stability has been a feature of New Zealand's monetary policy framework for over ten years. 

 "In an important sense the review is a review of how we have performed in the last decade and to the extent that I have carried responsibility for the Bank's decisions in that period then clearly the review is partly of my performance," Brash said. 

 Brash said the official cash rate, which the central bank uses to implement its monetary policy decisions, is working well so far. 

 "I think we are using the best instrument currently, namely the official cash rate, but of course that has been in place for only about a little over a year. We were using other forms of instruments prior to that and I think it is worthwhile looking at whether that was a sensible evolution," he said. 

 "There are those who feel that we should be using other forms of instruments, such as for example reserve asset ratios of direct kinds of quantitative restrictions on lending. I personally don't think those make sense, but lets have an expert internationally make a judgment on that," he said. 

 Similarly, Brash said the international experience suggests that it isn't very useful for central banks to directly intervene in foreign exchange markets, but there can't be any harm in the monetary inquiry offering its views on the issue. 

 The Reserve Bank of New Zealand hasn't used its reserves to intervene in foreign exchange markets since 1985, and the country's political parties also oppose the idea of the central bank intervening in currency markets. 

 Finance Minister Michael Cullen, speaking to reporters with Brash, reiterated that viewpoint Tuesday. 

 "I would be very surprised if the reviewer would have in mind to recommend that we went into direct intervention in foreign exchange markets and it would take an awful lot of convincing of me to suggest that we ought to be doing that," Cullen said. 

 Cullen said he expects to shortly announce who will chair or conduct the monetary inquiry. 

 He had decided to publish the inquiry's term of reference before the announcement of a chairman because he wanted financial markets to know what the inquiry is all about prior to Brash's departure on an overseas trip where he will meet investors and other players with an interest in New Zealand markets. 

 Cullen said Brash is traveling overseas shortly. 

 Cullen said one of the issues likely to be canvassed by the monetary inquiry is the central bank's governance structures. 

 Currently, Governor Brash is personally accountable for maintaining price stability under the terms of the Policy Targets Agreement he signed with Cullen last December. 

 The board of the Reserve Bank, which is chaired by Brash, monitors Brash's performance, but doesn't have input into monetary policy decision-making. 

 Brash told reporters there is a contradiction in the law, which has been recognized for long time, in having a board that he chairs acting as a monitor of his performance. 

 "It may well be that the reviewer (of the monetary inquiry) says that is a contradiction which should be changed," Brash said. 

 Cullen told reporters the role of the Reserve Bank's board is "quite unusual" by international standards. 

 He said the U.S. and U.K. central banks have more "openly collegial" decision-making structures than New Zealand's, and it is appropriate for the inquiry to examine if this should remain so. 

 Cullen earlier Tuesday listed six issues to be reviewed by the upcoming inquiry into monetary policy.

title: NZ Brash: Most People Now Endorse Jan Cash Rate Rise
text:
WELLINGTON -(Dow Jones)- Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash said Wednesday that he believes most people now endorse the central bank's surprise move in mid-January to raise official cash rates. 

 Brash told a parliamentary select committee that the outlook for world growth and inflation pressures was much different in January, when the decision was made, than in November when the bank completed its economic forecasts. 

 Brash was appearing before the committee to discuss the central bank's briefing paper to the incoming government, but questions were asked about the increase in the official cash rate to 5.25% from 5%, which was announced just hours before fourth-quarter inflation proved to be much less than expected. 

 Brash said he has negotiated a new agreement with the new center-left coalition government, and understands the government wants to avoid the sudden appreciation in the New Zealand dollar that occurred in the 1990s and which proved so painful for exporters. 

 He said it is in everyone's interest to avoid such rapid local dollar appreciation. 

 The increases in the official cash rate in November and January were the best way to avoid the risk of a repeat of those rapid local dollar rises because it "nabs inflation before it builds a full head of steam." 

 However, Brash said he can't guarantee the strategy. 

 Brash told the committee that he sees three potential advantages arising from the New Zealand government's proposal to sponsor an independent inquiry into the operation of monetary policy in New Zealand. 

 One possible outcome from the proposed inquiry, details of which Finance Minister Michael Cullen is expected to outline later this month, is that it will affirm or endorse the country's existing framework for conducting monetary policy, he said. 

 A second possible outcome of the inquiry is that it will offer useful advice on whether the Reserve Bank is fully utilizing all of the instruments available to it to influence monetary conditions. 

 He said it would be useful to have an independent authority express a view on whether the Reserve Bank ought to, for example, attempt a greater control over credit supply within the economy. 

 Brash also noted the Reserve Bank of New Zealand doesn't intervene in foreign exchange markets, but said it would still be useful for an independent person to lend an assessment on that stance. 

 A third possible outcome of the inquiry, Brash said, is that it may find that there is room to improve the internal structures of the New Zealand central bank, which deliberates and make decisions on monetary policy operations. 


Brash also said he thinks it would be better to have a non-New
Zealander conduct the inquiry.

title: Concerns about RBNZ independence overblown - NZPA.
text:
WELLINGTON, Jan 21 (Reuters) - Offshore investors have turned away from New Zealand because of a perceived dispute between Finance Minister Michael Cullen and the Reserve Bank which some believe may undermine the independence of the central bank, the New Zealand Press Association reported on Friday. 

 But a senior currency dealer said the perception that the bank's independence was under threat was exaggerated, NZPA reported. 

 Concern has arisen since the Reserve Bank increased its official cash rate on Wednesday, to 5.25 percent from 5.00 percent, only a couple of hours before the release of surprisingly low December quarter inflation figures. 

 Finance Minister Michael Cullen, not yet two months in the job since his leftist coalition took power, then said he would meet with bank governor Don Brash next week to discuss the timing of the hike and the accuracy of the bank's and Treasury's forecasts. 

 He also said he expected in future the bank would "not necessarily assume inflationary pressures are there when the published figures are showing they are not". 

 "Comments such as that have made the offshore market slightly jittery about how interventionist the new Government may wish to be," Bank of New Zealand manager of foreign exchange Greg Ball told NZPA. 

 Adding to foreign investor jumpiness is that just after his appointment Cullen altered the central Policy Targets Agreement with the Reserve Bank. It was a minor change but was read as an indication that the new Government wanted the bank to pay more attention to economic growth, rather than just inflation. 

 On Thursday, the stock market's key NZSE-40 capital index lost 1.74 percent as foreigners sold in response to the rate rise. 

 This morning, the currency was down more than a third of a US cent at 51.41 US cents from 51.78 US cents shortly before Wednesday morning's interest rate move. Overnight, the kiwi hit 51.28 US cents. 

 Economists are divided over whether Cullen should have spoken publicly, but Ball said foreigners were acting on fear of the unknown. 

 "It's been over-reported, it's been over-emphasised," Ball said. "I don't think it is that important." 

 Ball said the market was concerned next week's meeting would see Cullen telling Brash how to run monetary policy - anathema to markets which watched New Zealand's central bank lead the way in formalising independence from Government interference. 

 "There's no reason to believe that," Ball said. "Personally, I don't put a lot of credence on that. All this is is a change of government, and people do things slightly differently."

title: Asian markets tumble as investors cut and run.
text:
SYDNEY, Aug 28 (Reuters) - Asia-Pacific share markets tumbled early on Friday after a major sell-off on Wall Street appeared to confirm fears of a global economic downturn and investors scrambled for a way out. 

 Japan's benchmark Nikkei average fell 3.55 percent in early trade to 13,901.50 points - its lowest level since Japan's economic bubble burst in 1990. 

 As the Australia dollar again flirted with historic lows despite central bank intervention overnight, Australian stocks also dived at the start of trade. 

 The benchmark All Ordinaries index fell 94.8 points or 3.7 percent to 2,465.8. New Zealand's NZSE-40 Capital Index plunged more than four percent in the first hour of trading. 

 And economists said there was no end in sight to the carnage as nervous investors cut their losses and ran. 

 "Investors in emerging markets, those who have not already pulled their money out of Asia, will simply pull the plug and take these markets to historic lows," said Grant Fitzner, an economist at HSBC Markets in Sydney. 

 "A lot of people are liquidating their positions now, taking their losses and exiting these markets." 

 The Asian bailout was sparked by a torrid trading session on Wall Street, where the Dow dropped 357 points, or 4.12 percent, to 8166 points - its lowest level since February. 

 Markets were also in turmoil in Canada, which raised official interest rates to protect its dollar, and in Latin America. Toronto stocks spun down six percent, Argentina's main index lost 10.63 percent and Brazil's Bovespa index tumbled 9.95 percent. 

 "I think we are having a frantic exit from equity markets across the world. People are concerned and they are raising cash," Michael Metz, managing director at CIBC Oppenheimer, told Reuters in New York. 

 The global market turmoil has been largely blamed on a financial meltdown in Russia, where the rouble has gone into virtual freefall. 

 Fitzner said Russia's economy accounted for only one percent of global gross domestic product (GDP) but the country had a symbolic importance for emerging market investors. 

 The main victims of the Russian crisis have been commodity-linked currencies such as the Australian and Canadian dollars - and agriculture-dependent Latin American markets. 

 The Australian dollar swept to new record lows, falling to as low as US$0.5530 in New York trade, despite intervention by the Reserve Bank of Australia. The New Zealand dollar hit a fresh 12-year low of US$0.4790 overnight. 

 The U.S. dollar shed about one yen to trade at around 140.50 yen after Wall Street's weakness. 

 For many foreign exchange traders, the commodity link has been just a pretext for speculators trying to find a safe one-way bet. 

 "These guys lost large in Russia and now they're trying to make it up dumping defenceless currencies like the Australian dollar," said one Sydney dealer. "The commodity rationale is just a smokescreen."

title: FOCUS-NZ dollar assets win friends, for now.
text:
AUCKLAND, June 18 (Reuters) - New Zealand dollar assets won some unlikely friends on Thursday, courtesy of Japanese and U.S. central bank intervention to support the yen, but analysts doubted the friendship would last. 

 The New Zealand dollar's slippery slide over the last year has accelerated in recent weeks thanks to the likelihood of a credit rating downgrade by Moody's Investors Service and continued concerns about the large current account deficit. 

 The weak yen compounded the kiwi's woes until Wednesday night (NZ time), when Japan and the U.S. stepped in to shore up the yen, and the kiwi rallied more than two U.S. cents. 

 By noon the kiwi was holding onto most of its gains, trading at US$0.5188/95 from 0.4974/81 at Wednesday's close. 

 Market commentators were unsure whether intervention would work over the longer term and whether Japan's economic reform package would achieve what it set out to. 

 But the kiwi's reprieve and a sharply stronger Wall Street brought a sharp rally in New Zealand equities, the benchmark NZSE-40 Capital Index gaining almost two percent to 2,038.21. 

 Wholesale interest rates - which had been under pressure from the lower kiwi - fell back sharply. 

 By late morning, key 90-day bank bill rates were at 9.25 percent from almost 9.70 percent at Wednesday's close. 

 Ulf Schoefisch, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell NZ, said there was no doubt about the degree of determination behind the intervention. 

 "I think the market will not try to push the yen lower again in the short term, but as we have seen in previous periods of interventions, the markets have taken three to four weeks to break through the levels again," he said. 

 "So ultimately I think we will see a weaker yen again, but it may take a while." 

 While the kiwi had benefited, downside risk would open up again should the yen suffer a relapse. "The fundamentals have not changed, neither here nor in Japan," Schoefisch said. 

 Prime Minister Jenny Shipley was also cautious. 

 "What has happened overnight is helpful, but I will only personally have real confidence in whether or not we are going to find our way out if we see the sorts of reforms undertaken in Japan that not only I but very many other APEC leaders have discussed on many occasions in the recent past," she said. 

 Vicki St John at share brokers Credit Suisse First Boston said the recovery in equities looked brittle. 

 "At this stage it still feels fragile and vulnerable to any reasonable changes in currency. If the currency whipped back down again we would react pretty quickly," she said. 

Foreign exchange dealers agreed it was too early to say whether kiwi's downtrend had finished so soon after plumbing 12-year lows against the greenback. 

 "We've got to see what happens in Japan. If they don't do anything fundamental - if it is solely intervention - then it won't last," said one kiwi dealer. 

 While intervention had put a gloss on New Zealand assets for the time being, the fundamentals for the economy were still weak - private forecasters expect data due on June 26 to show flat growth in the March quarter. 

 And the March quarter current account defifit - the primary cause of Moody's concern - is expected to climb to about 8.0 percent of GDP in the March quarter from 7.7 percent in December. That data is due on June 24.

 The yen's relentless slide lower is pummeling emerging market currencies in Southeast Asia, East Europe and Latin America. Investors are shifting assets en masse into the dollar, sterling and U.S. Treasurys. 

 The Indian rupee, South Korean won, Malaysian ringgit, Singapore dollar, South African rand and Mexican peso all fell against the dollar. The Russian ruble was flat following intervention by that nation's central bank. The Australian and New Zealand dollar also declined. 

 Late afternoon in New York, the dollar was trading at Y146.15, up from Y144.33 Friday in New York. The U.S. currency was also trading at DEM1.8105, up from 1.8061 Friday. Sterling was trading at $1.6350, up from 1.6335. The dollar is at its highest level against the yen since August 1990. 

 "It's really more of the same," said Ricardo Gomes, managing director at Republic National Bank in New York. 

 Traders are selling the yen because Japan isn't attractive. Moreover, traders don't believe the U.S. Federal Reserve is prepared to jointly intervene with the Bank of Japan to defend the yen unless Tokyo shepherds in fundamental reforms to open up Japanese markets and slash taxes. 

 In lieu of U.S. support, traders don't believe Japan alone poses a credible threat to more than temporarily reverse the yen's decline. Despite the Bank of Japan spending around $20 billion in intervention two months ago, traders note, the yen is still falling quickly. As a result, traders are increasingly ignoring Japanese leaders almost daily threats to take decisive action to boost the yen. 

 In the meantime, some believe pressure is increasingly mounting on China to devalue its currency, the yuan, a step which traders believe could take other pegs with it, including the Hong Kong dollar, ruble and Brazilian real. 

 "The market is very nervous," said Gomes. This anxiety is reflected in currency options where volatilities soared and market participants snapped up dollar/call yen/puts, or the right to buy dollars and sell yen.
