title: RBNZ's hands seen tied by kiwi dollar's weakness.
text:
WELLINGTON, June 9 (Reuters) - New Zealand's central bank has little option but to let the kiwi dollar continue its downward spiral, analysts said on Tuesday. 

 The Reserve Bank on Wednesday morning faces the first major test of its recently introduced policy of only commenting or altering monetary conditions after its weekly Monetary Policy Committee meeting on Tuesdays. 

 Analysts believe the bank is hamstrung in using its major monetary policy lever - a change in the daily cash target - because of the fragile state of the economy. 

 A tightening at this stage could send the economy into reverse. 

 Conversely, if the bank does not want conditions to ease any more it is largely powerless. 

 Silence from the bank on Wednesday morning would be tantamount to sanctioning easier conditions, said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Bank economist Ulf Schoefish. 

 "It's all conditional on where the Monetary Conditions Index is. It might just sneak in to a level that is acceptable to the Reserve Bank," he said. 

 Monetary conditions have eased to over a hundred basis points below the RBNZ's target for the September quarter, as outlined by the bank in its May 26 statement. 

 The index was at 245 on Tuesday afternoon compared with the bank's current target of 350. 

 Last week, traders interpreted the RBNZ's silence after its monetary conditions meeting as effectively sanctioning the MCI at about 90 points below the 350 target. 

 The New Zealand dollar has fallen over two U.S. cents since the bank's May 26 set-piece and, apart from a short spike down in January 1993, is now at its lowest level since late 1986. 

 The RBNZ has never intervened directly in the currency since it was floated in 1985 and Governor Don Brash is on record as stating that he believes intervention would be largely futile. 

Foreign exchange traders believe the Reserve Bank of Australia has spent upwards of A$3 billion defending the Aussie, which plunged towards an all-time low on Tuesday. 

 Australian weakness has been a big factor in the New Zealand dollar's fall with both countries catching cold from Asia. 

 Schoefish believes there is a zero chance of the RBNZ lowering its cash target, due to the weak state of the economy. 

 He said the problem for the bank was its inability to direct the mix of monetary conditions to ensure any easing came via either the currency or interest rates, but not the other. 

 BNZ Chief Forex dealer Mike Symonds said that even if the RBNZ declined to comment, he doubted the market would ease too aggressively from this point. 

 "The MCI looks as though it will settle around the minus-90, minus-100 level but up towards minus-130 and minus-135 we are pushing the outer limits," he said. 

 The kiwi market would again take its lead from global forex markets overnight, he said. 

 "Given the way the Aussie is performing, the outlook is not particularly positive. But the kiwi is holding in there, just," he said. 

 Treasurer Winston Peters firmly ruled out any question of the New Zealand government supporting intervention. 

 "We are not getting into the business of risking the taxpayer's dollar against the investment decisions of thousands of people abroad in the way that Australia has," he told National Radio in an interview during the morning.

title: NZ dollar falls to 11-1/2 year low, under US$0.50.
text:
WELLINGTON, June 10 (Reuters) - The New Zealand dollar, which has been trading around 5-1/2 year lows against the U.S dollar for several days, slipped below a key level of US$0.5010 in Wednesday trade and reached levels not seen since late 1986. 

 A dip to just under US$0.5000 at about 10.40 a.m. (2240 GMT), took it to levels last seen on October 17, 1986, according to central bank data. 

 On that date the spot currency last closed under 50 U.S. cents at US$0.4997. 

 The slip, which came in tandem with a move by the Australian dollar below US$0.59, followed a comment earlier in the morning by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand that it would like to see New Zealand monetary conditions clos. 

 According to bank records, the TWI was last at around these levels in May 1994 when it hit 56.47. 

 The trade-weighted all-time low was hit on January 3, 1992, when it touched 52.74. 

 The spot kiwi's all-time low against the U.S. dollar comes from the time of its float, on March 4, 1985, when it hit US$0.4365. 

 Both the Australian and New Zealand currencies continued to stray below their respective key levels at 10.58 a.m. (2258 GMT), with the kiwi trading at US$0.4980/87 and the Aussie at US$0.5873/78. 

 Traders in Australia reported the usual rumours of intervention by the Reserve Bank of Australia. 

 The RBNZ has never intervened, and according to New Zealand politicians this week there is no political desire here to start doing so.

title: NZ ministers see kiwi fall as normal market action.
text:
AUCKLAND, June 9 (Reuters) - New Zealand's Finance Minister Bill Birch and Treasurer Winston Peters on Tuesday played down the significance of the recent sharp fall in the kiwi dollar, saying it showed international markets at work and was not going to spur extraordinary policy action such as intervention. 

 Birch, in Auckland, told Reuters he felt the movement in the New Zealand dollar was the result of "the market at work, and our framework accommodates that. 

 "We've got a robust framework of economic policies and I'm sure that's the best way to allow those adjustments to take place," he added. 

 Earlier, speaking on National Radio, Peters firmly ruled out any question of the New Zealand government supporting intervention in the foreign exchange market. 

 In recent weeks the Australian central bank, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), has intervened to prop up the tumbling Aussie dollar. 

 "We are not getting into the business of risking the taxpayer's dollar against the investment decisions of thousands of people abroad in the way that Australia has," Peters said in a morning radio interview. 

 Birch, speaking after giving a speech to a gas industry conference in Auckland, said he did not think the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) would be especially shocked by the movement in the currency either, given that it was mainly driven by prevailing trends in international markets including the U.S. dollar's significant strengthening against the yen. 

 Asked if he expected the RBNZ to comment on Wednesday morning after its weekly monetary poilicy meeting, Birch said: "I'm sure that the Reserve Bank will be monitoring it closely, but I don't think that the way international currency markets are working are a surprise to the Reserve Bank." 

 Peters said another factor in the currency's fall was that "we did have an over-rated dollar and it will probably settle at a far more acceptable level". 

 The Treasurer has said on several occasions that he considered the dollar to be over-valued in 1996 into 1997 and has welcomed the steady depreciation seen since the middle of last year. 

 He said he did not believe there had been any capital flight from New Zealand associated with its latest fall. 

 "It may well have stabilised for all we know," he added. 

 Asked if the currency's fall could justify the government abandoning its inflation target, Peters said the target had been widened after the 1996 election to a band of nought to three percent from nought to two. 

 He said the wider target allowed a far more flexible, long-term response from the governor of the Reserve Bank who would not have to make knee-jerk reactions of the type the bank could be forced into with the narrower target.

title: NZ Brash Repeats RBNZ Retains  Forex Intervention  Option

 In a briefing to the multi-party grouping, Brash reiterated his central bank continues to research the practicalities of direct foreign currency intervention as well as the opportunity costs associated with maintaining but not using the reserves.

title: Intervention  in NZ dollar won't work, say analysts.
text:
WELLINGTON, Dec 9 (Reuter) - New Zealand foreign exchange analysts on Monday dismissed as counter-productive apparent hints by Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen that the central bank should directly intervene in the market. 

 Cullen, who is Labour's candidate for finance minister if it clinches a coalition with the New Zealand First party, caused a mild stir in financial markets last week when he sent a coded message about intervention. 

New Zealand First is expected to decide on Tuesday whether it will support Labour or the conservative National Party. 

 In his speech, Cullen said there were various "highly orthodox and commonly practised ways" of addressing the exchange rate, which he has consistently described as overvalued. 

 He declined to go into detail, but said calls for dropping interest rates missed the point and the exchange rate itself was the primary problem. 

Foreign exchange experts all took Cullen to mean that the Reserve Bank should intervene directly to bring the dollar down, something never done since the kiwi was floated in March 1985. 

 The kiwi, which recently touched 8-1/2 year highs, is one of the freest floating currencies in the world but RBNZ Governor Don Brash reserves the right to intervene. 

 Brash last week told Reuters he did not wish to air his views on intervention. In the past he has pointed to the failure of intervention by other countries, notably Britain in 1992. 

 "It doesn't work very well and can be counter-productive under certain circumstances. The general view on intervention is that it is not particularly effective," said Bankers Trust economist David Plank. 

 "The very short term impact (of RBNZ selling) might be for the currency to dip, but the general experience around the world is (intervention is) very ineffective but good at wasting taxpayers' money." 

 Cullen has argued that part of the reason for the kiwi's steep climb -- up 25 percent on a Trade-Weighted Index basis in three years -- is that investing in the New Zealand dollar is a one-way bet, and he wants to dispel that notion. 

 Brash caused a stir in the currency market last week when he said that the New Zealand dollar appeared to be near the top of its cycle. Plank believes the currency is 10-15 percent overvalued. 

 But not everyone agrees. 

 National Bank chief foreign exchange dealer Stu Nattrass said the exchange rate had only recovered to the level it was at in 1988, after which the country went into deep recession. 

 He said inflation expectations are the seat of the problem and the reason why wholesale interest rates are at 8.5 percent while inflation is expected to be at one percent in 1997. 

 "Interest rates are far more relevant than exchange rates. I'm surprised people are focusing on the exchange rate and not interest rates as being way out of line," Nattrass said. 

 A dealer who did not wish to be named said that if the RBNZ directly sells New Zealand dollars it will simply provide cheap rates for investors to buy the currency. 

 "You would quickly find a level of willing buyers," he said. 

 One bank's chief bond dealer said any intervention would indicate the RB's autonomy had been undermined. 

 "It would not be the amount the bank sold, just that they are sellers. I would see that as being bearish, showing political influence coming back into the Reserve Bank and therefore they are losing their independence," he said. 

 Under the Reserve Bank Act, the finance minister can request an intervention but the governor is as liberty to ignore it if such a move would threaten the bank's goal of achieving price stability. The government can demand action but needs to get an Order in Council, a move requiring cabinet approval and signature by the governor-general. 

 Even exporters doubt intervention would work. 

 Malcolm Bailey, president of lobby group Federated Farmers and spokesman for an exporters' crisis summit on the exchange rate last week, said: "I don't think selling New Zealand dollars will be the answer." 

 He said exporters are not looking for quick fix solutions, although he agreed intervention could "burst the bubble of over-enthusiasm about investing in New Zealand". 

 "If you have the government behind the Reserve Bank pulling the levers, then you undermine confidence in the Reserve Bank Act," he said. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746

title: FEATURE - New Zealand inflation-tamer in control.
text:
WELLINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuter) - The man who has largely driven inflation out of New Zealand, central bank governor Don Brash, is far happier now he has curbed the annual rate back within a government-set target of 0-2 percent. 

 On Tuesday, New Zealand's annual underlying inflation fell to two percent from 2.2 percent at June 30 and Brash celebrated by sending out an easing signal which sent short-term interest yields scurrying 50 basis points downwards. 

 Asked in an interview on Wednesday if he still enjoys the job after seven years, Brash said: "I enjoy it far more when I am inside the range than when I am outside the range." 

 The very tall, 55 year-old Brash said he had no plans to retire voluntarily. 

 He is not quite half way through a five year contract he signs with the government which gives him operational independence to keep inflation within the agreed range and gives the finance minister the right to fire him if he fails. 

 New Zealand had inflation in the mid-teens when Brash was appointed in 1988, but since passing the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) Act 1989 has had one of the lowest rates in the world. 

 Twice the target band has been breached -- once in 1991 when the band was undershot during the very rapid disinflation process, and then in the June 1995 quarter when it was overshot. 

 Brash believes the act has delivered to New Zealand an "astonishingly stable" currency, lower interest rates than most developed countries as well as the low inflation rate. 

 While the act says nothing about economic growth targets, GDP in the June year rose 5.5 percent and Brash believes a rate of 3.5 percent-plus is sustainable. 

 Unemployment has also dropped dramatically, to 6.3 percent from over 11 percent in the early 1990s. 

 "If you had said 10 years ago that a country as small as New Zealand, without Switzerland's track record, would ever get its 10-year bonds under U.S. 10-year rates you would have been certified," Brash said. 

 (Ten year bonds now above U.S. rates at 7.14 percent.) 

 "I find it hard to think what other reason there might be (than the act)," he said. 

 He pointed to the fact that although the much larger economy of Australia had a lower ratio of public debt to GDP, its bond yields have been 100-200 basis points above New Zealand's for some years. 

 "You would have to conclude the reason for the substantial gap has to do with the credibilty of the legislation." 

 STEADY "KIWI" DOLLAR 

 While there has been huge volatility in even major currencies in recent years, New Zealand's curency has mostly maintained a gradual upward path. And since the "Kiwi" dollar floated 10 years ago, the RBNZ has never had to directly intervene in the market. 

 "The New Zealand dollar has sailed along within a remarkably narrow range," said Brash of the Kiwi's recent performance. 

 The Trade-Weighted Index (TWI) measuring the Kiwi against a basket of currencies has moved in a 59.0-62.75 band in the past seven months. 

 The RBNZ indirectly targets the TWI and interest rates as they impact on price stabilty and monetary policy but it sets no particular ranges. 

 "If you have a very precise inflation target and you are a small, open economy inevitably you have to form a judgement within which the exchange rate can move and still be consistant with inflation in the target band," Brash said. 

 Opposition Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen said that the RBNZ's use of the exchange rate to contain domestic prices unfairly hits the tradeable sector rather than service industries where most inflationary pressures have appeared. 

 However, Brash said there is not much he can do about that. 

 "I sometimes wish that I could control the mix of interest rates and the exchange but I have long since accepted that I can't," he said. "We can't control the mix, the market controls that. We can only tighten or ease." 

 HIGH REAL INTEREST RATES 

 Some critics of the RBNZ said that New Zealand appears doomed to have high real interest rates. Home lending rates are 10.5 percent compared with the two percent inflation rate. 

 "We have high real interest rates now because we had 20 years of high inflation and negative real interest rates so that savers got so badly burned that they haven't got used to the idea of accepting three to four percent on deposit as a prudent thing to do." 

 Other critics contend that high real rates choke off growth and every time the economy appears ready to take off, the RBNZ, fearful of inflation pressures, forces interest rates up. 

 The experience of five to six percent economic growth over the past two years which has pushed inflation outside the barrier has taught the RBNZ that New Zealand's sustainable growth rate is somewhat below that. 

 Some economists believe a rate of 3.5 percent is aiming too low when compared to countries like Singapore. 

 But Brash said that Singapore now sees its sustainable rate at four to six percent while the U.S. sees its sustainable rate at 2.5 percent and Britain at 2.25 percent. 

 "So 3.5 is quite respectable by the standards of other developed countries with which we often compare outselves." 

 The RBNZ forecasts New Zealand's growth will slow from 5.5 percent at June 30 to two percent next March year and then, boosted by planned government tax cuts, 3.3 percent in 1997. 

 Former RBNZ financial markets manager and now ANZ Bank New Zealand Treasurer, Grant Spencer, recently called for a review of the 0-2 percent inflation band. He suggested the RBNZ could avoid sharp policy changes as inflation nears edges of the band. 

 But Brash believes central banks with a wider target tend to react too late and the winding back costs more in terms of lost production and social costs. 

 Also he said New Zealanders are getting used to two percent. 

 "In New Zealand 0-2 has become symbolic of the commitment of successive governments to price stability. Any change would be perceived of a weakening of that commitment even if that was not the intention." 

 He remains confident that whatever the result of the election due next year under a new mixed member proportional system, a majority of members will support the Reserve Bank Act.

title: NZ's  Central Bank  -4: Brash Qualifies Statements On Policy
text:
The central bank is required under the Reserve Bank Act to keep underlying inflation (the CPI minus one-time price spikes and interest rates) below 2.0% annually. 

 Its failure to keep underlying inflation within that target range could be grounds for New Zealand Minister of Finance Bill Birch to request an explanation and possibly replace Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash for failing to hit the target. 

 Brash actually signed a contract with the government, the Policy Target Agreement in 1992, promising to keep underlying inflation within the 0% to 2% range. 

 It is unlikely that Birch will take such an extreme measure as replacing Brash. But he did confirm Wednesday he would ask the central bank's non-executive directors to submit a report on the operation of monetary policy should the underlying rate exceed the 2.0% range as forecast. 

 At a press conference before the release of the MPS, Brash said he had spoken to Birch Wednesday and that he doesn't plan on resigning from his post and wasn't asked to do so. 

 Brash said in his statement to the market that 'monetary conditions must remain firm.' 

 But he qualified the timing of how long short-term interest rates would remain above the current 9.0% level. Most mortgages in New Zealand are borrowed at a rate about 2.0 percentage points above the 90-day bank bill rate. Current rates are about 11.0%. The MPS says 'the 90-day bank bill rate is assumed to remain over 9.0% for at least the rest of 1995, before declining gradually.' 

 'As additional information is received, it may become apparent that an earlier easing of monetary conditions is warranted,' Brash said. 'Conversely, if indicators point to stronger momentum behind inflation than we currently estimate, not only would easing in monetary conditions be delayed, but a further firming would be required. Either way, the Reserve Bank will take whatever action is necessary to maintain price stability.' 

 The central bank doesn't intervene in currency markets, but uses about $20 million (New Zealand) to facilitate inter-bank daily cash settlements. The central bank can send the 90-day bank bill rate higher by withdrawing some or all of its daily settlement cash. The markets have moved in recent months to take the 90-day bank bill rates near the 9.0% level. 

 Brash said at a press conference before the release of the MPS that 'if monetary conditions were to ease,' a change in the cash target would be 'entirely possible.'

title: NZ/Brash -4: Kiwi On TWI Basis Below Mid-'84 Level
text:
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand doesn't intervene in the foreign-exchange market to influence the value of the nation's currency. However, the central bank does monitor closely the currency's trade-weighted value, and through its comments and adjustments to money market liquidity levels it can affect the value of the New Zealand dollar on a trade-weighted basis. 

 The most recent comment by the Reserve Bank on the currency occured in February, when the central bank indicated it was concerned with a decline in the currency's trade-weighted value. At that time the New Zealand dollar had dropped to 59.16 against its trade-weighted index. 

 The trade weighted index (TWI) is a weighted basket measuring the New Zealand dollar against the currencies of five major trading partners. The index currently is around 59.47. During 1994 it ranged between 55.24 and 60.28. 

 The Reserve Bank closely monitors the New Zealand dollar's trade-weighted value because the currency influences the nation's inflation rate through prices paid for imports. The central bank is legally mandated to keep the underlying inflation rate at 0%-2%. 

 In his speech to the farmers' group, Brash reaffirmed a Reserve Bank forecast for the appreciation of the New Zealand dollar's trade-weighted value. 'Our most recent projection for inflation is based on annual appreciation in the TWI of about 2%, and this appears at this stage to be consistent with underlying inflation moving gradually back towards the center of our 0% to 2% target,' he said. 

 Brash also noted that the current level of the trade-weighted index still is below the level reached after a major devaluation in mid-1984. 

 'It is relevant to note that between the beginning of 1991 and the beginning of 1995, the TWI appreciated by a total of little more than 3%, considerably less than an average of 2% annually. Indeed, at this stage the Kiwi (New Zealand) dollar on a TWI basis remains below its level immediately after the July 1984 devaluation,' he said.
